papers.title: WayPOP: A Panoramic Open-Set Panoptic Tracking Benchmark
papers.abstract: Holistic perception for autonomous agents requires reliably segmenting and associating scene elements across time and camera views, including objects outside a fixed semantic taxonomy. Existing open-set panoptic benchmarks focus on individual images or views, while panoramic tracking benchmarks assume closed-set taxonomies. Consequently, these benchmarks do not evaluate whether unknown objects can be consistently segmented and tracked across synchronized multi-camera sequences. We introduce WayPOP, a panoramic open-set panoptic tracking benchmark built on real Waymo PVPS sequences augmented with diverse out-of-taxonomy 3D assets from Objaverse. Inserted objects are placed at fixed locations in the 3D scene and rendered using calibrated vehicle-mounted cameras as the ego vehicle and surrounding traffic move, providing temporally and cross-view consistent panoptic annotations and auxiliary LiDAR range observations. WayPOP contains approximately 670 curated assets instantiated as 980 unique unknown-object tracks, yielding 53,452 unknown-object mask annotations across 21,300 camera images. Our evaluation protocol defines a hierarchy of tasks from view-independent open-set panoptic segmentation to full panoramic open-set panoptic tracking, using known/unknown PQ and (w)STQ metrics. We benchmark representative open-set and open-vocabulary segmentation methods with temporal and cross-camera association. Our results reveal substantial limitations of current methods in truly open-set scenarios, highlighting robust unknown-object localization and identity association across time and views as major open challenges.

papers.title: Large particle number asymptotics for point-interacting bosons in the plane
papers.abstract: We consider $N$ bosons in two dimensions interacting via point interactions, modeled by the TMS Hamiltonian. We prove that their ground state energy has the asymptotic behavior $-e^{C N }$ for large $N$, for an explicit constant $C$ related to the sharp constant in the Ladyzhenskaya-Gagliardo-Nirenberg inequality. Such asymptotic behavior was predicted in the physics literature, based on a variant of the mean-field approximation.

papers.title: ConceptARC at Scale: Studying Conceptual Understanding in Reasoning Models
papers.abstract: Large reasoning models (LRMs) perform well on challenging benchmarks, yet it remains unclear whether they form generalizable abstractions across conceptually related reasoning tasks. The Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus (ARC) provides a controlled testbed for studying abstraction, requiring solvers to infer transformation rules over two-dimensional grids from a small set of examples. While ARC evaluates rule abstraction within individual tasks, different tasks may share higher-level structure despite requiring different transformations$\unicode{x2014}$for example, several tasks may involve reasoning about objects contained within other objects. Benchmarks such as ConceptARC capture this structure by grouping ARC-style tasks into recurring spatial and semantic concepts, but they often contain only a few manually constructed tasks per concept. We introduce ConceptARC at Scale, a generator for creating thousands of ARC-style tasks targeting a specific concept. Using this generator, we construct ConceptARC-100, a dataset of 1,600 new, manually reviewed tasks, with 100 tasks for each of the 16 concepts defined by ConceptARC$\unicode{x2014}$ten times the size of the original benchmark. We evaluate a range of recent LRMs and models trained from scratch on ConceptARC-100 to characterize which concepts they solve reliably and where they struggle. We further analyze the models' internal representations and find clear semantic structure: task representations cluster according to the operations applied to objects, such as recoloring, removal, or translation, even when realized through substantially different rules and scenarios. Together, our results suggest that models form stable abstractions of transformation operations that generalize across diverse tasks.

However, the extent to which large reasoning models rely on generalizable abstractions when solving complex reasoning problems remains unclear (Beger et al., 2025; Opiełka et al., 2025). The Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus (ARC) (Chollet, 2019) provides a useful domain for studying this question. Each task presents a small number of input–output grid examples from which a solver must infer an underlying transformation rule and apply it to unseen inputs (see Figure 9 in the Appendix for an example). Abstraction, however, can also extend across tasks. Different ARC tasks may share higher-level structure even when they require different transformation rules (Acquaviva et al., 2022; Hodel, 2024). papers.title: Variational Learning with Lie Group Exponential Families
papers.abstract: Variational Bayesian learning for deep neural networks offers many potential benefits. The difficulty in implementation arises from constraints on the parameters of the variational distributions, as well as the need for low-variance gradient estimators. Our recent work proposes Lie group methods for multiplicative or affine groups that naturally overcome such difficulties. Lie groups are essentially parameter spaces with a binary operator such as addition or multiplication, which allows for natural updates within the parameter space. In this article, we streamline and extend our Lie group framework to any general Lie group, and give an explicit relation to standard natural-gradient variational learning methods such as the Bayesian learning rule (BLR). In particular, we prove that linear approximations of the Lie group algorithm give generalizations of the BLR. The key ingredient is the harmonic exponential family, a general class of Lie group exponential families associated to representations of Lie groups. Our work provides a systematic method to construct from such representations efficiently implementable algorithms for variational learning.

papers.intro:
Variational learning for neural networks (Hinton and Van Camp, 1993; Graves, 2011) offers many potential benefits over standard empirical risk minimization and can be used to motivate various deep-learning algorithms (Khan and Rue, 2023). Some of the benefits of variational learning are improved regularization and reduced overfitting, as suggested by the minimum description length principle (Hinton and Van Camp, 1993; Graves, 2011; Blier and Ollivier, 2018; Grünwald, 2007) and PAC-Bayesian bounds (Alquier, 2024). Depending on the form of the variational posterior, different deep learning algorithms can be obtained, for instance, Adam-like methods (Shen et al., 2024) for diagonal Gaussians, algorithms for binary neural networks for Bernoulli distributions (Meng et al., 2020) and biologically plausible multiplicative dynamics for log-normal distributions (Nishida et al., 2026). The Bayesian viewpoint also offers a fruitful framework for thinking about model adaptation and model understanding, for example, federated and continual learning (Nguyen et al., 2018; Ashman et al., 2022), model merging (Matena and Raffel, 2022; Daheim et al., 2024) or sensitivity analysis to perturbations in both the model and data (Nickl et al., 2023).

The de-facto standard approach for variational learning in neural networks is to update the distribution parameters using gradient-based methods to leverage backpropagation training (Graves, 2011). Khan and Rue (2023), for example, use a natural gradient method on the natural parameters of an exponential family. This method has two main difficulties. First, one needs to satisfy constraints on the parameters of the distribution, for example, positivity of the covariance matrix in the case of Gaussians (Lin et al., 2020). Secondly, the objective functions involve integrals with respect to the variational distribution, and obtaining low-variance stochastic gradients is a major challenge. Reparametrization tricks provide such estimators, but it is not clear whether they are available for the variational family at hand and they have to be derived case by case (Mohamed et al., 2020).

Recently, Kıral et al. (2023) proposed a learning algorithm which addresses the above difficulties by parametrizing the probability distribution through Lie groups. The constraints on the parameters are naturally handled through the group’s closure and lower variance gradients are available by default as the Lie group automatically enables the reparametrization technique. Furthermore the homogeneity of the group allows transporting the gradients on the Lie group to a common tangent space thus allowing for a natural application of momentum, and such transports are compatible with the Fisher information metric which is invariant under reparametrizations.

In this work we establish the connection between the Lie group updates and existing methods on exponential families (EFs) such as the Bayesian Learning Rule (BLR) by Khan and Rue (2023). The Lie group update rule does not require the family to be an EF, however many useful families are EFs. EFs are especially well suited to the Bayesian framework, which relies on multiplication and division of distributions to add, remove or modify information. This corresponds to simple addition and subtraction on the natural parameters of the family, connecting the Bayesian framework to optimizing on natural parameters. EFs come with a rich structure, such as dually flat coordinate systems of natural and expectation parameters studied in information geometry (Amari, 2016). As EFs have many desirable properties, the aim of this paper is to further study the Lie group learning rule of Kıral et al. (2023) when specialized to EFs and to understand its relation to the Bayesian learning rule (Khan and Rue, 2023) which is derived for EFs and gives a unifying and simplifying view of many other algorithms.

Those EFs which also have a Lie group structure are families of distributions which combine the best of both worlds, and it should therefore not be surprising that most of the eponymous EFs named after a mathematician share this property. They have the above desirable properties of EFs, but the additional group structure gives easy reparametrization tricks and allows for updating without breaking constraints. Developing a recipe to construct exponential families on homogeneous spaces from real representations of Lie groups, Tojo and Yoshino (2021) redefine the term harmonic exponential families subsuming the earlier definition coined by Cohen and Welling (2015) for homogeneous spaces of compact Lie groups via unitary representations. These families characterize all exponential families closed under a Lie group action. Using this characterization we establish a general and concrete connection between the Lie group update and BLR. Our main contribution is to prove that the linearization of the update proposed by Kıral et al. (2023) always recovers the Bayesian learning rule for exponential families with Lie group structure, see Theorem 13. Altogether, our work supplies the theoretical foundations for efficient algorithms for variational learning using Lie groups and exponential families.

papers.title: Ground-Wing: A Parametric 3D Wing-in-Ground-Effect Dataset for Benchmarking Neural Surrogate Models
papers.abstract: This paper presents a CFD dataset of a highly parametrized 3D wing operating in ground effect, designed for benchmarking neural surrogate models for aerodynamic prediction, using a wing shape and flow conditions typically encountered in motorsport applications. The dataset comprises 770 RANS simulations of 194 unique wing configurations, sampled across 27 airfoil profile variants and 4 distances from the ground, spanning variations in wing sweep, chord, taper, angle of attack, and tip twist. Six neural network architectures representing distinct paradigms --- convolutional (DoMINO), graph-based (X-MeshGraphNet), transformer-based (AB-UPT, GeoTransolver, GAOT), and JEPA-based (AeroJEPA) --- are evaluated on their ability to predict surface pressure coefficient and wall shear stress distributions, from which integral drag and lift coefficients are recovered. The dataset is intended to be used as a challenging benchmark for surrogate CFD models, due to the uniqueness of the ground effect being absent from other wing and airfoil datasets.

The aerodynamic design of front wings for automotive applications relies heavily on computational fluid dynamics (CFD), which, while accurate, demands substantial computational resources and turnaround time. The aerodynamic design of front wings for automotive applications relies heavily on computational fluid dynamics (CFD), which, while accurate, demands substantial computational resources and turnaround time. In motorsport applications, for example, fast-paced design cycles require hundreds of geometry iterations within months, making the computational cost of fluid simulations a significant bottleneck.

The reason for this cost is that a direct analytical solution to the equations which describe the motion of viscous fluids, such as air, has not yet been discovered. The equations in question are known as the Navier-Stokes equations [1], which CFD software aims to resolve iteratively through finite volume methods. Even with these strategies, however, simplified modeling of the most complex flow behaviors has to be employed in order to keep the simulation time within reasonable limits. One such simplification, used in this paper, is the usage of the RANS (Reynolds Averaged Navier Stokes) [2] equations instead, whose solution provides the time-averaged flow field across the simulation domain, while using models [3] to calculate the effects of instantaneous turbulence. In addition, to allow for these methodologies to produce meaningful results, newly designed geometries require extensive preprocessing even before the simulation itself can start. CAD surfaces need to be made perfectly watertight, discretization of the airflow volume needs to be obtained through meshing, and boundary conditions for all relevant surfaces need to be set, all of which require a combination of manpower and computational effort.

Data-driven surrogate models based on neural networks can help alleviate most of these issues. By learning a mapping from geometric inputs directly to flow field solutions, they can provide predictions of flow variables by avoiding the iterative residual minimization of traditional CFD solvers altogether. They also do not require a mesh to produce a result, as they can operate on simpler representations of the objects of interest, such as simple 3D point clouds, sampled directly from a CAD geometry. This reduces the need for resource intensive meshing pipelines. By leveraging architectures such as Neural Operators [4] they feature the possibility for predictions on arbitrarily (i.e. distinct from the training setup) dense grids.

papers.title: Non-Interfering Asymmetric AdamW Updates for Constrained Exploration of Equifinality in Hybrid Models
papers.abstract: Hybrid models let neural networks supply the unresolved parameters of a process-based simulator, and are fitted to observations that constrain aggregate fluxes and storages but not the internal partitioning that produces them. Such a fit is equifinal: configurations indistinguishable in the observed aggregates can disagree substantially about the unobserved internals, and therefore about the mechanism they attribute to the same data. We study evapotranspiration, whose total flux is observed while its split into transpiration and evaporation is not. A model ensemble built from random seeds alone spans only a narrow band of the partitionings the data admit. We produce the spread deliberately, training members under auxiliary repulsion on transpiration, subject to the fit to observations not degrading. Non-interference is usually arranged by making the auxiliary gradient orthogonal to the main one, but under AdamW the applied step is a preconditioned momentum direction, so orthogonality between raw gradients no longer implies it. We introduce Non-interfering Asymmetric Network Optimization (NANO), an update whose first-order effect on the main loss is exactly that of the main objective alone, whose auxiliary step is bounded, and which concentrates repulsion in the coordinates the main gradient leaves idle.

papers.title: Hybrid LLM-Deterministic Pipelines for Enterprise-Scale Code Migration at Bloomberg
papers.abstract: Large organizations carry a long tail of infrastructure migrations that are worth doing but rarely urgent enough to compete with feature work, because each one costs significant engineering time per repository. This paper reports on our industrial experience from Automated Uplift, a multi-month initiative applying LLM-assisted migration pipelines across thousands of Bloomberg repositories. We examine two distinct production campaigns: a heterogeneous Python packaging migration (approx. 1,900 candidate repositories) and a uniform C++ build system migration (approx. 6,700 candidate repositories). Together, these campaigns generated 2,333 pull requests, resulting in 729 successful migrations. We detail our hybrid architectural solution which maximizes deterministic processing, confines the LLM to bounded file transformations within a pre-computed context, and incorporates runtime production telemetry (such as execution logs and usage traces). Our findings show that generating migrations turned out to be the easier part; the bottleneck was the cost, for owning teams, of reviewing, testing, and deploying them. These costs were lowered when changes could be verified directly in the pipeline before opening a PR (as with C++ compilation and test validation), and when the population was uniform enough for fixes to carry over from one repository to the next. We conclude by distilling our experience and findings into actionable, transferable patterns for architecting hybrid LLM-deterministic pipelines and scaling code migrations across the enterprise

papers.title: Euclid. Predicting scaling relations for emission-line galaxies using simulated data
papers.abstract: The Euclid spectroscopic surveys will substantially increase the number of observed emission-line galaxies. We assess the ability of the Euclid Wide Survey (EWS) and Euclid Deep Survey (EDS), at the final DR3 depth, to recover the star-forming main sequence (MS), dust-mass relation (DMR), and mass-metallicity relation (MZR) from emission-line measurements. We use MAMBO (mocks with abundance matching in Bologna) spectroscopic simulations processed with the official Euclid pipelines. The MS is traced over $0\leq z\leq 4$ using Pa$\beta$, H$\alpha$, and [OII] as SFR tracers. The shallow EWS flux limit biases the MS towards higher normalisation and a flatter slope by selecting the brightest, most strongly star-forming galaxies. The deeper EDS enables almost complete sampling with Pa$\beta$ and H$\alpha$ at log$_{10}(M_*/M_\odot)\geq10.3$ over $0\leq z\leq 1.88$, with mild biases at both redshift limits. The [OII]-based MS is increasingly biased towards higher SFRs at the highest redshifts. The DMR is traced through the Balmer decrement over $1.45\leq z\leq 1.88$ and $0.9\leq z\leq 1.88$ in the EWS and EDS, respectively. The derived colour excess agree well with the input values, although detecting the faint H$\beta$ line restricts the sample to less obscured galaxies at fixed $M_*$, particularly in the EWS; the DMR is better sampled in the EDS. Finally, a golden sample detected in multiple optical rest-frame emission lines at $1.49\leq z\leq 1.88$ recovers gas-phase metallicities with typical accuracy of 0.1 dex at log$_{10}(M_*/M_\odot)\geq10$, while lower-mass galaxies show biases up to 0.15 dex. Relative to H-band limited sample, this sample preferentially traces the upper MS and lower MZR. Despite the simplified simulations lacking effects such as mutual spectral contamination and detector persistence, these forecasts provide a benchmark for future Euclid spectroscopic analyses.

papers.intro:
The Euclid mission (Laureijs et al. 2011; Racca et al. 2016; Euclid Collaboration: Scaramella et al. 2022; Euclid Collaboration: Mellier et al. 2025) is designed to investigate the nature of dark energy and dark matter through its two main cosmological probes: weak gravitational lensing (WL) and galaxy clustering (GC). Over its planned six-year duration, Euclid will map approximately one third of the extragalactic sky, covering about 14 00014\,000 deg2 away from the ecliptic and Galactic planes as part of the Euclid Wide Survey (Euclid Collaboration: Scaramella et al. 2022, EWS;). The EWS will be complemented by the Euclid Deep Survey (EDS; Scaramella et al., in prep.), covering 53 deg2 and reaching two magnitudes deeper in the HEH_{\scriptscriptstyle\rm E} band by the end of the mission, with a signal-to-noise ratio (S/N) roughly four times higher in emission-line flux than the EWS.

The mission has already begun delivering data products, starting with an initial public Quick Data Release (Euclid Collaboration: Aussel et al. 2026, Q1;). The first major public data release (DR1, at the end of 2026) will be followed by DR2 and DR3 approximately 2.5 and 5 years later, respectively, progressively reaching the final survey depth and sky coverage.

Euclid has a 0.5 deg2 field of view, observed simultaneously by two instruments. The Visual Imager (VIS) operates with a broadband filter IEI_{\scriptscriptstyle\rm E} ≃\simeq (rr+ii+zz) with a 5​σ5\,\sigma detection limit of mAB≤26.5m_{\rm AB}\leq 26.5 for extended sources (Euclid Collaboration: Cropper et al. 2025). The Near-Infrared Spectrometer and Photometer (NISP) has both a photometric channel (NISP-P), with three filters YEY_{\scriptscriptstyle\rm E}, JEJ_{\scriptscriptstyle\rm E}, and HEH_{\scriptscriptstyle\rm E} reaching mAB≤24m_{\rm AB}\leq 24 at 5​σ5\,\sigma for point-like sources (Euclid Collaboration: Jahnke et al. 2025), and a spectroscopic channel (NISP-S). NISP-S is a slitless spectrometer with two red grisms (RGS, 1.21–1.89 µ​m\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolMicro m}) and a blue grism (BGS, 0.93–1.36 µ​m\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolMicro m}), the latter operating exclusively in the EDS and calibration fields. NISP-S was designed to meet the requirements for: i) a resolving power of ℛ≥380\mathcal{R}\geq 380 and ℛ≥260\mathcal{R}\geq 260 for 0.5​″ diameter sources in the RGS and BGS, respectively; and ii) a 3.5​σ3.5\,\sigma line-flux sensitivity limit of 2×10−16​erg​s−1​cm−22\times 10^{-16}\,\mathrm{erg\,s^{-1}\,cm^{-2}} in the EWS at 1.6​µ​m1.6\,$\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolMicro m}$ (also for 0.5​″ diameter sources). These requirements were established to enable accurate redshift measurements, with σ​(z)≤0.001​(1+z)\sigma(z)\leq 0.001(1+z), for more than 1000 galaxies deg-2 in the range z∈[1,2]z\in[1,2] via H​α\mathrm{H}\,\alpha detection (Laureijs et al. 2011; Pozzetti et al. 2016). On-sky measurements from Q1 confirmed that the NISP-S sensitivity meets these expectations (Euclid Collaboration: Le Brun et al. 2026), while the spectral resolution exceeded the requirements, reaching ℛ≃500\mathcal{R}\simeq 500 for the RGS (Euclid Collaboration: Copin et al. 2026). At the end of the mission, the EDS is expected to reach sensitivities of 5×10−17​erg​s−1​cm−25\times 10^{-17}\,\mathrm{erg\,s^{-1}\,cm^{-2}} and 6×10−17​erg​s−1​cm−26\times 10^{-17}\,\mathrm{erg\,s^{-1}\,cm^{-2}} with the RGS and BGS, respectively (Euclid Collaboration: Mellier et al. 2025, for more details see).

In the coming years, Euclid will deliver the largest near-infrared spectroscopic datasets to date. Beyond redshift measurements, the tens of millions of spectra obtained will enable the study of fundamental physical and chemical properties of galaxies through rest-frame optical and near-infrared emission lines across a wide range of redshifts. The main targets of the mission, namely H​α\mathrm{H}\,\alpha-line emitters over z∈[0.84,1.88]z\in[0.84,1.88], are observed close to ‘cosmic noon’, a crucial epoch in galaxy evolution when star formation and black hole growth reached their peak (Madau and Dickinson 2014). This represents a step forward of several orders of magnitude in sample size compared to previous near-infrared spectroscopic surveys, which were limited to a few hundred to a few thousand galaxies at z≥1.3z\geq 1.3, such as 3D-HST (van Dokkum et al. 2011), FMOS-COSMOS (Silverman et al. 2015), MOSDEF (Kriek et al. 2015), KMOS3D (Wisnioski et al. 2019), and recent NIRSpec/JWST campaigns (Neufeld et al. 2024). Combined with stellar masses (M∗M_{*}) and other photometrically-derived physical properties (Euclid Collaboration: Tucci et al. 2026; Euclid Collaboration: Enia et al. 2024), these measurements will enable the study of three key scaling relations for emission-line galaxies, as described below.

Combined with stellar masses (M∗M_{*}) and other photometrically-derived physical properties (Euclid Collaboration: Tucci et al. 2026; Euclid Collaboration: Enia et al. 2024), these measurements will enable the study of three key scaling relations for emission-line galaxies, as described below.

The luminosity of recombination lines, such as H​α\mathrm{H}\,\alpha and Pa β\beta, and of forbidden lines, such as the [O ii]λ​λ\lambda\lambda3727,3729 doublet (hereafter, [O ii]), are direct tracers of the instantaneous star formation rate (SFR), re-emitting the ionising radiation from young, massive stellar populations with lifetimes shorter than 20 Myr (Kennicutt 1998). The correlation between SFR and M∗M_{*} defines the so-called star-forming main sequence (Noeske et al. 2007; Daddi et al. 2007; Elbaz et al. 2007; Speagle et al. 2014; Popesso et al. 2023, MS;), which exhibits a nearly constant slope and small intrinsic scatter across cosmic time, suggesting that most galaxies build up their stellar mass through smooth and continuous gas accretion rather than through stochastic merger-driven starbursts (Rodighiero et al. 2011). Its normalisation increases with redshift, reflecting the higher star formation efficiency at earlier epochs. Whilst the redshift evolution of the MS has been extensively studied up to z=5z=5 using photometric SFR indicators, including rest-frame UV (Wuyts et al. 2011; Nordon et al. 2013; Pannella et al. 2015) and far-infrared luminosity (Daddi et al. 2007; Elbaz et al. 2007; Schreiber et al. 2015), its evolution as traced through nebular emission lines remains comparatively less well explored.

papers.title: Euclid: Forecasting the number counts of bright line emitters in the Euclid Wide Survey and Euclid Deep fields
papers.abstract: The Euclid mission will revolutionize our understanding of the visible Universe by collecting images and spectra of millions of galaxies across cosmic time and environments. Here, we forecast the number counts of galaxies emitting [OII], H\b{eta}, [OIII], H{\alpha} and Pa\b{eta} lines in the Euclid Wide Survey (EWS) and Deep Survey (EDS). We compare predictions from different models, including semi-analytic models and empirical scaling relations. We then simulate spectra for galaxies in the MAMBO lightcone using FastSpec, designed to rapidly generate one-dimensional spectra as observed by Euclid. We process these simulated spectra with the official Euclid spectroscopic pipeline to recover redshifts and line fluxes and derive expected counts. Predictions for H{\alpha}+[NII] emitters are broadly consistent across mocks and with existing observations. In the EWS, relative RMS scatter among mock predictions for integrated counts is approximately 19% for H{\alpha}+[NII], 44% for [OII] and 41% for [OIII], reflecting greater model dependence for oxygen-line forecasts. After accounting for flux losses and redshift misidentification, corrected flux measurements recover most intrinsic line counts, especially in the EDS. From the MAMBO-based FastSpec simulations, we predict that Euclid will detect about 42 million H{\alpha} emitters in the EWS and 1.7 million in the EDS. The same simulations predict approximately 0.5 and 0.8 million [OII] and [OIII] emitters, respectively, in the EDS, and about 1.3 and 7.5 million in the EWS. These non-H{\alpha} forecasts remain subject to substantial model-dependent uncertainties, as shown by scatter among the different mocks. These samples will be instrumental in pushing large-scale structure and baryon acoustic oscillation studies beyond redshift z~2, extending Euclid cosmological and galaxy evolution studies beyond what is achievable with H{\alpha} alone.

papers.intro:
The European Space Agency (ESA) Euclid mission is designed to investigate dark energy, dark matter, and the evolution of cosmic structures by mapping the geometry and growth of structure over a large fraction of cosmic time (Laureijs et al. 2011; Racca et al. 2016; Euclid Collaboration: Scaramella et al. 2022; Euclid Collaboration: Mellier et al. 2025). Euclid will survey billions of galaxies over the extragalactic sky, providing optical and near-infrared imaging together with near-infrared slitless spectroscopy. The mission combines the VIS Instrument (Euclid Collaboration: Cropper et al. 2025) and the Near-Infrared Spectrometer and Photometer (NISP, Euclid Collaboration: Jahnke et al. 2025), enabling measurements of galaxy clustering and weak gravitational lensing, which are fundamental probes for cosmology.

The primary observing strategy of Euclid is divided between the Euclid Wide Survey (Euclid Collaboration: Scaramella et al. 2022, EWS;) and the Euclid Deep Survey (EDS). The EDS consists of three Euclid Deep Fields (EDFs), namely EDF-North, EDF-South, and EDF-Fornax. The EWS covers approximately 14 00014\,000 square degrees of the extragalactic sky, focusing on high-precision imaging and spectroscopy at unprecedented depths, and will constitute the main data set for the primary science goals of the mission. Galaxy evolution is one of the main scientific objectives of Euclid. By detecting galaxies across a broad range of redshifts and environments, Euclid will constrain processes such as star formation, quenching, and morphological transformation, which regulate the transition from star-forming to quiescent galaxy populations. Its data set, covering approximately one third of the sky, will make it possible to map galaxies over a large fraction of cosmic history (Madau and Dickinson 2014), from the local Universe to cosmic noon and to earlier epochs, and across different environments, from groups to proto-clusters and clusters. This will provide constraints on the physical mechanisms through which environment affects galaxy evolution.

A defining feature of Euclid spectroscopy is its capability to detect bright emission lines from galaxies over wide redshift ranges, including [O ii]λ​3727\lambda 3727 (hereafter [O ii]), H​β\mathrm{H}\,\beta, [O iii]λ​5007\lambda 5007 (hereafter [O iii]), H​α\mathrm{H}\,\alpha, and Pa β\beta. These lines provide complementary diagnostics of star formation (Kennicutt 1998; Jansen et al. 2001), dust attenuation, gas excitation, metallicity, and AGN activity (Baldwin et al. 1981; Baskin and Laor 2005; Kewley et al. 2006), and are therefore central to both galaxy evolution and cosmological applications of the Euclid spectroscopic surveys.

H​α\mathrm{H}\,\alpha is the primary tracer for the Euclid spectroscopic cosmology sample at 1≲z≲21\lesssim z\lesssim 2, where it provides a direct probe of star-forming galaxies and enables large-scale structure measurements. The [N ii]λ​λ​6548,6583\lambda\lambda 6548,6583 doublet lies close to H​α\mathrm{H}\,\alpha and can contribute to the blended H​α\mathrm{H}\,\alpha+[N ii] complex in low-resolution slitless spectroscopy. In this work, however, H​α\mathrm{H}\,\alpha is the main line of interest. Unless explicitly stated otherwise, H​α\mathrm{H}\,\alpha refers to the deblended H​α\mathrm{H}\,\alpha component. We use H​α\mathrm{H}\,\alpha+[N ii] only when comparing with models or observations that report the blended complex.

papers.title: DESI DR2 Results III: The Mass of the Milky Way
papers.abstract: We present measurements of the mass of the Milky Way using distant halo stars selected from the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI) Data Release 2 (DR2). We apply four dynamical modeling methods to 10,036 RR Lyrae (RRL) and blue horizontal branch (BHB) stars with 6D phase space coordinates that span from $\sim$10 to 95 kpc from the Galactic center, the largest samples of their kind. All methods are applied to mock surveys based on cosmological simulations that include generating individual tracer stars, convolving their phase-space coordinates with DESI and Gaia DR3-like uncertainties, and tailored models of the survey selection functions. By comparing the performance on these mocks, we quantify how systematic biases from both methodology assumptions and galaxy disequilibrium impact each estimate. The mock-based systematics, which differ by method and tracer, are used to correct the individual estimates and to derive joint estimates using a rigorous formalism that accounts for per-method biases and residual correlations between methods. We obtain a joint estimate of the mass within 80 kpc to be $M(r < 80 \mathrm{\,kpc}) = 6.36^{+0.53}_{-0.48} \times 10^{11}$ M$_\odot$ and a virial mass estimate of $M_\mathrm{200c} = 1.19^{+0.14}_{-0.12} \times 10^{12}$ M$_\odot$, with similar results when combining only RRL-based or BHB-based measurements. These results provide a roadmap for future DESI efforts, as well as those in other spectroscopic surveys, to reliably constrain the mass of our Galaxy.

Characterizing the mass distribution of the Milky Way is as scientifically relevant today as it was a century ago when the landmark stellar catalogs of Kapteyn [132] were published. While today we have a detailed picture of the distribution of the luminous component [26]11 1 Though there remain interesting discrepancies in recent measurements of the Milky Way’s stellar disk mass [156, 125]., we now face the more challenging task of characterizing the total mass, which includes the dark matter distribution within the Galaxy.

After four decades of increasingly compelling evidence, the cold dark matter (CDM) model with a cosmological constant (Λ\Lambda) has become the standard framework to describe the evolution of the large-scale structure of the Universe [59, 265, 204]. More recently, apparent shortcomings of the CDM model on galactic and subgalactic scales have been highlighted: the “missing satellites”, “too-big-to-fail”, “core-cusp” and “plane-of-satellites” problems [38, 218, see reviews by]. These small-scale challenges, along with the absence of a detection of the dark matter particle (22, though see 4), have motivated the development of diverse alternative hypotheses for the nature of dark matter that could alleviate the small-scale challenges while retaining the large scale success of CDM [182, see review by]. Examples include, but are not limited to, warm [28, 160, e.g.,], self-interacting [234, 243, e.g.,], or fuzzy [119, 223, 120, e.g.,] dark matter.

Simulations of these alternative models make distinctive predictions for the properties of structure on subgalactic scales, such as the number of dark matter subhalos and satellite galaxies [235, 255, 30, 159, 84, 187], the inner density slope of halos [162, 160, 216], the shape of the dark matter halo [78, 40, 30, 216, 246, e.g.,] and the presence or absence of figure rotation [79, 11, 35, 7].

A precise determination of the Milky Way’s total mass and its spatial distribution are fundamental inputs for constraining dark matter using local data. For example, the connection between dark matter halos and the galaxies that form within them, and the resulting scaling relations, are determined, to first order, by the halo mass [266, 49, 15, 222, 263, 221, e.g.,]. For a given halo mass, different model assumptions lead to different predictions for the structure and properties of Milky Way-like galaxies [52, 33, 99, e.g.,] and the number of subhalos and satellites in a given dark matter model [134, 186, 181, 180, 182]. Likewise, precisely measuring the local dark matter density is essential for a proper interpretation of direct dark matter detection experiments [see 18, for a review]. Another example is the reconstruction of the Milky Way’s history and the evolution of its different stellar populations, which often requires integrating orbits or calculating integrals of motion in an assumed potential.

Despite its importance, the mass of the Milky Way is still relatively uncertain, with estimates ranging between ≈0.5−2×1012​M⊙\approx 0.5-2\times 10^{12}\mathrm{\,M_{\odot}} [see 26, 256, 27, for reviews]. In the last decade, data from the Gaia mission [96] has stimulated the development, improvement and application of methods to estimate the Milky Way mass distribution [see 121, for a review]. A non-exhaustive list of commonly-used methods to estimate the total Milky Way mass includes: • variants of the virial theorem [89, 261, 262]; • application of the Jeans equations in spherical [100, 130, 258, 25] and axisymmetric geometries [158, 264, 189]; • modeling of stellar streams [116, 128, 147, 138, 145, 31, 29, 85, 165, 140, 124, 196, 188, 13]; • constraints from the escape velocity [150, 231, 202, 66, 208]; • distribution function (DF) fitting [169, 259, 168, 80, 65, 114, 171], including for DFs inferred from simulations [152, 154, 153, 42, 45], estimated in the space of integrals in trial potentials [109, 155, 17], or explored via the steady-state collisionless Boltzmann equation [6, 106]. Finally, there are methods that target the local dark matter density [210, 267, 37, 118, 157, e.g.,], rather than the global mass distribution.

Despite a plethora of methods (and often several implementations of the same method), there is relatively little comparison between methods to assess their relative performance. Most analyses perform internal validation tests on mock data, but analyses vary on three primary axes: (i) how many modeling techniques are considered, (ii) whether the mock data are based on analytic equilibrium models or cosmological simulations, and (iii) the inclusion of survey effects like selection functions and observational uncertainties. Several works have applied a single technique to mock data based on cosmological simulations, either with [152, 81, 154, 274, 142, 211, 228, 171, 194] or without [259, 219, 42, 66, 102, 213, 190, 34] survey effects. Some works have applied multiple techniques to the same dataset, but either used mock data based on equilibrium models [155] or cosmological simulations without survey effects [110, 257, 258]. Analyses that use nominally similar mocks (e.g., Gaia mocks produced in 105 or 220, with additional selections tailored to their data) rarely discuss performance relative to other efforts.

papers.title: Mock catalogues for the DESI DR2 Milky Way mass modeling effort
papers.abstract: The Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI) survey is an ongoing campaign to obtain millions of spectra, including for stars within the Milky Way. One of DESI's Key Projects for its second data release (DR2) is to measure the mass of the Milky Way using a variety of techniques applied to six-dimensional kinematics of distant halo stars. We present mock surveys generated from the Auriga cosmological simulations (AuriDESI) that are used to validate these techniques in several companion studies. The AuriDESI tracer catalogues are tailored to reflect key features of the DR2 Key Project dataset, including the selection of RR Lyrae and blue horizontal branch stars, uncertainties on line-of-sight velocities and proper motions, and variation in observational completeness within the survey footprint. We discuss how well the resulting AuriDESI tracer catalogues compare to their observed DESI counterparts, including suggesting improvements that can be generalized to similar mock survey efforts within the community. The AuriDESI tracer catalogues are publicly available on Zenodo.

papers.intro:
It has become cliché to say ‘we are in the era of large surveys’ for Galactic astronomy, but it is true nonetheless. Wide-area digital sky surveys including SDSS (York et al., 2000), DES (DES Collaboration, 2016), Pan-STARRS (Chambers et al., 2016), DELVE (Drlica-Wagner et al., 2021), and UNIONS (Gwyn et al., 2025) have covered the sky with uniform and deep photometry. The Gaia mission has provided parallax and proper motion measurements for nearly 2 billion stars in the Milky Way (Gaia Collaboration et al., 2018; Gaia Collaboration et al., 2023). Spectroscopic surveys including SDSS (York et al., 2000), DESI (DESI Collaboration et al., 2016a), and H3 (Conroy et al., 2019) have complemented a subset of these stars with line-of-sight velocities and chemical abundances, which will expand greatly as 4MOST (de Jong et al., 2019) and WEAVE (Jin et al., 2024) come online. Using some combination of the above datasets, Galactic astronomers have discovered more than 60 faint satellite galaxies (Drlica-Wagner et al., 2020; Pace, 2025) and more than 100 stellar streams (Grillmair and Carlin, 2016; Ibata et al., 2024; Bonaca and Price-Whelan, 2025), unravelled the Milky Way’s stellar halo into its constituent accretion events (Deason and Belokurov, 2024), and revealed time-dependent disequilibrium in the Milky Way’s disk (Antoja et al., 2018; Bennett and Bovy, 2019) and halo (Erkal et al., 2021; Petersen and Peñarrubia, 2021; Vasiliev, 2023; Yaaqib et al., 2024; Byström et al., 2025; Chandra et al., 2025).

One quantity of particular interest is the mass (and mass profile) of the Milky Way, which is a key input for mapping satellite counts to dark matter constraints (Newton et al., 2018; Nadler et al., 2020; Nadler et al., 2021), predictions for dark matter subhalo interactions with globular cluster streams (Ibata et al., 2002; Johnston et al., 2002; Ngan and Carlberg, 2014; Erkal et al., 2016; Nibauer et al., 2025), and models of the Milky Way potential used for orbit integration (Bovy, 2015; McMillan, 2017; Price-Whelan, 2017). The increase in tracers with available six-dimensional phase-space properties (positions and velocities) have enabled an explosion of measurements for the mass of the Milky Way (Patel et al., 2018; Callingham et al., 2019; Watkins et al., 2019; Eadie and Jurić, 2019; Shen et al., 2022; Ibata et al., 2024; Medina et al., 2025b, e.g.,) using a variety of tracers (see Wang et al., 2020; Bobylev and Baykova, 2023; Bayer et al., 2025 for recent compilations).

Yet even with this dramatic increase in the quantity (number of stars) and quality (information per star) of data, it is not obvious that our measurements are leading to a more correct understanding. In the case of the mass of the Milky Way, several works have highlighted the impact of observational uncertainties and selection functions (Wang et al., 2015; Rehemtulla et al., 2022), baryonic contraction in the dark matter profile (Cautun et al., 2020; Dado et al., 2026), and the dynamical influence of the LMC (Garavito-Camargo et al., 2019; Petersen and Peñarrubia, 2020; Erkal et al., 2020; Cunningham et al., 2020; Deason et al., 2021; Brooks et al., 2026) that bias, or at least complicate our interpretations of, the measurements.11 1 Similar concerns have been raised for mapping halo substructures to individual accreted systems (Thomas et al., 2025; Sante et al., 2026) and the census of faint tidal features (Shipp et al., 2023).

Many of these challenges can be addressed by testing measurement methods on adequately sophisticated simulated catalogues, where the answer is known. Broadly speaking, there have been two approaches to generating mock surveys of Milky Way data. The first assumes analytic density distributions that are in dynamical equilibrium, most prominently used in the Besançon (Robin et al., 2003), galfast (Jurić et al., 2008; Jurić, 2018), and TRILEGAL (Girardi et al., 2005) models. While this approach can be empirically tuned to match observed Milky Way data, it generally oversimplifies the structure of the Galaxy, particularly in the stellar halo where accretion-built substructures (satellites, streams) are modelled as one smooth component. The second approach is to sample distributions generated by particles in cosmological simulations. Originally pioneered by Sharma et al. (2011), successive improvements in this approach (Lowing et al., 2015; Thob et al., 2024) have culminated to produce sophisticated mock surveys from flagship cosmological hydrodynamical zoom simulations, including FIRE (Sanderson et al., 2020; Nguyen et al., 2024; Lucey et al., 2026a) and Auriga (Grand et al., 2018; Kizhuprakkat et al., 2024).

The Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI) is a state-of-the-art multiplexed spectroscopic instrument operating on the Mayall 4-meter telescope at Kitt Peak National Observatory (DESI Collaboration et al., 2022). DESI is able to obtain ∼\sim5000 spectra at once over a large (∼\sim3 deg) field of view (DESI Collaboration et al., 2016b; Miller et al., 2024; Poppett et al., 2024). While DESI’s primary survey objective is to investigate the nature of dark energy by measuring baryonic acoustic oscillations and redshift-space distortions (DESI Collaboration et al., 2025; Abdul Karim et al., 2025), it has also taken spectra of over 12 million stars in the Milky Way (Koposov et al., 2026, see Section 5.3 of). The Milky Way Survey (MWS) preferentially targets distant stars in the Galactic halo, including tracers like RR Lyrae (RRL) and blue horizontal branch (BHB) stars for which distances can be precisely measured (Fermani and Schönrich, 2013; Catelan and Smith, 2015; Barbosa et al., 2022; Garofalo et al., 2022). One of DESI’s Key Projects for its second data release (DR2) is to use halo BHBs and RRLs to measure the mass of the Milky Way, using several methods benchmarked against the same set of mock catalogues generated from cosmological simulations.

papers.title: Constraining the Milky Way Mass profile with data driven distribution function using DESI DR2 halo stars
papers.abstract: We employ a novel data-driven dynamical modeling method, the empirical distribution function (emPDF), to constrain the Milky Way mass profile using a large sample of halo stars from the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument Milky Way Survey (DESI MWS). The method does not assume any functional form of the tracer distribution. Deviations from the steady-state assumption and the effects of observational errors are further tested and calibrated using a number of realistic mock observations (AuriDESI). Applying the calibrated method to two classes of tracers in DESI, we derive a best-constrained virial mass and concentration of $\log M_\mathrm{200c}/M_{\odot}=12.05_{-0.12}^{+0.21}(_{-0.18}^{+0.26})$ and $\log c_\mathrm{200c}=1.20_{-0.16}^{+0.11}(_{-0.24}^{+0.20})$ for BHBs. For RR Lyrae stars we derive $\log M_\mathrm{200c}/M_{\odot}=12.15_{-0.14}^{+0.22}(_{-0.19}^{+0.26})$ and $\log c_\mathrm{200c}=1.16_{-0.12}^{+0.09}(_{-0.18}^{+0.16})$. The uncertainties quoted outside and within brackets are statistical and total errors including systematic errors calibrated from AuriDESI, respectively. The two tracer populations provide overall consistent measurements of the MW halo mass profile. Combining the halo star constraints with the independent constraint from satellite dynamics, we derive a robust and precise final measurement of the MW halo parameters of $\log M_\mathrm{200c}/M_{\odot}=12.12_{-0.05}^{+0.05}(_{-0.04}^{+0.06})$ and $\log c_\mathrm{200c}=1.16_{-0.03}^{+0.05}(_{-0.07}^{+0.05})$, with correlation coefficients of $\rho=-0.90(-0.54)$.

papers.intro:
Accurate constraints on the total mass and density distribution of the Milky Way (MW) dark matter halo are fundamental to understanding the formation and evolution of our Galaxy under the cosmological framework. For example, the “too big to fail” problem was raised more than ten years ago by [9]. They pointed out that the most massive satellite galaxies in our MW are less massive than the most massive subhalos predicted by Λ\LambdaCDM simulations of MW-mass systems. This problem, however, can be explained if the virial mass of our MW is smaller than that assumed by [9]. For example, [96] and [14] reported that the MW satellites are consistent with Λ\LambdaCDM predictions at a confidence level of 10% if the dark halo of the MW has a virial mass smaller than 1.3×1012​M⊙1.3\times 10^{12}M_{\odot}. This example demonstrates the importance of precisely constraining the MW host halo mass.

This example demonstrates the importance of precisely constraining the MW host halo mass.

The measurement of the dark matter halo mass of the MW is usually based on the modeling of various types of dynamical tracers, including halo stars, satellite galaxies, cold gas, and even the companion Andromeda galaxy. There are also various types of dynamical methodologies that can be used to model these tracer objects. The readers can refer to [97] for a review on different methodologies applied to various types of tracer objects, and also to some more recent studies [94, 104, 50, 75, 20, 7, 88, 49, 79, 36, 95, 12, 13, 63, 58, 83, 62, e.g.].

Among the different types of methodologies, a common approach for dynamical modeling is based on the phase-space distribution function (DF), in which the tracers are considered to be in dynamical equilibrium, and the model gravitational potential parameters are determined by fitting the model to the observed data [63, 20, 100, 95, 88, e.g.]. The DF provides a complete description of a dynamical system via its full 6D phase-space representation[6].

Despite numerous efforts over the past decades devoted to inferring the mass of our MW, the current constraints on the profile of the outer halo show considerable discrepancy [100, 97]. The discrepancy mainly arises from two aspects: 1) limited halo tracer populations with incomplete and inaccurate kinematic data (e.g. proper motions) at large distances; and 2) systematic uncertainties behind the modeling method that remain uncorrected or uncalibrated [43, 44, 36, 20]. To address these issues and establish reliable constraints on the MW mass profile, improved kinematic observations of halo tracers and reliable modelling methods are essential.

The large sample of DESI halo stars, especially those probing the more distant outer stellar halo, will provide invaluable new insights into the MW outer halo. By combining DESI line-of-sight velocities and spectrophotometric distances with Gaia proper motions, these halo stars provide a valuable resource with six-dimensional phase-space information. They can potentially help to constrain the dark matter distribution in the more distant outer stellar halo to better precision, in addition to the use of satellite galaxies as tracers [64, 63, e.g.]. Nevertheless, as we will show in this study, the Gaia DR3 proper motion measurements are subject to large uncertainties for halo stars beyond 50 kpc, and thus additional corrections or calibrations are required in our measurement.

With the sizable sample of halo stars as tracers, there is a demand for reliable methodologies that can fully exploit the tracer information to estimate the mass of the Galaxy, as well as a good understanding and control of the systematic errors involved. papers.title: A distribution-function estimate of the Milky Way mass profile from outer halo stars in DESI DR2
papers.abstract: We present measurements of the Milky Way mass using blue horizontal-branch (BHB) and RR Lyrae (RRL) stars from the second data release of DESI (DR2), covering its first three years of operations. We employ 279 BHBs and 213 RRLs at $\sim\!50$--$80$\,kpc from the Galactic center, selected from catalogs roughly twice as large as those of DESI DR1, used in our previous mass measurement. We apply the Galactic Mass Estimator (GME), a hierarchical Bayesian framework that assumes power-law forms for the potential and the tracer density, and accounts for distance and velocity uncertainties. Validating the method on 24 AuriDESI mock catalogs (six Auriga halos at four viewing angles), we find that it overestimates the enclosed mass by $\sim\!15\%$ at 80\,kpc, and correct our results accordingly. We obtain $M(<80\,{\rm kpc}) = 0.64^{+0.06}_{-0.06}$ and $0.53^{+0.05}_{-0.05} \times 10^{12}\,M_\odot$ for BHBs and RRLs, respectively, while including Sagittarius stream stars lowers these masses by $\sim\!10$\%. Extrapolating to 100\,kpc, we obtain $M(<100\,{\rm kpc}) = 0.74^{+0.07}_{-0.07}$ and $0.62^{+0.06}_{-0.07} \times 10^{12}\,M_\odot$, and anchoring an NFW halo to our GME constraints at 65\,kpc yields virial masses of $M_{200} = 1.12^{+0.14}_{-0.12}$ and $0.89^{+0.11}_{-0.10} \times 10^{12}\,M_\odot$. BHBs yield systematically higher masses than RRLs across the full radial range, reflecting the impact of tracer choice even within a single method. This work is part of a wider DESI DR2 Key Project effort to measure the Milky Way mass and constrain systematics arising from different samples and methodologies.

One of the main limitations of the use of tracers in the outer halo (at Galactocentric radii RGC≳20R_{\rm GC}\gtrsim 20 kpc) is the scarcity of tracers with complete and precise phase-space information, since distance and proper motion measurements at such distances remain challenging even with state-of-the-art space missions and telescopes (e.g., Gaia). Furthermore, line-of-sight velocity measurements of statistically significant samples often rely on large-scale spectroscopic surveys mapping the halo. Beyond observational limitations, the interpretation of outer-halo kinematics is further complicated by physical effects that violate the assumptions of equilibrium and spherical symmetry underlying most mass estimators, most notably the gravitational influence of the Large Magellanic Cloud [43, 85, e.g.,] and the presence of tidal substructure and stellar streams [53, 116, 114, 115, 50, 57, e.g.,].

The DESI survey is ideally suited to Milky Way mass studies, delivering spectroscopic observations of millions of halo stars over a wide sky area and providing full 6D phase-space information (i.e., 3D positions and 3D velocities) when combined with Gaia proper motions. Among the stellar tracers accessible to DESI, RR Lyrae stars (RRLs) and blue horizontal-branch stars (BHBs) are particularly valuable, as well-calibrated standard candles that yield precise heliocentric distances (with uncertainties at the ∼5%\sim\!5\% and ∼10%\sim\!10\% level, respectively; see e.g., Garofalo et al. 44 and Deason et al. 24). Here we extend that analysis to DESI’s second data release (DR2), which encompasses the first three years of survey operations, with a significantly larger sample of tracers extending to ∼120\sim\!120 kpc over a larger and more homogeneous on-sky footprint. This paper presents one of three independent Milky Way mass measurements carried out as part of the DESI Year 3 Key Project (Y3KP). This paper is organized as follows. In Section II, we describe the DESI DR2 BHB and RRL samples used in this work, including distance determinations, radial velocity measurements, and the selection cuts applied to the catalogs. Section III summarizes the GME framework and the hierarchical Bayesian model adopted in our analysis. We validate the method on cosmological simulations in Section IV, using mock BHB and RRL catalogs from the AuriDESI simulation suite, spanning a representative range of halo assembly histories and viewing angles. The mass estimates derived from the DESI DR2 samples are presented in Section V. In Section VI, we examine the sensitivity of the mass recovery to selection cuts and other potential biases, compare our results with the DESI DR1 measurements of 77, discuss the consistency between the BHB and RRL mass profiles, and place our estimates in the context of the broader literature. We summarize our findings in Section VII.

papers.title: $\mathcal{C}^\infty$ Smooth Trajectory Planning with Application to Soft Robots
papers.abstract: High motion performance and avoiding structural vibrations rely on smooth trajectory planning. The smoothness requirement depends on the robot's complexity in terms of the number of degrees of freedom and system order due to the flexibility of the joints and links. For industrial robots, the smoothness requirements have been determined and subsequently taken into account. Although unknown for soft continuum robots, the exact smoothness requirement can potentially be much larger than previously considered ones such as $\mathbf{\mathcal{C}^4}$ for collaborative robots and $\mathbf{\mathcal{C}^5}$ for quadcopter drones. To address this gap, we introduce a $\mathbf{\mathcal{C}^\infty}$-smooth trajectory generator that respects defined kinematic limits and generates infinitely differentiable trajectories. The generated path addresses and generalizes to all smoothness requirements, where a transition between sequential states is needed. Therefore, all trajectories have continuous velocity, acceleration, jerk, snap, crackle, pop, etc. Of particular interest is the case of null boundary conditions, i.e., all derivatives at the start and end of the trajectory are equal to zero. We verified and evaluated our proposed approach in simulations and on hardware.

Consider a soft continuum robot changing its shape from start to goal configuration. To achieve this, a trajectory generator is used to provide suitable intermediate values in actuation space, task space, or any intermediate space, e.g., joint space or arc space. The smoothness of those generated trajectories is important as non-smooth trajectories may cause vibrations due to the capability of exciting the eigenmodes of the mechanical system. That is why, as shown by De Luca & Book [1], the smoothness requirement for a robot with flexible elements can, e.g., go as high as twice the number of flexible joints and links, respectively. Following the widely assumed approach that, in the limit, a hyper-redundant robot is a soft continuum robot, a soft continuum robot has infinitely many flexible elements. Therefore, according to different authors from Chirikjian & Burdick [2] to Burgner-Kahrs et al. [3], those robots have infinite degrees of freedom. Consequently, soft continuum robots require infinitely differentiable smooth trajectories, i.e., 𝒞∞\mathcal{C}^{\infty} smooth trajectories.

Unfortunately, in soft continuum robotics, most authors do not specify the smoothness of the trajectory used. If any reference trajectory is utilized, linear interpolation between configurations is the current norm. For quasi-static motions, as required for safety in medical robots [9], soft continuum robots are often position-controlled, where the intermediate states are not interpolated. Furthermore, survey and review articles, e.g., [10, 3, 11, 12, 13], neither discuss nor identify trajectory generation as a potential open challenge. We believe that this represents an overlooked potential to improve the performance of downstream methods with low implementation effort.

When generating a trajectory, the boundaries at the beginning and the end of the trajectory need to match the previous and subsequent trajectory boundaries, respectively. For point-to-point trajectories, the boundaries of the time derivatives at the end and the beginning are zero, whereas the boundaries of the path match the start and goal configurations, see Fig 1. Therefore, using functions that can be differentiated infinitely many times is necessary but not sufficient. For example, a cosine function is such a function, where the fourth derivative is itself. Using τ∈[0,1]\tau\in\left[0,1\right] and the Havercosine function, (1−cos⁡(π​τ))/2\left(1-\cos\left(\pi\tau\right)\right)/2 as an interpolator for a trajectory generator seems to be smooth. However, the second derivative 0.5​π2​cos⁡(π​τ)0.5\pi^{2}\cos\left(\pi\tau\right) reveals that the acceleration of the generated trajectory jumps at τ=0\tau=0 and τ=1\tau=1. Hence, the Havercosine function as a trajectory is only 𝒞1\mathcal{C}^{1}. Similar arguments apply to the exponential function used by Rymansaib et al. [14] that has jumps at the end of its derivatives. Using a parametric Gaussian function for the velocity profile [5] or acceleration profile [15] leads to a path profile composed of non-elementary antiderivative with undesirable side effects. Another example is the use of logistic functions as used by Müller-Karger et al. [16] and other related functions that are infinitely differentiable and have two horizontal asymptotes. The asymptotic behavior violates the boundaries of the path, i.e., the path jumps at the beginning and the end, and, therefore, those trajectories are not even 𝒞0\mathcal{C}^{0}. To summarize, to the best of our knowledge, current trajectory generators cannot generate 𝒞∞\mathcal{C}^{\infty} smooth trajectories even if the underlying path primitive is a 𝒞∞\mathcal{C}^{\infty}-smooth function.

In this work, we propose point-to-point trajectory generators that respect defined kinematic limits and generate infinitely differentiable trajectories. The algorithm produces continuous velocity, acceleration, jerk, snap, etc. profiles. To achieve 𝒞∞\mathbf{\mathcal{C}^{\infty}} smoothness, we use a non-linear transformed normalized piecewise flat function as a geometrically scaled path primitive. This path primitive allows us to derive a simple trajectory generator that can consider kinematic limits such as maximum velocity, acceleration, and jerk. Our main contributions are as follows. We provide an infinitely differentiable path primitive and derive an easy-to-implement 𝒞∞\mathcal{C}^{\infty}-smooth trajectory with mathematically sound properties as an alternative to the compared methods. Additionally, our proposed approach has been verified and evaluated in simulation on a tendon-driven soft robot (TDSR), and on hardware on a 7-DoF FR3 arm.

papers.title: Assurance-Conditioned Continuous Authorization for Autonomous AI Agents
papers.abstract: Autonomous software agents can act through tools, delegate work, and change their models or execution environments while earlier authorizations remain in flight. We present Assurance-Conditioned Continuous Authorization (ACCA), an approach designed to be harness-independent, for maintaining operational authority according to currently justified assurance. It distinguishes evidence validity from contextual applicability, derives assurance claims from eligible evidence, and resolves a multidimensional effective-authority envelope within a principal-declared ceiling and applicable policy. A typed dependency graph supports selective re-evaluation of authorization-relevant changes. An authority epoch changes when effective authority changes; a distinct optional authorization-basis version supports revalidation of action-specific authorization conditions. Protected effect-time enforcement can reject stale actions before a consequential resource change, subject to the available commit mechanism. A compositional Domain Governance Profile expresses domain-specific semantics without granting authority. Controlled scenario tests implemented as a regression suite using a trading profile exercise default-deny rules, evidence-conditioned contraction and recovery, policy divergence, selective non-response, and stale-action rejection at a local gateway before the simulated-broker boundary. The study establishes implementation-level evidence in one domain, not a cross-domain guarantee of harmful-behavior prevention.
papers.intro:
Agentic AI changes the authorization problem in ways that go beyond tool invocation. A conventional application typically executes a relatively stable set of operations through predefined workflows and interfaces. An autonomous or semi-autonomous agent can instead select among actions, formulate intermediate plans, adapt its behavior as observations arrive, delegate work, interact with external systems, and continue acting as its environment changes. Consequently, authorization conditions that were appropriate when a task began may cease to be appropriate during execution. The agent itself may change—for example, through a model, prompt, tool, configuration, persistent memory, learned skill, routing, subagent, or harness update—but authority may also become inappropriate without any change to the agent. A dependency may degrade, an external environment may enter conditions outside those under which the agent was evaluated, a security control may fail, or a stakeholder’s risk posture may change. Static permission assignments are therefore poorly matched to autonomous systems whose operational context, dependencies, risk, and assurance basis can change while they act.

This problem is not merely technical. Traditional organizational and service workflows routinely delegate substantial authority to trusted insiders, but that authority is embedded within a broader institutional control system. Human discretion is constrained by professional judgment, procedural controls, separation of duties, approval requirements, supervision, organizational accountability, performance incentives, professional obligations, and the prospect of financial, employment, legal, or reputational consequences for misconduct. Together, these mechanisms create a balance between granting individuals sufficient discretion to perform useful work and constraining the risks created by that discretion. Many of these safeguards operate beyond technical access control: an employee may be technically capable of performing an action and formally authorized to do so, yet refrain because the action is inappropriate under the circumstances, requires escalation or additional approval, violates a professional obligation, or could create unacceptable consequences.

Many of these safeguards operate beyond technical access control: an employee may be technically capable of performing an action and formally authorized to do so, yet refrain because the action is inappropriate under the circumstances, requires escalation or additional approval, violates a professional obligation, or could create unacceptable consequences.

As service activities are increasingly delegated to autonomous agents, this institutional control model does not transfer directly to software. Some controls can be translated into machine-enforceable mechanisms—for example, separation of duties can become independent approval, procedural controls can be expressed as policy, and supervisory intervention can become human-in-the-loop authorization. Other safeguards do not have straightforward equivalents. Agents do not inherently possess professional responsibility, internalize organizational norms, respond to career or reputational incentives, or face penalties in the manner of human decision makers. Nor can organizations assume that an agent will exercise the contextual and prudential judgment through which trusted insiders recognize exceptional circumstances and voluntarily limit their own actions. Agentic automation therefore does not merely replace human labor; it changes the institutional mechanisms through which delegated authority has traditionally been made tolerable.

This distinction exposes a fundamental governance problem. Technical capability and access permission are insufficient bases for delegation. An agent may be capable of performing an action and possess legitimate access to the required resources while the available assurance evidence, current operating conditions, or applicable risk and governance policy no longer justify allowing it to exercise that authority. The relevant question is therefore not merely whether an agent can perform an action, or even whether an identity has permission to invoke an interface, but what the agent should currently be allowed to do, under what constraints, and with what degree of autonomy. The distinction between capability and justified authority consequently becomes a central governance concern.

The economic motivation for solving this problem is substantial. Agentic software may automate not only information-technology tasks but significant portions of professional and operational services, moving software from supporting workflows toward performing services themselves. This “service-as-software” trajectory increases the potential value of autonomy while simultaneously increasing the consequences of inappropriate authority. The objective is therefore not to eliminate autonomy, but to enable useful autonomy while continuously ensuring that the authority exercised by an agent remains justified by current evidence, operating conditions, organizational policy, and stakeholder risk tolerance.

papers.title: The spatial structure of solar magnetoconvection at scales up to $60$~Mm
papers.abstract: While convective motions at the scale of granules on the solar surface are well understood, those of mesogranular and supergranulation are not. At still larger scales, the lack of giant cells is a major mystery. We aim to slightly improve understanding of the radial and horizontal flows associated at mesogranular scales and supergranulation. We perform a deep MURaM small-scale dynamo simulation, extending from $50$~Mm below the solar surface and with a horizontal size of 60~Mm and sufficient resolution to begin to properly resolve the magnetic bright points in intergranular lanes. We determine the structure of the convective modes from the simulations at different scales, and compare the power spectra to those which have been previously observed. At all scales which are resolved by the simulation the simulated flows agree with the amplitude implied by Doppler measurements and local correlation tracking (LCT) measurements. The power in the vertical Doppler velocities at supergranular and larger scales is shown to be influenced by density perturbations near the surface. The structure of the modes at depth is simple as expected from the previous study of \cite{LordCameron2014} except the horizontal forcing scale scales like $H_\rho^{2/3}$ instead of $H\rho$. The simulations reproduce the observations up to scales of $60$~Mm. Within the simulated range, $l>=70$, we do not see the excess power associated with the convective conundrum.

papers.intro:
The structure of solar convection at the scales of granules (11 to 22 Mm) was essentially solved by Stein and Nordlund (1989), see also the review of Nordlund et al. (2009). Convection at scales greater than that of the granules remains poorly understood (Hanasoge et al. 2012; Hotta et al. 2023; Birch et al. 2024), although high-resolution simulations including the effects of the small-scale dynamo field has been shown to reduce the discrepancy between the observations and numerical simulations (Hotta and Kusano 2021; Hotta et al. 2022). In this paper we apply and slightly extend the analysis presented in Lord et al. (2014) to a simulation at higher resolution and including the magnetic fields generated by a small-scale dynamo. We share the same aims as the previous papers on this topic, to improving our understanding of convection at scales larger than granules.

We share the same aims as the previous papers on this topic, to improving our understanding of convection at scales larger than granules.

papers.title: StarWorld: A Cross-Layer World Model for Starlink Prediction and Streaming
papers.abstract: Starlink and other low Earth orbit (LEO) satellite broadband systems exhibit stochastic access dynamics whose effects propagate from network measurements to throughput prediction and adaptive bitrate (ABR) streaming, making reasoning over multiple plausible futures essential. Existing studies mainly characterize realized traces or individual system layers, leaving cross-layer world modeling of these evolving dynamics largely unexplored. To address this gap, we propose StarWorld, a cross-layer world model for Starlink prediction and streaming. StarWorld couples learned stochastic network dynamics with executable prediction, control, and playback processes to imagine multi-step cross-layer futures, while a calibrated Trust Gate determines whether these futures are sufficiently reliable for use. On real Starlink measurements, StarWorld achieves the lowest network-future distributional errors among the comparison methods at the principal horizons and reduces pairwise controller quality-of-experience (QoE) effect error by 76%. These results support StarWorld as a cross-layer imagination environment for studying prediction and streaming outcomes under uncertain Starlink access conditions.

Such cross-layer evaluation requires accounting for temporal dependence, uncertainty, and their effects on application behavior. Starlink throughput exhibits structure at multiple timescales [4], and prediction models use measurement histories to estimate future capacity [5]. Streaming controllers then combine capacity estimates with buffer state to select bitrates, coupling network conditions to playback quality [6, 7]. Within the user-side scope, future access capacity is treated as an exogenous process that is independent of application actions. Application actions instead determine prediction and playback outcomes under a given capacity evolution. A single replay evaluates these interactions on one realized network trajectory; it does not characterize the range of plausible continuations or their associated playback risks. papers.title: The kinematic Kelvin-Helmholtz instability-driven dynamo: implications for merging compact objects
papers.abstract: Binary neutron star (BNS) mergers excite a Kelvin--Helmholtz instability (KHI) in the shear layer between them. It is parasitized upon by the magnetic field to form a powerful magnetic dynamo. Using a large ensemble of high-resolution visco-resistive KHI-driven dynamo simulations we construct analytical, asymptotic in Reynolds number ($\rm{Re}$) models for the magnetic field growth rates and mean vertical field dynamo onset times. Our models suggest that in the $\rm{Re} \gg 1$ limit, the mean vertical field is seeded immediately, kinematic growth rates become asymptotic in $\rm{Re}$, and the dynamo moves out of the kinematic stage on $\mathcal{O}(0.1\,\rm{ms})$ timescales, readily attaining magnetar-strength fields during this transition. This suggests that most global BNS merger simulations are not time-resolving the correct KHI-driven dynamo regime.

papers.title: The two-loop Lamb shift: the final missing contribution
papers.abstract: The last significant unknown contribution to the two-loop Lamb shift, namely the electron self-energy with vacuum-polarization insertion into the photon line, is determined including higher-order effects in the parameter $\alpha Z$, with $\alpha$ being the fine-structure constant and $Z$ the nuclear charge number. Our calculation improves the accuracy of theoretical predictions for energy levels and transition energies in heavy hydrogen-like and lithium-like ions by up to one order of magnitude, enabling more stringent comparisons between theory and available experimental results. These results pave the way for more precise tests of quantum electrodynamics in the strong-field regime, as well as for accurate determinations of nuclear charge radii.

papers.title: Securing Web Agents with the Compile-Then-Execute Paradigm
papers.abstract: Web agents commonly follow the ReAct paradigm, selecting each action from runtime observations that inherently mix trusted and untrusted content. This design makes their control flow vulnerable to prompt injections embedded in webpages. We introduce Baya, a compile-then-execute web agent designed to prevent prompt-injection-driven control-flow hijacking by design. Before accessing the live website, Baya compiles the user's request into an executable Python program that calls a Trusted Website API. The planning model does not observe live website content; only the compiled program processes it. Untrusted data may determine program values or select among branches defined during compilation, but it cannot redefine the user task or cause the model to synthesize new website operations at runtime. The Trusted Website API gives the compiler a unified view of the website's action space, enabling ahead-of-time planning without the stepwise action discovery required by reactive agents. Our evaluation across 581 valid WebArena Verified tasks shows that Baya achieves 77.8% aggregate utility, outperforming browser-only ReAct (55.1%) and API-enabled ReAct (66.7%). On WASP, a security benchmark for web agents, Baya achieves 0% attack success rate, compared with 16.2% for API-enabled ReAct and 25.5% for browser-only ReAct.

papers.intro:
Web agents have emerged as a promising interface for automating complex web tasks, such as retrieving information, shopping online, or planning travel. Modern web agents typically operate in a reactive loop: they observe the current webpage, reason about the next action, execute it through a browser interface, and repeat until the task is complete [37]. This ability to adapt to information revealed during execution enables agents to operate on dynamic websites and complete complex, multi-step tasks.

Web agents have emerged as a promising interface for automating complex web tasks, such as retrieving information, shopping online, or planning travel. Modern web agents typically operate in a reactive loop: they observe the current webpage, reason about the next action, execute it through a browser interface, and repeat until the task is complete [37]. This ability to adapt to information revealed during execution enables agents to operate on dynamic websites and complete complex, multi-step tasks.

The same adaptability creates a fundamental security risk. Unlike traditional software interfaces, webpages inherently contain a mixture of trusted and untrusted information, including content from the website itself, users, and third parties. When a reactive agent incorporates this content into its reasoning, attacker-controlled content can influence not only the data it processes but also the actions it selects. This opens the door to indirect prompt-injection attacks [10, 38], in which malicious web content can cause the agent to deviate from the user’s intended task and perform attacker-chosen actions [33]. In this paper, we focus on preserving control-flow integrity: preventing untrusted web content from introducing attacker-chosen operations beyond the user’s intended workflow.

Separating planning from execution and committing to a pre-compiled plan provides a structural defense against control-flow hijacking. Instead of allowing the agent to continuously decide its next action based on runtime webpage content, the agent first compiles a task-specific plan and then carries out that plan against the web. In this architecture, information retrieved from webpages is treated as runtime data consumed by a compiled plan, rather than as instructions that can arbitrarily redefine the agent’s control flow. Prior work, such as CaMeL and FIDES, has demonstrated that compile-then-execute is an effective foundation for secure tool-calling agents [9, 8, 1, 20]. A prior analysis of WebArena found that all benchmark tasks are compatible with this paradigm, assuming complete trusted APIs [28]. However, applying compile-then-execute to web agents is more challenging than to conventional tool-calling agents.
