When integrated into a PIC, a nanowire comes into contact with other materials and is exposed to hybridization effects. Understanding the photonic and electronic coupling mechanisms behind this is fundamental to their integration, because these interactions can substantially alter light-matter coupling. Previous research has shown how the hybridization with metals increases the speed of the lasing emission.[14, 58] Research regarding the interaction of lasing nanowires with TMDs is scarce, even though TMDs, such as MoS2 and WS2, exhibit strong excitonic characteristics and a direct band gap in the monolayer limit, making them particularly promising for modifying the optical properties of nanowire lasers.[64] In our previous study, we investigated the interaction of nanowires with monolayer MoS2 and observed a partial suppression of the lasing emission.[15] We assumed a type-II band alignment between ZnO and MoS2 [42] as well as an associated charge transfer process. Thus, we attributed the change in the lasing characteristics to band filling and the Moss-Burstein effect. However, we did not consider further loss mechanisms for the lasing emission, such as optical absorption by the 2D material being in the evanescent field of the lasing nanowire.

papers.title: Migration and eccentricity damping timescales in overstable resonant planetary systems: hydrodynamic and N-body simulations
papers.abstract: Tidal interactions between planets and discs modify semimajor axes and eccentricities. These effects are represented by migration and eccentricity damping timescales in analytical and Nbody models, although they are assumed constant. This approximation is uncertain in resonant multiplanet systems, where coupled planet disc evolution can produce non-linear torque feedback. We investigate migration and eccentricity damping in two planet systems undergoing resonant and overstable evolution near the 2:1 mean motion resonance. Using hydrodynamic simulations with varying disc surface densities, viscosities, and aspect ratios, we measure both timescales from energy and angular momentum exchange between the planets and disc. We find that both timescales are time dependent and vary throughout the evolution. In resonant systems, sign reversals occur owing to eccentricity oscillations and disc torque variations. Moreover, migration timescales normalised by their expected dependence on planetary mass, disc surface density, and aspect ratio deviate between models. Likewise, the common relation between migration and eccentricity damping timescales is not recovered. We compare the hydrodynamic evolution with several Nbody approaches. Models with constant migration and damping timescales fail to reproduce the hydrodynamic evolution, whereas torque-based approaches provide better agreement. In particular, approaches including corotation torque saturation and planetary eccentricity reproduce the hydrodynamic evolution in the type I migration regime, whereas additional corrections are required when planets partially open gaps. These results show that time-dependent torque-based prescriptions provide a consistent physical link between hydrodynamic simulations and simplified Nbody models of resonant planetary systems.

These interactions drive orbital migration and damp planetary eccentricities, thereby shaping the final architecture of planetary systems.

The theoretical foundations of planet–disc interactions were established by Goldreich and Tremaine (1980) and Ward (1997). Since then, the theory of planetary migration and disc-driven orbital evolution has been developed through analytical, numerical, and hydrodynamic studies (see Kley and Nelson, 2012; Baruteau et al., 2014, for reviews). Because long-term hydrodynamic simulations remain computationally expensive, many investigations of planetary system formation rely on N-body calculations in which the effects of the disc are represented through prescribed migration and eccentricity damping timescales, τa\tau_{a} and τe\tau_{e}. Such approaches have been extensively used to study resonant capture, resonant chains, and the long-term dynamical evolution of planetary systems (Lee and Peale, 2002; Papaloizou and Szuszkiewicz, 2005; Goldreich and Schlichting, 2014; Batygin et al., 2015; Batygin and Petit, 2023, e.g.). In most applications, these timescales are assumed to be constant or are parameterised using simple analytical relations. Although this approximation has proven useful, its validity has rarely been investigated against hydrodynamic simulations of resonant multi-planet systems.

The reliability of these prescriptions is particularly important for planets undergoing convergent migration toward mean-motion resonances. Studies have shown that resonance capture results from a delicate balance between resonant excitation and disc-driven damping (Kley et al., 2004; Papaloizou and Szuszkiewicz, 2005; Delisle et al., 2015). Consequently, even modest changes in the migration or eccentricity damping rates can modify the resonant equilibrium, alter the amplitude of libration, and affect whether a resonant configuration remains stable over long timescales (Goldreich and Schlichting, 2014; Deck and Batygin, 2015; Xu et al., 2018).

In resonant systems, gravitational interactions between the planets continuously excite planetary eccentricities, whereas disc–planet interactions usually damp them, unless there is a depletion of gas around the planets’ orbits such as a clean gap or surface density drop (Goldreich and Tremaine, 1980; Papaloizou et al., 2001; Duffell and Chiang, 2015). The competition between these prcesses establishes an equilibrium eccentricity. Under certain conditions, however, perturbations about this equilibrium do not decay but instead grow with time, eventually leading to resonance escape. This behaviour is commonly referred to as overstability, was investigated analytically by Goldreich and Schlichting (2014) and subsequently extended by Deck and Batygin (2015), Delisle et al. The migration and eccentricity damping rates themselves have also been the subject of extensive investigation. Hydrodynamic studies demonstrated that the torques acting on eccentric planets differ substantially from those predicted for circular orbits and depend on the disc response, spiral-wave structure, and eccentricity evolution (Papaloizou and Larwood, 2000; Cresswell et al., 2007; Cresswell and Nelson, 2008). In addition, torque formulae accounting for Lindblad and corotation torques have revealed a complex dependence on disc structure and thermodynamics (Paardekooper et al., 2010; Paardekooper et al., 2011). These results suggest that migration and eccentricity damping may not always be accurately represented by fixed timescales.

This work aims to investigate migration and eccentricity damping timescales in resonant planetary systems that exhibit overstable behaviour and to evaluate the assumptions commonly adopted in N-body models. Using hydrodynamic simulations of two planets near the 2:1 mean-motion resonance, we measure these timescales directly from the exchange of angular momentum, orbital energy, and disc torques following Ataiee and Kley (2021). We then address two questions: (i) whether commonly used analytical scalings reproduce the measured hydrodynamic behaviour, and (ii) which N-body prescriptions provide the most faithful representation of the orbital evolution observed in the simulations. Establishing such a connection is essential if simplified N-body models are to be used reliably in studies of resonant capture, resonant stability, and overstability.

Establishing such a connection is essential if simplified N-body models are to be used reliably in studies of resonant capture, resonant stability, and overstability.

This paper is organised as follows. Section 2 describes the numerical setup and the method used to calculate migration and eccentricity damping timescales. Section 3 presents the hydrodynamic results and parameter study. Section 4 compares the hydrodynamic simulations with different N-body prescriptions. Section 5 discusses the physical interpretation and implications of the measured timescales. Finally, Section 6 summarises our conclusions.

papers.title: Balancing hierarchical representation and quantization: A performance trade-off in text embeddings
papers.abstract: Hierarchical text embedding models offer variable-length representations, while quantization reduces numerical precision; both aim to improve computational efficiency. This work is an empirical benchmark study of how these two orthogonal, already-established techniques interact. We evaluate 38 tasks from the Massive Text Embedding Benchmark (MTEB) using four transformer-based embedding models, covering 1D and 2D hierarchical representations combined with 32-bit, 8-bit, and binary quantization, for 168 configurations per task. We report each efficiency dimension separately: theoretical per-vector storage and end-to-end evaluation time. Under a Friedman test with Nemenyi post-hoc analysis, int8 quantization is statistically indistinguishable from float32 for pair classification and re-ranking and costs at most 1.5 percentage points overall, whereas binary quantization is significantly worse across every task category. Halving the embedding dimension once is not statistically detectable above $m=16$; two successive halvings always are. Combining an 8x dimensionality reduction with int8 yields a 32x reduction in per-vector storage at 94.4% of baseline effectiveness. Because evaluation times were measured once, we treat them as indicative: we find no evidence that quantization speeds up evaluation, whereas sampling from intermediate layers shortens it substantially. Retrieval degrades far faster than every other category, so we report findings per task category.

papers.intro:
Learned representations, commonly called embeddings, represent diverse data types (e.g., words, documents) as real-valued vectors, organized such that semantically similar items are positioned close together within the embedding space [1]. Since Word2Vec [2], embeddings have advanced further, notably with BERT [3], which marked a shift towards context-dependent embeddings, and with Sentence-BERT [4] and SimCSE [5], designed to learn embeddings for entire sentences. These representations then power a wide spectrum of downstream tasks, including classification, clustering, and retrieval [6]. Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) [7] stands as a prominent example: a typical RAG pipeline involves chunking and embedding documents, retrieving relevant chunks based on similarity to a user query, and then generating a response from a large language model.

papers.title: Perceptive Humanoid Motion from Simulation
papers.abstract: Humanoid robots have the potential to automate a wide range of physical tasks. Progress toward generalist humanoid autonomy, however, remains constrained by a data bottleneck: mapping pixels and free-form language to low-level joint commands requires paired supervision, and no corpus of such data exists at sufficiently large scale. Some approaches rely on human teleoperation and wearable capture devices, which require at least an hour of human time to produce an hour of data. We present HALO, a humanoid autonomy system powered by a pipeline that synthesizes vision-language-motion data across a thousand procedurally generated homes. The corpus scales with compute rather than human labor. HALO acquires a repertoire of physical skills, including sitting on chairs, navigating to named objects, stepping sideways through half-open doors, crouching and crawling beneath tables, and pushing boxes. It orchestrates these skills to solve composite, long-horizon tasks. Without ever seeing a real home during training, HALO transfers zero-shot to the physical world, achieving a 91% success rate across 360 trials in six unmapped real-world environments. See https://apple-aiml-research.github.io/ml-halo/ for code and videos.

papers.intro:
Humanoid robots can somersault, dance, and run. Yet none of them can be invited into an unfamiliar living room and asked to sit down. They are agile but blind: a backflip is choreographed in advance and executed against geometry the robot never has to perceive. The tasks that would make a humanoid useful are not like this. They take place in rooms nobody has scanned, among furniture nobody has annotated, and the robot has to find the chair before it can sit on it. Perception enters twice, and at two levels of abstraction. It is semantic, deciding what to do: which of the objects around me does the instruction refer to? And it is physical, deciding how to move: the seat has to be met where it actually is, and the robot’s weight transferred onto it without losing balance. Neither level is supervised the way a backflip is. A backflip requires only a reference motion clip and a tracker to follow it. Mapping pixels and free-form language to joint commands, however, demands paired supervision: an egocentric image, an instruction, and the precise whole-body trajectory that satisfies it.

Teleoperation systems such as ALOHA [2] and TWIST [3], or wearable capture devices such as UMI [4], can generate these demonstrations, but they couple data generation with physical labor. Because a person must manually act out every episode, an hour of data costs at least an hour of human time.

In this paper, we introduce HALO (Humanoid Autonomy, Learned in simulation, running Onboard), a humanoid autonomy system powered by a data generation pipeline that produces egocentric vision-language-motion data entirely in simulation. The resulting policy runs fully onboard the physical robot. Simulation unshackles data generation from human labor. A scene can be generated, a motion synthesized, and the corresponding egocentric video rendered with no human intervention. What would have taken hours (and days, and years) of human time can instead proceed autonomously and in parallel, bounded only by compute. To create a training episode, a motion diffusion model generates the whole-body humanoid motion, a procedural generator supplies the environment, and the simulator situates the motion in the environment to render the robot’s sensory inputs. Our training corpus comprises 300300 hours of episodes across a thousand procedurally generated homes, none of which anyone has had to visit or scan. Data scales with compute rather than human time. Quality is maintained by automated verifiers.

The HALO autonomy stack has three layers, illustrated in Fig. 2. An orchestrator (an off-the-shelf vision-language model invoked every two seconds) decomposes a free-form language request into a sequence of subtasks, each identifying one skill and the object it applies to. A motion generator running at 3 Hz combines a VLM-based encoder with a DiT-based decoder and maps an egocentric RGB observation and the subtask to a whole-body kinematic motion plan: five seconds of joint angles and pelvis poses. Finally, a 50 Hz motion tracker takes this motion plan in conjunction with onboard depth and proprioception, and drives the robot via joint-level actuator commands. The motion tracker is trained by large-scale reinforcement learning to follow motion plans while respecting balance, contact, and actuator limits. The first two layers settle the semantic half of the problem (which chair?); the tracker settles the physical half (meeting the seat where it actually is).

papers.title: FrontierPhysics: Evaluating Agents for End-to-End Physics Research
papers.abstract: AI agents are playing an increasingly important role in physics research. However, existing physics benchmarks only evaluate fixed questions, isolated sub-tasks, or paper reproduction with given solutions, and rarely check research quality alongside correctness. We introduce FrontierPhysics, an end-to-end benchmark with 56 tasks made by 42 physicists based on their own research, covering nine domains across theoretical, computational, and experimental physics. Each task requires agents to review the literature, develop a research plan, conduct research and experiments, and produce structured outputs and scientific manuscripts. Combining deterministic verifiers with expert-authored rubrics, FrontierPhysics evaluates whether agents' research is correct and publishable. Across 22 models in 26 configurations, no configuration passes more than 46 of its 168 rollouts. Manual review of agent trajectories shows that frontier agents' main weaknesses are insufficiently rigorous reasoning and limited expert intuition, rather than gaps in physics knowledge or execution errors.

papers.intro:
Large language models (LLMs) are evolving from passive scientific assistants into agents that take on parts of the research process. When equipped with external tools, these agents can search and summarize literature, formulate hypotheses, write and debug scientific code, and produce technical reports. Recent systems have demonstrated tool-augmented reasoning in chemistry, iterative code-based experimentation, multi-agent hypothesis generation, scientific-software optimization, and even interaction with laboratory instruments [30, 6, 29, 37, 17, 4, 33, 41, 20, 22, 18, 31, 15]. These systems point toward agents that contribute to more complete scientific workflows and projects, not only isolated subtasks [9].

Evaluating progress toward this goal requires benchmarks that capture the open-ended, multi-stage nature of scientific research. Scientific benchmarks are accordingly shifting from textbook-level questions [16, 23, 48, 35, 44] toward expert-level closed-ended questions [8] and research-level problems [40]. Among existing research-level benchmarks, some assess scientific reasoning [10, 50, 34, 25, 46], while others evaluate the agents’ ability to complete individual tasks within realistic scientific workflows [43, 19, 31, 28, 7, 21]. However, these benchmarks target isolated capabilities, and because many of their tasks are closed-ended with deterministic answers, models quickly saturate them, so the benchmarks lose signal. To move toward end-to-end research, some benchmarks formulate tasks as full-paper reproductions [36, 12, 49, 14]. Yet because agents are given the original publications, the research questions and solution structures are largely specified in advance, limiting their ability to evaluate open-ended scientific inquiry. More recent benchmarks address this limitation by converting published studies into research problems without revealing their solutions [32, 45, 47, 24]. Nevertheless, designing and evaluating such tasks involves many subtleties that require the expertise of the original authors: for example, how to write instructions that preserve as much open-endedness as possible while avoiding false negatives, and how to determine if an agent’s failure reflects true scientific misunderstanding or a lack of expert intuition and experience. To our knowledge, no existing benchmark is fully agentic, built by physicists from their own research, graded on both paper quality and result correctness, and designed to address these subtleties through manual task review and failure-mode analysis (Table 1).

In this paper, we introduce FrontierPhysics (Fig. FrontierPhysics: Evaluating Agents for End-to-End Physics Research), a benchmark evaluating whether AI agents can conduct end-to-end research across theoretical, computational, and experimental physics. FrontierPhysics tasks are designed by active physics researchers (including Ph.D. students, postdocs, and research scientists) from research projects they have personally conducted. On average, each task author has 420 citations. To preserve open-endedness while minimizing false negatives and positives, each task goes through manual general review, domain-expert peer review, and failure-mode analysis. For each task (Fig. 2), an agent receives a high-level prompt that resembles the instructions provided by a principal investigator (PI) at the beginning of a research project. The agent must then carry out the research and produce both a scientific manuscript and numerical outputs that can be verified deterministically. Much of this process is open-ended: the agent must investigate the topic, formulate a research plan, select appropriate methods, validate the results, and establish the significance of its findings. To evaluate these capabilities, FrontierPhysics combines a deterministic verifier (test scripts that check the numerical outputs) with rubric-based grading by reviewer agents.

papers.title: ReveaLLAGN 3: Revealing the Infrared Spectral Energy Distributions of Low Luminosity AGN
papers.abstract: The spectral energy distributions of active galactic nuclei (AGN) provide valuable information on the emission mechanisms taking place in their inner regions. Here we use the James Webb Space Telescope to study the near and mid-infrared spectral energy distributions of seven nearby low-luminosity active galaxy nuclei from 1.7 to 24 $\mu m$. We cleanly separate the AGN spectrum by performing spatial fits of the two-dimensional images across all wavelengths. We then compare these clean unresolved spectra to aperture-based spectra and show that they effectively remove galaxy contamination. Comparing our infrared measurements to X-ray emission, we find that low-luminosity AGN have enhanced near-infrared emission relative to more luminous AGN, a trend that correlates with radio-loudness, while their mid-infrared-to-X-ray ratios are comparable. A majority of our targets show strong compact silicate emission suggesting the presence of warm dust on parsec scales in these systems. We also quantify the near- and mid-infrared power-law slopes and colors of low-luminosity AGN. In the near-infrared we find AGN of all luminosities have similar spectral slopes and colors, however in the mid-infrared, we find low-luminosity AGN typically have steeper slopes and redder colors than more luminous AGN. Both the strong silicate emission and steep mid-infrared slopes disagree with existing models for low-luminosity AGN spectral energy distributions.

papers.intro:
Rapidly accreting supermassive black holes create some of the brightest objects in the Universe, however, a majority of supermassive black holes lying at the centres of galaxies are much fainter due to much lower accretion rates (Ho, 2009, e.g.). Relative to their rapidly accreting counterparts, these low-luminosity Active Galactic Nuclei (LLAGN) share a number of unique features. First, LLAGN show weaker ultraviolet (UV) emission and lack the "big blue bump" thermal continuum relative to bright AGN (Ho, 1999; Maoz, 2007; Ho, 2008; Eracleous et al., 2010; Fernández-Ontiveros et al., 2023; Kang et al., 2025). Second, they show very weak or frequently absent broad emission lines (Elitzur et al., 2014, e.g.) and have both weak high-ionization lines and strong low-ionization lines (Heckman, 1980; Goold et al., 2026, e.g.). Third, LLAGN are frequently radio-loud, with strong compact radio emission (Nagar et al., 2000; Nagar et al., 2005; Baldi, 2023).

These LLAGN phenomena can be explained by changes in the accretion structure that occur in systems accreting at rates somewhere below 1% of the Eddington accretion limit11 1 In this paper we define LLAGN as systems with Eddington ratios log(LBol/LEdd\rm L_{Bol}/L_{Edd}) <−3<-3.. At these lower accretion rates, the inner accretion disc becomes optically thin creating hot, radiatively inefficient accretion flows (Abramowicz and Fragile, 2013; Yuan and Narayan, 2014, RIAFs; see reviews by). Several subclasses of RIAF models exist including advection dominated accretion flows (ADAFs), where material is advected directly on to the black hole (Narayan and Yi, 1995; Yuan and Narayan, 2014), and models where the inefficiency is directly related to outflows or convection of energy (Blandford and Begelman, 1999; Quataert and Gruzinov, 2000, e.g.). The weak UV emission and the absence of broad lines in LLAGN are naturally explained by RIAF models due to the truncation of the inner accretion disc (Trump et al., 2011; Yu et al., 2011, e.g.). Modern general relativistic magneto-hydrodynamic simulations have enabled detailed numerical investigation of hot accretion flows and their application to data from the Event Horizon Telescope (Porth et al., 2019; Event Horizon Telescope Collaboration et al., 2022, e.g.) and to jet launching (Liska et al., 2018; Liska et al., 2020, e.g.). A substantial amount of energy in all AGN is emitted in the infrared part of the spectrum. A tight relation is found between the X-ray emission and the emission at 12 μ\mum in AGN at a wide range of luminosities (Krabbe et al., 2001; Gandhi et al., 2009; Asmus et al., 2015, e.g.) that likely reflects the balance between AGN heating and cooling (Spinoglio and Malkan, 1989). In the near-infrared at ∼\sim2 μ\mum, the correlation with X-ray is less tight, but still clearly found (Burtscher et al., 2015; Müller-Sánchez et al., 2018) with an apparent excess in LLAGN (Dumont et al., 2020). The dominant emission source at infrared wavelengths for higher luminosity AGN is thought to be dust emission from the torus or a disc wind (Ramos Almeida and Ricci, 2017; Hönig, 2019), however, as noted above, jet synchrotron emission in LLAGN can also contribute significantly at these wavelengths (Markoff et al., 2008; Prieto et al., 2016; EHT MWL Science Working Group et al., 2021; Fernández-Ontiveros et al., 2023). The relative contributions of these components remain unclear in LLAGN due to the challenge of separating the compact AGN emission from that of the underlying galaxy. In this context, the mid-infrared silicate features provide an important diagnostic of the dust surrounding the nucleus. While obscured Seyfert galaxies often show silicate absorption (Hatziminaoglou et al., 2015), LLAGN display a similar behavior as type 1s, with silicate features frequently detected in emission (Mason et al., 2012; Mason et al., 2013). However, previous studies based on Spitzer spectroscopy lacked the angular resolution needed to confirm the nuclear origin of this emission and the sensitivity required to obtain high-S/N spectra for large LLAGN samples. Conversely, previous photometric measurements did not provide the spectral resolution needed to characterize the silicate features themselves in these nuclei.

The SEDs of LLAGN have been modeled in the past, often under an assumption of their dominant emission mechanism. A number of studies interpret the power-law spectra of LLAGN in the radio and infrared in the context of jet models (Yuan et al., 2002; Markoff et al., 2008; Lucchini et al., 2019; Fernández-Ontiveros et al., 2023). Nemmen et al. (2014) fit 12 LLAGN SEDs and found some are ADAF-dominated, while others are jet-dominated. López et al. (2024) created a CIGALE (Yang et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2022) module for LLAGN that assumes an ADAF+Truncated Disc model using results of Nemmen et al. (2014). papers.title: Characterizing Gravitational Wave Electromagnetic Counterparts with the Schmidt Observatory System
papers.abstract: The emergence of gravitational wave (GW) multimessenger astronomy, marked by the detection of GW170817 and its associated kilonova, has opened a new window into the physics of compact binary mergers. Building a statistical population of kilonovae remains a challenge, limited by the low neutron star merger detection rates and the rapid evolution of these faint transients. The former problem will be overcome with upcoming LIGO/Virgo/KAGRA (LVK) sensitivity improvements leading to the fifth Observing Run (O5), while the latter will be addressed by the Schmidt Observatory System (including the Argus Array, the Deep Synoptic Array (DSA), and the Lazuli Space Observatory), in addition to ongoing and upcoming surveys (including the Rubin Observatory Legacy Survey of Space and Time). Using simulations of expected kilonovae at LVK O5 sensitivity, we find that Argus and Rubin could detect binary neutron star kilonovae at a rate of 0.3-4.2 yr$^{-1}$ and 0.6-7.0 yr$^{-1}$ respectively. For neutron star-black hole mergers, Rubin could detect up to 1 kilonova per year. Lazuli will be able to characterize this kilonova population down to $g \sim 26$ mag as early as 12 hours post merger. Additionally, $\sim35\%$ of these events are expected to exhibit a jet afterglow that will be detectable by DSA. We further characterize kilonova spectra to determine observable features of heavy element production. Finally, we develop an observing strategy that combines high cadence imaging and spectral monitoring, maximizing Lazuli's ability to constrain ejecta properties and composition of GW counterparts with reasonable observing time.

papers.intro:
The detection of GW170817 by the LIGO and Virgo collaborations marks the first gravitational wave (GW) observation of a binary neutron star (BNS) merger [2, 1]. This event was followed by GRB 170817A ∼1.7\sim 1.7 s after the merger [42, 99], by kilonova emission after ∼11\sim 11 hours [12, 18, 22, 23, 24, 31, 33, 53, 69, 81, 87, 102, 106, 109, 112, 116, 117], and by radio and X-ray afterglow emission on timescales of days to weeks [72, 114, 44, 7, 43, 63, 67, 89, 77]. Kilonovae trace the neutron-rich ejecta from the merger, while the afterglow traces the relativistic outflow launched from the remnant. Observing these electromagnetic (EM) counterparts allows us to probe heavy element production [52, 87], jet physics [114, 77, 8, 38, 115, 98], physics of neutron star mergers [21, 71, 27] and cosmology [3, 47, 16, 82], as well as the nature of the progenitor and remnant object [121].

Neutron star mergers have long been proposed as promising sites for the synthesis of rapid neutron capture elements via r-process nucleosynthesis [65, 32, 76]. Characterizing the composition of the kilonova ejecta that follows such a merger provides a unique observational window into the process. While photometry can constrain the broad luminosity and the color evolution of a kilonova, which can inform our understanding of its ejecta mass, velocity and electron fraction, spectroscopy provides a more direct way to probe the ejecta composition. Correctly identifying kilonova spectral lines remains a challenge because rapidly expanding ejecta possess a velocity gradient, which Doppler shifts the individual atomic transitions by different amount in different layers of the ejecta. This will broaden the line and cause lines with similar wavelengths to overlap and blend [52, 110, 39, 41]. As a result, the same spectral features can support competing identifications. In AT2017gfo, for example, Smartt et al. [106] attributed the early absorption feature at 1.8 μ\mum to Te I and Cs I, both second r-process peak elements, while Watson et al. [118] argued that Sr ii, a first r-process peak element, explains the same feature better.

Identifying the time at which a feature appears and tracing its subsequent evolution can help reduce ambiguities among blended features. This requires spectroscopic sequences that span optical to infrared wavelengths, since the kilonova cools and its emission shifts redward over time [41, 108]. AT2017gfo provided such a sequence because its proximity (∼40\sim 40 Mpc) made repeated high quality spectroscopy possible as the transient rapidly faded [75, 87, 106]. Moreover, the optical counterpart was rapidly identified (within hours of the GW trigger). Obtaining comparable observations for future events will be difficult as the increasing sensitivity of LIGO/Virgo/KAGRA (LVK) GW detectors will extend neutron star merger detections to distances of hundreds of Mpc, where their kilonova will appear much fainter. Additionally, GW localization regions can span tens to thousands of deg2, and a counterpart must first be identified through sensitive wide field imaging before spectroscopy can begin, so this may in general take longer than a few hours. Thus, obtaining spectroscopic sequences will become challenging for most ground based instruments, even at peak luminosity.

Beyond thermal emission, afterglow emission is also produced when a successfully launched jet interacts with the surrounding medium and generates synchrotron emission. If the jet is viewed close to its axis, the prompt gamma ray burst (GRB) and early afterglow are dominated by the jet core, making early optical and near-infrared monitoring important on timescales of hours to about a day after the merger. Off-axis events, however, are expected to constitute the majority of detectable GW sources, given that GW emission is sensitive to the inclination angle of the binary with respect to the observer. As a result, the viewing angle of the detectable GW source population peaks close to ∼30\sim 30 deg [100], resulting in a slowly-evolving jet afterglow peaking in luminosity hundreds of days after merger [54], which is close to what was observed for GW170817 [73, 82].

The Eric and Wendy Schmidt Observatory System11 1 https://www.schmidtsciences.org/schmidt-observatory-system/ is expected to provide new opportunities within this landscape of multi-messenger discovery and characterization in the coming years [94, 120]. By combining the large aperture equivalent, wide-field optical survey to be carried out by the Argus Array22 2 https://argus.unc.edu [66], with radio observations from the Deep Synoptic Array33 3 https://www.deepsynoptic.org (DSA; Hallinan et al. 45), rapid spectroscopic observations from the Large Fiber Array Spectroscopic Telescope44 4 https://astro.arizona.edu/research-groups/lfast (LFAST), as well as spectroscopic and imaging space-based data from the Lazuli Space Observatory [94], the System provides a unique opportunity for coordinated discovery and characterization of multimessenger sources. In addition, the NSF-DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST; Ivezić et al. 50) has recently started and is expected to discover EM candidate counterparts to GW events that can be further observed and characterized with this Observatory System.

In this work, we simulate BNS and neutron star-black hole (NSBH) merger GW events as expected during the LVK O5 observing run and as informed by available GW population studies. The O5 run is expected to start in ∼2029\sim 2029 and last about 3 years55 5 https://emfollow.docs.ligo.org/userguide/capabilities.html, and will have significant overlap with the Schmidt Observatory System expected operations. We attach kilonova and afterglow emission to the simulated GW events and evaluate their detectability with Argus and Rubin. For the detectable population, we estimate the Lazuli exposure times (ETs) needed for follow-up at different epochs. We then use AT2017gfo-like spectral models to determine when key spectral features are expected to be observable within Lazuli’s wavelength range, with a goal of developing possible observing strategies for future BNS and NSBH detections. Additionally, we estimate the potential for jet afterglow detections, including with DSA.

papers.title: CosmoVerse Data Challenge: How Tip of the Red Giant Branch Analysis Choices Shape the Inferred Hubble Constant
papers.abstract: Tip of the red giant branch (TRGB)-based determinations of the Hubble constant ($H_0$), the current expansion rate of the Universe, depend on choices made in selecting and analyzing stellar photometry and in assembling the sample of calibrator galaxies hosting Type Ia supernovae (SNe Ia). The CosmoVerse Data Challenge invites participants to analyze public photometric catalogs within a shared distance-ladder framework, opening each step of the measurement to the community and testing how these choices propagate into $H_0$. Participants independently selected photometric catalogs, galaxies, and TRGB measurement settings, while using a common SN Ia compilation and fitting procedure to convert distances into $H_0$. Supported by public notebooks and a training school, the challenge received 26 submissions from 22 participants. All submissions used the same analysis notebook, many participants were trainees at the school, and the true galaxy distances are unknown; the results therefore characterize the sensitivity of the submissions to analysis and sample-selection choices and are not a combined determination of $H_0$ or an estimate of the systematic uncertainty in published TRGB measurements. The inferred $H_0$ values have a median of $77.10\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}}$ and a standard deviation of $7.38\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}}$ $(5.11\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}}$ for the scaled median absolute deviation), $\sim 3.4$ $(\sim 2.4)$ times the typical quoted uncertainty of a submission. Differences in the measured tip of the anchor galaxy NGC 4258 add a coherent shift in the distance scale. The challenge shows how different choices within a common framework can produce substantially different values of $H_0$, and provides an open basis for tracing these differences and for making datasets and tools more transparent and accessible.

The Local Distance Network combines a range of local distance indicators within a distance-ladder framework (H0DN Collaboration et al., 2026). In the first rung of the distance ladder, geometric distances to nearby anchor galaxies, such as the distance to NGC 4258 from the orbital motion of water masers around its central black hole (Reid et al., 2019), calibrate the luminosity of standardizable candles such as Cepheid variables or the tip of the red giant branch (TRGB). In the second rung, the same candle is measured in more distant galaxies that have hosted Type Ia supernovae (SNe Ia); this step calibrates the luminosity of the SNe Ia. In the third rung, this calibration is applied to SNe Ia sufficiently far away that their redshifts are dominated by the expansion of the Universe (the Hubble flow; 0.023<z<0.150.023<z<0.15 for the SNe Ia used in this challenge), and the relation between their distances and redshifts gives H0H_{0}. SNe Ia are used in the last two rungs because they are luminous enough to be observed at these distances and, once their peak magnitudes are corrected using the shapes of their light curves, they become precise relative distance indicators (Phillips, 1993; Hamuy et al., 1996; Riess et al., 1996). SN Ia samples used for this purpose include the Pantheon+ compilation (Scolnic et al., 2022; Brout et al., 2022a; Riess et al., 2016; Riess et al., 2022), the Carnegie Supernova Project (CSP) sample (Hamuy et al., 2006; Freedman et al., 2019; Uddin et al., 2024; Freedman et al., 2025), and the Zwicky Transient Facility (ZTF) sample (Rigault et al., 2025; Dhawan et al., 2022).

In the third rung, this calibration is applied to SNe Ia sufficiently far away that their redshifts are dominated by the expansion of the Universe (the Hubble flow; 0.023<z<0.150.023<z<0.15 for the SNe Ia used in this challenge), and the relation between their distances and redshifts gives H0H_{0}. SNe Ia are used in the last two rungs because they are luminous enough to be observed at these distances and, once their peak magnitudes are corrected using the shapes of their light curves, they become precise relative distance indicators (Phillips, 1993; Hamuy et al., 1996; Riess et al., 1996). SN Ia samples used for this purpose include the Pantheon+ compilation (Scolnic et al., 2022; Brout et al., 2022a; Riess et al., 2016; Riess et al., 2022), the Carnegie Supernova Project (CSP) sample (Hamuy et al., 2006; Freedman et al., 2019; Uddin et al., 2024; Freedman et al., 2025), and the Zwicky Transient Facility (ZTF) sample (Rigault et al., 2025; Dhawan et al., 2022).

The discrepancy is not easily dismissed as a single measurement error, because each side is reached by multiple routes: several CMB experiments give consistent early-Universe values, and several distance indicators give consistent local values. The tension has been approached in two complementary ways: through searches for new physics beyond Λ\LambdaCDM that could reconcile the CMB-inferred value with the local one, and through renewed, independent scrutiny of the systematics in both approaches, including the local distance-ladder measurements themselves. The TRGB method, which this Data Challenge focuses on, provides a specialized, partial cross-check of the local measurement: it replaces Cepheids as the primary distance indicator that calibrates the SNe Ia, but its dependence on the geometric anchor distances and on the SN Ia data is essentially the same as that of Cepheids.

The TRGB method rests on a well-understood feature of the evolution of old, low-mass stars. Red giant stars grow steadily brighter as they evolve, until helium ignition abruptly ends the red giant phase at a nearly constant luminosity (Iben and Renzini, 1983). The bright end of the red giant branch (RGB), the TRGB, therefore appears as a sharp drop-off in the luminosity function of an old stellar population, and because this drop-off occurs at nearly the same luminosity in all such populations, comparing the apparent magnitudes of TRGB stars in a galaxy with their intrinsic magnitudes, calibrated with a geometric distance, gives the distance modulus of that galaxy.

In practice, the tip is located by selecting red giants from a catalog of resolved-star photometry, building their luminosity function, and detecting the sharp drop in star counts at its bright end. How cleanly and precisely this edge is detected depends on the stellar population of each galaxy and on analysis choices, such as which stars are selected and how much the luminosity function is smoothed; these choices can shift the inferred distance and therefore H0H_{0}. Measured in the outer halos of galaxies and most commonly in the II band, the TRGB is affected only weakly by several systematics that affect Cepheids: halo fields have low reddening internal to the host galaxy and little crowding or blending of the photometry, and the II-band tip has only a shallow, calibrated dependence on metallicity (Rizzi et al., 2007; Jang et al., 2021; Newman et al., 2024a; Newman et al., 2024b). In practice, however, the tip is often not a clean edge, and its localization relies on choices made case by case (Wu et al., 2023); in eleven Hubble Space Telescope (HST) fields around NGC 4258, for example, the measured F​814​WF814W tips can span a range of 0.3 mag (Li et al., 2023b). The tip contrast, the ratio of the numbers of stars half a magnitude fainter and brighter than the tip, has been used to assess the quality of tip measurements (Wu et al., 2023) and to standardize them (Li et al., 2023b; Scolnic et al., 2023). Other approaches have also been explored, such as utilizing the variability of red giants (Anderson et al., 2024; Koblischke and Anderson, 2024) and excluding subsamples of measurements based on their edge detector responses (Hoyt, 2023); in the context of measuring H0H_{0}, the applicability of these approaches can be limited in the hosts of SNe Ia.

papers.title: A pocket of oxygen in a near-pristine galaxy at z=4.2: chemical inhomogeneity at 10-parsec scales in LAP2
papers.abstract: We aim to constrain the oxygen abundance, the ionizing properties, and the spatial structure of LAP2, a strongly lensed (with a magnification $\mu$~50) oxygen-deficient galaxy at z=4.2 behind the galaxy cluster Abell 2744. We present new JWST/NIRSpec IFU PRISM observations (~13.6 hr) of LAP2, which we combine with archival JWST/NIRCam imaging. LAP2 is intrinsically extremely faint (M_UV=-12.7) and has a low stellar mass (M~$10^5~M_\odot$), comparable to that of massive star clusters. It consists of a compact core ($R_{eff}$~7 pc) embedded in a more diffuse emission (with $R_{eff}$~20 pc). Strong H$\alpha$ emission (EW$_{\rm rest}\simeq880$ \r{A}, $\log\xi_{\rm ion}\simeq25.3$), a blue UV slope ($\beta_{\rm UV}\simeq-2.5$, down to $\simeq-3.1$ in the core), and a Balmer decrement consistent with no dust attenuation indicate a young ($\lesssim10$ Myr), dust-free burst. [OIII]$\lambda$5007 is not detected in the integrated spectrum, implying [OIII]/H$\beta\leq0.61$ ($3\sigma$) and, using an extrapolated strong-line calibration, $12+\log({\rm O/H})\leq6.4$ ($\lesssim0.5\%\,Z_\odot$). This places LAP2 among the most metal-poor galaxies known. Faint [OIII] emission is, however, detected in the core (with $\rm4\sigma$ significance), where we derive $12+\log({\rm O/H})\simeq6.6$ ($\sim1\%\,Z_\odot$). This difference can be explained either by local self-enrichment, requiring only $\rm \sim0.2\,M_\odot$ of newly synthesized oxygen, or by a higher ionization parameter in the core. The upper limit on HeII$\lambda$1640 (EW$_{\rm rest}<39$ \r{A}, $3\sigma$) does not exclude a contribution from metal-free stars. LAP2 extends the census of spectroscopically confirmed EMPGs to star-cluster masses and to $M_{\rm UV}\approx-13$. Its location in a low-density region supports a scenario in which underdense environments preserve nearly pristine gas well after reionization.

papers.intro:
The metallicity of galaxies is closely linked to their stellar mass, giving rise to the well-established mass–metallicity relation (MZR, e.g. Garnett, 2002; Tremonti et al., 2004). This relation has been confirmed over a broad range of stellar masses, including the dwarf-galaxy regime (Lee et al., 2006; Andrews and Martini, 2013, e.g.,) establishing it as the fundamental scaling relation describing the chemical evolution of galaxies. The physical origin of the MZR is generally attributed to the interplay between the production of metals by stars, the accretion of relatively metal-poor gas, and the removal of metal-enriched material through galactic outflows (Larson, 1974; Davé et al., 2012; Maiolino and Mannucci, 2019, e.g.,). The dependence of metallicity on star-formation activity at fixed stellar mass led to the formulation of a more fundamental metallicity relation (FMR), providing a framework in which the evolution of the MZR can be interpreted in terms of the changing gas accretion and star-formation properties of galaxies across cosmic time (Mannucci et al., 2010; Lara-López et al., 2010, e.g.).

The evolution of the MZR with cosmic time was established progressively through observations of star-forming galaxies at high redshift, initially reaching z∼3−4\rm z\sim 3-4 (Erb et al., 2006; Maiolino et al., 2008; Mannucci et al., 2009; Kewley and Ellison, 2008, e.g.). The advent of the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), with its unprecedented sensitivity and wavelength coverage, provided access to the rest-frame optical emission lines over the entire redshift range up to z∼10\rm z\sim 10. Early JWST studies already extended metallicity measurements into the epoch of early galaxy assembly, finding only a mild decrease in the normalization of the MZR from z≈2−3z\approx 2-3 to z>4z>4 (Nakajima et al., 2023; Curti et al., 2024; He et al., 2026; Hsiao et al., 2026; Lam et al., 2026, e.g.). When star-formation rates are also taken into account, several studies find that galaxies at z≳6z\gtrsim 6 are, on average, more metal-poor than predicted by the FMR calibrated on local galaxies, by up to ∼0.5\sim 0.5 dex (Curti et al., 2024, e.g.), possibly indicating dilution by accretion of pristine gas (Heintz et al., 2023, e.g.). However, this offset is not universal,and some high-redshift galaxies lie on the local relations (Pérez-Díaz et al., 2026, e.g.,).

The low-mass and low-metallicity end of the MZR is particularly relevant for understanding the earliest stages of galaxy evolution. Extremely metal-poor galaxies (EMPGs), generally defined as systems with 12+log⁡(O/H)≲7.312+\log({\rm O/H})\lesssim 7.3 are rare in the local Universe. They are thought to result from a combination of inefficient metal retention, metal-poor gas accretion, and bursty star-formation histories (Izotov et al., 1999; Thuan et al., 2005; Lee et al., 2006; Kojima et al., 2020, e.g.). At high redshift, the low-mass end of the MZR is expected to extend towards even lower metallicities than in the local universe. Recent JWST observations of faint galaxies have begun to reveal this population, with measurements reaching estimated metallicities of a few per cent of the solar value and, in some cases, even lower (Vanzella et al., 2023; Vanzella et al., 2026; Maiolino et al., 2024; Maiolino et al., 2026a; Maiolino et al., 2026b; Nakajima et al., 2025; Hsiao et al., 2025; Morishita et al., 2025; Cai et al., 2025; Übler et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026, e.g.). Such low metallicities approach the regime expected for Population III (Pop III) stars, the first generation of stars formed from primordial metal-free gas (see Venditti et al., 2026b, for a recent review). Their metal deficiency can be probed through the absence or extreme weakness of oxygen and other metal emission lines, as expected for nebular gas with primordial composition (Zackrisson et al., 2011; Nakajima and Maiolino, 2022; Trussler et al., 2023; Fujimoto et al., 2025a, e.g.,). A complementary signature is strong He II emission, particularly the He II λ​1640\lambda 1640 recombination line, which arises from the exceptionally hard ionizing spectra predicted for hot, massive metal-free stars (Schaerer, 2002; Schaerer, 2003; Raiter et al., 2010, e.g.,). High He II equivalent widths can therefore provide a sensitive probe of a very hard, potentially primordial ionizing population.

The detection of Pop III stars, one of the most sought-after discoveries in modern astrophysics, faces multiple challenges. Due to the extremely short lifetimes of Pop III stars, their main spectroscopic features fade rapidly, already ∼3\sim 3 Myr after the initial burst, making them statistically rare to observe (Raiter et al., 2010; Zackrisson et al., 2011, e.g.,). This timescale, however, primarily characterizes the rapid fading of the hard ionizing spectrum following an instantaneous burst; more extended star-formation histories can sustain nebular emission for longer periods, while cooling radiation and supernova remnants may provide additional signatures after the most massive Pop III stars have evolved (Schaerer, 2002; Schaerer, 2003; Trussler et al., 2023, e.g.). Theoretical models expect Pop III stars to form in pristine low-mass halos (minihalos and atomic-cooling halos), or in the faint outskirts of more massive halos at high redshift that are still accreting pristine gas (Abel et al., 2002; Yoshida et al., 2003; Xu et al., 2013; Venditti et al., 2023; Venditti et al., 2024; Venditti et al., 2025; Koller et al., 2026; Storck et al., 2026, e.g.), resulting in faint continuum and line emission (Zackrisson et al., 2015). Because of this, many of the currently known Pop III candidates and EMPGs are gravitationally lensed systems, where the observed fluxes are magnified by factors of tens to hundreds, e.g. LAP2 at z=4.2z=4.2 (Vanzella et al., 2026), AMORE6 at z=5.7\rm z=5.7 (Morishita et al., 2025), LAP1 at z=6.6\rm z=6.6 (Vanzella et al., 2023; Nakajima et al., 2025) and Hebe at z=10.6\rm z=10.6 (Maiolino et al., 2024; Maiolino et al., 2026b; Übler et al., 2026). papers.title: The impact of Population III stars on the elemental enrichment of ultra-faint galaxies in the FIRE-3 zoom-in simulations
papers.abstract: The observed stellar mass-metallicity relation for ultra-faint galaxies in the Local Group (LG) is in tension with many theoretical predictions, suggesting the need for modified or additional channels of elemental enrichment at low metallicities. We present a suite of FIRE-3 cosmological baryonic zoom-in simulations of isolated ultra-faint galaxies run to z=0 (maximum baryonic resolution ~ 30 Msun, 0.1 pc) and LMC-mass environments (maximum baryonic resolution ~ 110 Msun, 0.5 pc), with different sub-grid models for Population III stars. Under our Pop. III model(s), star particles forming below a critical metallicity Z_crit represent an initial mass function (IMF) consisting of only massive stars (8-100 Msun). We examine how various stellar feedback processes impact the star formation histories (SFHs) and elemental abundances of ultra-faint galaxies. We find that our Pop. III model variants introduce an effective metallicity floor in ultra-faints at z=0, at Z_floor ~ 1e-5 Zsun to 1e-3 Zsun or [Fe/H]_floor ~ -7 to -5 depending on the model. However, simply including the Pop. III model does not systematically guarantee that all (or even most) ultra-faints enrich up to [Fe/H] ~ -2.5 to fully resolve the tension with the observed mass-metallicity relation, even though we obtain some galaxies at that level. Crucially, the ultra-faints that do enrich in [Fe/H] to this level observed in the LG have extended SFHs after Pop. III enrichment and significant iron enrichment from white dwarf (Type Ia) supernovae, indicating that iron enrichment from Pop. III alone is not sufficient. We also examine the ways in which early-time Pop. III feedback impacts the metallicity distributions and [Mg/Fe] abundance ratios in ultra-faint galaxies, and make a prediction for the stellar mass - [Mg/H] metallicity relation from our simulations.

papers.intro:
The first galaxies formed 200–300 million years after the big bang, hosting the first generations of stars (“Population III”, or Pop. III stars) and seeding the creation of all the luminous structures we observe in the Universe today [22, 75, see reviews by]. The era of Pop. III stars marked an important epoch in the cosmic timeline. They formed out of primordial gas composed almost entirely of hydrogen and helium from Big Bang nucleosynthesis, and their feedback and elemental enrichment commenced the build-up of heavy elements in the first galaxies as well as in the intergalactic medium (IGM), laying the foundation for the rich variety of elemental abundances we observe in stars and galaxies at present day [10, 21, 139, 23, 75].

Given that the conditions to form Pop. III stars likely only dominated at very early cosmic times, it remains extremely challenging to directly observe and measure their properties. As such, the nature of the Pop. III initial mass function (IMF), supernova rates and energetics, and nucleosynthetic yields remain key open questions in astrophysics [75]. Understanding Pop. III IMF, feedback properties, and yields is of vital importance for understanding how subsequent generations of star formation (Pop. II and I) proceeded and how galaxies enriched in metals over time.

papers.title: Polarimetry with the Giant Magellan Telescope: A Scientific Justification & Technical Requirements Document
papers.abstract: The photons we collect from astronomical sources are encoded with information about the physics behind their origin. To fully probe that physics, we must maximize the information we extract from those photons. At optical and near-infrared wavelengths, this is typically done with the use of filters or a disperser to extract flux as a function of color. An often disregarded piece of information that is also carried by those photons is the polarization state. Astronomical polarimetry is capable of revealing details about the source geometry and magnetic fields that are often unresolvable and, therefore, inaccessible by any other means. Polarimetry is typically a photon-starved science because crucial model discriminators are often only revealed when precisions of 0.1% in the degree of polarization are achieved. For spectropolarimetry, this necessitates the collection of over one million photons at each spectral bin, which demands the use of large aperture telescopes for typical objects of interest. The future completion of Giant Segmented Mirror Telescopes (GSMTs) promises the long-awaited light grasp to initiate an unprecedented era of discovery with astronomical polarimetry.

papers.title: Longitudinal-field particle acceleration in channels generated by strong electromagnetic waves in pair plasma
papers.abstract: Relativistically strong electromagnetic waves interacting with pair plasmas appear in astrophysical settings and may become accessible in future laboratory experiments using high-power lasers. Transverse modulations and filamentation can turn extended wavefronts into structures of a finite transverse width. We examine the interaction of such a finite-width wave incident on a cold, uniform pair plasma using a three-dimensional kinetic particle-in-cell simulation. The wave does not penetrate the plasma and instead advances by creating a fully evacuated channel. The wave loses energy at a rate that cannot be explained by plasma clearing alone. We find that the excess losses are caused by strong particle acceleration near the walls of the channel. The acceleration is driven by a longitudinal electric field associated with the transverse wave structure and the geometry of the self-generated channel.

In astrophysics, electron-positron plasmas and strong electromagnetic waves are found around compact objects. In particular, neutron stars produce intense radio waves, including extremely powerful fast radio bursts (FRBs) [11]. In the laboratory, there is strong interest in using high-power lasers to produce relativistic electron-positron pairs and to develop platforms for studying pair-plasma processes relevant to high-energy astrophysics [6].

In particular, neutron stars produce intense radio waves, including extremely powerful fast radio bursts (FRBs) [11]. In the laboratory, there is strong interest in using high-power lasers to produce relativistic electron-positron pairs and to develop platforms for studying pair-plasma processes relevant to high-energy astrophysics [6].

Pair plasmas respond to electromagnetic waves in a qualitatively different way from electron-ion plasmas. The key difference is the mass symmetry of the two species. Electrons and positrons have the same mass, so the wave-driven motion of the two species is symmetric. As a result, the strong charge-separation electric fields familiar from electron-ion plasmas are suppressed. The wave can still drive strong currents and transfer energy and momentum to the plasma, but the absence of an ion-electron mass disparity changes the plasma response.

Plane-wave models demonstrate basic features of this interaction. In particular, recent work has shown that a relativistically strong plane wave incident on a cold pair plasma can be completely reflected even when the plasma is underdense according to the usual linear cutoff criterion [17, 15]. In this regime, the reflected wave deposits momentum into the plasma and drives a moving reflection front. The plane-wave picture is useful because it provides analytic estimates for the front velocity, the compressed plasma density, and the energy transferred to the swept-up particles.

A more realistic picture of wave-plasma interaction may include transverse modulations and filamentation instability of the wave [10, 9]. These effects can create wave structures of a finite transverse width and allow plasma to leave the interaction region transversely. Once the wave has a finite transverse width, the basic questions have to be revisited: how does the wave transfer energy and momentum to the plasma, how is the transferred energy distributed among the plasma particles, and what controls the depletion length of the wave?

For the plasma density and wave strength considered here, the wave does not propagate through the pair plasma and instead advances by creating a fully evacuated channel (while an electron-ion plasma at the same electron density would be relativistically transparent). Section IV shows that channel clearing cannot account for the observed wave depletion. Section V identifies the longitudinal electric field as the dominant source of energy gain for the energetic particles. papers.title: Evolutionary Map of the Universe (EMU): Selection of active galactic nuclei and star-formation emission with machine-learning techniques
papers.abstract: Sources detected by recent large-area radio surveys require robust classification and characterisation. The Evolutionary Map of the Universe (EMU) is a prime example of machine-learning (ML) techniques efficiently enriching existing catalogues with classifications and derived physical properties that would be impractical to obtain from spectroscopy or colour selection alone. We aim to build a labelled sample of sources in the EMU pilot survey (EMU-PS, at 944 MHz, with rms ~ 30 uJy/beam over 270 deg2 in the southern sky) classified as being dominated by active galactic nuclei (AGNs) or non-AGN processes including star-formation. We will then use this sample to examine radio properties and redshift-dependent trends. We applied a pre-trained multi-stage ML pipeline to optical-to-infrared photometry of EMU-PS sources to derive classifications and photometric redshifts, which we used to compute additional radio properties, including luminosities. We increase the known number of AGNs and non-AGNs in the EMU-PS by more than a factor of 15 (recall 96 %) up to z ~ 5, and by nearly a factor of 100 (recall 94 %) for z > 1, respectively. In extrapolating these numbers for the full EMU survey, we expect to recover more than 3.4 million AGN candidates. A non-negligible low-redshift subsample of selected non-AGNs shows radio luminosities in excess of those expected from star formation alone, revealing detachment between photometric and radio classification. Radio-derived properties show expected trends for luminosities and a lack of evolution for in-band (800-1088 MHz) spectral indices. The ML-based pipeline provides a scalable way to produce large catalogues for the ongoing EMU survey and future Square Kilometre Array observations and reveals that multi-wavelength analysis can uncover radio populations and trends often missed by colour cuts or spectroscopy alone.

Thus, it is critical to determine whether the emission is dominated by AGN or star formation (SF) activity. A number of methods have been developed using spectroscopy, photometry, and other indicators to identify AGN emission and constrain their properties.

Using radio information and a redshift estimate, AGN can be selected based on their radio luminosity. If at a given redshift the luminosity of a source is higher than a certain limit, it can be classified as being dominated by AGN emission as SF activity alone is deemed not capable of reaching such levels (Magliocchetti et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2024). An additional selection method is based on radio morphology (Ndung’u et al., 2023). Depending on how concentrated the emission is and on its shape, radio sources can be classified into several types and subclasses (Rudnick, 2021; Barnes et al., 2025). However, based on the source luminosity, its distance, and the characteristics of the observations, morphology is not a reliable observable to assess the nature of a radio detection (Pović et al., 2015; Mingo et al., 2019, e.g.).

Widely used mid-infrared (MIR) criteria include colours from Spitzer (Lacy et al., 2004; Stern et al., 2005; Donley et al., 2012), the Wide-field Infrared Survey Explorer (Wright et al., 2010, WISE;), and the James Webb Space Telescope (Messias et al., 2012; Messias et al., 2014; Kirkpatrick et al., 2017; Kirkpatrick et al., 2023, JWST;). Alternatively, multiple broad- or narrow-band colours can be used to select sources and estimate their photometric redshifts (Wolf et al., 2001b; Wolf et al., 2001a; White et al., 2015, e.g.). However, colour selection suffers from degeneracies and overlaps that place multiple source types in the same parameter-space region (Messias et al., 2014; Daoutis et al., 2023, e.g.).

For spectral-energy-distribution (SED) fitting tools, the inclusion of AGN components in the template bases helps to determine the fraction of radiation produced by their central engine. Besides source classification, these tools can provide further properties of AGNs and their hosts such as stellar masses or SF rates. Example SED fitting tools with AGN components include SED3FIT (Berta et al., 2013), AGNfitter (Calistro Rivera et al., 2016; Martínez-Ramírez et al., 2024), CIGALE (Boquien et al., 2019; Yang et al., 2022), ProSpect (Robotham et al., 2020), Prospector (Johnson et al., 2021), and SMART (Varnava and Efstathiou, 2024). Despite their high reliability, which comes at the expense of long running times and the need for high-quality data, SED fitting methods can still reflect biases in their derived properties (Paulino-Afonso et al., 2022; Farrah et al., 2026).

With spectroscopic information, sources can be separated upon the dominant emission lines’ ionisation source, as quantified by line intensity ratios. For SF, emission is constrained by massive stars exciting their environments, while AGN produce harder X-ray photons (∼keV\sim$\mathrm{k}\mathrm{e}\mathrm{V}$) independent of the host stellar content (Stasińska et al., 2006). Commonly, BPT-VO diagrams (Baldwin, Phillips and Terlevich, 1981; Veilleux and Osterbrock, 1987) are used, which combine the line ratios [O iii]/Hβ\beta, [N ii]/Hα\alpha, [S ii]/Hα\alpha, and [O i]/Hα\alpha to classify sources. Nevertheless, these methods are observationally expensive, with spectra available for only a fraction of sources.

papers.title: Human Mobility Sensing Using Wall-Reflected Beamformed Millimeter-Wave Communication Signals
papers.abstract: Existing millimeter-wave (mmWave) communication beam patterns spatially weight human-scattered signals and shape the received-power signatures induced by human motion. We exploit these beam-shaped signatures for device-free walkingpace and walk-direction classification using a wall-reflected 60.8-GHz link with closely spaced phased arrays and fixed communication beamforming vectors. Human movement alters the interference between wall-reflected and scattered signals, producing power oscillations surrounding a central blockage fade. A beam-dependent interference model provides a physical interpretation of these signatures. Using received-power statistics from a continuous-tone experiment, we extract fade duration for walking-pace classification and pre/post-fade asymmetries for walk-direction classification. Measurements comprise 144 crossings from three participants along perpendicular and diagonal trajectories. Under leave-one-participant-out validation, logistic regression achieves 86.1% binary and 79.2% three-class walking pace accuracy, and 77.1% travel-direction accuracy. The results demonstrate mobility sensing using fixed communication beams without channel estimation, Doppler processing, or dedicated radar hardware

papers.intro:
Millimeter-wave (mmWave) communication systems rely on directional beamforming to overcome propagation loss but remain sensitive to human blockage and scattering [1, 2]. Although these effects are typically viewed as communication impairments, the resulting received-power variations can provide information about human movement and create opportunities for integrated sensing and communications (ISAC) [3, 4]. In phased-array systems, communication beamforming codebooks determine the spatial response of transmitted and received signals [5]. Their main lobes and sidelobes weight propagation components from different directions. As a person moves, human-scattered signals change relative to the dominant path. The selected beam patterns shape their interference and impose characteristic temporal signatures on the received power. These signatures can be opportunistically exploited for mobility sensing without relying on sensing-specific waveform design.

papers.title: CHEX-MATE: Density profile reconstruction in galaxy clusters
papers.abstract: We investigated the reconstruction of the intra-cluster medium radial density profiles in galaxy clusters, focusing on the impact of cluster morphology, dynamical state, and methodological choices, within the framework of the CHEX-MATE project. Using a sample of 109 simulated galaxy clusters analysed along 40 independent lines of sight, we compared azimuthal mean and median techniques for deprojection. We find that azimuthal median-based density profiles recover the true gas density with negligible bias over the radial range $[0.15-1.3] R_{500}$. Mean based profiles are affected by the presence of substructures. While an accurate masking of clumps or substructures can reduce the bias to $< 5\%$, the discrepancy increases substantially in disturbed systems or when substructures remain unresolved. The mean-to-median density ratio statistically traces projected gas inhomogeneities, although intrinsic scatter and projection effects limit its use for individual clusters. The complementary use of mean and median profiles therefore provides the most complete approach for large X-ray cluster samples.

papers.intro:
When considering the thermodynamic properties of the hot, ionised intra-cluster medium (ICM), it is typically assumed that the gravitational potential is spherically symmetric and that the gas has settled into hydrostatic equilibrium, where the density and temperature isosurfaces are aligned with the equipotential surfaces. In reality, both X-ray observations and hydrodynamical simulations of galaxy clusters show that the gas and the underlying dark matter distribution are continuously disturbed by the ongoing formation process. In cluster cores, departures from equilibrium are often associated with cavities and turbulent gas motions driven by active galactic nucleus feedback (e.g. McNamara and Nulsen 2007; Fabian 2012; and Gaspari et al. 2014) or sloshing caused by minor mergers (Markevitch and Vikhlinin 2007). In the outskirts, such departures are mainly linked to ongoing accretion and merger activity (e.g. Kravtsov and Borgani 2012 and Walker et al. 2019). As a result, the ICM is characterised by significant inhomogeneities, in both density and temperature, on a wide range of spatial scales.

Spherical symmetry is commonly assumed when deriving ICM properties from X-ray analyses, as it simplifies the deprojection procedure. It is also expected that geometric biases affecting individual systems average out over large samples because cluster orientations are randomly distributed. The impact of this assumption has been explored in several studies through comparisons of deprojection methods applied to idealised morphologies (e.g. Binney and Strimpel 1978; Piffaretti et al. 2003; and Buote and Humphrey 2012a; Buote and Humphrey 2012b). More recently, the impact of deviations from spherical symmetry on the reconstruction of ICM density profiles has been investigated in work based on cosmological hydrodynamical simulations (Veronesi et al. 2025). These authors show that non-negligible biases in the reconstruction of the mean density profile and its intrinsic scatter occur in the presence of large-scale substructures. These results highlight that projection effects, cluster morphology, and the presence of substructures play a crucial role in shaping the observed density profiles and their statistical properties.

We also explore the connection between density reconstruction techniques and gas inhomogeneities.

papers.title: AGN Host Galaxies in COSMOS-Web: Linking Structural Evolution and Star Formation Quenching up to $z=5$
papers.abstract: The role of active galactic nuclei (AGNs) in the suppression of star formation and structural evolution of galaxies during their transition from star-forming to quiescent systems remains unclear. We analyze 3,955 AGNs selected through five multiwavelength diagnostics at $0<z<5$. Using high-resolution JWST imaging from the COSMOS-Web survey and archival multi-wavelength photometry, we investigate the rest-frame optical size-mass distribution of AGN host galaxies and compare it with those of star-forming galaxies (SFGs) and quiescent galaxies (QGs). We find that the positions of AGN hosts in the size-mass plane depend on both redshift and stellar mass. At $z\gtrsim2$, massive AGN hosts ($M_\star/M_\odot>10^{10.5}$) generally exhibit sizes comparable to those of SFGs despite suppressed star formation. Toward lower redshifts, they increasingly approach the QG size-mass relation, accompanied by declining specific star formation rates (sSFRs) and increasing S\'ersic indices. In contrast, lower-mass AGN hosts remain close to the SFG relation across the redshift range. Overall, AGN hosts exhibit relatively mild size evolution, following $R_e\propto(1+z)^{-0.6}$ over $0<z<4$, shallower than that of typical SFGs and QGs. We further examine the relationship between star formation activity and structural compactness in the $\Delta\log\mathrm{SFR}_{\mathrm{MS}}$-$\Delta\Sigma_e$ plane. At $z<2.2$, AGN hosts predominantly occupy the compact star-forming and quiescent regions, broadly consistent with the compaction-quenching scenario. At $z>2.2$, however, some AGN hosts exhibit suppressed star formation while retaining relatively extended structures. These findings suggest that some AGN hosts may follow alternative evolutionary pathways in which star formation suppression precedes substantial structural compaction.

papers.intro:
The structural properties of galaxies are potential tracers of their assembly history, reflecting the interplay between star formation, gas accretion, mergers, and feedback processes [18, 62]. Observations have established distinct size–mass relations for star-forming galaxies (SFGs) and quiescent galaxies (QGs) across a broad redshift range [67, 72, 15]. At fixed stellar mass, QGs generally exhibit smaller effective radius and higher Sérsic index than SFGs, whereas SFGs tend to have more extended, disk-like structures and higher specific star formation rates (sSFRs; SFR/M⋆\mathrm{SFR}/M_{\star}). These differences suggest that the transition from star-forming to quiescent systems involves changes in galaxy structure as well as star formation activity. Identifying the physical mechanisms that drive this transformation is a central problem in galaxy evolution.

Active galactic nucleus (AGN) feedback has been proposed as a potential mechanism for regulating star formation, particularly in massive galaxies. Radiation, AGN-driven winds, and relativistic jets can transfer energy and momentum to the interstellar and circumgalactic media, potentially removing or preventing the cooling of gas required for star formation [20, 26, 30]. Meanwhile, there is some connection between AGN activity and galaxy structure [40]. For example, studies over 0.2≲z≲30.2\lesssim z\lesssim 3 have found that AGN hosts generally occupy an intermediate region between the size–mass relations of SFGs and QGs [59, 46, 47, 68]. Using COSMOS-Web observations, Zhuang et al. [73] found that X-ray-selected broad-line AGN hosts at 0.35≲z≲3.50.35\lesssim z\lesssim 3.5 broadly follow the size–mass relations of inactive galaxies, with star-forming AGN hosts showing slightly smaller sizes than their non-AGN counterparts. At higher redshifts (4≲z≲74\lesssim z\lesssim 7), Li et al. [48] also found that quasar host galaxies are systematically more compact than SFGs at similar stellar masses.

These findings suggest that AGN activity may be associated with both the regulation of star formation and the structural evolution of galaxies. However, the physical mechanism linking these processes, as well as their causal relationships and relative timing, remain poorly understood. In particular, it remains unclear whether AGN activity precedes, accompanies, or follows the structural transformation and quenching of its host galaxy. Therefore, studying the structural properties and star formation activities of AGN host galaxies is important to investigate the impact of AGN on galaxy evolution.

One possible physical interpretation is provided by the compaction–quenching framework. In this scenario, intense gas inflows—driven by processes such as mergers, counter-rotating streams [53], or violent disk instabilities—lead to dissipative contraction, build a dense central stellar core, and trigger central star formation [74, 65, 5, 29]. Following compaction, rapid central gas depletion, together with reduced gas inflow or replenishment, may initiate inside-out quenching. Observationally, massive compact SFGs at 0.5≲z≲30.5\lesssim z\lesssim 3 have shown an elevated incidence of AGN, and the probability of hosting an AGN increases with compactness among the SFGs [6, 4, 39, 28, 1]. AGN feedback could further promote quenching by removing or heating cold gas and suppressing subsequent cooling. In this framework, central gas inflows, black hole accretion, and galaxy compaction may be closely linked during the transition from SFGs to QGs.

Interpreting AGN host properties is complicated by the fact that different AGN selection techniques trace different emission components, with varying sensitivity to accretion rate and obscuration. Consequently, the resulting samples may exhibit systematically different host galaxy structures. Previous studies have found that radio-selected AGNs predominantly reside in massive, red, bulge-dominated galaxies, whereas mid-infrared selected AGNs are more often associated with bluer, disk-dominated hosts; with X-ray selected AGNs occupying an intermediate range in host color and morphology [32, 27]. X-ray selected AGNs tend to inhabit more massive and redder hosts [17], while IR selected AGNs are preferentially found in less massive galaxies with enhanced star formation [35]. IRAC-selected AGNs preferentially trace luminous, heavily obscured systems [37], whose host galaxies show higher incidences of irregular, asymmetric, and disturbed morphologies than those of X-ray-selected AGNs [24].

The COSMOS-Web survey provides an opportunity to address these questions by combining deep, high-resolution JWST imaging with extensive multiwavelength observations. In this work, we analyze 3,955 AGNs selected through mid-infrared, X-ray, radio-excess selection, as well as broad-line and DESI spectroscopic classifications (T. Kelly et al., in preparation). Using AGN–host image decomposition and spectral energy distribution (SED) fitting, we investigate the rest-frame optical size–mass relations, Sérsic indices, sSFR, and stellar mass surface densities of AGN host galaxies. Our primary objectives are to determine how these properties depend on stellar mass and redshift and to compare host galaxy structures across different AGN selection methods. Finally, we discuss the implications of our results for the relationship between AGN activity, structural compaction, and star formation quenching.
