papers.title: Neuromorphic Camera for Multi-Target Pointing Acquisition and Tracking in Free Space Optical Communication
papers.abstract: Pointing, Acquisition, and Tracking (PAT) in Free-Space Optical Communication (FSOC) applications must achieve both low jitter and a large Field of View (FoV) to support beacon acquisition and multi-target tracking. While conventional frame-based sensors provide the necessary angular coverage, their performance is limited by latency, available frame-rate, and motion blur. This work explores and demonstrates the application of an event-based vision sensor for PAT tasks in FSOC. The system employs a neuromorphic sensor that asynchronously records brightness changes (events) with microsecond-level temporal resolution. The main contribution of this paper is a comparative analysis of event-based tracking algorithms for the simultaneous acquisition and tracking of multiple optical beacons that operate directly on this asynchronous stream. The performance of these strategies is validated on an experimental dataset representing realistic operational conditions for dynamic High-Altitude Platform (HAP) and Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) networks. The analysis compares key metrics, such as tracking accuracy and processing latency, under various signal-to-background conditions.
papers.intro:
Free Space Optical Communication (FSOC) is a key technology for future high capacity wireless networks due to its large available bandwidth, immunity to Radio Frequency (RF) congestion, and license-free operation. However, compared to RF solutions, laser beams are highly directional and therefore require a very precise Pointing, Acquisition, and Tracking (PAT) system. Considering the receiver side, the following properties will enable simplified optical communication between multiple High Altitude Platforms (HAPs) or Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs): (i) large Field of View (FoV), (ii) high sensitivity, (iii) low latency / high tracking bandwidth and (iv) low cost, Size Weight and Power (SWaP).

papers.title: Online Control of the Family-wise Error Rate (FWER) for Multi-stage Platform Trials
papers.abstract: In platform trials, multiple intervention arms can enter or leave the study at any time, which brings the challenge of how to control the type I error rate. Online testing procedures, where a stream of hypotheses are tested over time and the total number of hypotheses is unknown, might be a viable choice for error rate control in platform trials. Interim analyses in a multi-stage design offer the opportunity of early stopping for success or futility in clinical trials by testing the same hypothesis at different time points. Some methods targeting false-discovery rate (FDR) or family-wise error rate (FWER) control for multi-stage platform trials have been proposed. However, a method which controls the FWER and allows new arms to be added at any time without prior information is yet to be established. The ADDIS-Spending (ADaptive DIScarding Alpha-spending) procedure controls the FWER in an online setting. We propose the group sequential ADDIS-Spending algorithm to enable interim analyses for each hypothesis in platform trials. The developed method can update the error level of an individual hypothesis at all (interim) analyses whenever new decisions on other hypotheses are made. We compare alternative approaches with our method in a simulation study. The proposed method yields competitive results in the conducted simulations.

papers.intro:
Platform trials, as well as basket and umbrella trials, have recently attracted increasing interest as innovative and efficient designs due to their efficiency and flexibility. They all fall under the concept of master protocols, in which multiple questions concerning the same disease or biomarker are addressed within a unified study [1]. Platform trials have especially come to the forefront of clinical research and contributed significantly to the development of treatments for COVID-19 [2]. However, this brings new challenges, such as controlling error rates under multiple testing. In this paper, we propose an approach to address the multiplicity issue in platform trials.

They all fall under the concept of master protocols, in which multiple questions concerning the same disease or biomarker are addressed within a unified study [1]. Platform trials have especially come to the forefront of clinical research and contributed significantly to the development of treatments for COVID-19 [2]. However, this brings new challenges, such as controlling error rates under multiple testing. In this paper, we propose an approach to address the multiplicity issue in platform trials.

While standard two-arm randomized clinical trials focus on a single intervention, multi-arm-multi-stage (MAMS) design allows the comparison of multiple treatments with a shared control. Platform trials can be considered as a boosted version of a MAMS trial, where multiple treatments can enter the platform at any time point (not fixed) and share the same control data [3, 4, 5]. This design improves efficiency and flexibility in identifying new treatments, but it also introduces multiplicity problems, since the total number of arms is not known when the trial starts [6]. While many papers have discussed the benefits and challenges of conducting a platform trial, fewer have focused on the problem of controlling the overall type I error rate of the trial. Cui et al. [7] introduce some statistical considerations of error rate metrics for platform trials, where they argue that FDR control does not comply with current regulatory policy. The false discovery rate is the expected proportion of false rejections among all rejected hypotheses. Bai et al. [8] and Nguyen et al. [9] investigated the possible multiplicity issues of shared control for platform trials. The family-wise error rate (FWER) control is usually the standard requirement in a confirmatory clinical trial. It is defined as the probability of making one or more false rejections among all hypotheses.

In a platform trial, typically only a few treatments are included in the beginning and additional arms will be added later. This setting also reflects an online multiple testing procedure, where hypotheses are tested sequentially over time and the total number of hypotheses remains unknown. Many online multiple testing algorithms have been proposed to ensure valid error rate control in an online setting. They adjust the testing boundaries dynamically based on the data collected at the testing time point. Robertson et al. [10] and Robertson and Wason [11] discussed how to control the online error rate for platform trials but without considering multiple stages. It would be worthwhile to establish a method controlling FWER for a multi-stage platform trial. Although the concept is related to MAMS designs, platform trials differ in that the number of arms and their dependence structure usually cannot be predetermined in practice. Therefore, online multiple testing algorithms are considered. Zehetmayer et al. [12] applied the LOND procedure [13] with multi-stage design on platform trials, which is valid for FDR control. The ADDIS-Spending (ADaptive DIScarding Alpha-spending) procedure proposed by Tian and Ramdas [14] is a method for controlling FWER in online testing, which solves the problem of an unknown number of hypotheses in the online testing setting.

An additional challenge is how to incorporate multi-stage designs into the online setting. Interim analyses are typically conducted at each stage of a multi-stage clinical trial to allow early stopping for efficacy or futility. This optimizes resource allocation and minimizes the required number of patients. Greenstreet et al. [15] proposed a method which controls the FWER of multi-stage platform trials in a pre-planned way, where the total number of arms must be pre-specified. The conditional error approach proposed by Burnett et al. [16] allows new arms to be added later without pre-specifying the total number of hypotheses. However, all decisions have to be made at the final testing time point because of the limitations of the closed testing procedure. The statistical power of a later entered arm might also be sub-optimal due to the property of the conditional error approach. In this paper, we propose a method to incorporate interim analyses for each hypothesis based on the ADDIS-Spending procedure. Our approach updates alpha allocations across (interim) analyses whenever formal testing decisions are made, thereby ensuring FWER control in multi-stage online settings. Simulation results show that our method performs well across a variety of scenarios, though performance naturally depends on trial characteristics.

papers.title: Synchronized Hearts, Desynchronized Brains: A Nonlinear Dynamics Perspective for Function and Failure
papers.abstract: Both the heart and the brain are built from electrically excitable cells, yet the emergent dynamics of these organs could not differ more. In the myocardium, a coherent traveling wave of action potentials ensures coordinated contraction; in the cerebral cortex, distributed, irregular spiking underlies efficient information processing and the generation of behavior. Here, we illuminate the principles that underlie the emergence of such distinct nonlinear dynamics using concepts from complex systems. We trace these principles across scales from ion channels and cellular action potential generation, through cellular coupling mechanisms and network architecture, to organ level dynamics and clinical phenotypes. Designed to support either synchronized waves or desynchronized information processing, the heart and the brain can thus be understood as operating on opposite sides of a synchronization phase transition. Crossing this transition implies pathological dynamics in both organs: Loss of synchrony in the heart produces arrhythmia; excess synchrony in the brain leads to epileptic seizures. We discuss how adaptation mechanisms, including plasticity, modulation, remodeling, and learning, maintain the appropriate level of (de)synchronization. Overall, we provide a unified excitable-system perspective, together with an educational notebook, to foster cross-disciplinary insights into cardiac and neural function and pathology.

papers.intro:
Already in the 18th century, Luigi Galvani recognized the importance of electrical activity in physiology [1]. His work paved the way for the later identification of electrically excitable cells as the building blocks underlying both cardiac contraction and neural information processing. In excitable cells, ion fluxes across the membrane maintain a negative resting potential; when this membrane potential is perturbed by a supra-threshold excitation, an electrical signal—a so-called action potential—is generated and propagates to excite or inhibit neighboring cells either electrically (heart) or biochemically (brain). By generating such cascades, impulses and information can propagate through tissue in a coordinated manner.

His work paved the way for the later identification of electrically excitable cells as the building blocks underlying both cardiac contraction and neural information processing. In excitable cells, ion fluxes across the membrane maintain a negative resting potential; when this membrane potential is perturbed by a supra-threshold excitation, an electrical signal—a so-called action potential—is generated and propagates to excite or inhibit neighboring cells either electrically (heart) or biochemically (brain). By generating such cascades, impulses and information can propagate through tissue in a coordinated manner.

Mathematically, cardiac and neuronal cells can be represented as excitable units that give rise to diverse emergent collective phenomena, such as coherent traveling waves that characterize cardiac tissue or distributed, ongoing activity that characterizes the brain. Generating the correct emergent activity is key to healthy organ function. However, healthy function can be compromised by changes at the cellular or even subcellular level that can result in macroscopic organ-level pathologies, such as disruption of a coherent traveling wave causing arrhythmia [2, 3, 4] or excessive excitation causing epilepsy [5]. Such pathologies can be identified at the organ-level by non‑invasive recordings of collective activity: electrocardiograms (ECG) for the heart [6] and electroencephalograms (EEG) for the brain [7, 8]. Conversely, the microscopic defects underlying these conditions can be detected only with sophisticated but invasive microelectrodes [9] or optical imaging approaches [10]. To overcome this experimental limitation and bridge microscopic mechanisms and macroscopic dysfunction, theoretical and computational approaches grounded in nonlinear dynamics are required. These approaches can bridge the scales, from micro-level modeling of membranes and cells, based on the classic membrane theories of Bernstein [11] and Hodgkin–Huxley [12] (see Fig Methods) to macro-level modeling of network topology and defects. Thereby, a thorough theoretical understanding can shed light on putative cellular origins of organ‑scale healthy and pathological collective dynamics.

From a nonlinear dynamics viewpoint, cardiac function can be described as the coherent propagation of electromechanical waves through sheets of coupled cardiomyocytes with regular single-unit dynamics (sinus rhythm). In a healthy heart, this wave is initiated regularly at the sinoatrial node, distributed by a specialized fiber network, and travels coherently across the cardiac tissue (myocardium) to produce the collective activity that underlies the mature ECG pattern and the coordinated contraction of the heart. In this context, we define cardiac activity as synchronized in the sense that the excitation wavefront propagates coherently along the physiologically intended conduction path, maintaining spatial integrity and phase alignment, and thus ensuring coordinated contraction. This definition quantifies deviations from healthy propagation: In cardiac arrhythmias, a broken, deformed, or reentrant wavefront deviates from this path and thus constitutes desynchronized, pathological activity. This can happen when the traveling wavefront is altered, either intermittently or persistently, by structural and electrophysiological defects. These defects range from cellular alterations to tissue‑level heterogeneities and can distort propagation, giving rise to a rich and challenging repertoire of spatiotemporal patterns [13, 14, 15, 16, 17] (see Fig. 3). Understanding how transitions from the regular sinus rhythm to these dysfunctional states emerge, informs the design of therapeutic strategies, including (i) low‑energy fibrillation control [18, 19, 20, 21], (ii) cardiac‑resynchronization therapy [22, 23], (iii) sub‑threshold cardiac‑contractility modulation [24, 25], (iv) antifibrotic interventions to improve heart function [26, 27], or (v) cardiomyocyte supplementation [28, 29]. These approaches aim at restoring the coordinated transmission of electrical signals necessary for efficient blood pumping based on the interpretation of pathological cardiac activity as a loss of synchronization in an excitable medium.

These approaches aim at restoring the coordinated transmission of electrical signals necessary for efficient blood pumping based on the interpretation of pathological cardiac activity as a loss of synchronization in an excitable medium.

In contrast, brain function relies on a complex network of excitatory and inhibitory neurons that processes inputs in parallel streams, employing a myriad of mesoscopic dynamical states. Such a variety of states originates from distributed activity with irregular single-unit dynamics, which is believed to support efficient encoding and processing of complex sensory inputs [30, 31, 32]. The resulting encoding is efficient in an information-theoretic sense because low correlations between units result in low redundancy and thereby higher information content of each pattern [33, 34]. We thus define neural activity as asynchronous in the sense that neural firing shows low redundancy, which increases the accessible coding space to store and process many different patterns [33, 35, 36]. Despite single-neuron statistics being predominantly asynchronous, coordination across brain areas emerges in the form of correlated fluctuations [37, 38, 35, 39] and transient wave-like patterns across spatial and temporal scales [40, 41, 42], which may reflect structured external inputs [43, 44] or specific physiological states such as REM sleep or attentive wakefulness [45, 46]. As a consequence, there is a tradeoff between transient correlations for reliable communication and minimizing correlations for efficient representation [44]. One hypothesis for how the brain achieves this tradeoff is that neural networks operate in the vicinity of a phase transition [47, 48, 49, 50]. Such phase transitions can give rise to emergent pairwise correlations and can also explain the waxing‑and‑waning of oscillations [51, 52, 53, 54, 55, 44]. However, being positioned close to a phase transition carries the risk of crossing that transition, which implies excessive synchrony and potentially produces pathological, epileptic states [56, 57, 58, 59, 60]. Interestingly, the role of synchronization is thus exactly opposite for the brain and the heart: the brain loses its function when synchrony becomes excessive, whereas the heart fails when the synchronization breaks down.

papers.title: PIMROP: A Feasibility Study of Return-Oriented Programming on Commercial Processing-in-Memory Architectures
papers.abstract: Processing-in-Memory places small programmable cores on the memory device, where they execute beside the DRAM banks and beyond the control-flow defenses that protect host programs. The security of this in-memory code is an attack surface that remains largely unstudied. We present PIMROP, to our knowledge the first demonstrated code-reuse attack on a commercial Processing in-Memory ISA. We show that return-oriented programming is feasible on a real, commercially shipped PIM instruction set, the UPMEM DPU, whose DRAM Processing Units run C compiled by a dedicated LLVM toolchain. We build Galileo-for-DPU, a gadget scanner adapted to the DPU's fixed-width, 8-byte-aligned RISC encoding, and run it entirely on the UPMEM functional simulator in a reproducible Docker and VM environment. We find the runtime library that every kernel links already yields 517 non-trivial gadgets covering all five canonical ROP primitive classes, and all 13 PrIM benchmarks we scanned carry gadgets as well. We then demonstrate two verified end-to-end attacks, each reproducible on 10 of 10 runs. In the first, a stack buffer overflow in a DPU kernel overwrites the saved return address and diverts control into a routine that copies a secret into host-readable memory. In the second, we leak the same secret using a chain of reused gadgets alone, without diverting control into any such routine. We further show that two standard defenses--stack canaries and _FORTIFY_SOURCE-style bounds-check fortification--fail on the DPU in ways specific to the platform (misplaced canary, silently inactive wrapper), and we verify a bounds-checked DMA that stops the attack on 10 of 10 runs with no effect on benign requests. To enable further research on PIM security, we open-source Galileo-for-DPU and our testing harness at https://github.com/wtegge2/ROP-in-PIM.

papers.intro:
For decades the cost of moving data between memory and the processor has grown faster than the cost of computing on it. For today’s memory-bound workloads, data movement dominates both time and energy [1]. Processing-in-Memory (PIM) attacks this problem directly by placing computation in or near the memory devices [1, 2, 3, 4]. The UPMEM DPU is the first commercially available, general-purpose PIM product [5], pairing each DRAM chip with programmable in-order cores (DRAM Processing Units) that run ordinary C compiled by a dedicated LLVM toolchain. A programmable processor now lives inside the memory module and with it, a new and largely unexamined attack surface.

None of them says anything about code executing on the DPU which runs on a different processor, with a different ISA, on the far side of the memory bus. PIM-security research so far has examined side and covert channels [6], RowHammer-style bit flips [7], and confidentiality of data offloaded to untrusted memory [8], and a recent threat-landscape survey [9] explicitly identifies code-reuse against programmable NDP cores as an open concern, but the integrity of control flow on the in-memory processor itself remains undemonstrated.

papers.title: FireOPS: A Human-Centric Emergency Operations Platform
papers.abstract: Volunteer fire brigades rely on fragmented alerting channels and radio plus paper for situational awareness, hindering a shared common operational picture (COP). FireOPS integrates smartphone alerting, navigation, a live geospatial COP, a district resource-load overview and contextual manuals into a human-centric decision-support surface for commanders and responders, running on an edge + cloud architecture whose dual-channel provides source-level redundancy against failure of either the radio or the provincial server feed; delivery to smartphones still depends on the cloud core and mobile networks. This lessons-learned report presents the design rationale, positions FireOPS within emergency-response information systems research, and reports operational findings from a primary log extract of a major regional flood in 2024 and from the 2025 public app release. A feature-matrix comparison with DIVERA 24/7, blaulichtSMS and the LifeRescue prototype identifies COP, decision support and dual-ingestion redundancy as the main differentiators, and we map the operational gaps observed during the flood to concrete engineering responses, deployed or in active development.

papers.intro:
Time-critical emergency response relies on personnel and commanders building and maintaining an accurate model of the evolving situation. In Endsley’s three-stage theory of situation awareness—perception, comprehension and projection—anticipating future states is crucial for high-quality decision-making [8]. In multi-agency operations, information must cross organisational boundaries to form a common operational picture (COP), and crisis-management research shows that COPs support collective sense-making when they structure problems and let responders negotiate meaning rather than simply displaying more data [30]. Recent work on human-centred crisis informatics identifies mobile applications, bidirectional warnings and responder-side dashboards as priority directions [13].

Volunteer fire brigades are staffed not by career professionals but by unpaid community members responding to alarms on an on-call basis, a distinctive context for information integration: members may be off-site when an alarm arrives, have limited training on specialised IT systems, and depend on community resources. Fragmentation across dispatch apps, paper maps, radio communications and separate reference manuals introduces delays and increases cognitive load. The FireOPS project arose from these challenges in the Upper Austrian district of Perg. Its central objective was to give incident commanders and responders a shared, district-wide COP unifying, in a single platform, a live map of incidents, dispatched units, vehicles, hydrants and weather; a district-load overview that surfaces municipal hotspots during peak events; mobile alerting with explicit “coming / not coming” acknowledgment; one-click navigation; and context-specific manuals and rescue cards. Together these layers constitute an information-integration problem at the intersection of three topic areas: IoT and edge computing (per-brigade paging receivers, on-premise brokers, brigade-information displays); web services and API integration (REST Core API, operational-management platform synchronisation, mobile push notifications, and a redundant feed from Austria’s fire-service Warn- und Alarmsystem (WAS) radio alerting network [6]); and large language models for web intelligence (an assistant with retrieval-augmented generation over a fire-service corpus). Heterogeneous sources must be fused into a single human-centric decision-support surface usable by volunteer practitioners under real-time load.

papers.title: Today's Work, Tomorrow's Workforce: Incentivizing Learning in AI-Assisted Work
papers.abstract: At work, people develop skills through experience: novices acquire skills by completing tasks, while experts retain theirs through continued practice. AI assistance changes this process by offering workers a choice between solving tasks independently and accepting the AI's answers. While relying on AI saves immediate effort, it can also displace the practice needed to acquire and retain skills, including those required to oversee the AI. We extend an existing accept-or-solve model to a sequence of tasks in which workers' skills evolve through independent practice and reliance on AI. We compare myopic workers, who maximize immediate utility, with strategic workers, who also value their future skills. We show that novices can become trapped at low skill levels, while experts may lose skill, even as AI-assisted outcome accuracy remains high. Strategic workers, by contrast, may choose to solve independently even when AI is more accurate, recognizing the future value of acquiring and retaining their skills. We then study incentives that reward correct independent work and characterize the payments needed to encourage skill acquisition and retention. We show that independent work can become self-sustaining once workers acquire sufficient skill, eliminating the need for continued incentives. Counterintuitively, supporting a higher skill target can sometimes reduce long-run incentive costs, either by enabling self-sustaining independent work or by lowering the payments needed to maintain proficiency. Our findings thereby shift the focus from whether workers should rely on AI on individual tasks to how organizations can sustain human expertise over time, and which skills are worth investing in.

papers.intro:
Astronauts on a six-month mission aboard the International Space Station need little physical strength for their work, but without gravity and physical effort, muscles and bones deteriorate. Since no work in space requires this physical strength, this loss often goes unnoticed until astronauts return to Earth. Once this loss becomes evident, space agencies began scheduling about two and a half hours of exercise into every mission day. This exercise retains the capacity that astronauts need once gravity returns. What gravity and physical effort are for an astronaut’s body is cognitive effort for a worker’s skills.

Traditionally, work has trained the people who perform it: novices acquire skill by solving tasks, and experts retain their skill through regular use [12, 42, 26]. AI loosens this link as workers can now accept an AI’s answer instead of solving a task themselves [20], often finishing faster and with higher quality [24]. The effort that AI saves, however, is the very effort through which workers learn. For example, novices who relied on AI while learning a new programming library acquired less skill [53], and endoscopists who had worked with AI detected fewer adenomas once the AI was withdrawn [18]. Work performed with AI assistance therefore risks workers not acquiring or retaining skill.

Even as AI capabilities grow, acquiring and retaining skill remains important because skills build on each other and are therefore needed to acquire other skills [29]. For example, programmers may use AI for routine coding yet still need coding skill to acquire additional skills that enable them to debug failures and make architectural judgments. This matters most early in a career, when novices perform routine tasks to build the foundation for becoming an expert [14, 35]. However, the importance of skills also extends to a longer horizon, where it is needed to oversee the AI itself, i.e., to detect its errors and take over when it fails [7, 39]. For high-risk systems, oversight is even legally mandatory through the EU AI Act [27].

Research on human–AI decision-making has evaluated workers’ choice to solve alone or use an AI by appropriate reliance: a worker should accept the AI’s answer when it is more likely to be correct and solve the task independently otherwise [43, 52]. This accept-or-solve choice is represented in formal models by maximizing the utility of a worker on a single task [8, 34]. In particular, Holstein et al. [34] show that independent effort can make accepting the AI’s answer rational even when the worker is more skilled and therefore more likely to answer correctly. With skill held fixed, however, these models miss two dynamics: A novice acquires skill by solving tasks that the AI would answer more accurately, which appropriate reliance scores as underreliance. Similarly, an expert who accepts the AI’s answer to save effort gradually loses their advantage over the AI. Dynamic models relax the assumption of fixed skill: Huang and Vishnoi [37] show that reliance driven by observed performance can lock people into low skill. Closest to our work, Aouad et al. [4] model dynamic skill and show that AI assistance can make workers less productive by saving the effort that leads to skill acquisition. Their workers, however, choose how much effort to exert rather than whether to accept the AI’s answer, so it remains open how the choice that reliance research evaluates changes once skill evolves. Once skill evolves, the answer depends on whether workers weigh only the current task or also how today’s choice shapes the skill they bring to future tasks. This motivates our first research question: RQ1: When do workers solve tasks independently instead of accepting an AI’s answer, depending on their skill, the AI’s accuracy, and their strategic behavior?

Practice pays off for a worker only if the skill gained earns more on future tasks than the effort and accuracy given up today. To answer these questions, we extend the accept-or-solve model of Bansal et al. [8] and Holstein et al. [34] from a single task to a sequence of tasks. We adopt the skill model of Aouad et al. [4], in which skill improves through independent work and decays at a constant rate, but replace their choice of how much effort to exert with the accept-or-solve choice. A myopic worker weighs only the effort and accuracy of the current task, whereas a strategic worker also weighs today’s effort against future skill. We then examine how incentives for correct independent answers can encourage workers to acquire and retain skill. Our work makes three contributions: • Dynamic accept-or-solve model. We extend the accept-or-solve framework with skill acquisition and decay and characterize how the value of future skill shapes reliance decisions. Strategic workers may solve independently even when the AI is more accurate, because doing so builds or preserves their skill. • Low-skill trap and expert deskilling. We identify conditions under which reliance on AI leads to stagnating or eroding skill without a visible decline in task performance. Novices remain trapped at low skill levels, and experts lose proficiency while output accuracy stays at the AI’s level. • Learning incentives. We derive the minimum payment for correct independent answers that makes myopic workers acquire and retain skill. papers.title: Colloidal 2D WS2 nanosheets exhibiting high-purity single photon emission
papers.abstract: The search for quantum emitters, delivering single photons "on demand" at cryogenic and elevated temperatures for photonic technologies is ever progressing. For example, micrometer-sized WS2 monolayers exhibit single photon emission by elaborated local defect or strain engineering. Here, we show that wet-chemically synthesised monolayered two-dimensional (2D) WS2 nano sheets (NSs) with lateral sizes of 14 (+/- 6 nm) readily emit single photons from exciton recombination without the need for substrate-induced patterning, strain/defect engineering or spectral filtering. Single particle spectroscopy of 70 individual NSs shows photoluminescence from excitons (2.02 eV), trios (1.94 eV) and defect-localized states (1.85 eV) with fast emission (t1<0.2 ns, t2=3.2 ns), allowing highly frequent excitation cycles. Pulsed at 80 MHz, colloidal WS2 NSs exhibit limited spectral diffusion, no blinking and distinct photon antibunching (g2(0)=0.07 at 5 K), thereby tackling challenges of established colloidal quantum dot systems (blinking, longer emission cycles), while retaining high single photon purity as key quality of deterministic quantum emitters.

papers.title: SHARP: A spectrograph proposal to fully exploit ELT capabilities
papers.abstract: The Extremely Large Telescopes (ELTs), with their large apertures and cutting-edge Multi-Conjugate Adaptive Optics (MCAO) systems, promise to deliver data sharper and deeper than even the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) across large fields. SHARP is a concept study for a near-IR (0.95--2.45 $\mu$m) spectrograph specifically designed to fully exploit the collecting area and angular resolution capabilities of the upcoming ESO's ELT. The instrument concept is driven by the goal of tackling the most important questions in astrophysics and cosmology, bridging the gap between the local and distant Universe. This requires versatility to accommodate diverse observational needs. SHARP (http://sharp.brera.inaf.it) is composed of two main units: NEXUS, a Multi-Object Spectrograph (MOS) optimized for detecting the faintest sources, and VESPER, a multi-object Integral Field Unit (multi-IFU) designed for brighter ones. This presentation provides an overview of the scientific design drivers, the solutions developed to meet them, and the resulting optical design that achieves the required performance.

papers.intro:
The upcoming generation of ground-based Extremely Large Telescopes (ELTs) will peer into the Universe with unparalleled clarity, delivering sharper and deeper data than the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) [18, JWST, Ref.]. These capabilities are fundamentally due to their large apertures, providing a massive photon collecting area, coupled with advanced multi-conjugate adaptive optics (MCAO) systems designed to uniformly correct large fields for atmospheric turbulence. The ELTs will achieve data significantly sharper than JWST, up to four times in the case of the Giant Magellan Telescope [26, 6, GMT, Ref.] (∼\sim25 m diameter), and six times sharper with the ESO’s Extremely Large Telescope [20, 51, ELT,] Specifically, ESO’s ELT is positioned to set new standards in astronomical observations, thanks to its 39m diameter primary mirror and its advanced MCAO system, MORFEO [9, 10, Ref.]. MORFEO corrects an area with a diameter of 160 arcsec, an AO system that allows supported instruments to explore the Universe with unmatched depth and clarity over large scales.

papers.title: A Construction Framework for Three-Dimensional Topological Magnetic Textures
papers.abstract:
Three-dimensional magnetic systems offer diverse possibilities for constructing complex topological textures from simpler magnetic configurations. Here, we present different routes for constructing complex three-dimensional magnetic textures from simpler parent configurations and discuss their impact on the topology of the resulting structures. We identify four construction principles: (i) adding transverse modulations, (ii) adding structures, (iii) entangling textures (e.g. braiding, or twisting), and (iv) introducing singularities.
  Using the skyrmion tube as an explicit parent configuration, we show how these principles give rise to several known three-dimensional magnetic textures. We then apply the same principles to predict novel textures derived from a meron tube, which are confirmed by micromagnetic simulations to be metastable in chiral magnets. Our results establish general principles for the systematic construction and discovery of complex three-dimensional magnetic textures.

Topological magnetic textures emerge from the interplay of competing magnetic interactions. In two dimensions, this interplay gives rise to well-established structures such as skyrmions [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6] and merons [7, 8, 9]. papers.title: A general technique for explicit quantile representations
papers.abstract: This work proves existence of contours independent of probability level for exact quantile integrals of strictly positive real-analytic densities. Explicit constructions cover five broad distribution families and yield a finite-interval representation of Black-Scholes implied volatility using forward functions.

Riemann boundary-value methods likewise yield explicit expressions for roots and inverse functions (Burniston and Siewert, 1973; Pickett and Millev, 2002). Other approaches characterize quantiles through differential equations and power series (Steinbrecher and Shaw, 2008), construct Taylor approximations from density derivatives (Yu and Zelterman, 2017), or invert saddlepoint approximations to obtain approximate quantiles (Arevalillo, 2003). papers.title: Ermakov--Based embeddings as a parameter-free layer for physics-informed neural networks
papers.abstract: Evolution equations with time-dependent coefficients force a neural solver to spend capacity on a scale that the equation already determines. We show that a single classical object, the Ermakov-Pinney scale function $\rho$, can be written into the input layer of a physics-informed neural network as a parameter-free embedding. One construction covers three problem families through the two signs of the Pinney constant $c$: linear diffusion ($c=-1$, $\omega\equiv0$), diffusion in a time-dependent confining trap ($c=-1$, $\omega\neq0$), and the quantum oscillator with time-dependent frequency ($c=+1$). An exact moment identity gives $\rho$ in closed form from the initial data alone, so no auxiliary network or knowledge of the solution is needed. Our central finding is comparative: each family requires a different component of the construction and has a different honest control. In family I, the diffusive-time reparametrisation alone reproduces most of the gain, so that family is a poor test of the idea and shows why an ablation is mandatory. In family II no time reparametrisation exists, the control degrades accuracy, and the amplitude prefactor becomes essential (40.8x). In family III the adiabatic approximation also fails, and the quadratic phase factor is what matters (5.7x). The method does not help when the reduced solution does not converge to a fixed point: its extrapolation advantage then disappears. The reduction itself is the classical scaling-variable change of the self-similar-asymptotics literature; what is new is the moment identity that makes it architectural for time-dependent coefficients, and the comparative anatomy above.

papers.title: Shapiro spikes in driven quantum fluids
papers.abstract: Periodic driving of a Josephson junction produces resonant transport signatures known as Shapiro spikes, conventionally described by effective circuit models. Here, we demonstrate Shapiro spikes in a neutral quantum fluid using simulations of a potential-biased atomic Josephson junction. The dc-current resonances follow the expected Bessel-function scaling, including the suppression and revival of individual resonances with increasing modulation strength. We uncover their microscopic mechanism by showing that the phase-winding frequency develops finite plateaus at integer multiples of the drive frequency. These phase-locked states are sustained by quantized-vortex nucleation and the associated $2\pi$ phase slips. Remarkably, within a locking plateau, the dc current and density transfer can reverse direction while the phase-winding frequency remains locked to the drive, giving rise to negative-mobility transport. Our results establish a microscopic link between vortex-mediated phase slips, Shapiro resonances, and anomalous transport in a neutral quantum fluid, revealing how quantized vortices convert resonant transport into phase-locked dynamics with negative mobility.

papers.title: The PAU Survey: Self-supervised image denoising for flux-preserving photometry
papers.abstract: Context. Deep photometric surveys increasingly rely on low signal-to-noise imaging, where noise affects source detection, flux measurements, photometric redshifts, and sample selection. Self-supervised denoising methods are attractive because they do not require ground-truth images, but applying them to quantitative photometry requires controlling the flux biases they may introduce. Aims. We evaluate and improve Noise2Void (N2V) for denoising real astronomical images, focusing on preserving fluxes, reducing photometric scatter, and retaining the main source features across a wide magnitude range. Methods. We use real observations from the Physics of the Accelerating Universe Survey (PAUS) together with PAUS-like simulated images. We show that standard N2V systematically underestimates galaxy fluxes, especially for faint galaxies. To mitigate this bias, we add a bounded-output layer that limits large negative outputs, and fine-tune the model with low-rank adaptation (LoRA) and two flux-aware loss terms that preserve the flux scale and improve repeated-exposure flux consistency. Results. For PAUS galaxies with 22 <= i_AB < 23 in the NB645 band, the standard N2V flux-ratio distribution peaks far below unity, while the bounded-output model restores it close to the original PAUS flux scale. The flux-aware LoRA fine-tuning reduces the width of the repeated-exposure flux-difference distribution to sigma_68 = 0.529 in NB645, an effective 47% reduction in random flux scatter relative to the original PAUS uncertainty scale, while keeping the median flux ratio close to unity. Conclusions. Denoising methods for astronomical surveys must be evaluated with photometric diagnostics, not image-quality metrics alone. With flux-aware modifications, self-supervised denoising can be adapted to low-SNR survey images while preserving the flux information needed for quantitative analysis.

papers.intro:
Noise is a major source of uncertainty in deep astronomical imaging. It arises from photon-counting statistics, detector readout noise (Newberry, 1991), and sky-background variations (Howell, 2000; Starck and Murtagh, 2007), degrading both data quality and downstream measurements. In particular, these noise sources can obscure faint extended features of low-surface-brightness galaxies, hinder source separation in crowded stellar fields, and introduce biases or additional uncertainties into morphological and photometric measurements. These effects propagate into a wide range of quantitative astronomical analyses, including weak gravitational lensing (Mandelbaum, 2018; Kaiser, 1992; Refregier, 2003), galaxy-clustering measurements (Alam et al., 2021), supernova light-curve analysis (Scolnic et al., 2018), cosmological-parameter inference (Chen et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2025; Hong et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2021), and photometric-redshift estimation (Bolzonella et al., 2000). Consequently, image-restoration methods can be valuable components of imaging-survey data-processing pipelines, but their scientific use requires that they preserve photometric information and be validated with diagnostics tied to the intended measurements (Robertson et al., 2019).

Image denoising is an ill-posed problem: suppressing noise requires assumptions about the underlying signal, and inappropriate assumptions can blur compact sources, erase faint emission, or bias flux measurements. These assumptions can be viewed as image priors, and their design has shaped the development of denoising methods (see Elad et al. 2023 for a review). Classical methods, such as linear filtering (Gonzalez, 2009) and wavelet-based approaches (Starck et al., 2015), impose explicit image priors, such as smoothness or sparsity, together with assumptions about the noise properties. In astronomy, however, high-precision measurements often avoids full image restoration because restoration priors can bias the quantities of interest. Instead, many analyses use task-specific inference methods, such as model-fitting photometry (Peng et al., 2002; Bertin and Arnouts, 1996), which estimate fluxes and source parameters directly from noisy data.

Rather than imposing explicit priors, deep learning networks can learn image priors directly from training data (LeCun et al., 2015). Many high-performing neural denoisers are trained in a supervised manner, using paired noisy or degraded inputs and clean reference images, often generated synthetically (Mohan et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2023). Applying these methods to astronomical imaging is challenging for two main reasons. First, noiseless ground-truth images are generally unavailable for real astronomical observations. Second, many neural denoisers are trained or pre-trained on natural-image datasets (Meng et al., 2020; Sriram et al., 2020), whose image statistics differ markedly from those of astronomical images. Astronomical sources often occupy only a small fraction of an image and can be faint relative to structured sky backgrounds, while the noise is shaped by the detector, observing conditions, and data-reduction pipeline (Chen et al., 2021).

These limitations motivate self-supervised denoising strategies that are trained directly on the target observations, rather than on external clean reference images. A family of self-supervised approaches exploits statistical assumptions about the noise to train models from noisy data alone (Schawinski et al., 2017; Lehtinen et al., 2018; Batson and Royer, 2019). This makes them particularly attractive for astronomical surveys, where paired noisy–clean images are generally unavailable. Although clean reference images are lacking, repeated observations, simulations, and survey-specific noise estimates can be used to test the assumptions of these methods and to validate their impact on measured fluxes.

Although clean reference images are lacking, repeated observations, simulations, and survey-specific noise estimates can be used to test the assumptions of these methods and to validate their impact on measured fluxes.

In this work, we apply Noise2Void (N2V; Krull et al. 2019) to narrow-band images from the Physics of the Accelerating Universe Survey (PAUS). N2V is a self-supervised denoising method that can be trained directly on noisy images. We show that visually cleaner denoised images can yield biased photometry: standard N2V systematically underestimate the fluxes of faint galaxies, both in simulations and in PAUS observations. In the low-SNR regime, local noise fluctuations can be comparable to the galaxy signal, making flux preservation particularly challenging. This bias reflects a mismatch between the standard N2V objective, which optimised pixel-level reconstruction, and the photometric quantities needed for science. We address this by modifying the network architecture with a bounded-output layer and by fine-tuning the model with flux-aware loss terms.

Section 3 presents the denoising methods, including the classical baselines, standard N2V, Probabilistic Noise2Void (PN2V; Krull et al. 2020) and the proposed flux-aware modifications. In Sect. 4, we test the models on simulated data and PAUS observations, focusing on image quality, flux preservation, and repeated-exposure flux consistency. Besides, we also do tests with the denoised flux. Finally, Sect. 5 discusses the implications of the results and summarises the conclusions.

papers.title: Quantitative infrared absorption imaging of vapor concentration fields during evaporation
papers.abstract: Quantitative full-field measurements of vapor concentration remain challenging near receding liquid-gas interfaces. We develop and quantitatively assess an infrared absorption imaging method for measuring vapor mole-fraction fields during evaporation. Broadband mid-infrared attenuation is converted into mole fraction using a spectrally weighted absorption coefficient. A vertical Hele-Shaw cell provides a controlled, nearly one-dimensional evaporation benchmark, with calibrated object-plane sampling of $30.5\,\mu\mathrm{m/pixel}$. Small transverse concentration variations in the central measurement region justify reducing the two-dimensional fields to axial profiles. Five profiles spanning different retained gas-phase interval lengths and three hydrocarbon liquids are compared with Stefan predictions using only measured interval lengths and endpoint concentrations, without fitting interior concentration data. At the higher vapor loading of n-pentane, the measurements resolve the nonlinear Stefan concentration profile and distinguish it from the linear diffusion limit. At the lower vapor loadings of n-hexane and n-heptane, the profiles progressively approach that dilute limit. The profiles agree with Stefan predictions, with normalized root-mean-square deviations of 0.0055-0.0185, and collapse onto the predicted identity relation after the logarithmic Stefan transformation. These results demonstrate quantitative recovery of both the magnitude and spatial structure of vapor concentration fields under the tested conditions. The method provides a full-field, tracer-free diagnostic for investigating evaporating flows in geometries and regimes where analytical concentration fields are unavailable.

Spatially resolved measurements of this concentration field are therefore valuable for testing transport models and for studying more complex evaporating flows.

Most experimental studies of evaporation infer the mass-transfer rate from liquid-side quantities, such as the temporal variation of droplet volume, interface position, or total sample mass [40, 31]. These measurements provide an integral evaporation rate but contain limited information about the structure of the gas-phase concentration boundary layer. Non-intrusive optical diagnostics have enabled spatially resolved measurements in gas flows that are difficult to access using mechanical probes, including measurements of velocity fields [1, 6, 26] and scalar quantities [3, 27]. For quantitative measurements of vapor concentration specifically, several optical approaches have been applied. Schlieren and interferometric techniques can visualize refractive-index variations associated with vapor concentration gradients [8], however, the refractive-index signal is not intrinsically species-selective, and quantitative interpretation may be further complicated by simultaneous temperature variations and by the indirect relation between the measured optical signal and species concentration. Laser-induced fluorescence and related tracer-based methods provide improved spatial resolution, but require suitable fluorescent species or tracers and may be affected by quenching, photophysics, and calibration uncertainties [24, 9]. Laser absorption spectroscopy, in contrast, provides an intrinsically species-selective and quantitative relation between optical attenuation and molecular concentration and has been widely used for gas-phase species measurements [12, 37, 42, 35]. However, conventional absorption measurements are commonly implemented along individual lines of sight or at discrete measurement locations, rather than as instantaneous two-dimensional concentration fields. Recent studies have extended laser absorption spectroscopy to spatially resolved measurements through beam scanning and tomographic reconstruction or rapid spatial sampling [5, 4, 41, 17]. These approaches enable quantitative vapor-field measurements, but remain inherently sequential, with spatial resolution limited by beam size and scan spacing and temporal resolution by the time required to scan the measurement domain.

Infrared absorption imaging provides a direct route to combine the species selectivity and quantitative nature of absorption spectroscopy with spatially resolved imaging. In contrast to scanning-based absorption measurements, the entire field of view is recorded simultaneously on an imaging detector, enabling instantaneous two-dimensional measurements without mechanical beam scanning. Camera-based absorption imaging in the ultraviolet and visible spectral ranges has enabled quantitative imaging of ions, atoms, and their compounds through electronic transitions [28, 29, 36]. In the mid-wave infrared, molecular rovibrational transitions have been exploited to image hydrocarbons, CO, CO2, and temperature, progressing from two-dimensional measurements to time-resolved and volumetric reconstructions [38, 25, 39]. When the absorption band of the target species lies within the spectral response of the imaging system, the transmitted intensity can be converted through the Beer–Lambert relation into a spatial map of absorbance and, after calibration, species concentration. The technique is therefore inherently tracer-free, species-selective, and quantitative, while retaining the parallel acquisition capability of an imaging system. These features are particularly attractive for evaporating flows, for which introducing fluorescent tracers into the vapor phase may be difficult and steep concentration variations can occur close to the liquid–gas interface.

When an evaporating species diffuses through a stagnant carrier gas, the condition of zero carrier-gas molar flux produces a nonlinear vapor-concentration profile, rather than the linear profile predicted by the dilute Fickian approximation. This problem therefore provides several independent theoretical features against which the experimental measurements can be evaluated.

Mid-infrared absorption images are converted into two-dimensional vapor mole-fraction fields using a spectrally weighted absorption coefficient, and the measurement method is evaluated through a hierarchy of increasingly stringent tests. First, the spectroscopic conversion is assessed to establish the absolute concentration scale. Second, the transverse uniformity of the two-dimensional concentration field is quantified to examine the validity of the one-dimensional approximation within the central measurement region. Complete dimensional concentration profiles obtained at different gas-layer thicknesses and for different hydrocarbon liquids are then compared with the Stefan solution using only the experimentally measured endpoint conditions, without fitting the interior concentration data, thereby testing the spatial accuracy of the measurement. Finally, normalized and logarithmically transformed concentration profiles are used to examine the predicted similarity and functional structure independently of the dimensional length scale, and thus to determine whether the measurements reproduce the nonlinear structure of Stefan transport.

papers.title: Cell-type-specific modularity in E/I networks shapes dynamical regimes and computational capabilities
papers.abstract: Structural modularity is a ubiquitous feature of brain networks that shapes neural dynamics and information processing. Yet excitatory and inhibitory populations can differ in their modular organization, and it remains unclear how this asymmetry affects network dynamics and computation. Here, using dynamical mean-field theory and simulations of networks performing complex temporal tasks, we show that independently tuning excitatory and inhibitory modularity controls the dynamical regimes of balanced E/I networks. In particular, such tuning can generate a dominant spectral outlier despite overall E/I balance, producing a topology-controlled transition between bulk- and low-rank-dominated regimes, with different dynamical bifurcations leading to chaos and bistability, respectively. In chaotic time-series prediction tasks, computational performance is enhanced near these dynamical boundaries, including both the onset of chaos and the transition to bistability. Favorable configurations exhibit strongly modular excitation and comparatively homogeneous inhibition, similar to what is observed in cortical connectivity.

papers.intro:
Connectivity in biological neural networks is highly structured and inhomogeneous, often organized into modules or clusters with dense intra-module and sparse inter-module connectivity [1, 2, 3]. Modular and clustered connectivity structures have been shown to significantly impact network dynamics, for example, by controlling population bursting [4], generating cascading dynamics [5], and increasing the robustness of attractor dynamics [6]. Beyond this, modular network connectivity has been linked to cortical-like activity patterns [7, 8] and shown to impact information processing [9] and task performance [10].

At the same time, biological neural networks are comprised of diverse neuron types that follow distinct and highly specific connectivity patterns [11]. In particular, excitatory and inhibitory neurons differ not only in their functional roles but also in their local and long-range connectivity, with various inhibitory subtypes forming heterogeneous and spatially structured networks [12, 13]. This cell-type specificity of wiring suggests that modular organization may differ between excitation and inhibition.

Using dynamic mean-field theory, we characterize how independent tuning of excitatory and inhibitory modularity shapes the network’s dynamical regime. We then relate these dynamical states to computational performance on a complex time-series prediction task using an echo state network framework, and examine how structured external inputs interact with E/I-modular recurrent connectivity. Together, this approach links cell-type–specific network architecture, emergent population dynamics, and computational performance within a unified theoretical framework.

papers.title: Optical linear polarization of the Be--X-ray pulsar binary LS V +44 17
papers.abstract: We present the optical $BVR$ polarization measurements for the Be--X-ray pulsar binary LS V +44 17 from its giant outburst in early 2023 and subsequently over three years. We detect a significant polarization of about $\approx1.1$--$2.1\%$, which includes the interstellar contribution. Polarization evolves significantly with time since the outburst. The interstellar polarization was found to be $\approx2.5$--$2.9\%$. The obtained intrinsic optical polarization of LS V +44 17 after correction is between $0.5$--$1.7\%$, perpendicular to the interstellar polarization direction. We consider various plausible sources of optical polarization and infer scattering in the Be decretion disk to be the most dominant source based on time and spectral evolution. Changing intrinsic PA with time hints at a plausible precession of the Be disk.

papers.intro:
X-ray binaries are binary star systems in which a compact object accretes matter from a stellar companion, typically a main sequence donor star. These systems provide valuable insights into accretion processes that occur in the vicinity of compact objects where matter is subject to extreme magnetic and gravitational fields. In case of Be–X-ray pulsar binaries (see Reig, 2011; Reig, 2026, for reviews), the donor is a Be star and the accretor is a neutron star (NS) operating as an X-ray pulsar (XRP, see Mushtukov and Tsygankov, 2024, for review). The Be star is surrounded by a geometrically thick quasi-Keplerian decretion disk (Lee et al., 1991). A close encounter of the NS with the Be disk during the course of its orbit results in the so-called Type I outbursts with X-ray luminosities ≈\approx1036–1037 erg s-1 due to increased accretion (Okazaki et al., 2013). Typically, these outbursts occur once per orbit. Brighter type II or giant outbursts with X-ray luminosity exceeding 103710^{37} erg s-1 are also possible in Be XRPs and are associated with the warping of Be disks (Stella et al., 1986; Negueruela et al., 1998; Okazaki et al., 2013). Generally, such outbursts last longer than Type I outbursts and occur once every few years.

LS V +44 17 (RX J0440.9++4431) is a Be–XRP binary (Motch et al., 1997) situated at a distance, d≈2.4d\approx 2.4 kpc (Bailer-Jones et al., 2021). Reig and Roche (1999) confirmed the source as an XRP with a pulsar period of 202.5±0.5202.5\pm 0.5 s. Reig et al. (2005) have extensively studied the companion star in the system. They identified the donor as a Be star of type B0.2V. The consistent presence of the Hα\alpha line in the optical spectra, as well as its correlation with infrared magnitudes led to the conclusion that there exists long term optical and infrared variability in the system. Both observational signatures, the emission lines and the infrared excess, are thought to be due to the presence of an equatorial decretion disk, plausibly produced as a result of the rapid rotation of the star (Porter and Rivinius, 2003). The variability suggests long term structural changes in the Be disk. LS V +44 17 went into type I outburst in 2010 and 2011, during which the orbital period was measured at ≈\approx155 d (Morii et al., 2010; Finger and Camero-Arranz, 2010) and the magnetic field was estimated at ≈3×1012\approx 3\times 10^{12} G (Tsygankov et al., 2012) using timing and spectral X-ray analyzes. The orbital period was later updated to 150.0±0.2150.0\pm 0.2 days by Ferrigno et al. (2013).

During this outburst, the source was also observed with the Imaging X-ray Polarimetry Explorer (Weisskopf et al., 2022) and X-ray linear polarization in the 2–8 keV band was measured by Doroshenko et al. (2023). Polarimetry is a unique technique to probe the geometry of the emitting region. XRPs are expected to have a high degree of polarization (PD) in X-rays due to the strong birefringence of magnetized plasma in the presence of strong magnetic fields (Gnedin et al., 1978). The electric vector position angle (aka polarization angle, PA) is thought to be related to the projection of the magnetic dipole of the XRP on the sky plane and is hence expected to evolve with the pulsar phase, as described by the rotating vector model (Radhakrishnan and Cooke, 1969; Meszaros et al., 1988; Poutanen, 2020, RVM;). The geometry of the X-ray source in LS V +44 17 was interpreted using a two-component model (Doroshenko et al., 2023; Zhao et al., 2025). The first component that depends on the pulsar period was described using the RVM. In addition, a second component, constant with respect to the pulsar phase, is potentially produced due to the scattering of the pulsar radiation in the accretion disk wind (Nitindala et al., 2025). Its presence was required to describe the evolution of X-ray polarization between supercritical and subcritical accretion states.

The polarized optical emission in such systems can originate from various components such as the Be star and its decretion disk, the NS accretion disk and disk wind, reprocessed X-ray emission from the XRP in the disk and/or the companion star, and from the strong magnetic field of the NS and the interaction of the Be disk material with this magnetic field. The data is described in Sect. 2. The results are presented in Sect. 3 and are discussed in detail in Sect. 4. Lastly, we summarize our findings in Sect. 5.

papers.title: A Counterexample to the Weak Gibbs and Regularity Conjectures
papers.abstract: We provide a counterexample to the weak Gibbs and regularity conjectures. The example is a spin-one system on the square lattice with a translation-invariant nearest-neighbor interaction. At high temperatures and high on-site field strengths, it has a unique KMS state that does not have the weak Gibbs or regularity properties.

papers.title: BIOTRAM: Biochemistry-informed Transformer for Relative Abundance via Metabarcoding
papers.abstract: Arthropod monitoring at scale begins with metabarcoding of bulk samples: trap collections of hundreds to thousands of specimens processed as one unit, extraction of DNA from the bulked specimens, then sequencing of the DNA from all specimens together. Metabarcoding reveals which taxa such a sample contains, but due to factors such as differing DNA amplification rates and body sizes, its read counts do not neatly correspond to how abundant the different taxa are relative to one another. This lack of relative abundance limits the data's utility for the multitude of ecological analyses that depend on it. We propose BIOTRAM: a neural network that estimates per-taxon specimen counts by dividing the observed read counts by a learned read yield per specimen, which it factors into the DNA each specimen contributes and how efficiently that DNA is amplified. It also generalizes to out-of-domain data better, beating all baselines on bottles from unseen regions, later collection dates and unseen sequencing batches, and transferring to data from an unseen laboratory. Insects are by far the most diverse multicellular taxon on Earth (Colwell et al., 2026) and are fundamentally important for human existence given their foundational role in ecosystem processes (Yang and Gratton, 2014). Yet, they are undergoing extensive global declines (Wagner et al., 2021; Hallmann et al., 2017); efforts to quantify this are limited by the paucity of reliable data (Didham et al., 2020). Malaise traps—tent-like structures that passively capture flying insects and direct them into a bottle of preservative—are widely used for capturing insects for study (Karlsson et al., 2020). BIOTRAM, a biochemistry-informed transformer for relative abundance via metabarcoding, is instead structured around the steps of the experimental pipeline: it estimates specimen counts by dividing each taxon’s reads by a learned read yield per specimen, factored into per-specimen DNA contribution and amplification efficiency, so it can produce estimates for taxa absent from training. Its taxonomic unit is the Barcode Index Number (BIN), a cluster of near-identical barcodes proxying for species that usually agrees with species assigned by morphology (Ratnasingham and Hebert, 2013). Our contributions are as follows: (1) A paired DNA barcoding-metabarcoding dataset (Section 3). 1,188 bottles processed with both metabarcoding and (for ground-truthing) individual barcoding, yielding 414,640 matched (reads, count) pairs across 132,184 unique BINs and 578 sites—more than an order of magnitude larger than existing data. (2) A bespoke architecture built on biological and chemical knowledge (Section 4.3). Rather than a naïve model, we propose a staged model based on the biochemical properties of the metabarcoding process. (3) Latent predictions of primer binding efficiency and body size (Section 4.1). Our model produces physically interpretable latent estimates of both properties, which directly shape the relationship between specimen counts and read counts per BIN and bottle. (4) Controlled evaluation under distribution shift (Section 5). We compare BIOTRAM against deep baselines trained with the same objective and inputs, generalizing to novel collection locations (spatial blocking), novel time-points (temporal cut-off), and across metabarcode sequencing methods (data from another laboratory).

papers.title: Construct Validity of Coding Benchmarks for LLM-based Agentic Coding Tools
papers.abstract: Software developers increasingly adopt LLM-based agentic coding tools to assist them with development tasks. To provide developers with up-to-date information on these tools' effectiveness, prior work introduced benchmarks that enable comparisons across tools. Despite the widespread adoption of such benchmarks, however, recent work has shown that they suffer from issues threatening their validity. Aims. In this work, we aim to complement prior work by analyzing the construct validity of agentic coding benchmarks. Methodology. We analyze nine benchmarks commonly used to evaluate the effectiveness of agentic coding tools. We identify the constructs that the benchmarks claim to measure, the metrics used to operationalize them, and potential confounders that interfere with the measurement. Results. Our findings show that benchmarks commonly operationalize broad concepts such as coding capability with only a small set of metrics. The reported attributes that might confound the measurements vary between benchmarks, indicating a lack of standardization. Conclusions. We conclude with recommendations to strengthen construct validity in agentic coding benchmarks and encourage further empirical work to better understand the effectiveness of agentic coding tools.

papers.intro:
A benchmark is a systematic evaluation framework for assigning a quantitative score to a tool or method under assessment [1]. The goal of benchmarking is to enable reproducible comparisons of different approaches by measuring a given property. Critical realism is a philosophy of science that assumes reality exists independently of our beliefs, while recognizing that our knowledge of it is fallible. From this perspective, measurement depends on theoretical assumptions and value judgments [2]. For example, measuring the quality of agent-generated code requires a theory of code quality. People with different values and goals may disagree on the quality of the same code, even if they agree on an overall theory of code quality. When value conflict is low and the theory underlying a measurement is widely accepted and well understood, we say that the measurement is “direct.” Direct measurements are assumed to have inherent validity. In contrast, if there is value conflict or a measure depends on theories in which we are less confident, then the measurement’s validity requires explicit justification. Such properties are modeled as constructs and require explicit operationalization. The construct validity of an operationalization requires several forms of evidence. Face validity concerns whether an indicator plausibly represents the construct; content validity concerns coverage of its dimensions. Convergent validity concerns expected relationships among indicators of the same construct, while discriminant validity concerns their distinction from indicators of other constructs. Predictive validity concerns whether measurements predict theoretically related outcomes. In reflective measurement models, convergent and discriminant validity are assessed using multiple indicators, with shared variance used to estimate the latent construct [3]. Since agentic coding tools such as Claude Code and Codex were introduced in 2025, researchers have proposed a range of benchmarks to evaluate their effectiveness for software engineering tasks [4]. For example, after the introduction of SWE-bench by Jimenez et al., their benchmarking approach was applied to an increasingly diverse set of repositories spanning multiple programming languages [5], human-verified task samples [6, 7], or long-horizon tasks [8]. Based on these benchmarks, companies such as OpenAI and Anthropic compare a newly introduced model, which can serve as the backbone of an agentic coding tool, against results from earlier model generations to demonstrate the superiority of the new model at the time of its release [9, 10, 11]. Similarly, SE researchers commonly adopt these benchmarks to compare approaches for improving agentic coding systems [12, 13, 14, 15]. However, despite the widespread adoption of agentic coding tools, recent work has raised various concerns about the validity of the estimated scores in current benchmarks [16]. Understanding these threats can guide the design of new benchmarks whose task samples and evaluation metrics better represent the capabilities they claim to measure. Previous analyses have indicated threats to the validity of the benchmarks, arising from issues such as misalignment between the description of an issue and the associated code change [17], weaknesses in the validation of a generated candidate solution [18], or the contamination of benchmarks in the training of LLMs [19]. We complement this prior work by presenting a preliminary study of potential threats to the construct validity of current agentic coding benchmarks. Our research questions are:

papers.title: Optimizing Geo-replicated Deterministic Databases
papers.abstract: In transactional databases, achieving active-active replication among geo-distributed replicas is challenging due to the high coordination cost in ensuring the serializability of concurrent cross-node transactions. Deterministic concurrency control (DCC) has emerged as a promising alternative: it establishes a global order for a batch of transactions before execution and thereby amortizes this coordination cost across the batch. To better understand the performance characteristics of DCC, we conduct a theoretical analysis of traditional two-phase locking and optimistic concurrency control to account for geo-replication and introduce a model for DCC. We compare the three paradigms and identify the conditions under which DCC is advantageous. Guided by the insights from this analysis, we then present Quirinus, a DCC-based geo-replicated database that optimizes transaction execution through speculative execution, transaction reordering, integration of conflict-free replicated data types (CRDTs), and fast-path commit. Even without these optimizations, Quirinus achieves up to 6.2x the TPC-C throughput of Tiga under our configuration.

papers.intro:
Geo-replication is essential for globally scaled databases, as it provides extremely high availability to the applications that serve global users. Commonly, a geo-replicated OLTP database consists of transaction execution nodes and replicated storage nodes distributed across different data centers (DCs) for horizontal scalability and fault tolerance.

Commonly, a geo-replicated OLTP database consists of transaction execution nodes and replicated storage nodes distributed across different data centers (DCs) for horizontal scalability and fault tolerance.

To provide serializable isolation, databases use concurrency control protocols such as two-phase locking (2PL) and optimistic concurrency control (OCC) to resolve conflicts and establish a serial transaction order. Under geo-replication, however, these protocols incur significant coordination overhead (Zhang et al., 2018) because a transaction cannot commit until its writes have been durably and consistently replicated. This guarantee is typically provided through consensus replication (Ongaro and Ousterhout, 2014; Lamport, 2001), which adds cross-DC communication to the commit path (Zhang et al., 2024a). Because round-trip times (RTTs) between geo-distributed DCs can reach hundreds of milliseconds (Bailis et al., 2013), this coordination lengthens transaction lifetimes. Both 2PL and OCC resolve conflicts at runtime for each transaction, so longer lifetimes increase exposure to conflicts (Yu et al., 1993): 2PL transactions hold locks longer, whereas OCC transactions are more likely to abort and retry.

Deterministic concurrency control (DCC) brings batching to transaction ordering. It predetermines a global order for a batch of transactions before execution, thereby removing runtime order resolution while preserving serializability (Thomson et al., 2012; Faleiro and Abadi, 2015; Faleiro et al., 2017; Thomson and Abadi, 2010; Abadi and Faleiro, 2018; Qin et al., 2021; Lu et al., 2020; Hildred et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2023; Han et al., 2025; Hong et al., 2025). It thus removes the need for strongly consistent replication at the storage layer; instead, the replication moves to the execution layer that replicates transaction inputs and runs the same deterministic execution at each replica. By decoupling ordering from execution, DCC amortizes the ordering coordination cost across a batch instead of paying it for each transaction. However, this design introduces two costs: (1) every transaction incurs batching delay, even without contention; and (2) execution is repeated at each replica, making execution efficiency critical.

We observe that OCC has become a popular choice for geo-replication, while DCC is gaining traction in recent years. Although the strengths and weaknesses of these concurrency control paradigms are intuitively clear, we need to understand their advantageous regimes and trade-offs. DCC is found to achieve favorable performance when the network RTT dominates execution time, whereas 2PL and OCC can suffer from unbounded latency under high contention. The replication speed and deterministic execution time are still the bottleneck for DCC, which requires optimization.

The core idea that allows these optimizations to be realized is to synchronize replica state only at batch boundaries, creating a consistent snapshot (Eldeeb et al., 2023) between consecutive batches. This design allows transactions within a batch to be freely reordered to reduce the total execution cost, provided that all replicas derive the same deterministic order. For example, a transaction with a read–write dependency can instead read from the snapshot, allowing it to execute concurrently with the writer.

papers.title: Odd and even fake quadrics isogenous to a product
papers.abstract: A $\mathbb{Q}$-homology quadric is a smooth compact complex surface which has the same $\mathbb{Q}$-homology as a quadric surface, that is, the product of two $2$-dimensional spheres. It is called fake if it is minimal and not rational. Among them are the fake quadrics which are isogenous to a product of complex curves. In this paper, we determine the parity of the intersection forms of all fake quadrics isogenous to a product of unmixed type. In particular, we show that there are fake quadrics with odd intersection forms.

papers.title: SBVUL: Statement-Based Vulnerability Detection
papers.abstract: Many recent approaches for vulnerability detection use large language models (LLMs) to classify functions as vulnerable or benign, leaving developers to locate the exploitable statements. Furthermore, while these approaches have shown performance improvements, they still fall short in distinguishing vulnerable from patched real-world functions. This paper presents SBVul, an agentic approach that detects exploitable statements in C/C++ functions. In Phase~1, an LLM agent explores the function and its repository and identifies candidate statements. In Phase~2, a second agent analyzes the control and data flow of each candidate and confirms it, rules it out, or marks it uncertain. We created a manually verified ground truth of exploitable statements for 200 pairs of the PrimeVul Paired test set and ran SBVul with the open-weight models Qwen 3.8 and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and Anthropic's Sonnet 5.5 and Opus 5.5. Phase~1 identifies ground-truth statements in 56--77% of the vulnerable functions, and Phase~2 confirms such a statement with an explanation accepted by an LLM judge in 26--73%. However, all models also confirm candidates in 23--61% of the patched functions. Across vulnerable and patched functions, the highest statement-level precision is 0.315 at a recall of 0.605 obtained with Opus 5.5 (xhigh). At the function level, SBVul with Opus 5.5 classifies 42.0% of the pairs correctly, compared with 33.8% reported for the best previous approach.
