This was followed by a demonstration of deeper imaging by de Jong et al. (2024b) using 32 hours of observations. While these studies highlighted the potential of sub-arcsecond wide-field imaging with LOFAR, scaling up to ultra-deep imaging with hundreds of hours of LOFAR observations remained non-trivial. The primary challenges included processing and imaging 16 TB of visibility data per 8-hour observation11 1 These data are typically reduced to around 4 TB using Dynamical Statistical Compression (Offringa, 2016, Dysco;), although the total number of visibilities remains unchanged. within a computationally feasible timescale, automatically selecting and precisely calibrating high signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) calibrator sources across the wide field of view (FoV) under varying ionospheric conditions, the difficulty of jointly calibrating the short baselines from the Dutch stations with the long baselines from the European stations, and the need for human-interventions for validation and quality assessment.

Recent work has addressed the aforementioned challenges. These include general developments in the calibration software facetselfcal (van Weeren et al., 2021) that have improved calibration performance and reliability (e.g. van Weeren et al., 2026b, Appendix A), also when jointly calibrating short and long baselines (de Jong et al., 2025b). Automated self-calibration parameter selection and quality assessment by combining quality metrics with a machine learning algorithm have removed the need for human intervention (de Jong et al., 2024b; de Jong et al., 2025b). The high computational costs for the final deep imaging with multiple observations are mitigated through sidereal visibility averaging (SVA; de Jong et al. 2025a). This approach averages calibrated visibilities from different epochs with similar baseline coordinates, which, after applying all calibration solutions, reduces the total data volume of tens of observations to that of one or two. Combining this with recent improvements in automated processing strategies (de Jong et al., 2025b), the overall computational cost of processing for ultra-deep imaging with hundreds of hours of LOFAR data has been lowered by more than an order of magnitude compared to the first successful LOFAR sub-arcsecond wide-field imaging by Sweijen et al. (2022). By making use of the Common Workflow Language (Amstutz et al., 2016; Crusoe et al., 2022, CWL;), Toil (Vivian et al., 2017), and Simple Linux Utility for Resource Management (Yoo et al., 2003, SLURM;) for data processing on high-performance computing clusters, we have also enabled efficient automated parallel processing of numerous observations, as detailed in van der Wild et al. (subm.). CWL workflows are reusable, interoperable, and portable, which aligns CWL-based pipelines with FAIR principles (Wilkinson et al., 2016, e.g.) and supports scalable processing of large numbers of LOFAR observations.

In this work, we use the most recent data processing strategies for LOFAR long-baseline imaging to release ultra-deep sub-arcsecond wide-field images across a FoV of 2.5×2.52.5\times 2.5 deg2 of the European Large Area ISO Survey-North 1 (Oliver et al., 2000, ELAIS-N1;) deep field, using 200 hours of LOFAR-HBA observations in the 115–168 MHz band. The highest resolution image represents the deepest LOFAR image to date and is among the deepest radio images ever produced at any frequency. Located at a right ascension (RA) of 16:11:00 and declination (DEC) of +54:57:00, ELAIS-N1 has been extensively studied across a broad range of wavelengths, including X-rays (Manners et al., 2003, e.g.,), ultraviolet (Martin et al., 2005; Chaturvedi et al., 2026, e.g.,), optical (McMahon et al., 2001; Aihara et al., 2018, e.g.,), infrared (Lawrence et al., 2007; Mauduit et al., 2012; Oliver et al., 2012, e.g.,), and radio (Sirothia et al., 2009; Ocran et al., 2020; Sinha et al., 2022; Kondapally et al., 2022; Best et al., 2023, e.g.,), and is one of the selected LOFAR deep fields (Kondapally et al., 2021; Duncan et al., 2021; Tasse et al., 2021; Sabater et al., 2021; Bondi et al., 2024). papers.title: Partially Dynamic Algorithms for Single-Source Temporal Paths
papers.abstract:
We present efficient partially dynamic algorithms for maintaining earliest arrival times from a fixed source in temporal digraphs with $n$ vertices.
  For the incremental scenario where updates are arc insertions, our algorithm has a constant query time and requires a total update time of $O(n + m \log m)$, where $m$ is the total number of arcs added to the arc-less graph. For the decremental scenario where updates are arc removals, our algorithm has a constant query time and requires a total update time of $O(n + m \log m)$, where $m$ is the number of arcs in the graph upon its initialization. We also consider earliest-arrival queries with an arbitrary departure-time threshold and develop an incremental algorithm with $O(n+\Delta_s m\log m)$ total update time, $O(\log m)$ query time, and $O(n+m)$ space, where $\Delta_s$ is the number of distinct departure times of arcs leaving the source. All of our algorithms are also capable of reporting an earliest arrival path from the source to the queried vertex $v$ in constant time per edge once the earliest arrival time at $v$ is known.
  We complement our positive results with conditional lower bounds based on the Online Boolean Matrix-Vector Multiplication conjecture (a.k.a. OMv conjecture). For both the incremental and the decremental scenarios, we show the non-existence of an algorithm with $O(n^{1-\varepsilon})$ amortized update time and $O(n^{2-\varepsilon})$ amortized query time, even if the algorithm is randomized and latencies on the arcs are uniform. For arbitrary departure-time queries, we also establish an OMv-based conditional lower bound showing that our incremental algorithm is optimal up to logarithmic factors on dense temporal graphs. Thus, efficient total running time is essentially the best outcome we can get. Our conditional lower bounds hold also for the case of undirected temporal graphs.

Temporal graphs are graphs in which edges are available only at specific time instants. They are a standard model for networks whose interactions change over time, such as communication networks, transportation systems, social networks, and contact networks. In these settings, the time at which an interaction occurs is often essential, and cannot be ignored without losing important information.

They are a standard model for networks whose interactions change over time, such as communication networks, transportation systems, social networks, and contact networks. In these settings, the time at which an interaction occurs is often essential, and cannot be ignored without losing important information.

The most basic model of a temporal graph was introduced by Kempe, Kleinberg, and Kumar [22]. In this model, a temporal graph consists of an underlying graph together with a set of integer labels assigned to each edge, representing the times at which the edge is available. As movement through the network must respect time, the basic notion is that of a temporal path, i.e., a path whose edge labels appear in non-decreasing order. Several variants of this model have been studied, including strict temporal paths, paths with waiting constraints, continuous-time models, and stochastic models; see, e.g., [11, 20].

Many algorithmic problems on temporal graphs have been considered in the literature. These include the computation of temporal paths optimizing different objectives, such as earliest arrival, minimum duration, or minimum number of hops [1, 25, 12]; sparsification and temporal spanners [6, 7, 13, 14, 22]; exploration problems [15, 16]; temporal versions of covering problems [2, 17]; and network creation games [4, 5]. Among these topics, temporal reachability is one of the most basic. Given two vertices uu and vv, one asks whether there exists a temporal path from uu to vv. Unlike the static case, the answer may depend on the starting time, the allowed waiting time, and the chosen path model. Moreover, temporal reachability is in general not symmetric, and its behavior is often more complex than standard graph connectivity.

papers.title: Optimal Subcubic Byzantine Agreement with Plain PKI
papers.abstract:
We consider Byzantine Agreement (BA), where $n$ parties run a distributed protocol to agree on a common value, despite $t$ parties being byzantine. In the synchronous setting, a choice must be made between the weaker unauthenticated setting, which only allows $t < n/3$ byzantine parties, and the stronger authenticated setting that allows up to $t < n/2$ byzantine parties. For this latter setting, BA can be solved with optimal resiliency and optimal bit complexity. However, so far, all optimal solutions rely on the use of threshold signatures. This shows a gap compared to regular signatures, where only protocols with cubic complexity are known for optimal resiliency $t < n/2$.
  We wonder whether this cubic complexity is required without the use of threshold signatures and show that this is not the case. More specifically, given $\kappa$ an upper bound on the size of a hash or signature, we describe a deterministic protocol solving BA with bit complexity $\mathcal{O}(\kappa^{(\sqrt{13} - 1)/2} n^{(\sqrt{13} + 1)/2}) \approx \mathcal{O}(\kappa^{1.303}n^{2.303})$ while having optimal resiliency $t<n/2$ and round complexity $\mathcal{O}(n)$.

papers.title: Mutual linearity in semi-Markov networks
papers.abstract: Despite their microscopic complexity, stochastic networks show a surprising degree of universal, parameter-independent properties. One example is mutual linearity, which has recently been characterized as a generic, pairwise-linear relation between observables of Markov processes under local perturbations, valid for both stationary dynamics and for transient dynamics in Laplace space. Here we show that mutual linearity arises if a certain global affine relation is satisfied. This allows us to demonstrate that mutual linearity also holds for a broad class of local perturbations in semi-Markov networks, which, unlike Markov networks, have memory in terms of the dwell time in the current state. However, exceptions exist, meaning that mutual linearity does not extend to all possible perturbations of semi-Markov networks. Strikingly, this restriction disappears for first-passage times. Thus, semi-Markov networks exhibit a fundamental asymmetry between occupation and first-passage statistics, different from Markov networks. Finally, we show that our results are directly applicable to stochastic resetting in semi-Markov networks, where the Laplace-space relations acquire a physical interpretation in terms of stationary occupations and the probability to reach a target before reset. This provides a natural setting in which the predicted affine relations can be probed.

papers.title: Scythe: Semantic-Aware Rewriting for Fast,Effective Program Reduction
papers.abstract: Automated program reduction shrinks a program into a smaller one that preserves a property of interest. Language-agnostic grammar-based reducers are easy to retarget across languages, but because they reason only about syntax, they cannot perform the coupled edits needed to remove whole declarations, e.g., a method cannot be deleted while it is still called. As a result, they waste oracle calls on edits that cannot succeed and often leave irrelevant declarations behind. We present SCYTHE, a fast, semantic-aware pre-processing step that runs in front of any grammar-based reducer without modifying it. SCYTHE encodes the program as a typed declaration dependency graph and applies a set of semantic-aware operators that decouple declarations from their use sites, making them removable while keeping the program well-typed. Fine-grained token-level minimization is then left to the downstream reducer. On 73 benchmarks across C, Java, and Solidity, combining SCYTHE with PERSES never yields a larger result than PERSES alone, and a strictly smaller one on 70 of 73 cases. On average, the combination produces programs 55.6% smaller (up to 95.5%) and is 2.3$\times$ faster (up to 7.4$\times$). SCYTHE also boosts LATRA, a reducer that, unlike the purely syntactic PERSES, also applies language-specific transformations: the combination produces programs 10.6% smaller (up to 61.8%) and is 2.4$\times$ faster on average. papers.intro:
Automated program reduction is integral to debugging and bug deduplication in software systems that take programs as input, such as compilers, interpreters, and static analyzers. Given a program PP that exhibits a property of interest, such as a compiler crash, a miscompilation, or a static-analysis report, a reducer produces a smaller program P′P^{\prime} that still exhibits it, querying an oracle (a script that checks the property) on each candidate [1]. Existing reducers fall into two families. Language-specific reducers, such as C-Reduce [1], apply transformations tailored to one language (e.g., C). These transformations make reduction effective, but the tools are hard to retarget to other languages. Language-agnostic, grammar-based reducers [2, 3] instead delete syntax while guaranteeing that the result still parses, so they can be retargeted to a new language simply by supplying its grammar. However, this generality comes at a cost. Language-agnostic reducers can be slow, even on small programs, and often leave behind code that is irrelevant to the property of interest.

papers.title: Who Gets Counted? Large Language Models, Informative Refusal, and Downstream Bias in Name-Based Demographic Classification
papers.abstract: Researchers routinely infer gender, race, and ethnicity from names, yet the standard tools used for this task misclassify the groups that diversity research most needs to measure. Large language models (LLMs) have been proposed as a remedy because they label diverse names accurately. We ask whether that accuracy carries over to the estimates researchers report. Across 10,000 Chinese names, 19,998 North Carolina voters with self-reported race, and 300 political science authors with human reference codes, we compare three LLMs with seven traditional tools and link the voter sample to party registration and age. Selective labeling explains part of the LLMs' accuracy advantage. Claude Haiku labels half of the voters, and a traditional tool limited to its most confident half is more accurate. Hard labels from every tool understate the White--Black gap in Democratic registration by 36% to 65%, while BIRDiE estimation on BISG posteriors comes within 0.03 of it. Haiku's missing labels select on age, inflating the age gap by six years. Combined with BISG, LLM answers sharpen individual labels without a demonstrated gain in BIRDiE accuracy. Classifiers should be judged by the estimates they produce, including the consequences of missing labels

papers.intro:
Studies of representation in citation networks, hiring, legislatures, and public office routinely infer the race and gender of individuals from their names, while computational tools have been used to scale these practices to millions of records (Dion et al., 2018; Dworkin et al., 2020; Bertrand and Mullainathan, 2004; Imai and Khanna, 2016; Lee and Velez, 2024). Yet the tools that make this possible fail unevenly. Threshold-based Bayesian Improved Surname Geocoding (BISG), the standard method for race, undercounts Black individuals by about 19% and overcounts White individuals by 16% (Kozlowski et al., 2022). In a survey of 19,924 scholars who reported their own identities, the best-performing gender tool misgendered 43% of Chinese women (Lockhart et al., 2023). Classification errors often concentrate among the groups that diversity research sets out to count.

Large language models (LLMs) appear to address some of these challenges. Given only a name, they have been shown to assign the correct self-reported race to between 75% and 85% of people in recent benchmarks, while their errors fall less heavily on non-White names than those of surname dictionaries (AlNuaimi et al., 2024; Dasanaike, 2026). For gender, leading LLMs have the lowest error rates of the tools tested (Domínguez-Díaz et al., 2024). These benchmarks rank classifiers by their accuracy among the names each tool labels, which remains a focus for researchers when choosing a tool.

Accuracy across labeled names leaves out two things that decide whether a classifier improves applied work. One is which names each tool declines to label. Dropping unlabeled cases biases estimates whenever the reason a case is missing is related to the outcome (King et al., 2001; Knox et al., 2020). This is particularly relevant as safety-tuned LLMs often refuse requests to classify race. As a result, where refusals fall on hard names or on particular groups, high accuracy on the labeled names says little about the full sample. The other is what the labels do to the estimand. Researchers use inferred categories to estimate group shares and group differences, and misclassification can pull group differences toward zero even when accuracy is high (Blackwell et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2019; Argyle and Barber, 2024). Existing benchmarks that do not track refusal and downstream bias thus cannot tell us whether LLMs improve the estimates researchers publish.

papers.title: Perceived Trust and Transparency in AI-Altered vs. Human-Written LinkedIn Posts
papers.abstract: People increasingly draft a social media post themselves and then let an AI model refine it (AI-altered), a common but understudied middle case between fully human-written and fully AI-generated content. We ask whether this changes how trustworthy and transparent readers perceive the post to be, and whether they can even tell. We first analyze real ChatGPT conversations (WildChat) to find how people actually alter social media posts, which we use to design realistic alteration prompts. We then run a pre-registered, within-subjects online experiment (n=214) in which participants rate unlabeled human-written and AI-altered LinkedIn-style posts for perceived trustworthiness and transparency, and separately judge whether each post was AI-altered. We find that AI-alteration itself has no detectable effect on either perceived trustworthiness or transparency (both estimates near zero, not significant). At the same time, readers did not reliably detect AI-alteration (49\% accuracy, near chance) and defaulted to assuming human authorship when unsure. However, our analysis shows significant differences in transparency and trustworthiness ratings across the specific post, the AI model, as well as the prompt used to alter it. For instance, more detailed prompts raise both perceived trustworthiness and transparency but also make the alteration more detectable. Surprisingly, the prompt that shifted ratings most also asked the model to add one new idea absent from the original post: readers nonetheless rated this AI-invented, unverifiable content as more trustworthy and transparent.

papers.intro:
People often say they would trust a message less once they suspect AI wrote it: in an experiment on real, entirely human-written Airbnb profiles, hosts explicitly labeled as using an AI writing assistant were rated less trustworthy than hosts believed to write their own (Jakesch et al., 2019). Yet this suspicion may not track anything real: across six later experiments with over 4,600 participants, people could not reliably tell genuinely AI-generated self-presentations from human-written ones in professional, hospitality, and dating contexts (Jakesch et al., 2023), so when distrust of “AI-sounding” text does occur, it likely falls on the wrong content as often as the right one. Nor is disclosure’s effect itself settled: a larger, more recent experiment that labeled real AI-generated misinformation and real human-written content alike as AI-generated found no significant effect of the label on perceived accuracy or credibility (Li and Yang, 2024), where Jakesch et al. (2019)’s comparable labeled condition had found a significant drop. Whether, and under what conditions, knowing or suspecting AI involvement changes how content is judged is thus still unresolved, and this paradox plays out wherever people write for others online. And such AI-assisted writing is becoming the default: about half of marketers already use AI to create or optimize content (SurveyMonkey, 2025), and by the end of 2024, almost 40% of the US working-age population reported using generative AI, and 78% of organizations reported using AI that year (up from 55% in 2023), an adoption curve faster than the computer or the Internet’s (Bick et al., 2024; Maslej and others, 2025). That capability cuts both ways: the same models that can polish an existing post can just as easily generate a persuasive one from scratch, at a scale no individual writer could match (Salvi et al., 2025; Chergarova and others, 2025).

A pre-registered experiment addresses the RQ directly, combining three steps. First, we analyze the WildChat dataset (Zhao et al., 2024) to see how people actually use ChatGPT to alter social media posts, informing the prompting styles used in the next step. This analysis also shows LinkedIn is the most common target platform for such requests, and professional networks are a high-stakes case in their own right: posts there are tied to a real name, a real employer, and colleagues who can check what is claimed (Guillory and Hancock, 2012), and the platform is projected to grow from 644 million users in 2019 to 942 million by 2028 (Statista Research Department, 2023). We then gather real LinkedIn posts, alter them with two LLMs and four prompts, and compare originals to alterations with text metrics. Building on this, a pilot and the pre-registered main experiment let participants rate perceived trustworthiness and transparency of AI-altered LinkedIn posts, and later separately judge, for each post, how likely it is human-written, testing whether readers can detect AI-alteration at all, which can affect how much they trust it (see Method below).

Our hypotheses are the following: • H1 (Trustworthiness): AI-altered social media posts are perceived as more trustworthy than human-written social media posts. • H2 (Transparency): AI-altered social media posts are perceived as more transparent than human-written social media posts. We expect AI-altered posts to be rated higher on both scales, as they are more clearly written than human-written ones. We also expect this effect to outweigh people’s skepticism towards AI-altered posts, which may come up if they detect that a text was created with the help of AI. We expect however that, for LinkedIn-style posts, the AI-detection task is not trivial, since the platform is used by professionals who tend to write clearer posts, which could be more easily confounded with those altered with an AI tool. Additionally, we explore which LLM model and prompt style have a greater impact on perceived trustworthiness and transparency.

Our hypotheses are the following:

H1 (Trustworthiness): AI-altered social media posts are perceived as more trustworthy than human-written social media posts.

H1 (Trustworthiness): AI-altered social media posts are perceived as more trustworthy than human-written social media posts.

H2 (Transparency): AI-altered social media posts are perceived as more transparent than human-written social media posts.

H2 (Transparency): AI-altered social media posts are perceived as more transparent than human-written social media posts.

We expect AI-altered posts to be rated higher on both scales, as they are more clearly written than human-written ones. We also expect this effect to outweigh people’s skepticism towards AI-altered posts, which may come up if they detect that a text was created with the help of AI. We expect however that, for LinkedIn-style posts, the AI-detection task is not trivial, since the platform is used by professionals who tend to write clearer posts, which could be more easily confounded with those altered with an AI tool. Additionally, we explore which LLM model and prompt style have a greater impact on perceived trustworthiness and transparency.

Two results anchor the paper. First, altering a post with AI does not, by itself, move perceived trustworthiness or transparency in any significant way: these perceptions can still be raised or lowered by which model altered a post and which prompt was used, even though AI-alteration itself is invisible on average. Second, this null result has a straightforward cause: the experiment revealed that participants could barely tell an altered post from an unaltered one, and when in doubt, assumed a human had written it. Therefore, an alteration that raises no suspicion just gets judged as trustworthy and transparent as when a person had written the whole post. A further, more practical finding is that richer prompts raise both perceived trustworthiness and transparency at the cost of making the alteration itself easier to spot, including when the prompt explicitly asks the model to sound less like AI. The richest prompt also asked the model to add a new idea the post did not originally contain (content invented by the AI rather than supplied or verified by the human author) and readers still rated it as more trustworthy and transparent. We use these results to situate AI-alteration on a four-stage spectrum of AI involvement in social media writing, distinct from fully AI-generated content.

papers.title: Geometric Pumping of Optical Work in Coherent Wave Scattering
papers.abstract: Optical work exchanged between light and time-varying matter underlies a wide range of emerging photonic technologies, yet a general geometric theory describing its generation and control has been lacking. Here we establish such a theory for coherent electromagnetic scattering. We show that the net optical work accumulated during an adiabatic modulation cycle is a geometric quantity determined by the Berry curvature of the outgoing field in parameter space. Nonzero optical work can thus be generated by cyclically modulating two or more independent system parameters. In contrast to conventional adiabatic pumping between incoherent reservoirs, optical work pumping vanishes under maximally mixed illumination. Greater illumination coherence increases the maximum work attainable through wavefront shaping. For fully coherent illumination, we derive the optimal incident wavefront and modulation trajectory that maximize the optical work per cycle. Our framework unifies time-varying photonics, optomechanics, and geometric transport within a common scattering formalism.

papers.title: CMS ECAL VFE Production Qualification
papers.abstract: Upgrading the CMS ECAL barrel for the HL-LHC requires replacement of all on-detector electronics, including 12240 Very-Front-End (VFE) cards employing CATIA and LiTE-DTU ASICs for amplification and digitisation of signals from ECAL's 61200 lead-tungstate crystals. All production VFEs undergo the same qualification procedure: functional testing, environmental stress screening, and calibration. We have received and functionally tested 13596 unique VFEs; two never passed our test criteria. Results for other VFEs are uniform and within expectations, demonstrating the excellent quality of the cards. Key metrics, such as a gain ratio of $10.21 \pm 0.07$ and power consumption of $1.805 \pm 0.013~\mathrm{W}$, demonstrate high consistency across the batch.

papers.title: CMS ECAL Phase-2 upgrade: characterisation and stability analysis of a three-stage low-voltage power-conversion system
papers.abstract: As part of the High-Luminosity upgrade of the Large Hadron Collider, the front-end electronics of the Compact Muon Solenoid electromagnetic calorimeter barrel are being replaced. A three-stage low-voltage power-conversion system supplies the upgraded electronics. As the cascade dynamics require characterisation to ensure stable operation, interactions between the three converter stages are assessed at their two interfaces using the Nyquist criterion. A validated shunt-injection setup using a Bode 100 frequency-response analyser provides in-situ impedance measurements under load to assess the accuracy of the averaged converter models. Results show that both interfaces are stable over the evaluated configurations, with modelled minimum distances to the critical point of 0.76 and 0.79, respectively. A turn-on study identifies capacitor charging at Stage 3 as the main cause of inrush currents triggering Stage 2 overcurrent protection. Two Stage 3 board variants stagger converter enables within and between boards, keeping the measured two-tower current below 5 A, within the 8.0 A protection threshold.

papers.title: Turbocharging PiPNN for Proximity and $k$-NN Graph Building
papers.abstract:
Graph-based Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search (ANNS) indexes such as HNSW and Vamana deliver state-of-the-art query performance at the cost of large indexing times. The recently introduced PiPNN method drastically accelerated index construction by way of a partitioning-based algorithm leveraging dense matrix multiplication and top-$K$ aggregation kernels.
  In this paper, we unlock the full potential of PiPNN's hardware-friendly algorithm design. We introduce PiPNN II, which optimizes multiple steps of the PiPNN recipe, giving up to $8\times$ speedups for graph-based ANNS index construction. In addition, we present GPiPNN, a GPU implementation which builds comparable ANNS indices up to $43.7\times$ faster than Jasper and up to $50\times$ faster than CAGRA. We also extend PiPNN II and GPiPNN to compute high-quality $k$-NN graphs directly, which unlocks massive speedups over methods used in many existing systems for clustering, anomaly detection, and more. For 10-NN graph building at $90\%$ recall, we obtain up to a $13\times$ speedup on CPUs and $6.6\times$ on GPUs as compared to the prior best methods. PiPNN II can build a billion-scale 10-NN graph in under 16 minutes.
  Common to both PiPNN II and GPiPNN is the use of quantization to reduce memory traffic and leverage fast low-precision matrix operations. Top-$K$ emerges as a new bottleneck, which we optimize with specialized code for specific $K$, and by fusing with the matrix kernel to avoid materializing the distance matrix to memory. On CPUs, we demonstrate further performance improvements by leveraging our matrix kernels in the RobustPrune procedure proposed in Vamana and used in PiPNN. On GPUs, we flatten recursive partitioning into segmented batches, use one fused top-$K$ abstraction for partitioning and leaf scoring, and prune with already-witnessed direct edges rather than new candidate-to-candidate scoring passes.

papers.intro:
Vector embeddings power modern search, recommendation, entity resolution, and retrieval-augmented generation systems (Li et al., 2020; Zeakis et al., 2023; Lewis et al., 2020; Gao et al., 2023; Mitra et al., 2018; Roy and Dutta, 2022; Xiong et al., 2021). These systems rely on approximate nearest-neighbor search (ANNS) because exact search is prohibitively expensive and small errors are tolerable. Graph-based indexes such as HNSW, Vamana (DiskANN), and NSG have become the standard for high-recall, low-latency ANNS (Malkov and Yashunin, 2018; Jayaram Subramanya et al., 2019; Fu et al., 2019). Unfortunately, their excellent query performance has come at the cost of slow index construction: building a high-quality search graph (also termed “proximity graph”) over a large dataset has historically required many hours or even days of compute on powerful multi-core machines (Manohar et al., 2024).

Unfortunately, their excellent query performance has come at the cost of slow index construction: building a high-quality search graph (also termed “proximity graph”) over a large dataset has historically required many hours or even days of compute on powerful multi-core machines (Manohar et al., 2024).

Fast index construction is not merely a convenience: build time is often a major factor in the total cost of the system. Indexes must be rebuilt as data drifts, parameters need to be tuned across datasets, and ANNS appears as an inner loop in fundamental tasks including accelerated kk-means (Spalding-Jamieson et al., 2025), hierarchical clustering (Yu et al., 2025; Dhulipala et al., 2023), minimum spanning trees, and single-linkage clustering (Andoni and Zhang, 2023; Beretta et al., 2025; Azarmehr et al., 2025; Bateni et al., 2017). Small modifications to graph-index construction also yield high-quality kk-NN graphs (Carey et al., 2022), a primitive that we directly target in this paper. An indexing method that takes hours or days is simply unusable in many modern workflows.

The recently introduced Pick-in-Partitions Nearest Neighbors (PiPNN) method significantly speeds up high-quality index construction by replacing build-time graph search with regular partition-local scoring work (Rubel et al., 2026). It recursively partitions the input vectors into small overlapping collections (termed “leaves”), generates candidate edges through batched all-pairs distance comparisons and top-KK aggregation inside each leaf, and streams those candidates through an online history-independent pruning procedure (HashPrune) to retain sparsity. The payoff of this approach is that the existing version of PiPNN is up to 11.6×11.6\times faster than the ParlayANN implementation of Vamana on CPU and produces indexes with equivalent QPS-recall performance (Rubel et al., 2026).

In addition, it processes multiple collections of points in a single kernel using a segmented top-KK primitive, which ameliorates workload imbalances. papers.title: Beyond the Landing Page: Website Blocking, Tracker Visibility, and Human Alignment in Automated Web Crawls
papers.abstract: Web tracking studies largely rely on automated crawlers, yet their measurements can differ from what people encounter while browsing. Conventional crawlers follow predefined navigation rules, whereas LLM-driven agents decide how to navigate and interact with websites, potentially changing the tracking they encounter. We compare agentic and non-agentic crawlers to examine how websites respond to them, what tracking they record, and how closely their observations match human browsing. Across 2,000 popular websites, we evaluate different navigation strategies, automation frameworks, and stealth configurations, alongside browsing data from 26 participants. We find that website denials increase beyond landing pages for standard browser automation, while a detection-resistant automation framework largely prevents this escalation without increasing recorded tracking. On the same URLs, agentic crawlers record tracking activity from 1.5-1.7 times as many third-party organizations, particularly on consent-managed pages. Agentic crawlers recover 82-87% of tracker organizations observed by participants, compared with 58-68% for non-agentic crawlers, yet roughly half of their own observations are absent from human participant visits. These findings show that avoiding website interventions, increasing tracking visibility, and achieving closer agreement with human observations do not necessarily go hand in hand, highlighting the need to select and validate crawlers according to the measurement objective.

papers.intro:
Tracking is pervasive on the Web, raising concerns about users’ privacy and the collection of their browsing data. Understanding the extent of Web tracking is important for assessing these risks and evaluating protections. Yet measuring what people actually encounter while browsing remains difficult. Most large-scale studies instead rely on automated crawlers (Englehardt and Narayanan, 2016; Acar et al., 2014; Iqbal et al., 2021; Vekaria et al., 2025). A crawler, however, is not a neutral observer: its browser configuration, automation framework, and browsing behavior can affect how websites respond and what tracking activity it records (Ahmad et al., 2020; Jueckstock et al., 2021; Cassel et al., 2022). Consequently, automated measurements can differ substantially from human browsing (Zeber et al., 2020). A recent comparison with study participants found that an automated crawl missed fingerprinting on 45% of the websites where participants encountered it, a gap that the authors attributed to authentication, bot detection, and scripts that run only after user interaction (Annamalai et al., 2025).

A recent comparison with study participants found that an automated crawl missed fingerprinting on 45% of the websites where participants encountered it, a gap that the authors attributed to authentication, bot detection, and scripts that run only after user interaction (Annamalai et al., 2025).

More recently, LLM-driven browsing agents have emerged that interpret Web pages and decide how to navigate and interact with them (Zhou et al., 2024; He et al., 2024; Zheng et al., 2024). Unlike traditional crawlers that follow predefined navigation rules, these agents can make context-dependent decisions about which links to follow and which elements to interact with, potentially resembling aspects of human browsing. These differences raise two questions: how does agentic browsing affect the tracking activity that crawlers record, and how do the resulting measurements compare with what people encounter when browsing the Web?

Their stealth variants incorporate browser fingerprint spoofing, with the Chromium variant also using Patchright, a modified version of Playwright designed to reduce automation detection. The two agentic crawlers are an agent built on the browser-use framework (Browser Use, 2026) and SuperScraper, a research crawler we built that perceives pages only through screenshots and acts through operating-system input. Because each crawler chooses its own pages, a non-agentic crawler revisited every URL that the agents had visited, which lets us compare crawlers on identical pages. Our results reveal several ways in which crawler design affects measurement outcomes. First, website denials are similar across configurations on landing pages but increase on subsequent pages for browsers driven by unmodified Playwright. Replacing Playwright with Patchright largely eliminates this escalation, whereas browser fingerprint spoofing and simulated mouse movement do not. Yet Patchright does not increase recorded tracking, demonstrating that avoiding interventions and increasing tracking visibility are distinct. Second, on matched URLs, the agentic crawlers record trackers from 1.5–1.7 times as many organizations as non-agentic crawls. This difference is particularly pronounced on consent-managed pages. The interaction-logging crawl shows that our browser-use agent frequently accepted consent and that confirmed consent actions were followed by additional third-party scripts. Finally, the agentic crawlers recover 82–87% of the tracker organizations observed by participants on shared URLs, compared with 58–68% for non-agentic crawlers. However, only 48–49% of the agents’ own observations also appear in the participant visits. Thus, greater tracking visibility does not necessarily translate into closer agreement with human browsing.

papers.title: Consistent Submodular Maximization with Full Foresight
papers.abstract:
Online algorithms with bounded recourse face three intertwined obstacles: uncertainty about the future, computational limits, and a limited budget for changes. We ask a fundamental question that separates consistency from the other two: what does solution stability cost when the entire future is known and computation is unlimited?
  We answer this question for monotone submodular maximization, where an algorithm must maintain a solution of at most $k$ arrived elements, with a constant number of changes per step. We determine the optimal approximation thresholds: $3/4$ for deterministic algorithms and $\xi^\star \approx 0.7942$ for randomized algorithms. For every $\varepsilon>0$, we get within $\varepsilon$ of these thresholds with worst-case recourse polynomial in $1/\varepsilon$, independent of $k$ and the stream length. We prove matching impossibility results even for coverage functions.
  We attain the sharp bounds by optimally balancing two opposing forces: preparing for future arrivals and protecting the current solution. For randomized algorithms, we use addition robustness against prefixes of the known future, which we analyze tightly via an interval-selection problem. For deterministic algorithms, we introduce certificates, paths in a fractional relaxation that maintain high value, which we round into an update schedule.

papers.intro:
Online algorithms with recourse have emerged as a central paradigm for optimization over evolving inputs: they maintain good solutions as the input changes, while limiting how much these solutions change, either at each update or in aggregate over the entire sequence. This paradigm has been developed for a broad range of fundamental problems, including Steiner trees (Imase and Waxman, 1991; Gu et al., 2016), minimum spanning trees and TSP (Megow et al., 2016), scheduling (Sanders et al., 2009), bin packing (Feldkord et al., 2018), set cover (Gupta et al., 2017), bipartite matching (Bosek et al., 2014; Bernstein et al., 2019), kk-clustering (Lattanzi and Vassilvitskii, 2017; Fichtenberger et al., 2021), and submodular maximization (Dütting et al., 2024; Dütting et al., 2025).

We study this question for monotone submodular maximization under a cardinality constraint (Nemhauser et al., 1978; Krause and Golovin, 2014). We give the algorithm full knowledge of the arrival sequence and unrestricted computational power. Each maintained solution must use only elements that have already arrived, and consecutive solutions may differ by only a constant number of elements. Even with full foresight, preparing a solution for future arrivals can compromise its current value, while postponing changes can leave too little time to complete them. The challenge is to plan solutions and transitions that remain close to the current optimum while respecting the recourse bound.

papers.title: HELIX: HEterogeneous LLM Inference with FleXible and Fine-Grained Partitioning
papers.abstract: LLM inference is inherently heterogeneous, with performance bottlenecks shifting throughout inference phases down to individual operators. This has motivated heterogeneous serving systems that disaggregate execution across specialized accelerators, typically through fixed partitions such as prefill/decode or attention/FFN. However, these approaches commit to a partitioning strategy in advance, limiting their ability to adapt to different workloads and model architectures while forcing emerging accelerators into predefined roles. We present HELIX, a vLLM-based software stack that discovers, compiles and dispatches workload-aware partitions across heterogeneous accelerators at the operator granularity. At engine initialization, HELIX automatically determines hardware-specific operator placements that minimize execution latency, accounting for profiled execution costs, communication overheads, device capabilities, and memory constraints. It combines dynamic programming, piecewise compilation, and heterogeneous subgraph dispatch, enabling accelerators with partial operator coverage to participate in LLM inference without predefined model partitions. HELIX provides an open-source unified framework for exploring, evaluating, and integrating heterogeneous accelerators for LLM inference, lowering the barrier to emerging hardware by exposing them as subgraph executors. In systems combining H100 and B200 GPUs with emerging accelerators, HELIX resolves LLM partitions that multi-query decoding latency by up to 3$\times$ for dense and sparse transformer models and up to 3.5$\times$ for hybrid state-space models, relative to standard attention-FFN disaggregation.

papers.intro:
The rapid adoption of LLMs for conversational assistants, code synthesis and complex reasoning tasks has made inference efficiency a first-order systems concern.

The rapid adoption of LLMs for conversational assistants, code synthesis and complex reasoning tasks has made inference efficiency a first-order systems concern.

Achieving efficient hardware mapping requires recognizing that LLM inference is far from monolithic, as the hardware demands it imposes vary substantially depending on which stage of the inference pipeline is examined. At the phase level, prefill processes the input prompt in parallel and is predominantly compute-bound, whereas decode generates tokens in an auto-regressive fashion and is typically bandwidth-bound. This asymmetry has motivated prefill/decode (P/D) disaggregation Qin et al. (2025); Zhong et al. (2024), which assigns each phase to a dedicated hardware pool optimized for its respective bottleneck (see Figure 1a). Within the decode phase itself, a similar asymmetry emerges at the operator level: for high-concurrency multi-query serving, feed-forward networks (FFN) amortize the large set of weight parameters fetched from memory to generate multiple tokens. Instead, attention is strictly memory-bound as each new token must attend over the entire growing KV-cache, requiring repeated memory reads that scale with sequence length rather than reuse of loaded data. This operator-level asymmetry has encouraged Attention–FFN (A/F) disaggregated systems Team (2025); Liang et al. (2025); Zhu et al. (2025); Aubrey and Ghodsian (2026), which map attention and FFN or expert layers onto separate resources (see Figure 1b). However, even these operator-level bottlenecks are not invariant. At the workload level, batch size modulates the arithmetic intensity of FFN kernels during decode He et al. (2025), since larger batches amortize the loaded weights. Therefore, variations in the serving scenario can cause individual kernels to transition between memory- and compute-bound regimes, making them better suited to different hardware architectures.

This heterogeneity has led to the development of disaggregated inference systems, with A/F emerging as a prominent direction. Beyond GPU-only deployments, the introduction of specialized accelerators has also encouraged heterogeneous disaggregation, since hardware properties favor specific operators, such as LPU-based FFN offloading from GPU Aubrey and Ghodsian (2026) and DRAM process-in-memory (PIM) for memory-bound attention Park et al. (2024); He et al. (2025); Hong et al. (2026). These heterogeneous systems commonly use model-specific partition boundaries and focus the disaggregation decision on the sharding exploration rather than jointly deciding fine-grained placements down to the individual operators. The disaggregation strategy is inherited from the A/F framing and never revisited against the particular model, hardware combination and serving scenario. As hardware architectures diversify, fixed partition boundaries cannot account for the trade-offs introduced by combining different hardware capabilities, adopting new model structures, and varying serving regimes. This paper argues that LLM serving must be rebuilt around dynamic, fine-grained partitioning. Here, dynamic denotes deployment-specific placement resolved during compilation time. What to offload and where to place it are decision variables searched over the LLM computational graph and resolved against the hardware’s capabilities, interconnect and computation cost for a model and a target serving regime. We formulate partitioning as a dynamic programming problem over the LLM computational graph. Using profiled per-operator execution and communication costs, our method finds latency-minimizing partitions for a given model, hardware configuration, and serving regime. We present HELIX, a heterogeneous execution stack built on vLLM Kwon et al. (2023), which compiles and executes partitioned LLM graphs across available accelerators. Figure 1 places our approach in this landscape, moving from static P/D and A/F toward the dynamic partitioning that accommodates workloads, models, and hardware pool. In summary, this paper makes the following contributions: • We develop a profile-guided dynamic programming method for partitioning search to determine, at compilation time, how to split LLM inference stages across heterogeneous hardware, given workload, system, and model. • We design HELIX, a heterogeneous execution stack built on vLLM, that along with resolving partitions, runs LLM inference across the available devices, backed by pluggable per-device profilers and backends. • We evaluate HELIX on dense Transformer, MoE, and hybrid SSM models across four hardware platforms and four heterogeneous configurations where found partitions can reduce multi-query decoding latency up to 3.5×\times compared to attention-FFN disaggregation.

papers.title: Conjugator length of Bestvina-Brady groups
papers.abstract: We classify the conjugator length functions of Bestvina-Brady groups. We show that the conjugator length function, when non-trivial, grows as a linear or quadratic polynomial. In fact, we give explicit criteria on the defining graph to determine the precise degree of the polynomial. The proof generalises ideas of Bridson, Riley, and Sale by exploiting the framework developed by Chang and the authors to classify the Dehn functions of Bestvina-Brady groups.

Formulated by Dehn, over a century ago, the Conjugacy Problem is one of the three decision problems for finitely generated groups [Deh11]; it asks for an algorithm to determine whether two words on the generators of a group represent conjugate elements. Geometrically, if the group is the fundamental group of a manifold MM, this problem asks if two loops in MM are freely homotopic to each other.

Formulated by Dehn, over a century ago, the Conjugacy Problem is one of the three decision problems for finitely generated groups [Deh11]; it asks for an algorithm to determine whether two words on the generators of a group represent conjugate elements. Geometrically, if the group is the fundamental group of a manifold MM, this problem asks if two loops in MM are freely homotopic to each other.

The first problem posed by Dehn, the Word Problem, asks whether there is an algorithm that decides if a given word represents the identity in the group. Since the conjugacy class of the identity is itself, the Word Problem can be thought as a special case of the Conjugacy Problem. As there are groups with unsolvable Word Problem, there are groups with unsolvable Conjugacy Problem [Nov54, Nov58, Boo59]. Remarkably, there are groups with solvable Word Problem, but with unsolvable Conjugacy Problem [Bok68, Col69, Mil71, OS20].

papers.title: Correct Robots Before They Make Mistakes: Proactive Human-in-the-Loop Intervention via Preference Learning
papers.abstract: This paper presents Proactive Human-in-the-Loop (PHIL), a framework for proactive policy correction and preference-based post-training. PHIL enables operators to preview policy-predicted future motion and intervene before anticipated undesirable actions. During takeover, PHIL continues querying the policy and displaying its predicted trajectories in the physical workspace through an extended reality (XR) interface. PHIL pairs rejected policy predictions with corrective action chunks subsequently executed from the same physical state over the same horizon, and preference-based post-training encourages the policy to favor these corrections. This paper evaluates PHIL on four real-world manipulation tasks using a diffusion policy and a pretrained vision-language-action policy. With five correction episodes per condition, PHIL increases mean success rates across the evaluated tasks and demonstration budgets from 44.0% to 70.3% for the diffusion policy and from 57.8% to 76.9% for X-VLA, compared with HG-DAgger. Separately, policies trained with proactive corrections show fewer unnecessary recovery behaviors in successful episodes. Project page: https://intuitive-robots.github.io/PHIL-page/.

papers.intro:
Robot policies, including visuomotor policies and vision-language-action (VLA) models, have shown strong performance on a broad range of manipulation tasks. However, policies trained from offline demonstrations may still encounter states that are beyond the coverage of their training data. In such situations, the policy may produce undesirable motions or fail to complete the task. Improving performance in such cases requires additional task-specific data.

Robot policies, including visuomotor policies and vision-language-action (VLA) models, have shown strong performance on a broad range of manipulation tasks. However, policies trained from offline demonstrations may still encounter states that are beyond the coverage of their training data. In such situations, the policy may produce undesirable motions or fail to complete the task. Improving performance in such cases requires additional task-specific data.

Human-in-the-loop imitation learning addresses this gap by collecting corrective data during policy rollouts. During these rollouts, the policy may visit states that are absent from, or underrepresented in the offline demonstrations. Most existing human-in-the-loop methods collect correction data reactively. In reactive correction, the operator decides whether to intervene based on the robot’s currently observed execution, without a preview of the policy’s predicted future motion. It is straightforward to deploy and allows corrective data to be collected during policy rollouts. The resulting recovery actions can also be valuable when the robot must recover from an error and retry a task [11]. This approach has enabled effective policy refinement through interactive data aggregation, remote teleoperation, and corrective residual control [14, 17, 23]. When reactive corrections begin after an error has occurred, they include recovery actions in addition to actions that advance the task. The proportion of reactive correction data in the dataset can affect how often recovery motions appear in the policy output. A higher proportion increases the likelihood of producing recovery motions even when no recovery is needed.

The proportion of reactive correction data in the dataset can affect how often recovery motions appear in the policy output. A higher proportion increases the likelihood of producing recovery motions even when no recovery is needed.

These limitations motivate proactive correction, in which the operator reviews the policy’s proposed motion and provides corrections before an anticipated error occurs. By visualizing the policy’s predicted future motion, proactive correction enables the operator to identify and correct potential errors before the robot enters safety-critical states. This predictive preview reduces the operator’s cognitive burden of continuously anticipating the policy’s behavior. It can also reduce the need for repeated reactive corrections as an error unfolds. Although proactive correction shows considerable promise, it has received limited attention. Existing work has considered simulated tasks in autonomous driving and robotic manipulation [2], while its application to complex physical robot manipulation remains unexplored. Extending proactive correction to such tasks requires an interface that allows the operator to intuitively assess the robot’s proposed three-dimensional motion before an anticipated error occurs. Although a screen-based preview can overlay this motion on a camera view, judging its depth and spatial orientation from a two-dimensional display can be difficult. To address this challenge, we propose PHIL, a proactive human-in-the-loop imitation learning framework that uses an Extended Reality (XR) interface to visualize proposed policy action chunks in the physical workspace. Each action chunk is converted into a sequence of three-dimensional end-effector poses and spatially registered with the physical workspace. The operator can therefore inspect upcoming motion in three dimensions within its execution context while the robot executes the current action chunk.

Extending proactive correction to such tasks requires an interface that allows the operator to intuitively assess the robot’s proposed three-dimensional motion before an anticipated error occurs. Although a screen-based preview can overlay this motion on a camera view, judging its depth and spatial orientation from a two-dimensional display can be difficult. To address this challenge, we propose PHIL, a proactive human-in-the-loop imitation learning framework that uses an Extended Reality (XR) interface to visualize proposed policy action chunks in the physical workspace. Each action chunk is converted into a sequence of three-dimensional end-effector poses and spatially registered with the physical workspace. The operator can therefore inspect upcoming motion in three dimensions within its execution context while the robot executes the current action chunk.

When the preview indicates that the proposed motion may lead to an error, the operator takes control and provides corrections before the anticipated undesirable action occurs. During the takeover, PHIL continues to query the policy at the unchanged query schedule and display updated action chunks in the XR headset. PHIL constructs contrastive pairs from the displayed policy action chunks and the corresponding executed corrective robot trajectories. For each retained policy query during intervention, the displayed action chunk is recorded as rejected, denoted by At−A_{t}^{-}. The next HH executed robot actions starting at that query form the corresponding corrective action chunk At+A_{t}^{+}, which may include policy-controlled actions after release. Both action chunks in each pair start from the same physical state. When the operator judges the most recently displayed action chunk to be acceptable, they release control and the robot returns to policy control. After data collection, PHIL uses the contrastive pairs to fine-tune the policy, encouraging it to favor executed corrective action chunks At+A_{t}^{+} over rejected policy action chunks At−A_{t}^{-} from the same physical state. We evaluate PHIL on four real-world manipulation tasks, with experiments covering both diffusion and pretrained VLA policies. Compared with HG-DAgger, PHIL increases the average success rate from 44.0% to 70.3% for the diffusion policy and from 57.8% to 76.9% for X-VLA. Proactive correction data reduce unnecessary recovery behaviors approximately tenfold compared with reactive correction data.

papers.title: Single-crystal X-ray diffraction of BC8 carbon near terapascal pressures
papers.abstract: Whether carbon forms crystalline structures beyond diamond at terapascal pressures remains unresolved. Predicted for nearly four decades, the denser BC8 phase has lacked direct crystallographic evidence. Here we report the first direct crystallographic identification of BC8 carbon, formed as a single crystal from molten carbon during laser-driven decaying-shock compression of [100]-oriented diamond following loading above 1.1 TPa. Using in situ orientation-resolved single-crystal X-ray diffraction, we observe discrete Bragg spots whose spacings and angular relationships are reproduced by a common orientation matrix within each indexed BC8 reflection group, providing constraints beyond powder peak matching. Our single-crystal formation strategy and direct diffraction evidence resolve the decades-long quest for a post-diamond carbon structure, demonstrating how dynamic loading pathways can make predicted high-pressure phases experimentally accessible.

papers.title: The Kato square root property for fractional elliptic operators in divergence form
papers.abstract:
We establish the Kato square root property for fractional elliptic operators $L = -\operatorname{div}^\alpha(\mu 
abla^\alpha \cdot)$ of order $2\alpha \in (0,2)$ on $\mathbb{R}^d$, built from the Riesz fractional gradient and divergence, with bounded, measurable and uniformly elliptic complex coefficients $\mu$. More precisely, we show that the domain of $L^{1/2}$ coincides with the distributional fractional Sobolev space $\mathrm{S}^{\alpha,2}(\mathbb{R}^d)$ and that $\|L^{1/2} u\|_{\mathrm{L}^2} \simeq \|
abla^\alpha u\|_{\mathrm{L}^2}$, with constants that are locally uniform in $\alpha$. As a consequence, we recover the Kato square root property for elliptic operators $-\operatorname{div}(\mu
abla\cdot)$ in the limit $\alpha 	o 1$, and we obtain continuity of the square root with respect to the parameter $\alpha$. The proof follows the second-order approach to the Kato problem. Its two new ingredients are nonlocal off-diagonal estimates of polynomial order for the resolvents of $L$, and a construction of $T(b)$-test functions that circumvents the nonlocality of $
abla^\alpha$ by factorizing it through Riesz potentials.

papers.title: Phase matching and mode coupling in photonic-crystal ring resonators
papers.abstract: Photonic-crystal ring resonators, in which periodic refractive-index modulations couple counter-propagating modes, have become a widely used platform for nonlinear photonics, offering mode-by-mode dispersion engineering. When several modulation components are superimposed, their relative angular alignment (phase) is an additional degree of freedom whose impact on the nonlinear dynamics has remained unclear. Here we show that the relative phases between the modulation patterns have a decisive impact. Through the interference of the nonlinear processes in forward and backward direction, they add a phase and mode selection rule to the established phase-matching conditions, which can fully suppress nonlinear coupling. They also impose a relative spectral chirp between forward- and backward-propagating waveforms. We illustrate these effects for parametric oscillation and dissipative Kerr solitons. Our results extend the concept of phase matching to resonators with interfering nonlinear pathways and establish the alignment of index gratings as a design dimension for nonlinear microresonators.

papers.title: Generative Learning on Dynamic Text-Attributed Graphs
papers.abstract: Dynamic text-attributed graphs capture evolving interactions among entities with rich textual information, but future-link prediction remains difficult when nodes have little interaction history or appear as new targets. We propose \method, a generative framework that represents nodes with compact semantic identifiers (SIDs) learned from text and autoregressively predicts a target SID conditioned on the source SID, recent interaction events, and relative time gaps. A lightweight structural calibration further incorporates repetition, co-occurrence, and popularity. At inference time, \method encodes each query context once and reuses SID likelihoods to rank prescribed candidates, providing a candidate-efficient prediction interface. Experiments on nine datasets show broadly competitive performance across domains and graph densities. Source-side inductive evaluations demonstrate that text-derived SIDs provide a useful representation when a test source has no observed interaction history, while two recommendation-oriented case studies evaluate controlled new-user adaptation and first-arrival ranking for inductive new items. Further analyses characterize SID uniqueness, capacity, and temporal stability. Overall, the results support combining text-derived SIDs with temporal histories for dynamic link prediction.

Dynamic graphs capture evolving interactions in applications such as online review platforms, social networks, collaborative knowledge bases, recommender systems, and citation networks (Feng et al., 2026; Li et al., 2024a; Pareja et al., 2020). These interactions are often accompanied by rich textual attributes, including reviews, posts, profiles, item descriptions, paper abstracts, and relation descriptions (Zhang et al., 2024; Peng et al., 2025). As these graphs evolve, a key challenge is how to combine textual semantics with temporal interaction evidence when nodes have highly uneven interaction histories.

Such data naturally form dynamic text-attributed graphs (DyTAGs), where temporal structure and textual attributes jointly shape dynamic graph learning (Lei et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2026). As these graphs evolve, a key challenge is how to combine textual semantics with temporal interaction evidence when nodes have highly uneven interaction histories.

This challenge is particularly evident across source-history regimes (Li et al., 2024b; Zheng et al., 2023). For inductive or rarely active source nodes, structural evidence is weak or absent, making textual attributes the primary history-independent signal. A diagnostic with DyGFormer illustrates this gap: on Wikirevision, IMDB, and Weibo-Daily, its Hits@10 for sources with no training or validation interactions is only 54%, 17%, and 2%, respectively, of that for sources with more than ten prior interactions. This disparity motivates a model that relies on text-derived semantics when source history is unavailable and progressively incorporates event-level temporal evidence as interactions accumulate.

Most dynamic graph learning methods follow a discriminative prediction paradigm. Memory-based methods maintain node states updated by interaction streams (Rossi et al., 2020; Kumar et al., 2019; Trivedi et al., 2019; Tian et al., 2023), while neighborhood- and sequence-based methods encode temporal neighborhoods or interaction histories (Xu et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2021; Yu et al., 2023; Cong et al., 2023). Despite architectural differences, they typically predict future interactions by scoring sampled or enumerated candidate targets. As illustrated in Figure 1, discriminative methods score candidate targets directly, whereas generative methods model the identifier of the next target. Recent generative retrieval approaches represent targets as sequences of discrete semantic codes and autoregressively estimate their likelihoods (Rajput et al., 2023; Ju et al., 2025; Tay et al., 2022). papers.title: Compounding Physical RSI: Turning Execution Failure into Inherited Capability
papers.abstract:
Generalist robot policies are trained on static offline datasets, yet physical manipulation unfolds sequentially across stages. Because a weakness in a downstream stage remains unobservable until the policy passes earlier ones, each resolved bottleneck exposes the next hidden failure mode. This staged structure calls for Recursive Self-Improvement (RSI), in which a policy iteratively executes, diagnoses failures, and updates itself. Moreover, because task completion behaves like a product of stage-level pass rates, recursive gains can multiply across generations. In physical environments, three bottlenecks obstruct compounding: terminal execution feedback rarely localizes the stage that caused a failure, failed trajectories do not supply the corrective action, and updating shared parameters can degrade previously mastered skills.
  We propose Compounding Physical RSI, a self-evolving policy framework that turns execution failures into heritable capability. First, automated capability-gap assessment traces failed rollouts to the task stage where progression breaks down and formulates a structured improvement objective. This limitation stems from the sequential, stage-gated nature of manipulation. A robot must approach an object before grasping it, and must establish a stable grasp before transporting or placing it. Consequently, a deficiency in a downstream stage remains masked until the policy reliably passes all preceding stages: a policy that fails during grasping never reveals how it would fail during transport, because its rollouts never reach that state. Moreover, the failure modes encountered during transport depend directly on the contact configuration produced by the grasp, as each policy induces its own closed-loop state distribution [12]. We define the earliest task stage that a policy cannot yet pass reliably as its capability frontier. Because behavior beyond this frontier remains unobserved during execution, a fixed dataset cannot anticipate how the evolving policy will fail once it crosses the current barrier. Each successful fix advances the capability frontier and exposes the next latent failure mode.

Rooted in classical formulations of self-referential learning [13, 14] and renewed in modern foundation-model research [15], RSI recognizes that when a policy’s next bottleneck becomes visible only after the current one is resolved, improvement cannot be reduced to a single static training run. Second, failed rollouts lack corrective supervision: even a precisely localized failure shows what went wrong without specifying the counterfactual action the policy should have executed. papers.title: Using AI Predictions to Augment Rather Than Replace Surveys
papers.abstract: LLMs can predict human survey responses with nontrivial accuracy. What this means for the future of social surveys remains hotly contested. Optimists anticipate a coming era of synthetic respondents; skeptics see a fragile and overhyped substitute. This article advocates a position: AI predictions cannot replace surveys, but they can augment them. Using prediction-powered inference (PPI), a statistical framework rooted in survey methodology and known in sociology as "mixed subjects design", the study tests whether AI predictions can improve the statistical efficiency of social surveys when combined with census-scale auxiliary information. Applying the framework to 83 social outcomes in the General Social Survey (GSS) and National Health Interview Survey (NHIS), with American Community Survey (ACS) being the auxiliary file, we find that supervised predictors yield effective-sample-size gains of about 7-12 percent when estimating the mean, while LLM gains are smaller but positive.

AI is no longer a distant future; it is already part of the infrastructure of social science. Across fields, predictive systems now support tasks ranging from classification to simulation. Sociology has entered this moment as well, as generative models increasingly shape debates about measurement and routine research practice (Bail 2024; Alvero et al. 2026).

A separate trend sociologists are facing is the increasing difficulty of fielding social surveys. When these two trends meet, we see an emerging interest in the use of AI for social surveys. Large language models can be prompted with demographic profiles and then requested to answer common social survey questions, and they often produce responses that resemble human answers in nontrivial ways (Argyle et al. 2023; Santurkar et al. 2023; Bisbee et al. 2024; Kim and Lee 2023; Rosenbusch et al. 2023; Xie et al. 2026). Supervised learning trained on earlier survey waves can also predict many survey outcomes from demographic and socioeconomic covariates (Salganik et al. 2020; Zheng and Cheng 2025; Rahal et al. 2024). These results make it tempting to imagine a future in which surveys become smaller, with predictive models filling in what humans would have said.

That temptation requires caution. AI-generated survey responses can contain arbitrary and hard-to-audit bias. They can be too centered or under-dispersed, muting the heterogeneity that surveys are designed to measure. They can also be too discriminative, reproducing stereotypes or group-specific distortions in the name of prediction (Santurkar et al. 2023; Bisbee et al. 2024; Kozlowski and Evans 2025; Westwood 2025; Xie et al. 2026).

Treating AI predictions as replacements for survey responses gives models more authority than their bias can support. Discarding those predictions altogether leaves useful information unused. We advocate a middle path, using AI predictions to augment actual surveys. A prediction can be wrong in level or distribution and still be useful if it is correlated with the true outcome. That correlation lets the model summarize the part of the outcome that is predictable from observed covariates in a large auxiliary file. The probability survey then measures prediction error by comparing predicted and observed responses among sampled humans. The resulting estimator uses AI for the predictable component and uses the survey to correct what AI misses, preserving design-based validity while reducing sampling variability.

Prediction-powered inference (PPI) formalizes this augmentation strategy (Angelopoulos et al. 2023; Angelopoulos et al. 2024; Zrnic and Candès 2024b). Its central operation is outcome prediction followed by correction. Predictions on a large unlabeled file are combined with a correction estimated from observed outcomes in a smaller labeled sample. In our application, we also incorporate survey weights to account for the sampling designs, whereas prediction-powered augmentation uses additional information to improve precision. For mean estimation, this correction follows the logic of the classical difference estimator, linking PPI to the model-assisted survey tradition (Cassel et al. 1976; Deville and Särndal 1992; Särndal et al. 1992; Breidt and Opsomer 2017; Mozer 2026).

PPI is especially useful when collecting additional observed outcomes is expensive but a much larger unlabeled file from the same population distribution is available. The objective is to improve precision for the same inferential target, not to establish representativeness or justify extrapolation to a different population. Gains depend on whether predictions sufficiently reduce the variation that must be estimated from the labeled sample; a large unlabeled file alone does not guarantee improvement. Social surveys offer an important application because additional interviews are costly, while files such as the American Community Survey (ACS), harmonized through IPUMS, provide compatible covariates for many more individuals without measuring the focal survey outcomes.

We test how much PPI can help with routine quantitative tasks in sociology, including estimating population means and estimating regression coefficients. We apply the framework to a range of opinion outcomes in the General Social Survey (GSS) and health outcomes in the National Health Interview Survey (NHIS), with ACS as the auxiliary file. We compare historical supervised learning, cross-fitted supervised learning, and LLM respondent simulation, and we evaluate both predictive performance and downstream inferential gain. For mean estimation, supervised predictors yield effective-sample-size gains of about 7 to 12 percent, while LLM gains are smaller. In this benchmark, gains are generally larger for health outcomes than opinion outcomes and for means than regression coefficients. These differences matter for how researchers use PPI: a predictor that improves estimation of an outcome mean may provide little benefit for an adjusted demographic association. Predictors should therefore be evaluated for the intended estimand, rather than by outcome-level predictive accuracy alone.

papers.title: Energetic Nonthermal Electrons within the Above-the-looptop Regions in Solar Flares: Acceleration, Feedback, and Quasi-Periodic Pulsations
papers.abstract:
Solar flares are among the most dramatic events in the solar system, releasing substantial magnetic energy and accelerating a large number of electrons to high energies. Notably, in certain events, the above-the-looptop region may contain a significant population of nonthermal electrons, both in number and energy. For the first time, we adopt a novel numerical method that combines magnetohydrodynamics with energetic particles incorporating feedback from nonthermal electrons to investigate electron acceleration and transport in solar flares. We find that a large fraction of energetic electrons are accelerated via the current sheet and termination shock regions. Most energetic electrons are concentrated in the above-the-looptop region, carrying a sizable amount of the released energy.
  We observe that greater feedback of nonthermal electrons leads to steeper energy spectra. The energy density of the nonthermal electrons oscillates due to the periodic impact of magnetic islands into the above-the-looptop, which may help explain the observed quasi-periodic pulsations (QPPs). Our simulations provide new insights into the origin of nonthermal electrons and associated emissions in the above-the-looptop region.

A significant portion of the released energy is believed to be carried by nonthermal electrons [39, 52, 53, 66, e.g.,], and understanding the mechanisms behind their acceleration remains a central focus of solar flare research.

A significant portion of the released energy is believed to be carried by nonthermal electrons [39, 52, 53, 66, e.g.,], and understanding the mechanisms behind their acceleration remains a central focus of solar flare research.

The multi-wavelength emissions (hard X-rays and microwaves), generated by these accelerated electrons, provide valuable insights into particle acceleration, transport, and radiation processes. These observations have revealed that nonthermal electrons typically exhibit a power-law energy spectrum, f⁡(ε)∝ε−δf(\varepsilon)\propto\varepsilon^{-\delta}, with a median spectral index of δ∼5\delta\sim 5 [39, 52, 53, 19]. Hard X-ray observations suggest that, in certain events, a significant fraction of electrons are accelerated into the nonthermal range, carrying energy comparable to the released magnetic energy [39, 52, 53]. Especially, recent EOVSA observations along with other multiwavelength observations have provided unprecedented imaging spectroscopy of the X8.2-class eruptive flare event SOL2017-09-10 [23, 12, 20]. These observations show that the nonthermal electrons are partially confined to the above-the-looptop region with a relatively weak magnetic strength, referred to as the “magnetic bottle” [35, 12, 11]. It has been suggested that the above-the-looptop region is the primary region for energetic particle acceleration and trapping in this event, although further studies are needed to see if this is a universal scenario.
