papers.title: ReveaLLAGN 2: Exploring the Nuclear Gas and Stellar Kinematics of Nearby LLAGNs with JWST/NIRSpec IFU
papers.abstract: Low-luminosity active galactic nuclei (LLAGN) represent the most common mode of black hole accretion in the local Universe, yet their nuclear structure, stellar and gas kinematics remain poorly constrained at parsec scales. We investigate the nuclear regions of eight nearby representative LLAGN, the ReveaLLAGN sample: M87, M104, M94, M81, NGC1052, NGC4258, NGC5128 and NGC4395. Using JWST/NIRSpec data, we probe the stellar, molecular hydrogen, hydrogen recombination, and high ionisation coronal lines kinematics and their spatial distribution, exploring how detectability and spatial distributions of these lines vary across different Eddington ratios. The stellar LOSV maps reveal a slowly rotating disk in the nuclei of all our targets, characterised by an anti-correlation with the h3 Gauss-Hermite moment. Across the sample, the stellar velocity dispersion rises toward the central black hole. Only in M104 and M94 does the velocity dispersion display a more intricate pattern that departs from a simple disk configuration, indicating the presence of multiple kinematic components in these galaxies. Across the sample, the gas distribution and kinematics exhibit rotation that is frequently decoupled from the stellar rotation, suggesting that the stellar gravitational potential is decoupled from the current accretion state. The gas kinematics are often visually aligned with the radio jet, presenting broader velocity dispersions along the jet direction. Line-ratio maps indicate that the dominant excitation mechanism is photoionisation by the central AGN, with mechanical heating from shocks becoming important only at higher Eddington ratios. Across the sample, we detect coronal lines in all LLAGN when using nuclear-aperture spectra, and we can obtain spatially resolved kinematics only in NGC5128 and NGC4395, the highest Eddington ratio sources.

papers.intro:
The majority of supermassive black holes (SMBHs) accrete material from their surrounding accretion disks at rates far below the theoretical Eddington limit (Hasinger et al., 2005; Ho, 2008). This is commonly expressed in terms of the Eddington ratio, defined as the ratio between their bolometric luminosity (Lbol) and their Eddington luminosity (LEdd). Such systems are referred to as low-luminosity active galactic nuclei (LLAGN) and are distinguished by Eddington ratios of ≲0.01\lesssim 0.01. The majority of supermassive black holes (SMBHs) accrete material from their surrounding accretion disks at rates far below the theoretical Eddington limit (Hasinger et al., 2005; Ho, 2008). This is commonly expressed in terms of the Eddington ratio, defined as the ratio between their bolometric luminosity (Lbol) and their Eddington luminosity (LEdd). Such systems are referred to as low-luminosity active galactic nuclei (LLAGN) and are distinguished by Eddington ratios of ≲0.01\lesssim 0.01. Although LLAGN are far more numerous than their high-Eddington ratio counterparts (Hasinger et al., 2005; Ho, 2008), they remain relatively poorly understood because their intrinsic emission is weak, making it challenging to disentangle the nuclear contribution from the host galaxy light.

In contrast to quasars and Seyfert galaxies, LLAGN may also exhibit different accretion flows: the gas density is reduced, making the inner accretion disk optically thin and geometrically thick, so that the inflowing gas radiates inefficiently and forms a radiatively inefficient accretion flow (RIAF) (Narayan and Yi, 1995; Quataert, 2001, e.g.). As a result, LLAGN tend to show a diminished or absent broad-line region (Elitzur and Ho, 2009; Elitzur et al., 2014, e.g.), a truncated or absent accretion disk (Yuan et al., 2009; Eracleous et al., 2010; Taam et al., 2012; Nemmen et al., 2014; Fernández-Ontiveros et al., 2023, e.g.), and lacking the “blue bump” seen in brighter AGN(Ho, 1999; Yuan and Narayan, 2014). Additionally, LLAGN observations also reveal a similar correlation between X-ray emission from the hot corona and the infrared emission from dust reprocessing, as observed in brighter AGN (Kotilainen et al., 1992; Alonso-Herrero et al., 1996; Civano et al., 2012; Burtscher et al., 2015; Müller-Sánchez et al., 2018; Ohlson, submitted and others, 2026), suggesting a possible scaled down AGN scenario for LLAGN. But deviations from this correlation have been found at extremely low-luminosities (Dumont et al., 2020).

The mass of the central SMBH is a fundamental parameter to characterize the AGN. Dynamical measurements of black holes masses in nearby galaxies have revealed a correlation between the SMBH mass (MBH) and the stellar velocity dispersion of the host bulge (σe\sigma_{{\rm e}}), known as the MBH–σe\sigma_{\rm e} relation (McConnell and Ma, 2013; Kormendy and Ho, 2013; Saglia et al., 2016, e.g.). This key relationship is based on both gas and stellar dynamical measurements. The consistency of these methods has been tested only in a handful of cases (Neumayer et al., 2007; Cappellari et al., 2009; Feldmeier et al., 2014; Feldmeier-Krause et al., 2017; Krajnović et al., 2018; Davis et al., 2020, e.g), and the measurements do not always agree (Ferrarese et al., 1996; de Francesco et al., 2006; Walsh et al., 2012; Walsh et al., 2013; Gebhardt et al., 2011; Thater et al., 2021, e.g). Since MBH is small compared to the galaxy bulge mass (∼0.3%\sim 0.3\%) (McConnell and Ma, 2013) gravitational influence cannot explain the MBH–σe\sigma_{\rm e} relation, and instead radiation pressure from AGN feedback is thought to be responsible. This relation suggests that SMBHs and their host galaxies may have grown in lockstep, with SMBHs potentially playing a significant role in galaxy formation (Croton et al., 2006, e.g.).

AGN feedback can be radiative, or be due to shocks or outflows from a jet. This feedback can be traced through its impacts on the gas surrounding the AGN, disturbing its kinematics and changing its ionization state. The gas and jet interaction becomes particularly important at low accretion rates, because LLAGNs show a possibly enhanced jet activity (Ho, 2002; Sikora et al., 2007; Ho, 2008, e.g.). Jets can accelerate and compress the gas and produce shocks. These process can produce observable non-circular signatures in the gas kinematics (Riffel et al., 2008; Davies et al., 2009; Hicks et al., 2009; Shimizu et al., 2019; Riffel et al., 2020, e.g). Jets have also been observed to be responsible for producing extended coronal emission in some LLAGNs (May et al., 2018; Rodríguez-Ardila et al., 2025). In the ReveaLLAGN sample, Goold et al. (2024) suggested that outflows may explain the increase in emission line broadening with ionization potential observed in some LLAGNs. Goold et al. (2026) found also that kinetic mode feedback may explain the higher excitation temperatures of molecular hydrogen in the ReveaLLAGN sample compared to brighter AGNs. At the same time, AGN feedback is closely linked to the availability of gas that can fuel SMBH accretion. Inflow of cold molecular gas in LLAGNs has been observed (Combes et al., 2013, e.g) as well as inflow of warm molecular gas, for example in the LINER NGC 1097 (Davies et al., 2009) and the Galactic Center (Hsieh et al., 2017). In other cases, such as NGC 5128, no signs of inflows are observed in the warm gas but there is a compact rotating disk (Quillen et al., 2010; Espada et al., 2017), indicating large reservoirs of gas in nuclear regions. Whether cold gas can reach the vicinity of the SMBH in LLAGNs, as observed in Seyfert galaxies, remains unclear. The enhanced radio loudness of LLAGNs compared with brighter AGNs may indicate that jets can expel gas before it reaches the innermost regions. One example is M87, whose jet has a very wide base, potentially consistent with this scenario (Ly et al., 2007, e.g.).

The James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) integral field units (IFU) provide unmatched sensitivity and spatial resolution in the near- to mid-infrared range (1.7–28 μ\mum)) (Böker et al., 2022; Wells et al., 2015; Argyriou et al., 2023), enabling detailed mapping of both stellar emission and ionized/molecular gas tracers in the nuclear regions of LLAGN. Compared with classical optical coronal lines, NIR coronal lines are less affected by dust obscuration and less contaminated by star formation from the host galaxy, making them distinct signatures of LLAGN accretion (Satyapal et al., 2021).

papers.title: From the quantum group $U_{q^{1/2}}( {\widehat {\mathfrak{sl}}}_2 )$ to the Kronecker quantum cluster algebra
papers.abstract: Let $\mathcal A_q$ be the Kronecker quantum cluster algebra with principal coefficients. We construct an explicit algebra homomorphism from the whole quantum group ${U_{{q^{1/2}}}}( {{{\widehat {\mathfrak{sl}}}_2}} )$ to $\mathcal A_q$, whose images together with either of the two frozen variables generate $\mathcal A_q$. As an application, we obtain algebra homomorphisms from the split $\imath$quantum groups of affine $\widehat {\mathfrak{sl}}_2$ to $\mathcal A_q$. Moreover, we explicitly determine the images of the positive and negative real and imaginary root vectors of ${U_{{q^{1/2}}}}( {{{\widehat {\mathfrak{sl}}}_2}} )$ in terms of quantum cluster variables.

papers.title: Quiescent galaxies at cosmic noon: from individual element abundances to star formation histories
papers.abstract: Understanding the formation and early evolution of massive quiescent galaxies is crucial for a complete picture of galaxy formation in a cosmological context. Such a comprehensive picture can be obtained through measurements of individual elemental abundances, which encode the timescales and physical conditions of their star-formation and assembly histories. While extensive work at low and intermediate redshift has revealed strong correlations between stellar mass, metallicity, and abundance ratios, studies at z ~ 2-3 remain extremely limited. Their faintness and compactness make medium-resolution near-infrared spectroscopy for detailed chemical analysis extremely challenging. We present a science case to measure full elemental abundance patterns in a representative sample of massive quiescent galaxies at cosmic noon, exploiting rest-frame optical absorption features. We show that deriving robust stellar population constraints for these systems requires spectra with S/N ~ 20 per resolution element, together with a spatial resolution comparable to their ~ 0.1 arcsec sizes. We show that such requirements can only be met with a 40m class telescope equipped with a powerful adaptive optics system. In this context, SHARP-NEXUS, in combination with MORFEO-MCAO capabilities, emerges as the only viable ELT instrument capable of enabling this science, providing both the sensitivity and angular resolution needed. Although massive quiescent galaxies are rare at these redshifts, their study can efficiently exploit the instrument's multiplexing by targeting galaxy overdensities and coordinating with surveys of star-forming galaxies. Such synergistic strategies, proven feasible in high-redshift clusters and by multiplex-sharing facilities like 4MOST, would allow SHARP-NEXUS to open a new window on the chemical enrichment of the earliest massive galaxies.

papers.intro:
Understanding how massive quiescent galaxies form and evolve is key to a complete picture of galaxy formation in a cosmological context. In a Universe dominated by cold dark matter, hierarchical assembly makes it challenging to build these galaxies rapidly and maintain them in a predominantly passive state over most of cosmic time, as revealed by the fossil record of local systems (e.g. Carnall et al. 2023; Valentino et al. 2023). Their well-behaved redshift evolution also makes them valuable cosmological probes (e.g., BOSS, Eisenstein et al. 2005). By measuring the elemental abundances of their stellar populations, we can probe the physical processes that governed their assembly. Indeed, the chemical composition of a galaxy results from the intricate balance between several physical processes, including the accretion of pristine gas, the expulsion of metal-enriched material through galactic winds, the efficiency of star formation, the cumulative effect of mergers, and ultimately, the stellar initial mass function (IMF). While the metallicity of the interstellar medium traces the chemical state of the galaxy at the epoch probed by the observations, the elemental abundances locked in its stars record the integrated history of chemical enrichment throughout its formation and evolution (e.g., Thomas et al. 2010). For this reason, stellar abundance patterns provide a powerful diagnostic of both the star formation and assembly pathways of galaxies (e.g., Maiolino and Mannucci 2019 and references therein). In particular, for quiescent systems, where strong stellar absorption lines dominate the spectra, stellar chemical compositions serve as especially sensitive tracers of their past star forming activity.

In the early Universe, only hydrogen, helium, and trace amounts of lithium were produced through primordial nucleosynthesis. The formation of heavier elements, collectively referred to as metals, began only with the first generation of stars. Inside them, thermonuclear reactions progressively synthesise heavier elements, with the yield depending on stellar mass and evolutionary stage. Massive stars (M≥8​M⊙M\geq 8M_{\odot}) evolve rapidly (∼1−30\sim 1-30 Myr) and end their lives as core-collapse supernovae (Type II SNe), enriching the interstellar medium (ISM) with so-called α\alpha-elements (e.g., O, Mg, Si, Ca, Ti). In contrast, Type Ia supernovae, which originate from long-lived, lower-mass progenitors in binary systems, are the main producers of iron peak elements, and release their products on longer timescales (e.g., ∼1\sim 1 Gyr Greggio 2005; Nomoto et al. 2013). This delayed enrichment plays a crucial role, as the ratio between α\alpha-elements and iron traces the timescale over which star formation occurred in a galaxy (Thomas et al. 2005).

Analyses of stellar populations and chemical abundances in galaxies at z∼0z\sim 0 have provided key insights into the formation pathways and evolutionary histories of massive quiescent systems. A well established result is that the most massive early-type galaxies in the local Universe are also the most metal enriched (e.g., Trager et al. 2000; Gallazzi et al. 2005; Thomas et al. 2010). This correlation is generally interpreted as a consequence of the galaxy gravitational potentials: in deeper potential wells, stellar winds and supernova-driven outflows are less efficient at expelling the metal enriched gas (e.g., Tremonti et al. 2004 and references therein).

A well established result is that the most massive early-type galaxies in the local Universe are also the most metal enriched (e.g., Trager et al. 2000; Gallazzi et al. 2005; Thomas et al. 2010). This correlation is generally interpreted as a consequence of the galaxy gravitational potentials: in deeper potential wells, stellar winds and supernova-driven outflows are less efficient at expelling the metal enriched gas (e.g., Tremonti et al. 2004 and references therein).

Massive quiescent galaxies are also observed to host the oldest stellar populations and to exhibit enhanced α\alpha-element abundances, commonly quantified through the [α\alpha/Fe] ratio (e.g., Thomas et al. 2005; McDermid et al. 2015; Conroy et al. 2018). These findings point toward a scenario in which the most massive galaxies assembled their stellar content early and over very short timescales (de La Rosa et al. 2011). Moreover, detailed studies of individual elemental abundance patterns have shed light on the nucleosynthetic origin of various elements in massive systems. For instance, the Fe peak element cobalt appears to receive a non negligible contribution from core collapse supernovae (Conroy 2013), whereas α\alpha-elements such as calcium and titanium show evidence of significant production in Type Ia events (e.g., Saglia et al. 2002; Thomas et al. 2003; Johansson et al. 2012; La Barbera et al. 2025).

Surveys targeting galaxies at redshifts 0.5<z<1.20.5<z<1.2, (e.g., LEGA-C, van der Wel et al. 2016; VANDELS, Carnall et al. 2019). have provided an important bridge between the early universe and local quiescent systems. Yet, even at these epochs, roughly halfway through cosmic history, the interpretation remains complex due to processes such as rejuvenation episodes and morphological transformations. Establishing a direct evolutionary connection with present-day early-type is further complicated by the so called progenitor bias. Since galaxies quench at different cosmic times, the passive population continuously grows, meaning that passive galaxies observed at high redshift correspond only to the earliest quenched systems. Therefore, they are not necessarily representative of all passive galaxies observed in the local Universe.(van Dokkum and Franx 2001). Some galaxies cease star formation earlier and stay compact, while others quench later, typically exhibiting larger sizes. Consequently, to best constrain the mechanisms that shaped quiescent galaxies, it is essential to observe them near the time of their formation and quenching, around redshift z∼2z\sim 2, before subsequent mergers alter their stellar populations (Barro et al. 2013, Sampaio et al. 2025). At that epoch a substantial fraction of the progenitors of the present-day passive galaxy population is thought to have already undergone quenching, making this epoch particularly suitable for investigating the stellar populations of the progenitors of massive quiescent galaxies in the local Universe. Indeed, the extent to which progenitor bias affects the interpretation of the results obtained for z ∼\sim 2 samples remains debated. Importantly, systematic differences in the stellar population models and analysis techniques adopted at different redshifts can themselves introduce significant variations in the inferred stellar ages. For example, Ditrani et al. (2026) showed that systematic differences of up to 1.5-2 Gyr in the inferred ages of massive quiescent galaxies at z ¡ 0.8 can emerge simply from the choice of different evolutionary models adopted for the spectral analysis, even when the same galaxies, datasets, and spectral indicators are considered. By performing a homogeneous analysis of BOSS and DESI data for galaxies spanning z ∼\sim 0.8 to the local Universe, they found that the stellar populations of intermediate redshift massive quiescent galaxies are consistent with quenching epochs at z>>1.5-2, depending on the adopted spectrophotometric model. These results suggest that, while progenitor bias cannot be completely neglected, its impact on the interpretation of the massive quiescent population at z∼\sim 2 is likely negligible.

papers.title: On symmetry and monotonicity of singular solutions to critical fractional Hartree equations
papers.abstract: This paper continues the study initiated in \cite{GuJevnikarYang2026b} of fractional Hartree equations with zero capacity singular sets. We are concerned here with the critical case, i.e. \[ (-\Delta)^s u=\left(\int_{\mathbb{R}^N\setminus\Gamma} \frac{u^{2_{\mu,s}^*}(y)}{|x-y|^\mu}\,d y\right)u^{2_{\mu,s}^*-1} \quad\text{in }\mathbb{R}^N\setminus\Gamma, \] where $N\ge2$, $s\in(0,1)$, $\mu\in(0,N)$ and $2_{\mu,s}^*$ is the critical exponent associated to this class of problems. We prove symmetry and monotonicity with respect to the singular set $\Gamma$. The Kelvin transforms centered at regular points provide sufficient decay at infinity for both the transformed solutions and their associated Hartree coefficients, without imposing global integrability assumptions. Combined with a moving plane argument and a comparison estimate in critical Lebesgue spaces, this allows the moving plane method to cover the full interaction range.

papers.title: Logarithmic corrections for four-dimensional loop percolation
papers.abstract:
We study the one-arm probability of the discrete random-walk loop soup on $\mathbb{Z}^4$ at small positive intensity. Using the small-loop crossing and macroscopic attachment estimates of Gao, we prove that the expected capacity of the origin cluster formed by loops contained in a box grows at most as the square of the logarithm of the box radius. Consequently, there are constants $\alpha_0,c,C,\beta>0$ such that, for $0<\alpha\le\alpha_0$, \[
  c\alpha R^{-2}[\log(R+2)]^{\beta\alpha}
  \le \mathbb{P}_\alpha(0\leftrightarrow B_R^c)
  \le C\alpha R^{-2}[\log(R+2)]^2. \] The interval $(0,\alpha_0]$ is strictly subcritical. The upper bound rests on a simultaneous capacity estimate for neighborhoods of loop ranges, followed by an expansion over chains in which sufficiently small intermediate loops have been removed. A deterministic bound on the variation of the surviving scale sequences makes the expansion summable. The positive logarithmic-power lower bound is already known from work of Chang and Sapozhnikov; we give a proof using macroscopic attachments and a layer-cake argument, with constants uniform at small intensity. In particular, the one-arm exponent equals two, and the logarithm of its correction has order $\log\log R$, for every fixed intensity in this interval. We also derive polynomial tail exponent one for the cardinality and capacity of the full cluster, determine their positive moment thresholds, and give an application to random wires.

papers.title: Polylogarithmic bound for the Gy\'arf\'as-Sumner conjecture
papers.abstract: The classical Gy\'arf\'as-Sumner conjecture asserts that for any fixed forest $F$, any graph $G$ not containing $F$ as an induced subgraph, with bounded clique number $\omega(G)$, has bounded chromatic number $\chi(G)$. Recently, Nguyen, Scott, and Seymour proved that every such graph has chromatic number at most $|G|^{o(1)}$. We improve this bound to a polylogarithmic one $(\log |G|)^{O(1)}$.

papers.intro:
One of the most basic questions in graph theory asks when the chromatic number of a graph is controlled by its clique number. It is immediate that it is a lower bound, but when can one also upper bound the chromatic number by a function of the clique number? Sadly, the answer is in general no, since one of the most classical results in probabilistic combinatorics, due to Erdős [11], established the existence of graphs with high girth (so in particular no K3K_{3}) with arbitrarily large chromatic number. This construction is highly random, and leads to a very natural question of whether assuming the graph we are working with is structured changes the answer. This question lies at the core of the theory of chi-boundedness, which has attracted considerable attention over the years with many interesting results; see [25] for a recent survey on the topic. One of the most natural structural assumptions that one might make is to require the graph to not contain a fixed small graph HH as an induced subgraph. It is immediate from the above-mentioned high-girth, high-chromatic number construction that this can not work if HH contains a cycle. This leads us to the conjecture, independently raised by Gyárfás and Sumner in the late 1970s and early 1980s, that forbidding a tree (or equivalently a forest) does suffice.

This beautiful conjecture remains open, despite a lot of work on the topic. Let us highlight one of the first results on the topic due to Gyárfás, which settled the conjecture for paths [13], introducing a technique now called the Gyárfás path argument that has proved extremely useful over the years since. Gyárfás, Szemerédi and Tuza proved the radius-two case for triangle-free graphs [12]. The latter was subsequently extended to arbitrary bounded clique number by Kierstead and Penrice [14]. Further special families of trees have been settled since then, including brooms, subdivisions of stars, and several related classes; we direct the reader to [25] for more details and further references.

Our proof is naturally split into several steps.

Step 1. We use TT-freeness to find many closed walks of length 44. This is done by observing that we can find many not necessarily induced copies of TT, where many here is in terms of the density of GG. Since each such copy must, in fact, not be an induced copy, it must contain an edge which completes a cycle with some subpath of TT. This cycle is very short (since TT is of constant size), giving us a lot of short cycles in the graph, even when accounting for possible overcounting. Sidorenko-style inequalities allow us to translate this count to the desired count of length four closed walks. In reality, this step is not done via counting due to regularity issues, but is instead carried out via a stationary TT-indexed random walk which attempts to embed a tree in a certain carefully chosen random way which allows us to do a “weighted” probabilistic version of the above counting argument; see Section 2.2 for more details.

Step 2. We use the high count of closed walks of length four to obtain many dense induced bipartite blocks with little density between them. This is done by repeatedly extracting such blocks and finally subsampling them to ensure lower density between them. Here, the blocks themselves are provided by the high count of closed walks of length four by simply picking the edge which is used in the largest number of the walks and observing that each walk gives an edge between the neighborhoods of the endpoints of this edge. We can then invoke the fact that these neighborhoods are qq-colorable to find independent sets on both sides which still retain a lot of the density, giving us the desired block. We then remove this block and repeat so long as we have many closed walks. The final step, to ensure there is little density between the blocks, is to subsample the blocks with appropriate probability. We refer to this final collection of dense induced bipartite blocks with little density between them as a block-system. See Section 2.3 for more details.

papers.title: Explainable Anomaly Detection in 5G Networks through Continuous Time Graphs
papers.abstract: 5G networks increasingly resemble distributed systems in their design. It then becomes crucial to move beyond traditional network-based detection methods and to explore alternative approaches. In this work, we propose a formalization of 5G network exchanges as a dynamic graph, on which we apply techniques from the field of graph-based learning to detect anomalies effectively. This representation allows for fine-grained analysis of packet-level semantic content, while simultaneously capturing sequential and topological contexts, both of which are essential for identifying sophisticated and multi-stage attacks. To assess the effectiveness of this formalism, we evaluate it with the most popular dynamic graph models, demonstrating its potential for 5G anomaly detection.

papers.title: Descriptor representations of geometric port-Hamiltonian systems on Hilbert spaces
papers.abstract: We establish conversions in both directions between geometric and descriptor representations of linear port-Hamiltonian systems on infinite-dimensional Hilbert spaces. For the geometric-to-descriptor conversion, we represent the possibly multivalued inverse Dirac relation by a skew-adjoint operator on enlarged Hilbert spaces, retaining the original operator-domain restrictions. The construction accommodates internal and external ports. We show that the conversions preserve trajectories and the power balance. An incompressible Kelvin--Voigt solid illustrates the results.

Algebraic constraints arising from Dirac structures are already familiar in finite dimensions. The additional difficulty in infinite dimensions is that the operator part of a Dirac relation may be unbounded. Its domain can encode spatial regularity and boundary conditions that cannot be recovered merely from the algebraic constraints. A conversion to descriptor form must preserve these domain restrictions as well. Moreover, the spaces associated with algebraic constraints may themselves be infinite-dimensional, as in models of incompressible continua.

Every closed linear relation admits bounded image and kernel representations. The challenge here is therefore not simply to write the geometric inclusions as operator equations. Rather, we seek a structured descriptor representation in which the Dirac interconnection is realized by a skew-adjoint operator on enlarged Hilbert spaces. The transition from a structured descriptor equation to geometric relations is comparatively direct: the inverse graph of the interconnection operator gives a Dirac structure. For the converse direction, we use the operator–multivalued decomposition of the inverse Dirac relation to obtain a skew-adjoint operator representation. An auxiliary variable accounts for the multivalued part, while the original operator domain is retained. The construction draws on the theory of linear relations Arens (1961); Cross (1998); Hassi et al. (2009); Behrndt et al. (2020); related infinite-dimensional Dirac representations are studied in Iftime et al. (2014). Combined with parametrizations of the storage and resistive relations, this gives a closed descriptor operator with internal and external ports. We prove an exact correspondence of classical trajectories, including preservation of the power balance.

papers.title: Finite-time mixing and reaction in packed bed reactors
papers.abstract: We investigate mixing dynamics in porous media at finite times, using pore-scale lattice-Boltzmann simulations combined with Lagrangian particle tracking. We compute fluid deformation in randomly packed beds based on the moving Protean frame approach introduced by Lester 2018. From the extracted Lagrangian kinematics, we construct a mixing model based on lamellar aggregation that well predicts the Eulerian scalar fields obtained from simulations. Our results reveal an early time mixing regime dominated by shear-driven fluid deformation, where solute mixing arises from the random overlap of diffusive concentration elements. In this regime, mixing proceeds slowly and follows a temporal decay of concentration variance, $\sigma_c^2 \sim Pe^{-\alpha/(2\alpha+1)} t^{-1/2}$, where Pe is the Peclet number and $\alpha$ the exponent characterizing shear deformation. This dynamic arises when the Peclet number is small relative to the ratio between the exponential-mixing and shear-deformation timescales. This analysis also demonstrates that shear-induced mixing govern the homogenization of early-stage reactions at the fluid-solid interface in finite-size random packed beds, typically operating at moderate Peclet numbers $Pe =O(10^2)$.

papers.intro:
Although fully developed mixing in porous media has been widely studied, the dynamics of mixing at early, finite times remains less well understood.

Although fully developed mixing in porous media has been widely studied, the dynamics of mixing at early, finite times remains less well understood.

In porous systems of limited size or characterized by finite-time processes such as reactions, finite-time mixing plays a decisive role in controlling the homogenization of an injected solution. Consider, for instance, small compact porous reactors: in such systems, while molecular diffusion is too slow to support mixing, pore-scale advection contributes to distributing the solute effectively within the limits of the reactor’s longitudinal size LL. Nevertheless, the residence time L/UL/U has to be long enough to allow complete molecular conversion (Maggiolo et al., 2020), implying that the device must operate at a limited mean flow velocity UU and Péclet number. As a result, advection-driven mixing is weak and constrained by the limited physical reactor space LL.

Limited-size porous systems are also encountered in a range of other applications, such as membranes and electrodes (Farzaneh et al., 2021). Furthermore, in highly reactive media, mixing may be limited at very short times, because species transport is subsequently inhibited by reaction. Under such conditions, fully developed mixing may not be achieved and the mixing dynamics are fully realized at finite times.

At finite or large Péclet numbers, solutes transported through porous media often organize into thin, high-concentration filaments separated by low-concentration voids (Dentz & de Barros, 2015). Mixing refers to the transition of a scalar field–such as concentration–from an initially heterogeneous, segregated state to a final, spatially homogeneous distribution (Villermaux, 2019). In porous media, this process relies on the ability of the flow to eliminate small-scale concentration contrasts through kinematic deformations generated by the pore-scale geometry at very early times. In other words, mixing is completely mediated by the pore-scale architecture.

Unlike two-dimensional flows, three-dimensional porous structures inherently generate chaotic flow (Lester et al., 2013; Lester et al., 2016), where random sequences of stretching and folding events produce long-term exponential stretching of concentration fields (Heyman et al., 2020). The average long-term growth rate of infinitesimal fluid element lengths is quantified by the Lyapunov exponent, λ\lambda, which determines the onset of chaotic mixing at tm∼d/(2​λ​U)​ln⁡(\Pen)t_{m}\sim d/(2\lambda U)\ln(\Pen). Lamellar theories have been developed to capture these dynamics. Initially proposed for turbulent flows (Duplat & Villermaux, 2008) and later extended to random porous flows (Dentz et al., 2023), these models describe mixing as the formation of elongated lamellae (or sheets) of high concentration and their subsequent random aggregation. This framework highlights an early stretching–compression regime, during which advection (i) redistributes regions of high concentration randomly in space, bringing previously segregated pockets into proximity, and (ii) amplifies transverse concentration gradients within lamellae, thereby accelerating diffusion-driven dilution. Both processes act as powerful mixing mechanisms. After tmt_{m}, the overlapping lamellae can be modeled as undergoing random aggregation, either fully or partially correlated depending on the pore-scale dynamics (Duplat et al., 2010; Heyman et al., 2024).

papers.title: Empirical Bayes Flow Matching for Continuous Cryo-EM Heterogeneity
papers.abstract: We address the problem of learning generative priors over high-dimensional latent variables from indirect, noisy observations, with a focus on continuous heterogeneity in cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM). In this setting, 3D atomic structures $x \in \mathbb{R}^{3N_a}$ are never directly observed and must be inferred from 2D projection images $y$ generated by a complex, non-linear forward operator. We propose Empirical Bayes Flow Matching (EB-FM), a method that learns a flow matching prior $p_\theta(x)$ directly from observations using a Monte Carlo stochastic approximation Expectation-Maximization framework. EB-FM alternates between an E-step that performs approximate posterior sampling from $p_\theta(x \mid y)$ via guided flow-based generation while maintaining persistent latent estimates through stochastic approximation, and an M-step that updates the flow model using these stabilized latent variables as training targets. This approach eliminates the need for pretraining on clean data and naturally accommodates non-linear forward models. We validate our method on controlled inverse problems using two-moons and MNIST data, and demonstrate its effectiveness on simulated cryo-EM data with known poses, showing that EB-FM can recover continuous distributions of protein conformations directly in atomic-coordinate space.

In the natural sciences, quantities of interest are typically not directly observed but inferred from indirect measurements. This inverse-modelling task is central to experimental science, and its success depends on how faithfully we can represent the distribution of the underlying quantities of interest.

In the natural sciences, quantities of interest are typically not directly observed but inferred from indirect measurements. This inverse-modelling task is central to experimental science, and its success depends on how faithfully we can represent the distribution of the underlying quantities of interest.

Inferring protein structure using cryogenic electron microscopy (cryo-EM) is a prime example of this task Frank (2002); Egelman (2016); Nogales and Scheres (2015). Proteins carry out their biological functions as dynamic molecules, adopting multiple conformational states that mediate essential cellular processes such as transport and signalling Frauenfelder et al. (1991); Motlagh et al. (2014). Cryo-EM is uniquely positioned to observe this structural heterogeneity: a biological sample is flash-frozen, preserving the ensemble of conformations present in solution, and an electron beam then produces thousands of noisy 2D projection images of the 3D structures, each in a random, unknown orientation Frank (2002); Egelman (2016); Nogales and Scheres (2015); Vulović et al. (2013). In contrast to models like AlphaFold Jumper et al. (2021); Abramson et al. (2024), which primarily target high confidence static structures, cryo-EM data directly reflects the full distribution of conformations that a protein occupies, and recovering this distribution is essential for understanding function Giri et al. (2023). The task is therefore not to reconstruct a single 3D structure, but to infer a distribution p⁡(x)p(x) over 3D atomic configurations from indirect observations. This can be framed as an Empirical Bayes problem Robbins (1964); Casella (1985); Efron (2014).

Classical cryo-EM reconstruction pipelines Scheres (2012); Punjani et al. (2017) target single consensus structures and handle heterogeneity only through discrete clustering. Recent deep-learning methods (cryoDRGN Zhong et al. (2021), 3DFlex Punjani and Fleet (2023), cryoFIRE Levy et al. (2022), cryoSPHERE Ducrocq et al. (2025), mixture-of-neural-fields Levy et al. (2024b)) learn continuous latent representations of conformational variability, but all share a structural limitation: they operate in a two-stage regime in which the 2D projections are first used to reconstruct 3D density / voxel grids, and atomic models are fit to those densities only as a separate downstream step. This decoupling of the generative model from the underlying atomic physics prevents the use of strong structural priors: the density stage has no access to atomic-coordinate priors, and the atom-fitting stage no longer has access to the raw observations. This matters most when the observations are under-determined and have low signal-to-noise ratios, precisely the regime where a strong atomic prior should help the most. The exception in the literature is Rosenbaum et al. (2021), which operates directly in atomic-coordinate space and couples an atomic-coordinate prior to the raw image observations using a variational autoencoder. We follow this direction, incorporating modern generative-modelling approaches for the prior.

Like Rosenbaum et al. (2021), we operate in atomic-coordinate space, but we depart from its VAE framing in two important ways. Second, instead of an amortised encoder, we maintain persistent per-observation latents {x~i}\{\tilde{x}_{i}\} that are inferred via optimization during the model training. This is formulated as a Monte Carlo stochastic approximation Expectation-Maximization algorithm Delyon et al. (1999). We optimize the marginal likelihood of the observations by alternating between an E-step, where each latent x~i\tilde{x}_{i} is refined via deterministic approximate posterior sampling using the current prior and the observation yiy_{i}, and an M-step, in which the flow matching prior is retrained on the stabilized latent ensemble {x~i}\{\tilde{x}_{i}\}.

Several lines of work train generative priors directly from corrupted observations rather than clean data, including AmbientDiffusion Daras et al. (2023) for structured measurement corruption. Most relevant to our setting, DiEM Rozet et al. (2024) proposes a similar empirical Bayes scheme with a diffusion prior, but under two restrictions that prevent its application in our setting. First, DiEM is formulated exclusively for linear Gaussian forward models p⁡(y∣x)=𝒩⁡(y∣A​x,Σy)p(y\mid x)=\mathcal{N}(y\mid Ax,\Sigma_{y}), for which the intermediate-state marginal likelihood admits a closed form via moment matching. Our cryo-EM forward model is structurally non-linear as the 3D atomic coordinates enter the projected image through a sum of radial-basis exponentials. Second, DiEM’s E-step relies on solving a large linear system via a Conjugate-Gradient method at every discretization step. This requires evaluating Vector-Jacobian Products through the generative network, which becomes computationally prohibitive in the case of high dimensional observations. EB-FM bypasses these limitations, targeting non-linear differentiable forward models with a tractable E-step.

papers.title: Virtual Microphone Array for Direction-of-Arrival Estimation Based on Fiber-Optic Position Sensing
papers.abstract: This paper presents a virtual microphone array approach for estimating the direction of arrival of a sound source using a moving microphone and a stationary reference microphone. The method exploits the microphone motion to generate a time-varying array geometry, using fiber-optic position sensing to reconstruct the trajectory and determine the resulting virtual microphone configurations. For each configuration, the estimated time difference of arrival between the two microphone signals and the corresponding microphone geometry define a hyperboloid representing all possible sound source positions consistent with the time difference. By combining multiple hyperboloid constraints, the direction of arrival can be estimated in azimuth and elevation relative to the microphone coordinate system. In contrast to conventional arrays with fixed geometries and approaches based on predefined microphone trajectories, the proposed method derives the virtual array geometry directly from the measured microphone motion, enabling a spatially distributed virtual array to be formed using only two physical microphones and offering potential for size- and weight-constrained applications. The approach was experimentally evaluated under controlled low-reflection conditions for different source positions, source distances, and signal characteristics. The influence of microphone motion was further examined, and the method was tested with a moving sound source. The results demonstrate the feasibility of direction-of-arrival estimation using a virtual microphone array without requiring a predefined microphone trajectory.

papers.intro:
Determining the direction of sound sources is a fundamental task in numerous audio engineering applications and systems. The information can be used, for example, to enhance desired signal components, suppress unwanted interference, or localize noise sources [1]. Such methods are used in applications such as hearing aids, conference systems, acoustic cameras, and drone-based sound source localization [2]. To extract spatial information from the sound field, microphone arrays with predefined geometries and a fixed number of microphones are typically employed. The performance of direction estimation is influenced by the array aperture as well as by the number and spatial arrangement of the microphones [3]. To avoid spatial aliasing when processing broadband signals, dense spatial sampling of the sound field is required. This typically necessitates a large number of microphones and therefore increases the technical complexity of array design, synchronization, calibration, and data processing [4].

Determining the direction of sound sources is a fundamental task in numerous audio engineering applications and systems. The information can be used, for example, to enhance desired signal components, suppress unwanted interference, or localize noise sources [1]. Such methods are used in applications such as hearing aids, conference systems, acoustic cameras, and drone-based sound source localization [2]. To extract spatial information from the sound field, microphone arrays with predefined geometries and a fixed number of microphones are typically employed. The performance of direction estimation is influenced by the array aperture as well as by the number and spatial arrangement of the microphones [3]. To avoid spatial aliasing when processing broadband signals, dense spatial sampling of the sound field is required. This typically necessitates a large number of microphones and therefore increases the technical complexity of array design, synchronization, calibration, and data processing [4].

One approach to reducing the required number of sensors is to exploit the motion of one or more microphones. By analyzing phase or frequency changes in the recorded signals, information about the direction of a sound source relative to the microphones can be obtained [5, 6]. Existing systems typically achieve this by moving the microphones along predefined trajectories. While this simplifies the determination of microphone positions, it constrains the resulting virtual array geometry, which can complicate the implementation of such systems in applications with strict size and weight constraints. An alternative is to derive the virtual array geometry from non-predefined microphone motion. By temporally segmenting the recorded signals and associating each segment with the corresponding microphone position, a virtual microphone array comprising multiple spatially distributed microphone positions can be constructed [7]. The resulting sequential measurements provide relative propagation-time information between different spatial positions that can be used for direction-of-arrival estimation. However, this approach places stringent requirements on the position sensing system, since the microphone trajectory must be determined with high spatial accuracy and sufficient temporal resolution.

A promising approach to addressing these requirements is the use of fiber-optic interferometric sensing. Such systems enable highly accurate measurements of the displacement of mechanical structures and are used in a wide range of technical applications, including vibration analysis, manufacturing metrology, and geophysical structural analysis [8]. The measured displacement can further be used to derive kinematic quantities and to reconstruct the motion of mechanical structures. Combining virtual-microphone-array-based direction-of-arrival estimation with fiber-optic position sensing for determining the virtual microphone positions forms the basis of the approach presented in this paper (Fig. 1).

papers.title: The Hearpiece Database of Binaural Room Impulse Responses and Driver Responses on KEMAR
papers.abstract: This document describes the measurement setup, signal processing, data organization, and MATLAB file format of a database of acoustic responses measured on a Knowles Electronics Manikin for Acoustic Research (KEMAR) using the Hearpiece, a multi-microphone, multi-driver in-ear research device. The data include binaural room impulse responses (BRIRs) and Hearpiece driver responses, together with center-microphone room impulse responses and a loopback impulse response of the playback and recording system. The BRIRs cover two Hearpiece configurations, three room conditions, three independent insertions per configuration, and 24 horizontal source directions. The database supports reproducible research on binaural and hearing-device signal processing, with potential applications in speech enhancement, spatial filtering and source separation, dereverberation, active noise and occlusion control, and acoustic feedback cancellation. The database, MATLAB loading script, and technical documentation are publicly available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23667308.

papers.title: Construction, Enumeration and Duality of Perfectly Balanced Musical Sets of Order $2pq$
papers.abstract: In this paper, we present a comprehensive study of perfectly balanced musical sets, also known in the literature as vanishing sums of roots of unity, in the particular case of order $2pq$. Starting from the well-established result concerning the decomposition of such sets as an integer linear combination of regular polygons, we first provide an algebraic formalization that allows to explicitly construct all these sets. We then propose six different decompositions of each set into regular polygons. Moreover, by investigating their combinatorial enumeration, we derive a formula for the exact number of these sets for a given order $2pq$, and describe their distribution and cardinality for the particular case of order $6p$. One of the main results concerns the duality that can be established between these sets. In particular, we prove that every non-periodic minimal perfectly balanced set of order $2pq$ can be combined with another one to produce a self-complementary $2p$-periodic set, and the reciprocal also holds. Finally, we demonstrate that the modulus of the discrete Fourier transform coefficients of dual sets are related. All these results shed new light on the distribution of perfectly balanced sets of order $2pq$ and suggest new mathematical questions in a more general case.

papers.title: Impact of Negative Weights on Performance in Reservoir Computing
papers.abstract: Reservoir computing provides an efficient framework for time-series prediction because only the readout layer is trained while the recurrent reservoir remains fixed. In this study, we examine how the negative sign ratio of a signed Erdos-Renyi reservoir affects the internal dynamics and forecasting performance of an echo state network on the Mackey-Glass benchmark. To characterize the reservoir responses, we use two Shannon-entropy-based observables, namely node-state entropy and node-frequency entropy, as empirical proxies for the diversity of reservoir states and temporal activation patterns. We find that intermediate negative sign ratios are associated with richer internal dynamics and substantially lower prediction error than the sign-homogeneous extremes for the task considered here. These results suggest that link-sign composition can be a useful structural parameter in reservoir design for chaotic forecasting. The present findings should be interpreted within the scope of the current benchmark and reservoir setting, and broader validation will be required to establish their generality across other tasks, topologies, and controlled spectral conditions.

papers.intro:
Artificial neural networks (ANNs) have become increasingly ubiquitous across diverse domains of scientific and technological applications, fundamentally transforming fields ranging from autonomous vehicle navigation to computational creativity in image synthesis algorithms [1, 2, 3, 4]. Their computational capabilities extend to natural language processing and environmental modeling, where they contribute significantly to the accuracy and reliability of prediction systems [5, 6, 7, 8]. Recent advances in representation learning have further enabled efficient retrieval and similarity search in large-scale document corpora, such as patents, by embedding textual data into latent spaces using pretrained language models and contrastive learning techniques [9]. The exponential growth in computational resources and data availability has facilitated the evolution of increasingly sophisticated ANN architectures [6, 10, 11]. This technological advancement has enabled the development of deep learning models capable of extracting intricate patterns and generating predictions with unprecedented accuracy, including representation learning frameworks that embed complex user characteristics into latent spaces using metric learning approaches such as triplet loss [12]. Nevertheless, the substantial computational demands and extensive training time required by state-of-the-art ANN architectures remain significant challenges, particularly in resource-constrained computational environments.

Nevertheless, the substantial computational demands and extensive training time required by state-of-the-art ANN architectures remain significant challenges, particularly in resource-constrained computational environments.

Within this context, reservoir computing (RC) has emerged as a compelling computational paradigm offering distinct advantages. Characterized by reduced computational overhead and efficient training protocols, RC presents a robust alternative to conventional ANN architectures [13, 14, 15, 4]. The defining feature of RC, a fixed reservoir network structure maintained throughout the learning phase, enables a streamlined training procedure that circumvents the need for extensive iterative weight optimization characteristic of deep learning approaches [16, 13]. Furthermore, the architectural stability inherent to RC proves particularly advantageous for physical neural network implementations, where hardware constraints impose limitations on system flexibility and adaptability. This fixed architecture substantially simplifies the physical realization of ANNs, establishing RC as a promising methodology for developing computationally efficient artificial intelligence systems deployable across diverse applications, from edge computing devices to large-scale industrial systems [1, 6, 7, 16, 5, 8].

This separation between nonlinear dynamical transformation and lightweight readout learning makes RC highly effective for tasks in which temporal memory and nonlinear mixing are both essential [17, 18, 19]. Although random reservoirs are often treated as generic dynamical substrates, their detailed sign structure can strongly influence the resulting internal dynamics. In signed directed networks, positive and negative connections encode qualitatively different modes of interaction, and changing their ratio alters the balance between amplification and suppression in the network response [20, 21, 22, 23]. In the context of RC, such structural changes are expected to modify the reservoir’s eigenvalue distribution, state diversity, temporal complexity, and ultimately its predictive utility [24, 25]. However, the role of the negative sign ratio in reservoir design has not been systematically clarified.

papers.title: EviSeek: An Evidence-Centric Agentic Framework for Embodied Active Information Seeking
papers.abstract: Active embodied question answering requires agents to acquire evidence through viewpoint changes and physical interaction. The central challenge is to avoid undirected interaction: taking plausible actions without specifying what evidence they should reveal for answering the question. Action plans and accumulated histories alone can leave the informational purpose of an interaction implicit. We introduce EviSeek, a training-free framework that makes question-derived evidence demands explicit acquisition objectives, linking observation-conditioned actions and selectively retained evidence to the information the agent seeks. On 3,436 ESI-Bench questions, EviSeek improves accuracy over the Single-model agent by 7.1 percentage points with Qwen3-VL-32B and 3.7 points with Gemini 3.1 Pro, while improving visual-support-weighted accuracy and reducing mean token usage. These findings support making the informational purpose of interaction explicit, with action selection and evidence retention organized around what the agent needs to learn to answer the question.

papers.intro:
Active embodied question answering (A-EQA) requires agents to acquire information through interaction with a partially observed environment (Das et al., 2018a; Gordon et al., 2017; Majumdar et al., 2024). Relevant evidence may be occluded, distributed across locations, or revealed only by viewpoint changes and physical intervention (Bajcsy, 1988; Sawyer et al., 2024). Agents must decide what to observe, how to acquire those observations, and what to retain for answering.

Relevant evidence may be occluded, distributed across locations, or revealed only by viewpoint changes and physical intervention (Bajcsy, 1988; Sawyer et al., 2024). Agents must decide what to observe, how to acquire those observations, and what to retain for answering.

ESI-Bench highlights action blindness: poor action choices yield inadequate observations and subsequent reasoning errors (Hong et al., 2026). We focus on three related difficulties: questions may leave the required observations unspecified; acquiring them may require several stages of interaction; and limited visual history may discard earlier evidence before answering. For example, assessing a stacking configuration requires observing its state after a physical test and retaining that outcome. A plausible manipulation sequence alone does not establish that the relevant evidence was acquired or preserved.

ScoutVLA seeks missing visual evidence (Lu et al., 2026), MemoryEQA shares memory across planning, stopping, and answering (Zhai et al., 2025), and R4 decomposes questions for structured retrieval (Sohn et al., 2026). Building on these directions, we ask whether explicit evidence demands can serve as a shared reference for acquisition and retention, improving active question answering with a fixed pretrained vision-language model (VLM).

We introduce EviSeek, a training-free framework organized around this representation. Evidence-Demand Planning derives observational targets from the question and initial view without assuming a candidate answer is correct, then assigns acquisition subtasks to them. Evidence-Seeking Interaction pursues these goals through viewpoint changes or physical intervention, conditioning actions on observations and execution feedback. Evidence-Oriented Memory selectively retains views and action outcomes on an evidence board, linked to their originating subtask and demand. Subtasks organize acquisition, while the board separates retained answer evidence from transient control observations. Spatial reasoning and evidence interpretation remain dependent on the pretrained VLM.

papers.title: EvoGuard: Mitigating Degradation in Online Skill Evolution
papers.abstract: Skills let language agents reuse experience across tasks as natural-language documents. Recent work evolves skills from interaction, but existing methods have limitations when skills evolve online. Prior methods update a skill offline from a batch of trajectories collected over many tasks. Some then adopt the new skill without any check, which can degrade the skill over time. Others keep it only if it improves performance on a held-out validation set, which is too slow and costly to run after every update. We introduce EvoGuard, a pairwise skill selector that mitigates skill degradation at low latency and cost. We first run the agent iteratively to build pools of skills and score each skill on a private test set to obtain utility labels. We pair the skills and use rejection sampling to keep only pairs with a clear utility gap. The selector is trained on the logits of two label tokens to pick the better skill. At deployment it decides in a single forward pass, which is significantly faster than evaluation on the private test set. Compared with adopting every new skill, EvoGuard improves success by 11.0% on ALFWorld, 5.9% on ScienceWorld, and 2.7% on LiveCodeBench.

Language agents increasingly face streams of related tasks. Solving each task from scratch wastes what earlier interactions have revealed. A skill packages such experience as a reusable natural-language document. It records procedures, decision rules, and recovery strategies. A frozen agent can then adapt through external text instead of weight updates (Wang et al., 2024a; Anthropic, 2025; Xu and Yan, 2026). Recent work builds and evolves skills from interaction (Xia et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2026b; Yao et al., 2026). However, existing methods face three limitations when skills evolve online. In this setting a deployed agent updates its skill after every task.

In this setting a deployed agent updates its skill after every task.

Gap 1: Offline multi-trajectory evolution does not match deployment. Most methods update a skill offline from a batch of trajectories (Xia et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2026b). The update runs in a training phase before deployment. It analyzes trajectories from many tasks at once. A deployed agent rarely works this way. Each task arrives once and is attempted once. The next task is usually a different one. The skill must therefore be revised from a single trajectory and then reused by later tasks. SkillRise carries a skill across tasks in this way (Yao et al., 2026). However, it trains the executor jointly with skill curation and does not check individual updates.

Gap 2: Adopting every new skill causes degradation. A rewrite based on one trajectory can overfit that trajectory. A failed search may add a rule tied to one room. Even a successful episode may add redundant or misleading advice. This risk is measurable. We collect single-trajectory rewrites on ALFWorld and score every skill on a private test set of its task family (Figure 1).

To address these gaps, we propose EvoGuard, a pairwise skill selector that amortizes validation. Tasks are grouped into task families, and each family keeps one skill. After each task, a fixed generator writes a new skill from the latest trajectory. EvoGuard then decides whether this new skill replaces the current skill. This decision only requires the relative order of the two skills, not their absolute utilities. We therefore cast it as a pairwise preference problem. We pay the cost of validation once before deployment and use it to train the selector. After that, each decision only compares two skill texts.

EvoGuard works in three stages (Figure 2). (1) Multi-source skill pool construction. We run the rewrite loop on training tasks with a base generator and an expert generator, and collect the generated skills into a pool. (2) Utility-grounded pairwise preference learning. We estimate the utility of every skill on a private test set of its family. Rejection sampling keeps pairs from the same family with a clear utility gap. We then train a pairwise selector to predict which skill in a pair has the higher utility. (3) Online skill selection. After every task, the frozen selector reads the family description and the two skills. It keeps the skill it predicts to be better. This takes one forward pass and runs no extra rollouts in the environment.

papers.title: Anduin: A sybil-resistant agentic marketplace reputation system
papers.abstract:
As autonomous AI agents enter permissionless onchain markets, selecting new service providers remains a core challenge. Existing reputation systems depend on scarce resources like human curation, identity credentials, or voluntary reviews, while naive volume rankings are vulnerable to Sybil attacks.
  We evaluate whether existing onchain payment histories can yield provider ratings that are resilient against Sybil attacks. Using a 157-day dataset comprising 66M agentic transactions worth $6.1M across 16 blockchains, we model payment flows as a bipartite graph between buyers and providers. A provider's rating is derived from graph paths linked to a buyer's existing trusted network. We propose three Sybil-resistant rating algorithms: a max-flow rating and two relaxed algorithms optimized for stronger rating performance.
  Evaluating these algorithms against simulated adversaries across 813 buyers, we show that rating manipulation costs 20% of those buyers' total spend and is around 23x harder to manipulate than the standard similarity rule (collaborative filtering).

papers.title: Szeg\H{o} quasiforms: a Schottky-scheme construction for vertex operator superalgebras
papers.abstract:
We study the half weight ($N=\half$) analogue of the Bers quasiform on a Schottky group $\Gamma$ of genus $g$: the Poincar\'e series $S_\eps(x,y)=\sum_{\gt\in\Gt}j(\gt,x)/(\gamma x-y)\,(dx\,dy)^{1/2}$ over a lift $\Gt\subset\mathrm{SL}_2(\C)$ of $\Gamma$. The $\Ng:=2^{g}$ lifts give $\Ng$ trivial $\alpha$-holonomy even spin structures $\Lg$.
  The remaining $2^{2g}-\Ng$ spin structures
  are not treated in this paper.
  We prove, on an open set (H) of Schottky parameters and more generally whenever the critical exponent of $\Gamma$ is below $\half$ (any genus $g\ge 1$) the following:
  absolute and locally uniform convergence on $\Omega_0\times\Omega_0$, where $\Omega_0$ is the full region of discontinuity including the point $\infty$ (treated in homogeneous coordinates);
  invariance without Eichler-type defect; skew-symmetry; a simple pole on the diagonal as the only singularity; $H^0(\Sg,\Lg)=0$; and hence identification of $S_\eps$ with the Szeg\H{o} kernel of $\Lg$. At genus one the kernel is computed explicitly and the relations between lifts and theta characteristics are determined. We further prove that the diagonal coefficient defines a projective connection that differs from the Bergman projective connection by a quadratic differential
  constructed from $\theta[\delta](0)$, a residue-reconstruction formula for half-differentials with poles of any order, an expansion in the Schottky multipliers, and a formula for the free fermion stress tensor.

papers.title: ProofStudio: Five Proof Assistants in the Browser
papers.abstract: Recent advances in AI-assisted proof automation are extending the use of proof assistants in software verification and mathematics. However, greater proof automation does not remove users' responsibility to assess whether formal statements capture their intended requirements, making education in formal specification and reasoning essential. To lower the installation and learning barriers associated with mature proof assistants, we present ProofStudio, a browser-based environment integrating Isabelle/HOL, Lean, Rocq, HOL4, and HOL Light with corresponding worked examples, preconfigured proof search, and contextual AI assistance. With ProofStudio, users can explore formal specifications and proofs across five systems without local installation, inspecting native prover feedback and experimenting with automation through a common interface.

Recent advances in AI-assisted proof automation are expanding the practical scope of formal verification. Anthropic and Theorem recently reported using Claude to produce Rocq-checked proofs of no-crash properties for 239 entry points across 123 open-source libraries, subject to explicit execution assumptions and input bounds [1]. In mathematics, OpenAI released a large collection of AI-generated manuscripts, many accompanied by Lean formalizations [2]. These developments make proof assistants increasingly relevant to software engineers and scientists beyond the formal methods community.

Recent advances in AI-assisted proof automation are expanding the practical scope of formal verification. Anthropic and Theorem recently reported using Claude to produce Rocq-checked proofs of no-crash properties for 239 entry points across 123 open-source libraries, subject to explicit execution assumptions and input bounds [1]. In mathematics, OpenAI released a large collection of AI-generated manuscripts, many accompanied by Lean formalizations [2]. These developments make proof assistants increasingly relevant to software engineers and scientists beyond the formal methods community.

Greater automation, however, does not remove the need to understand and scrutinize what is being proved. OpenAI withdrew three manuscripts after a sign error invalidated an argument and two dependent proofs [3]. Beyond errors in reasoning, a separate concern remains even when a formal proof is accepted: verification establishes that a statement follows from its assumptions, whereas validation asks whether that statement captures the intended requirement. Anthropic’s report explicitly identifies the adequacy of specifications and machine models as limitations of its guarantees [1]. Recent work on AI-generated mathematics likewise reports discrepancies between natural-language arguments and their formalizations [4]. Scientists and engineers therefore still need the skills to read formal statements, inspect assumptions, and assess the scope of automated results.

Developing these skills requires opportunities to experiment. Mature proof assistants offer different logics, libraries, proof languages, and automation, with complementary strengths. However, trying each system often requires a separate installation and editor configuration. These barriers affect newcomers and make it harder even for experienced users to explore other provers. Corresponding worked examples can help users compare how different systems specify and verify familiar algorithms.

Earlier Lean 4 installation instructions explicitly acknowledged this requirement [5], while the current guide includes a publisher-trust prompt for the Lean extension [6]. Lean’s official FAQ further warns that opening files, building projects, or updating dependencies can execute arbitrary code, and recommends isolation for potentially malicious code [7]. papers.title: BobFlow: Towards Human-Agent Collaborative Data Science Using Dataflows
papers.abstract: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have established human-agent collaboration as a promising paradigm for data science. Effective collaboration requires a shared computational abstraction that enables agents to reason about processing logic while allowing human analysts to understand, guide, and refine the analysis. Although scripts written in Python or SQL provide precise control, their syntax and execution details can be difficult for analysts to understand and modify. In this paper, we argue that dataflows are an effective abstraction for human-agent collaboration in data science. We introduce BobFlow, a system that combines the dataflow abstraction with the ReAct paradigm. It enables agents to iteratively construct and execute dataflows for data science tasks while allowing analysts to inspect the analysis and provide feedback. Our user study shows that BobFlow helps analysts understand, inspect, and verify agent-generated analyses. A thorough experimental evaluation across proprietary and open-weight LLMs shows accuracy score gains of up to 18.6 points at just over 1/3 of a script-based ReAct agent's inference cost.

Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) are fundamentally transforming how humans and AI agents collaborate on data science tasks (Luo et al., 2026; You et al., 2025). Most commonly, agent-assisted data science has followed a human-led paradigm, where human analysts drive the analytical process, and AI agents assist with individual tasks, such as code generation, data transformation, and result interpretation (Wang et al., 2025a; Kazemitabaar et al., 2024). Recently, a growing number of LLM-powered agents have demonstrated the ability to plan and execute complex analytical tasks autonomously. Systems such as Claude Science (Anthropic, 2026a), OpenAI’s in-house data agent (OpenAI, 2026b), and Google’s multi-agent Co-Scientist (Gottweis et al., 2026) exemplify this trend. As a result, data science is shifting toward an agent-led, human-guided paradigm, in which analysts increasingly supervise agent-driven analyses, evaluate analytical decisions, and provide high-level guidance.

This shift introduces new challenges for effective human–agent collaboration (Kazemitabaar et al., 2024; Xie et al., 2024). In traditional human-led analytics, analysts maintain a natural understanding of the analytical process because they directly perform and control its individual steps. In contrast, when agents autonomously carry out complex, multi-step analyses, potentially involving multiple collaborating agents (You et al., 2025; Gottweis et al., 2026; Wu et al., 2024), human analysts may no longer be directly involved in the decisions and operations that produce the results. To effectively supervise these processes, humans must be able to quickly understand what agents have done, evaluate their analytical decisions, and provide timely feedback to guide subsequent steps (Zeng et al., 2025; Schmidgall et al., 2025). Moreover, analysts may wish to intervene in ongoing analyses or revisit earlier analytical states to explore alternative directions. This calls for interaction mechanisms that let humans efficiently understand, evaluate, and steer agent-driven analyses while preserving agents’ autonomy.

A central design choice for such human–agent collaboration is the computational abstraction, an intermediate representation through which humans and agents conduct and interact with an analysis. We argue that dataflows, represented as directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) of declarative operators and data dependencies, provide an effective shared abstraction for human–agent collaboration. Each operator represents an analytical step, such as scanning, filtering, joining, or aggregating data, while directed edges capture the dependencies between these steps. As illustrated in Figure 1, dataflows offer three key benefits. First, precise: each operator explicitly specifies an analytical operation, such as filtering movies with ratings above a threshold or computing the average budget for each release decade. Second, intuitive: the visual representation exposes analytical steps and their dependencies, allowing analysts to follow the analysis without navigating program syntax or intermediate variables. Third, easier to give feedback: analysts can inspect intermediate results and modify individual operators to refine the analysis. For example, an analyst can examine the average budget for each decade and ask the agent to compare movies by genre instead, allowing the agent to revise the relevant operators while preserving the remaining analysis.

papers.title: Does RRT* Work on Uneven Terrain Meshes?
papers.abstract: The optimal rapidly exploring random tree (RRT*) is proven asymptotically optimal on open subsets of Euclidean space with straight-line local planning. We ask whether it works on a triangle-mesh terrain, a two-dimensional surface in R^3. First, the original RRT* cannot run on a mesh: the surface has zero volume, so uniform sampling never hits it, no clearance ball fits in it, and chords across a fold leave it. Second, the surface reformulation we call Mesh RRT*, with its naive edge, the chord costed by its length, solved every run on heightfields with slopes up to 75 degrees but minimises the wrong objective: its cost, the straight-line length of a polyline whose vertices lie on the surface while its segments may leave it by a tolerance tau, is the length of no route on the surface and lies strictly below the geodesic length on any curved mesh. In numeric simulation and after 30,000 iterations the reported cost is on average up to 2.7% below the exact geodesic, a cost no path attains, and the returned route on average 0.1-0.5% longer than it. Rewiring keeps the biased edges, the bias decays only linearly with the step on polyhedral surfaces, and shrinking tau trades bias for connectivity. Third, replacing each chord by a path on the surface above it, built from projected points joined across the mesh edges they straddle and costed by its own length, makes every edge cost the exact length of a feasible path; with no other change the exact length of the returned routes is on average within 0.07-0.16% of the geodesic at every roughness tested, two to 3.4 times closer than with chords on the rougher terrains. The planner is in MeshNav3D 0.2.0 (release pending).
papers.intro:
Ground robots on rough terrain and surface-bound aerial vehicles plan on a surface, usually a triangle mesh, and the natural cost is geodesic length. The established tools are graph planners on the mesh (Dijkstra, A∗, Theta∗) and geodesic solvers such as the exact Mitchell–Mount–Papadimitriou (MMP) algorithm [1], fast marching [2] and the heat method [3]. Sampling-based optimal planners, led by the optimal rapidly exploring random tree (RRT∗) of Karaman and Frazzoli [4], are rarely applied here, and their guarantees are stated for Euclidean free space. This paper is about one of their primitives, Line, the routine that connects two tree nodes and prices the connection.

Jaillet and Porta extended RRT∗ to implicitly defined configuration manifolds such as closed kinematic chains, with local charts built by higher-dimensional continuation, and argued asymptotic optimality on the manifold [5, 6]; here the manifold is an explicit triangle mesh whose faces are the charts and whose geodesics can be computed exactly. Mesh geodesics are a mature field [1, 7, 3]; exact MMP is our ground truth. Sampling-based mesh planning has been used for ground robots with the basic rapidly exploring random tree (RRT), where the geodesic computations between tree nodes are a heavy load that the method reduces [8]; surface-bound aerial vehicles have instead been steered along the mesh by Riemannian motion policies on a planar parametrisation of it [9]. A∗ on the mesh graph and Theta∗ [10] serve as graph-planner reference points. We know of no prior work measuring sampling-based mesh planners against exact geodesics or identifying the cost inconsistency studied here.

This paper keeps two quantities apart. The length of a route is geometry: how far it runs along the mesh surface, measured here exactly with a geodesic solver. The cost of a route is what the planner computes, optimises and reports: the number its Line primitive assigns to each edge, summed along the route. In Karaman and Frazzoli’s setting the two coincide, because an edge is a straight segment inside the free space and its cost is its length. On a mesh they coincide only if the primitive makes them: a straight chord between two surface points is not a path on the surface, so its length is the length of no route, and a planner that charges it optimises and reports a cost below the surface length of the route it returns. Whether that happens on terrain meshes, by how much, and with what effect on the returned route is what we measure.
