papers.title: XuanJian-DINOSAR: A SAR Foundation Model Based on Global and Local Semantic Consistency
papers.abstract: Self-supervised pre-training on synthetic aperture radar (SAR) imagery enables transferable representations, but the optical-SAR domain gap and speckle perturbations limit representation stability. Most SAR foundation models use masked image modeling (MIM) through pixel reconstruction or structural feature prediction, which is sensitive to speckle or relies on predefined operators. Joint modeling of cross-view semantics and perturbation stability at corresponding spatial locations remains underexplored. We propose XuanJian-DINOSAR, a SAR foundation model based on global and local semantic consistency. We curate over 360K publicly available SAR target chips, detection images, and scene images spanning diverse targets, scenes, and sensors, and adapt an optically pre-trained DINOv2 model to SAR through self-supervised learning. The framework combines DINO global semantic self-distillation, iBOT local masked modeling, and KoLeo feature-distribution regularization to learn globally discriminative and locally structure-aware representations. We introduce a local semantic consistency branch tailored to SAR intensity statistics and coherent imaging characteristics. Shared geometric transformations produce spatially aligned teacher weak views and student strong views. Intensity transformations and Gamma multiplicative speckle perturbations are applied to student views, while a cosine consistency loss aligns patch tokens at corresponding locations, promoting stability under radiometric perturbations. This objective complements the cross-region and cross-scale semantic consistency of DINOv2 multi-crop training, jointly enforcing global and local semantic consistency. Experiments on multiple downstream classification and detection datasets demonstrate state-of-the-art performance on most evaluation metrics, validating the generality and transferability of the learned representations.

papers.title: Sublinear Approximations for Spanning Tree Congestion
papers.abstract:
The spanning tree congestion of a connected graph \(G\) is the minimum, over all spanning trees \(T\) of \(G\), of the maximum number of edges of \(G\) crossing a cut induced by deleting an edge of \(T\). In the spanning tree congestion problem we are asked to compute a spanning tree with minimum congestion.
  We describe two sublinear-ratio approximation algorithms for the spanning tree congestion problem (STC): a simple $\Ot(n^{8/9})$-approximation, and a more involved $\Ot(n^{2/3})$-approximation, where the notation $\Ot$ hides factors polynomial in $\log n$.. Until now, no algorithm with sublinear ratio was known.
  We also prove that for any fixed $0<\varepsilon<1$, approximation of the spanning tree congestion within $2-\varepsilon$ is NP-hard. This improves the previous best known lower bound $6/5$.

Both approximation algorithms for spanning tree congestion use the following structure. Identify the high-degree vertices, called hubs. Separate them into connected regions containing one hub each. Within a region, remove its hub and partition the remaining vertices into connected parts with small boundaries. The algorithms differ in the two partitioning phases: how to obtain regions with only one hub, and how to partition the region with exactly one hub.

papers.title: Strain control of magneto-optical properties of ultra-thin Ni-Mn-Ga films grown by magnetron sputtering
papers.abstract: Ultra-thin epitaxial Ni-Mn-Ga films, 10-15 nm thick, were grown by magnetron sputtering on MgO(001), either directly on the substrate or on a Cr buffer, and studied by X-ray diffraction, magnetometry, and magneto-optical Kerr effect (MOKE) spectroscopy. The films were austenitic, with the cubic cell tetragonally distorted in opposite directions. The film on bare MgO was stretched in-plane ($c/a=0.989$) and the film on Cr was compressed in-plane ($c/a=1.021$), while their unit-cell volumes differed by less than $0.3\%$. As the thermal expansion mismatch was expected to stretch the films in-plane in both cases, the opposite distortions were attributed to the lattice misfit. The room-temperature magnetization loops of the two films did not show significant differences, but their polar and longitudinal MOKE spectra differed in the amplitude, sign, and energy of the spectral structures over the whole 0.76-5 eV range. Magneto-optical simulations showed that the absence of the Cr buffer accounted only for the stronger low-energy polar MOKE rotation extremum of the film on MgO. We attributed the other changes to the strain-induced change of the electronic structure, consistent with theoretical predictions in which the $d_{x^2-y^2}$ and $d_{3z^2-r^2}$ sub-bands of the minority-spin Ni $e_g$ states exchange their order when the distortion changes sign. In parts of the spectrum, the two films showed Kerr rotation or ellipticity of opposite sign, so the choice of the growth template or a dynamically induced distortion can switch the sign of the magneto-optical response at a given photon energy.

The magnetic shape memory alloy Ni-Mn-Ga is a ferromagnetic Heusler alloy whose cubic L21 austenite transforms into lower-symmetry martensitic phases. Since its discovery in a Ni2MnGa single crystal [1], the magnetic-field-induced strain caused by twin-boundary motion has reached, respectively, 5.1 %, 9.5 % and 12 %5.1\text{\,}\mathrm{\%}9.5\text{\,}\mathrm{\%}12\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} in bulk single crystals of the 10M, 14M, and NM martensites [2, 3, 4]. A Cr buffer has low misfit to Ni-Mn-Ga, which enables epitaxial growth without significant interdiffusion and the release of freestanding films by selective etching [17, 18]. papers.title: Nuclear recoil with electron vacuum polarization in muonic atoms
papers.abstract: Using the heavy-particle QED approach, we derive the last missing $\alpha\,(Z\alpha)^5\,m^2/M$ nuclear recoil correction in muonic atoms, which originates from the combination of the $(Z\alpha)^5\,m^2/M$ recoil with the electron vacuum polarization. Numerical results are presented for the $1S$, $2S$, and $2P$ states of $\mu$H, $\mu$D, $\mu^3$He$^+$, and $\mu^4$He$^+$. For the $2P-2S$ Lamb shift in muonic helium ions, our results are of opposite sign and about four times smaller in magnitude than the previous logarithmic estimates.

papers.intro:
Energy levels of muonic atoms are sensitive probes of nuclear structure. Since the Bohr radius of the muon is about 200 times smaller than that of the electron, all nuclear structure effects are strongly enhanced. Thanks to this enhancement, laser spectroscopy of the 2​S−2​P2S-2P transitions in μ\muH, μ\muD, μ3\mu^{3}He+, and μ4\mu^{4}He+ [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] has yielded charge radii of light nuclei with unprecedented precision, and X-ray spectroscopy of heavier muonic atoms aims at further improvements for nuclei with Z=3Z=3–1010 [6]. The extraction of these nuclear charge radii from spectroscopic measurements relies on accurate theoretical predictions of all QED and nuclear structure contributions [7, 8, 9, 10, 11].

In muonic atoms, the electron vacuum polarization (evp) is the dominant QED effect. The reason is that the electron Compton wavelength is comparable to the muonic Bohr radius, me≈mμ​Z​αm_{e}\approx m_{\mu}\,Z\alpha, so that the ratio β=memμ​Z​α\displaystyle\beta=\frac{m_{e}}{m_{\mu}\,Z\alpha} (1) is of order one. Consequently, it is necessary to account for higher-order iterations of the evp potential as well as for its combination with other corrections. Therefore, for muonic systems, it is advantageous to include the evp potential directly in the nonrelativistic Schrödinger equation and solve it numerically [12]. The combined effect of evp and the leading nuclear recoil at order (Z​α)5(Z\alpha)^{5} has so far been known only in the logarithmic approximation [16], and its uncertainty was estimated at 100% [7]. In this work, we derive the complete (Z​α)5(Z\,\alpha)^{5} recoil correction with the Uehling potential [17] included, using the heavy-particle QED (HPQED) approach [18]. The Uehling potential modifies the Bethe logarithm, the Araki–Sucher [19, 20] term, and the Dirac-δ\delta terms through the wave function, the nonrelativistic Hamiltonian, and the energy, and gives rise to additional effective potentials and local terms. Higher-order evp potentials (Källén–Sabry [21], Wichmann–Kroll [22]) are not included in the nuclear recoil corrections, as their contribution is negligible; in muonic hydrogen, for instance, the Källén–Sabry correction amounts to about 0.7% of the Uehling correction [7], so we omit it here.

papers.title: Spectral properties of twisted soft waveguides
papers.abstract: We discuss a model of a soft waveguide described by Schr\"{o}dinger operator whose potential is a twisted straight channel of non-circular profile. We show that a compactly supported twist makes the operator subcritical, the property being expressed in terms of a Hardy-type inequality. On the other hand, a periodic twist raises the essential spectrum and its local slowdown may give rise to isolated eigenvalues below the essential spectrum threshold.

papers.intro:
Among relations between spectral properties and the geometry, the dynamics in the vicinity of curves plays an important role. It is well known, for instance, that the Dirichlet Laplacian in a tubular region which is bent but asymptotically straight has nonempty discrete spectrum due to the effective attractive interaction coming from the tube geometry; such operators are used as models of quantum waveguides cf. [EK15] for a survey. Other geometric perturbations can have different consequences. In particular, twisting of tube of a noncircular profile gives rise to an effective interaction which is of a repulsive nature. This effect was first observed in [CB96] and put on a solid mathematical basis in [EKK08].

Recently another waveguide model, labeled as ‘soft’ and more realistic from the physics point of view, has attracted attention. In this case the confinement is not realized by a hard wall modeled by Dirichlet boundary conditions, but rather by an attractive potential in the form of a channel. The effect of ‘binding by bending’ appeared to be robust; its existence was demonstrated in this setting too, both in two [Ex20, KKK21, EV24] and three [Ex22] dimensions. The question naturally arises whether a twisting of a three-dimensional waveguide modeled by a potential channel of an asymmetric profile produces an effective repulsion. The aim of this paper is to provide an affirmative response to this question.

papers.title: Extremal-Phase-Guided Sequential Convex Optimization: Model Order Reduction
papers.abstract: Fixed-order frequency-weighted H-infinity approximation is a nonconvex problem, and local optimization methods can be sensitive to initialization. We present extremal-phase-guided sequential convex optimization (EPGSCO) for stable fixed-order rational approximation. We introduce a novel phase-guidance technique motivated by the all-pass structure underlying optimal Hankel-norm approximation, with a phase template fitted to the error-magnitude derivative at dominant peaks. We integrate this guidance with dominant-peak selection, focused frequency grids, and adaptive pole-residue and polynomial-coefficient updates to address stagnation and improve approximation accuracy. CD-player examples and benchmarks with known optimal errors evaluate the algorithm against established methods. Comparisons with classical sequential convex optimization (SCO) under shared settings for the common components assess the combined contribution of phase guidance and adaptive frequency refinement. Results demonstrate improved accuracy in most of the tested cases and attainment of the known optimum from four tested initializations for a constructed order-42 benchmark, with additional computation in some cases.

papers.intro:
High-order rational and infinite-dimensional models arise in distributed-parameter systems, electrical circuits, power networks, and systems with communication or actuator delays [1, 2, 3]. Although these models describe the underlying dynamics accurately, their direct use can be impractical for repeated simulation, optimization, or real-time implementation [4]. Model-order reduction replaces them with low-order models that preserve relevant input-output properties [5, 6]. The required accuracy depends on the application. Sequential convex optimization (SCO) constructs local convex subproblems and validates finite steps using the nonlinear objective [22, 23]. In this paper, we propose extremal-phase-guided sequential convex optimization (EPGSCO) for stable fixed-order frequency-weighted ℋ∞\mathcal{H}_{\infty} approximation from frequency-response data. The proposed algorithm combines dominant-error-peak selection and focused optimization grids with phase-guided joint pole–residue second-order cone programs. Second-order cone programming (SOCP) is a class of convex optimization problems with a linear objective and constraints expressed as Euclidean-norm inequalities involving affine functions [30]. We use this formulation to bound the magnitudes of the linearized complex error responses and to impose parameter trust regions. papers.title: All reweighted paths lead to Rome: Unification of reweighting schemes for stratified path sampling
papers.abstract: Path sampling-based stratification algorithms such as Transition Interface Sampling (TIS) enable the evaluation of kinetic rate constants and mechanisms of complex molecular rare event transitions. By sampling only short dynamical trajectories, TIS allows constructing an estimate of the unbiased dynamics by reweighting the interface path ensembles. In the past decades several methods have been developed and applied to achieve such path reweighting, based on statistically optimal use of the trajectory data. Why and how this reweighting exactly works has been underexplored up to now. Here we discuss several different schemes to compute the reweighted path ensemble (RPE), notably point-wise matching, Weighted Histogram Analysis Method (WHAM), Multistate Bennett Acceptance Ratio (MBAR), variance based reweighting (VBR) and survival analysis reweighting (SAR). We show that except for the point-wise matching the other methods are leading to the same outcome, and in fact can be seen as identical. Moreover, the SAR links to a well-established nonparametric maximum-likelihood estimator of product-limit form. This allows a synthesis of all path reweighting schemes, identifying the common underlying nature. All schemes follow from this common origin. We illustrate the reweighting with some simple examples, and show that care has to be taken when applying WHAM, if the number of interfaces and histogram bins do not match.

papers.intro:
Molecular dynamics (MD) simulation has become a standard tool for investigating complex molecular systems, and can predict both thermodynamic and kinetic properties, provided a sufficiently accurate force field is available. Kinetic properties include the rate constants for rare but significant molecular transitions between metastable states, such as protein conformational changes, nucleation events, or chemical reactions. However, when dealing with high free energy barriers these rare transitions are interspersed with long waiting times in metastable states, rendering the direct approach very inefficient.

Molecular dynamics (MD) simulation has become a standard tool for investigating complex molecular systems, and can predict both thermodynamic and kinetic properties, provided a sufficiently accurate force field is available. Kinetic properties include the rate constants for rare but significant molecular transitions between metastable states, such as protein conformational changes, nucleation events, or chemical reactions. However, when dealing with high free energy barriers these rare transitions are interspersed with long waiting times in metastable states, rendering the direct approach very inefficient.

Numerous enhanced sampling techniques were developed to address this issue, usually by biasing the system along a preselected collective variable (CV) that mimics the reaction coordinate[57, 17, 1, 34, 65, 42, 21, 33]. The success of these methods depends on the choice of an appropriate CV, and failure to do so can result in inaccurate estimates of barrier heights, rate constants, and even mechanistic details[19]. Moreover, the biasing approach distorts the natural dynamics itself. These challenges led to the development of path-based techniques that optimize trajectories connecting reactant and product states, and enabling the identification of the minimum (free) energy pathway between them. Prominent examples include Nudged Elastic Band[36, 37, 35], string method[29, 30], action minimization[47], and dominant reaction pathway[31].

In the case of a complex rough energy landscape at finite temperature, a more effective strategy is to sample from a distribution of dynamical paths[20]. Transition path sampling[22, 24, 6, 25, 26, 7, 5, 10] achieves this by collecting an ensemble of pathways that connect initial with final state, through performing a Markov Chain Monte Carlo random walk through trajectory space. Starting with an initial trajectory, TPS generates a new trial path by selecting a frame and initiating a new trajectory by integrating the equations of motion both forward and backward in time[23, 9]. In a Metropolis-Hastings acceptance rule based on detailed balance, the trial path is then either accepted or rejected, and is rejected if it fails to connect the two stable states. Repeating this process results in the transition path ensemble, providing unbiased insight into the mechanism of the rare molecular transition.

Repeating this process results in the transition path ensemble, providing unbiased insight into the mechanism of the rare molecular transition.

By evaluating the reversible work between the reactive transition path ensemble and an ensemble of all trajectories originating in the initial state, TPS also allows for computation of the rate constant. However, efficiency was greatly enhanced with the advent of transition interface sampling (TIS), which samples a series of path ensembles conditioned to cross a hypersurface, or interface, positioned between the stable states[58, 59, 63]. Central to TIS is the crossing probability, the probability that a trajectory crossing one interface will also cross the subsequent interface. The final interface then determines the probability of transitioning into the final state. Multiplying the crossing probabilities of all interfaces with the flux through the initial interface enables precise calculation of rate constants. By stratifying the problem in this manner, TIS avoids the exponential increase in sampling cost with barrier height that is characteristic of direct simulations. Each interface is defined by an order parameter or collective variable, typically represented with the variable λ\lambda. While TIS theoretically provides exact rate constants regardless of the chosen order parameter, this choice does affect the sampling efficiency, although the resulting loss in efficiency due to a suboptimal order parameter is generally less pronounced than that observed in many other sampling methods[62, 63]. The introduction of replica exchange TIS (RETIS) and variants thereof improves these statistics, i.e. converges quicker, by enhancing the decorrelation between sampled paths, particularly for those paths near the stable states[64, 12, 16, 67].

However, if a sufficiently large number of paths is sampled, this crossing probability can also be estimated from other path ensembles conditioned on interfaces closer to the reactant state. Incorporating this additional information is desirable as it leads to a more accurate estimate of the overall crossing probability between the stable states.

Similar to how biased configurational samples in enhanced sampling techniques like umbrella sampling[57] or metadynamics[42] can be unbiased by reweighting, entire TIS trajectories can also be reweighted to correct for their overabundance, by ensuring that the reweighted trajectories matches the crossing probability statistics. This notion led to the concept of the reweighted path ensemble (RPE)[53], which assigns to each sampled path in the TIS simulation a weight such that the resulting weighted ensemble provides a representative description of the trajectory statistics that would be obtained from exhaustive unbiased direct MD. Weighted averages computed on the RPE trajectories approximate equilibrium expectations, including, but not limited to, free energy projections and rates.

papers.title: Tight bounds for fractional and randomized truthful scheduling
papers.abstract: We resolve one of the longest-standing open problems in algorithmic mechanism design by showing that randomization cannot yield a sublinear approximation for truthful scheduling on unrelated machines, even when truthfulness is required only in expectation. Our main technical result concerns fractional scheduling, where tasks may be split among machines. We prove that every deterministic truthful fractional mechanism on $n$ unrelated machines has worst-case approximation ratio at least $(n+1)/2$, even against the optimal integral makespan. This matches the known upper bound exactly and settles the optimal approximation ratio of truthful fractional scheduling. Since the expected allocations and payments of a truthful-in-expectation mechanism define a truthful fractional mechanism, the same lower bound applies to all truthful-in-expectation mechanisms and, in particular, to all universally truthful mechanisms. On the positive side, we give a universally truthful mechanism with approximation ratio $n/2+o(n)$. Together, these results establish the optimal leading constant $1/2$ for randomized truthful scheduling. Thus, randomization improves on the optimal deterministic approximation ratio by an asymptotic factor of two, and no more.

Randomized mechanisms come in two flavors: universally truthful and truthful-in-expectation. A randomized mechanism is called universally truthful if it is defined as a probability distribution over deterministic truthful mechanisms. A randomized mechanism is truthful-in-expectation when agents cannot strictly improve their expected utility by misreporting. The class of truthful-in-expectation mechanisms is broader, but the universally truthful mechanisms have the important characteristic that they are truthful even ex post (that is, even when the random coins become known). papers.title: Mock CSST NUV-NIR imaging of TNG50 galaxies with resolved stellar populations
papers.abstract: Aims. We aim to develop a framework for producing CSST-like mock images of resolved stellar populations from simulated galaxies, demonstrated here using two TNG50 galaxies as illustrative test cases. Methods. Starting from simulated galaxies from TNG50, we use the population synthesis code TRILEGAL to sample individual stars from star particles, retaining bright stars explicitly and treating the remaining unresolved light, including faint stellar light and nebular emission from star-forming regions, as a diffuse background component of the galaxy. Based on the dust distribution inferred from the gas mass and metallicity of gas cells, we use the radiative transfer (RT) code SKIRT to construct the dust model. From this model, we compute the line-of-sight extinction for individual stars, while image-level transmission maps for the diffuse light are derived through RT simulations. For young stars still embedded in their natal molecular clouds, we additionally include birth-cloud attenuation. The resulting dust-attenuated stellar catalogues and diffuse-light images are then processed with the CSST simulation pipeline, which applies PSF convolution, sky background, and instrumental noise. Results. Our framework produces mock CSST images for both a spiral galaxy and a dwarf irregular galaxy from TNG50 in the seven photometric bands. The mock images combine resolved stars, unresolved diffuse light, and dust attenuation within a unified framework, and include the main observational effects expected for the survey. The images are provided with known astrometric and photometric calibration information, and are intended as realistic image-level inputs for subsequent source detection, photometric recovery, and completeness analyses of resolved stellar populations. papers.intro:
Resolved stellar population studies provide direct constraints on galaxy evolution by linking individual stars to spatially resolved star-formation and chemical-enrichment histories. To date, UV–optical resolved-star work beyond the Milky Way has been driven primarily by HST and its legacy programmes. HST’s exquisite angular resolution has enabled landmark surveys across the Local Group and nearby galaxies, including the Panchromatic Hubble Andromeda Treasury in M31 (PHAT; Dalcanton et al. 2012), its southern extension PHAST (Chen et al. 2025), PHATTER in M33 (Williams et al. 2021), the Hubble Tarantula Treasury Project in the LMC (Sabbi et al. 2013), and nearby-galaxy programmes such as the Legacy ExtraGalactic UV Survey (LEGUS; Calzetti et al. 2015), PHANGS–HST (Lee et al. 2022), and the Local Ultraviolet to Infrared Treasury (LUVIT; Gilbert et al. 2025). However, these observations typically cover limited areas or selected fields. In the coming decade, JWST, Euclid, and, later, Roman will greatly expand resolved-star capabilities in the near-infrared (NIR), with particular sensitivity to evolved and dust-obscured stellar populations. However, wide-field UV–optical mapping of young resolved stellar populations over large areas remains comparatively scarce.

Compared with HST programmes that often target limited fields, the wide FoV of CSST will enable contiguous, galaxy-wide maps of resolved luminous stars for many nearby galaxies, with uniform multi-band photometry and slitless spectroscopy where feasible. These data will provide spatially comprehensive constraints on star-formation histories (SFHs), stellar-population gradients, and dust attenuation across galaxy disks and, where depth and crowding permit, into central regions and outer halos. The NUV coverage is particularly valuable for identifying young massive stars, tracing recent star formation, and constraining dust attenuation in young stellar populations. Together, these capabilities will extend resolved stellar population studies from localised case studies to more uniform, statistically controlled, galaxy-scale analyses of nearby galaxies.

Resolved stellar population studies with CSST will critically depend on reliable source detection, photometry, and stellar-parameter inference, all of which are challenging in realistic images of nearby galaxies. In crowded fields, source confusion and blending reduce completeness and degrade photometric accuracy. Spatial variations in the contrast between stars and the local background, set by unresolved stellar light, nebular emission, and sky background, produce position-dependent detection limits and systematic flux biases. Dust attenuation further complicates the problem: patchy extinction from the diffuse interstellar medium (ISM) alters colours and suppresses fluxes along different sightlines, while young stars may experience additional localised attenuation from their birth clouds, introducing age-dependent selection effects. These effects bias the recovered luminosities and colours and, consequently, the inferred attenuation and stellar properties. This motivates realistic, truth-matched mock observations that include crowding, complex image backgrounds, physically motivated dust attenuation, and the dominant image-level observational effects. In this work, we construct synthetic galaxy images and forward-model them through the CSST simulation pipeline, applying PSF convolution, sky background, and instrumental noise, to produce CSST-like mock images.

Hydrodynamical cosmological simulations provide a natural basis for such mocks. Existing efforts broadly fall into two categories. Image-level RT calculations, for example those performed with SKIRT, enable comparisons with imaging surveys in integrated-light morphology and colours (Rodriguez-Gomez et al. 2019; Baes et al. 2024, e.g.), but typically do not provide truth-matched catalogues of individually resolved stars. Conversely, catalogue-level products, often constructed from Milky Way (MW) analogues in simulations such as Auriga and FIRE, are well suited to resolved-star diagnostics, but do not by themselves produce realistic images and therefore do not capture PSF blending, complex image backgrounds, or image-level noise. In many catalogue-based applications, dust attenuation is treated with simplified prescriptions, including external MW extinction maps (Grand et al. 2018), distance-dependent laws (Valentini et al. 2018), or per-star extinctions inferred from line-of-sight gas columns mapped to E⁡(B−V)E(B-V) (Sanderson et al. 2020). These prescriptions are useful for MW studies, but do not straightforwardly generalise to external galaxies with different dust compositions, geometries, and viewing angles.

papers.title: Developing the Field Selector System for the SHARP Multi-IFU: Optomechanical Design and First Prototype Validation
papers.abstract: This paper presents the innovative Field Selector System (FSS) developed for VESPER, the multi-Integral Field Unit of the SHARP near-infrared spectrograph. The proposed system employs an array of movable light-collection probes (Field Selectors) that travel along parallel, vertically offset planes to avoid mechanical interference and vignetting. The true novelty lies in its opto-mechanical synchronization: as each probe translates by {\Delta}y to select a target, a set of folding mirrors shifts by {\Delta}y/2. This maintains a constant optical path length, allowing multiple independently moving probes to share a single focal plane and form a continuous image on it, easy to slice by the slicer. A dedicated optical test setup was developed to characterize the positioning stability and repeatability of the probe motion. The measured mechanical errors were converted into equivalent optical tilts and incorporated into the SHARP optical model to assess their impact on instrument performance. The experimental results identified the dominant sources of positioning error and provided valuable insight into the relationship between mechanical tolerances and optical performance. The study also highlights several design improvements capable of significantly reducing probe tilting and enhancing system stability. The results demonstrate the viability of the proposed concept and indicate that, with the identified improvements, the system represents an excellent field-selection solution for SHARP and other multi-integral-field-unit (mIFU) spectrographs.

papers.title: Supermassive black holes and nuclear star clusters in galaxies: constraining formation and co-evolution with SHARP and MICADO
papers.abstract: Nuclear star clusters and supermassive black holes are the dominant compact components in galaxy nuclei. They can coexist within the same system, and their relative prominence traces the history of gas inflow, star formation, and dynamical evolution on parsec scales. Key questions remain open concerning the physical channels that assemble nuclear star clusters, the mass regimes in which supermassive black holes become dynamically dominant, and the conditions under which compact stellar nuclei are suppressed, destroyed, or replaced by cusp-like structures. We describe how near-infrared integral-field spectroscopy with SHARP on the Extremely Large Telescope, combined with high-resolution imaging from MICADO, enables quantitative tests of nuclear formation and evolution scenarios within a unified framework. The joint analysis of stellar dynamics, stellar populations, and nuclear structure allows black-hole masses, internal kinematics of nuclear star clusters, and signatures of gas inflow to be measured consistently within the same systems, and defines the mass and distance ranges where robust constraints can be obtained. Recent discoveries of compact active nuclei at high redshift indicate that efficient black-hole growth can occur in systems with weak or compact stellar components. Although nearby galaxies are not evolutionary analogues of early systems, the diversity of nuclear configurations accessible with SHARP and MICADO provides a local laboratory for isolating the physical mechanisms that regulate the coupled evolution of central black holes and nuclear stellar structures.

papers.title: Primary and Secondary Star Formation in the Spiral Waves of NGC 628
papers.abstract: To determine the role of spiral arms and stellar feedback on the formation of stars, we examine the positions of optically identified and emerging star clusters in NGC 628. We find that the youngest clusters extend further into the spiral arms at small radii than at large radii, as expected when the angular flow rate through a wave-like arm increases with greater distance from corotation. The embedded or emerging star clusters (eYSCs) are identified relative to four distinct morphological features in the 7.7 micron image: spiral arm filaments, spiral arm spurs, spiral interarm feathers, and bubbles. Spiral arm-related eYSCs are presumably first-generation stars made from interstellar gas that was directly compressed by the density wave, while clusters along the rims of bubbles are secondary generations produced by feedback compression. The mass functions of the first and second generations differ: eYSCs in spiral arm filaments extend to significantly higher masses than eYSCs in bubbles. Secondary star formation continues downstream from primary star formation, removing the expected age gradient through the arms. Bubble eYSCs account for approximately one-third of all the emerging cluster mass. The outer arms have a more mixed distribution of spiral- and bubble-related eYSCs than the inner arms, potentially providing a way to distinguish wave and material arms and to find corotation in wave-like arms. Among the 17 most massive clusters with log M(Msun)>4, eight of them are in four tight pairs; in at least one case, the dynamical time for the pair is comparable to the cluster ages.

We begin with a detailed summary of star formation, spiral arms, feedback bubbles and young clusters in NGC 628 (Sect. II). We then summarize our data sources in Section III. The first step in our analysis is to determine the location of the crest in the old stellar spiral (Sect. IV). The positions of young optical clusters are examined with respect to this crest to look for evidence of a time sequence or steady flow through the spiral pattern (Sect. V). We consider the emerging clusters next (Sect. VI) and determine their locations with respect to three main spiral wave features, i.e., the main arms, bright spurs that jut off from the main arms, and interarm feathers; these features are explained in Sect. II.4. We also identify emerging clusters that are at the edges of bubbles (cf. Sects. II.2, VI.1). This characterization of the youngest star-forming regions is used to determine the relative numbers and masses of clusters that recently formed by gas collapse associated with specific dynamical processes. In Section VI.4, we compare the cluster mass functions for each environment to examine the claim that spiral arms make more massive clusters (Sect. II.1). From the relative cluster masses we also suggest approximate proportions of interstellar turbulence that is driven by spiral arms and feedback (Sect. VII.4). A surprising discovery is the presence of three tight binary clusters and one moderately tight binary among the 17 most massive clusters (Sect. VI.5). The results are summarized in Section VIII.

papers.title: The dwarf galaxy NGC 185: the flagship of Andromeda's dwarf galaxies for the study of evolved multiple stellar populations
papers.abstract:
Reaching galaxies at 10-15 Mpc with HST and JWST requires star
  formation history (SFH) diagnostics that do not rely on the faint
  main sequence turn-off. We investigate whether horizontal branch (HB),
  red clump (RC), and red and asymptotic giant branch (RGB, AGB) stars can
  fill this role for dwarf elliptical galaxies, using NGC 185 as a test case.
  We use stellar evolution models of low- and intermediate-mass stars as inputs
  to population synthesis simulations that reproduce the colour distribution and
  luminosity function of stars in the (mF606W-mF814W, mF814W)
  diagram. The study of the stars populating the HB is used to derive
  the distance modulus and reddening, the average mass loss suffered by the stars during
  the ascending on the RGB and the SFH occurred during the ancient epochs, before 7 Gyr ago.
  The luminosity function of the RC gives us constraints on the recent SFH (<8 Gyr).
  The distribution of HB stars yields a reddening E(B-V)=0.20 mag and a distance
  modulus DM=24.10 mag for NGC 185. The average mass lost by low-mass stars during
  the RGB phase is 0.22 +- 0.01 Msun. Star formation
  was concentrated at early epochs, with half of the stars formed more than 11 Gyr ago.
  The morphology of the HB indicates essentially no metallicity spread among stars older
  than 8 Gyr, whereas the slope of the RGB suggests that part of the stars younger than
  5-6 Gyr are slightly enriched in metals. Once RGB mass loss is adequately constrained, evolved stars can provide a
  reliable SFH for dwarf elliptical galaxies well beyond the reach of MSTO-based methods.
  We discuss the implications for more distant systems and the remaining uncertainties in
  the underlying stellar models.

papers.intro:
Significant effort has recently been dedicated to reconstructing the star formation history (SFH) of individual nearby galaxies through their resolved stellar populations. Detailed SFHs in the solar neighborhood (Gallart et al., 2024), Andromeda (Williams et al., 2015), nearby dwarf galaxies (Savino et al., 2023), and the stellar halos of nearby MW-mass galaxies (Brown et al., 2006; Rejkuba et al., 2005; Durrell, Sarajedini, & Chandar, 2010) have begun to constrain the physical processes that form and shape galaxies, including gas accretion and consumption (Cohen et al., 2025), stellar feedback (Hunter et al., 2022), and the mechanisms that quench star formation, such as the infall of low-mass dwarf galaxies into the MW (Fillingham et al., 2015; Slater & Bell, 2014, e.g.,) and cosmic reionization (Benítez-Llambay et al., 2015; Weisz et al., 2014, e.g.,).

The traditional method for reconstructing galaxy SFHs is fitting the main sequence turn-off (MSTO) in the colour-magnitude diagram (CMD) (Brown et al., 2006; Barker et al., 2011; Bernard et al., 2012; Bernard et al., 2015a; Bernard et al., 2015b; Monachesi et al., 2012; Geha et al., 2015; Monelli et al., 2016; Savino et al., 2023). However, the faintness of the MSTO restricts this method to nearby galaxies (<<1 Mpc). To reach larger distances (10–15 Mpc) with HST and JWST, it is important to develop techniques that derive the SFH from brighter, more evolved populations: stars on the red giant branch (RGB) and asymptotic giant branch (AGB), and those undergoing core helium burning on the horizontal branch (HB) and red clump (RC).

Several attempts have used the statistics of evolved stars to constrain galaxy SFHs. RC stars, together with the RGB stars from which they evolve, can constrain the SFH over the last 5–6 Gyr (Girardi & Salaris, 2001): the size and shape of the RC (Caputo, Castellani, & degl’Innocenti, 1995, e.g.,) and the relative number of RC to RGB stars (Tolstoy, 1999, e.g.,) both trace the age of the dominant population. Martin et al. (2017) used HB and RC stars to show that many M31 dwarf galaxies have extended SFHs, inconsistent with rapidly shut-down early star formation episodes. In recent years, this approach has largely been superseded by modern CMD-reconstruction methods, which derive the best-fitting SFH from a galaxy’s entire observed CMD, though often with a systematic mismatch between the observed and modelled RC. Weisz et al. (2014) showed that CMDs reaching only as deep as the HB (including the RC and HB but not the oldest MSTO) still retain significant SFH information, provided systematic errors arising from the models are accounted for. The largest source of uncertainty in age-dating a population via RC stars remains the uncertainty in mass loss along the RGB (δ​MRGB\rm\delta M_{RGB}), at the ∼20%\sim 20\% level.

Using the rest of the HB to derive ancient populations has proven more difficult, limited to a few dwarf galaxies with independent metallicity constraints. In Carina, Smecker-Hane et al. (1994) found two morphologically distinct horizontal branches, confirming that star formation occurred in two well-separated episodes at 6 and >10>10 Gyr, later confirmed quantitatively by de Boer et al. (2014) using MSTO photometry. Salaris et al. (2013) performed the first detailed synthetic HB simulation of Sculptor, using an independently derived SFH and metallicity evolution with RGB mass loss as the only free parameter, an approach Savino, Salaris, & Tolstoy (2015) extended to Carina, showing HB data can refine the SFH derived from red giants and turn-off stars alone. This culminated in the MORGOTH code (Savino et al., 2018), which showed that including the HB significantly increases SFH precision; applied to the more distant Tucana, it resolved three ancient star-formation phases at finer temporal resolution than previously possible, linked to three discrete HB clumps (Savino et al., 2019). While great progress has been made, HB stars work best as a complement to MSTO/RGB analysis rather than a standalone diagnostic, remaining fundamentally limited by RGB mass loss — a free parameter current theory cannot predict from first principles.

papers.title: Adaptive Optics for the Extremely Large Telescope: overcoming Point Spread Function challenges with MORFEO
papers.abstract: MORFEO is the multi-conjugate adaptive optics (MCAO) relay for the Extremely Large Telescope (ELT) of the European Southern Observatory. It combines the adaptive mirrors of the telescope (M4-M5) with two post-focal deformable mirrors to deliver a stable, diffraction-limited point spread function over a field approaching 1'. MORFEO senses the atmosphere using six sodium laser guide stars and up to three natural guide stars distributed across a $\sim$160'' technical field, enabling sky coverage levels of order 50% at the South Galactic Pole. Through its two gravity-invariant ports, MORFEO feeds the MICADO first-light imager and spectrograph with a corrected field of 51''and HARMONI, the high-angular resolution integral field spectrograph. SHARP, a concept for a multi-object near-infrared spectrograph at the ELT, adopts MORFEO as its reference MCAO architecture for evaluating achievable image quality and scientific performance. In this paper, we summarise the MCAO capabilities delivered by MORFEO, its optical quality, tomographic performance, stability of the corrected focal plane, and the accuracy of telemetry-based PSF reconstruction, and discuss their relevance for the development of SHARP and other wide-field spectroscopic concepts at the ELT.

papers.intro:
Adaptive optics (AO) has transformed ground-based optical and near-infrared astronomy by restoring diffraction-limited performance on large telescopes and thereby enabling high-contrast, high-resolution imaging and spectroscopy. The Extremely Large Telescope (ELT) (Gilmozzi and Spyromilio (2007)) integrates AO at the system level through the adaptive quaternary mirror M4 and the fast tip–tilt mirror M5; together with the Laser Projection System (Nijenhuis et al. (2022)), these enable several AO modes ranging from Single-conjugate AO (SCAO) (Babcock (1953)) and Ground Layer AO (GLAO) (Rigaut (2002)) to Laser Tomography AO (Foy and Labeyrie (1985)) and Multi–Conjugate AO (Beckers (1988)). Achieving stable diffraction-limited imaging at ELT aperture scales requires wide-field AO architectures capable of mitigating anisoplanatism and telescope-induced aberrations across arcminute fields.

Achieving stable diffraction-limited imaging at ELT aperture scales requires wide-field AO architectures capable of mitigating anisoplanatism and telescope-induced aberrations across arcminute fields.

MORFEO (Multi-conjugate adaptive Optics Relay For ELT Observations), formerly MAORY (Diolaiti et al. (2016)), is the MCAO module of the ELT. It combines telescope adaptive optics with two post-focal deformable mirrors (DM) conjugated at high-altitude layers (nominally ∼\sim6.5 km and ∼\sim17.5 km). The AO system uses the ELT constellation of six sodium Laser Guide Stars (LGSs) for high-order sensing, along with up to three faint Natural Guide Stars (NGSs) for low-order and truth sensing. This architecture delivers an adaptive correction over a technical field of ∼\sim160′′and supports the AO needs of two gravity-invariant instrument ports: the MICADO (Davies et al. (2010)) first-light imager/spectrograph and a second port assigned to the HARMONI spectrograph (Thatte et al. (2016)). For MICADO, MORFEO optimises diffraction-limited performance over the field imaged by the camera, allowing precision photometry, astrometry, and morphology studies in a range of science cases (Davies et al. (2021); Rodeghiero et al. (2021); Clenet et al. (2022)). The wider corrected field accessible from the second port, of order ∼\sim2–2.5′, enables concepts such as multi-object spectroscopy at the ELT scale.

A central challenge for ELT-class AO is the time- and field-dependent variability of the point-spread function (PSF), driven by atmospheric turbulence, telescope-induced perturbations, and residual control errors. In high-latitude extragalactic fields, the scarcity of suitably bright stars complicates empirical PSF characterisation. MICADO therefore adopts a blind telemetry-driven PSF reconstruction strategy (Veran et al. (1997); Wagner et al. (2018); Grazian et al. (2022)), which uses AO telemetry and control matrices to recover the science PSF without relying on isolated point sources. MORFEO is designed to provide sky coverage of at least 50% at high Galactic latitude, K-band Strehl ratios of ≳30%\gtrsim 30\% under median conditions, and the PSF stability required to minimise PSF-driven systematics in photometry and morphology (Busoni et al. (2022); Ciliegi et al. (2022)).

papers.title: Decentralized Impedance Specifications for Grid-Connected Converters: a Sequence-Domain Gershgorin Method, and a Frequency-Wise Framework for Combining Different Criteria
papers.abstract: In complex grid scenarios, with many power electronics (PE) converters connected, having specifications for converters can ease the design process. A practical approach is to impose the specifications on the converter's small-signal impedance in the frequency domain. This is advantageous since impedance is a physical property that can be measured. This paper focuses on providing decentralized impedance specifications for each converter connected to an ac bus. With decentralized specifications, each converter has its own specifications, which are independent of other converters' impedance. This enables a competitive multi-vendor environment while guaranteeing system stability. Existing methods of imposing decentralized specifications, based on the small-gain, passivity and Gershgorin theorems, are formulated within a common frequency-domain framework. Building on this, two new solutions that reduce the conservativeness of the specifications are proposed. First, Gershgorin-based decentralized specifications are formulated in the modified sequence domain. Second, a framework for combining different specification types across frequency ranges is developed and mathematically proven. The methods are compared on examples covering sub-synchronous and harmonic-range interactions of grid-following converters, grid-forming converters, and a mixed grid-forming/grid-following system, using analytical models, black-box impedance measurements, and time-domain responses obtained from simulations and an experimental setup.

papers.intro:
The global transition toward renewable energy sources has significantly increased the penetration of power electronics (PE) converters into electrical grids, introducing challenges such as converter interactions and small-signal stability issues. Traditional stability assessment techniques—state-space pole analysis and frequency-domain control loop-gain methods—are effective for individual converter design, but become complicated when multiple converters are interconnected, even for simple practical cases.

The global transition toward renewable energy sources has significantly increased the penetration of power electronics (PE) converters into electrical grids, introducing challenges such as converter interactions and small-signal stability issues. Traditional stability assessment techniques—state-space pole analysis and frequency-domain control loop-gain methods—are effective for individual converter design, but become complicated when multiple converters are interconnected, even for simple practical cases.

Impedance-based stability assessment offers an effective framework for studying converter interactions. First applied by Middlebrook for input filter design [1] and later extended to grid-connected converters [2, 3], the method partitions the system into source and load subsystems, each represented by its Thévenin or Norton equivalent. Stability is then assessed by applying the Nyquist criterion to the source-to-load impedance ratio, known as the minor loop gain.

Stability is then assessed by applying the Nyquist criterion to the source-to-load impedance ratio, known as the minor loop gain.

While a single-input single-output (SISO) representation is sufficient to capture the dynamics at the dc terminal of PE converters, the ac-side typically requires a multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) representation, usually in the d​qdq frame [4, 5, 6] to capture all relevant dynamics. Consequently, the ac-side impedance is a transfer function matrix, which necessitates the use of the generalized Nyquist criterion.

Since applying the Nyquist criterion offers limited insight into shaping the desired individual impedances, alternative impedance-based stability specifications were first proposed by Middlebrook [1] and later extended by Wildrick et al. [7]. For MIMO systems, several approaches to defining such specifications have been introduced, including methods based on matrix norms [8], on the diagonal dd- and qq-axis elements of the impedance matrix (applicable when the impedances are diagonally dominant) [9], passivity theory requiring both source and load subsystems to be passive [10], net damping criteria requiring the combined damping of both subsystems to be positive [11, 12, 13, 14], and, more recently, a rotated passivity index [15].

In the case where specifications are needed for multiple converters, the decentralized impedance specifications [16] were proposed. Here, the goal is to define individual conditions that each converter should satisfy independently of the others so that, once all converters are connected together, the system remains stable. This can be of great interest when many converters are planned for connection to the grid since the specifications for each converter can be given without knowing the impedance of the others up front.

Although impedance specifications for a single converter are well established in the literature for both dc systems [1, 7] and ac systems [8, 13, 15], decentralized specifications for multiple converters have predominantly been developed for dc systems—including a single dc bus [16, 17], series-type dc microgrids [18], multi-bus dc systems [19, 20], and dc distribution systems connected to an ac grid [21]—and only recently extended to converters connected to a common ac bus [22, 23], which is also the focus of this paper. For converters connected to different ac buses, decentralized conditions have been derived based on passivity of large-signal grid-forming models [24], on combining the small-gain and small-phase theorems [25], and, for multi-vendor grids, on robust stability analysis of grey-box converter models [26]. Related control-theoretic conditions have also been proposed for dc microgrids [27] and for generic networked systems [28, 29]. However, these conditions are formulated on control-loop transfer functions rather than on the terminal impedance [26], address large-signal rather than small-signal stability [24], or rely on properties, such as sectoriality, that converter impedances often do not satisfy [25, 23]; imposing them directly on measured frequency data is therefore not straightforward. In contrast, for converters connected to a common ac bus, the specifications reduce to simple per-converter conditions on the measured impedance.

In contrast, for converters connected to a common ac bus, the specifications reduce to simple per-converter conditions on the measured impedance.

In our previous work [22], we proposed a method that formulates decentralized specifications for the d​qdq-frame impedance based on the Gershgorin theorem, previously mainly employed for stability analysis [30, 31, 32, 33, 34]. It is recognized in [22] that the approach introduces a certain degree of conservativeness; however, alternative decentralized-specification methods and a systematic comparison of their conservativeness are not addressed. More recently, [23] proposed decentralized specifications based on a combination of the net-damping criterion and a rotated passivity index. Similarly to [22], it is demonstrated that assigning individual specifications to each converter can effectively prevent instability in multi-parallel converter systems.

Despite these advances, several gaps remain for converters connected to a common ac bus. First, comparisons between decentralized-specification methods are limited: [22] does not compare against alternatives, while [23] compares its extended-passivity condition only with conventional passivity and small-gain conditions for a grid-forming case, without considering Gershgorin-based specifications. Second, both [22, 23] primarily address low-frequency (near-synchronous) interactions, leaving the harmonic frequency range largely unexplored. Finally, combinations of methods across frequency ranges have so far been limited to passivity- and small-gain-type conditions: [15, 23] combine the rotated passivity index at low frequencies with the net-damping criterion at high frequencies, and [35] unifies small-gain, passivity, and rotated-passivity conditions through frequency-dependent multipliers. However, Gershgorin-based specifications are not covered by this framework, and [35] is validated only on a single-converter system, without deriving per-converter specifications for multi-parallel converters.

papers.title: On the Optimality of Implicit Feedback in Markov Decision Processes over Imperfect Links
papers.abstract: Goal-oriented communication protocols are explicitly designed to support the objectives of target applications, such as the monitoring and control of remote processes, while minimizing data traffic. This study considers a transmitter node that observes the environment state and sends it to a remote agent, which then performs control actions. This problem can be modeled as a remote Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (POMDP), a subclass of decentralized POMDPs. Existing studies limit transmissions through communication costs, but neglect the effect of channel impairments and non-ideal or delayed feedback. In this work, we study the optimal joint transmission and control policies over lossy forward channels without explicit acknowledgments. We introduce \emph{revealing} policies, under which the receiver's action, observed directly by the transmitter, discloses the outcome of the forward transmission, keeping the two agents synchronized without a feedback channel. We derive sufficient conditions for the optimality of time-invariant policies in this implicit feedback regime for general POMDPs, along with strictly weaker sufficient conditions in the special case of contextual bandits. Our simulations over a family of remote POMDPs show that these conditions are conservative, and revealing policies are optimal over a substantially wider parameter range than the conditions warrant.

papers.title: Efficient estimation of regression models for recurrent events in presence of terminal events
papers.abstract: Recurrent events are common in biomedical studies, and efficient methods are needed to analyse them, particularly when a terminal event may occur. Regression modelling of the marginal mean of recurrent events provides a simply interpretable approach, but standard estimation based on inverse probability of censoring weighting may not fully exploit observed event histories in multiple events settings. We demonstrate how the popular Ghosh-Lin proportional means model can be estimated efficiently by developing an augmentation procedure that is also applicable to composite endpoints. Using semiparametric efficiency theory, we characterize the fully efficient estimator. First, we investigate its construction under frailty models. We then propose a dynamic censoring-augmented estimator that is straightforward to compute and does not require a fully specified joint model for recurrent and terminal events. We show theoretically that it improves on the standard Ghosh-Lin estimator and derive an explicit expression for its asymptotic variance reduction. We also establish conditions under which tests of no treatment effect remain valid in randomized trials when the proportional means model is misspecified. Extensive simulations examine performance under dependence between recurrent and terminal events, unobserved heterogeneity, censoring-model misspecification, and auxiliary covariates. The practical gain of the proposed methods is illustrated with an analysis of catheter-related bloodstream infections in patients with chronic intestinal failure receiving home parenteral support.
papers.intro:
The use of recurrent events modelling has gained increased popularity in recent years both in theoretical work and in practical settings. In the pharmaceutical field, a recent industry qualification, see Akacha et al. (2018), advocated that going beyond a time to first event analysis can be of interest because it more fully describes the phenomenon studied and often it will also lead to a more efficient use of the data. This is particularly important in the setting of expensive randomized clinical studies. On the theoretical side, new developments are ongoing and a recent summary can be found in Cook and Lawless (2007), see also Andersen and Ravn (2023); Cook and Lawless (2018).

The regression modelling of recurrent events can roughly be grouped into intensity-based or rate-based modelling where the intensity/rate of the events of interest can be modelled alongside the intensity/rate of the terminal event. This line of work includes, for example, the Andersen-Gill model (Andersen and Gill, 1982), the Prentice-Williams-Peterson model (Prentice et al., 1981), and the Wei-Lin-Weissfeld and Lin-Wei-Yang-Ying models (Wei et al., 1989; Lin et al., 2000).

This line of work includes, for example, the Andersen-Gill model (Andersen and Gill, 1982), the Prentice-Williams-Peterson model (Prentice et al., 1981), and the Wei-Lin-Weissfeld and Lin-Wei-Yang-Ying models (Wei et al., 1989; Lin et al., 2000).

Another line of work instead has been focussing on what is called marginal mean regression modelling, which aims to model the marginal mean of the recurrent events. Here notably, the Ghosh-Lin model has been a pioneering approach that has been frequently used in applications (Ghosh and Lin, 2002). There have been several extensions of the Ghosh-Lin model to combine multiple events into composite endpoints (Mao and Lin, 2016) and, along the same lines, making composite endpoints in the context of competing risks (Furberg et al., 2022). The Ghosh-Lin model is a Cox-type regression extension of the simple nonparametric marginal mean estimator that was considered by Cook and Lawless (1997); Ghosh and Lin (2000) and recently, it was shown how the marginal mean parameter can be estimated efficiently (Cortese and Scheike, 2022).

The Ghosh-Lin model and its composite endpoint extensions are semi-parametric Cox-type models and the estimated parameters and inference for these models are often based on inverse probability of censoring (IPCW) adjustment. The current paper presents how this estimation procedure can be easily made more efficient by building on the theory of efficient estimation for censored data; see, e.g., Tsiatis (2006); Van der Laan and Robins (2003); Robins and Rotnitzky (1992); Bang and Tsiatis (2000) In addition, we show that the efficiency gain can be quite large and leads to an important advantage: it further introduces certain double robustness properties that make the parameter estimation less sensitive to the IPCW model selection for censoring, which is typically needed to provide unbiased estimates. We show theoretically how to obtain the most efficient Ghosh-Lin type estimator that relies on correctly specifying and estimating the working models involved in the augmented term of the estimating equations. Therefore, we propose a novel approach that develops augmented estimating equations based on a dynamic prediction model with time-varying coefficients for the augmented term due to censoring. The performance of this estimator is studied in extensive realistic simulations and the novel method gives a surprisingly large efficiency gain. The suggested estimator has the advantage of being computationally quite simple and keeping the computation time linearly in the sample size of the data.

papers.title: Spectral and mapping properties of the inverse Ornstein--Uhlenbeck operator
papers.abstract: We investigate the spectral and boundedness properties of the inverse Ornstein--Uhlenbeck operator $\mathcal{A}^{Q,B}$ and its associated semigroup in $L^p$ spaces with respect to the inverse Gaussian measure. We establish strong continuity and contractivity of this semigroup in $L^p$ for $p \in [1, \infty)$, and obtain a complete characterization of the spectrum of $\mathcal{A}^{Q,B}$. For $p \in (1, \infty)$, the spectrum is independent of $p$, consists entirely of eigenvalues and exhibits a spectral gap. For $p=1$, the spectrum is instead the left half-plane. Furthermore, we discuss ultracontractivity and hypercontractivity properties of the semigroup.

papers.title: Delay-induced multirhythmicity in a 3-cell inhibitory network
papers.abstract: We study the dynamics of a delayed three-cell central pattern generator network using return-map analysis and a phase-reduced description derived from generalized FitzHugh-Nagumo oscillators. The phase model captures the emergence and stability of synchronous, pacemaker, and traveling-wave rhythms and provides a systematic, computationally efficient framework for characterizing the network dynamics beyond direct return-map calculations. We conduct extensive two-parameter analyses of both the full and phase-reduced models, revealing rich multi-rhythmic dynamics and transitions among coexisting rhythmic states. The close agreement between the two descriptions establishes phase reduction as an efficient and reliable framework for characterizing the dynamical organization of delayed neural oscillator networks.

Central pattern generators (CPGs) are neural circuits that produce rhythmic motor patterns without rhythmic external input [14, 28, 10]. Interactions within biological CPGs are not instantaneous: finite synaptic transmission and signal-propagation times introduce delays into network coupling [21, 27, 23]. Such delays can substantially reorganize the network dynamics, affecting synchronization, phase locking, and the coexistence of rhythmic states even in small networks of coupled relaxation oscillators [17, 22, 2].

Phase reduction provides a complementary description of coupled-oscillator dynamics. In the weak-coupling regime, a high-dimensional network of oscillators can be reduced to a low-dimensional system governing their phase interactions [6, 12, 20, 29]. Early studies of delay-coupled oscillators incorporated transmission delays explicitly into the phase arguments [18, 26, 5]. Subsequent work established that, under weak coupling, these delays can instead be represented as effective phase shifts in the interaction functions of the reduced equations [4, 1, 2, 13, 15, 11, 6] as long as the delay is not too long [8].

Previous studies have shown that, in CPG networks without delays, phase-difference models accurately reproduce the fixed-point organization and stability properties revealed by return maps [29]. Whether this correspondence persists in delayed CPG networks, however, remains largely unexplored. Delays can generate more complex dynamical structures, including invariant curves, whose location and stability are not readily determined from return-map constructions alone. This limitation motivates a systematic comparison of return-map and phase-reduced descriptions of delayed CPG networks.

In this work, we investigate a delayed three-cell inhibitory CPG network by combining return-map analysis with phase reduction of a network of generalized FitzHugh–Nagumo oscillators [19, 3, 16, 17]. Using phase-response curves (PRCs) and coupling functions [6], we derive a two-dimensional phase-difference system and systematically compare its predictions with the dynamics of the full delayed network. We show that the phase-reduced model not only reproduces the principal rhythmic structures revealed by the return maps but also provides a more detailed characterization of the phase space. In particular, it identifies stable synchronous states with extremely small basins of attraction that can be difficult to detect through direct return-map simulations. The reduced model also permits the location and stability of limit cycles in the phase-difference plane to be determined directly, thereby clarifying the dynamical origin of the invariant curves observed in the return maps. Using both the full and reduced models, we perform extensive two-parameter analyses of rhythm generation and transitions among coexisting states. The close agreement between the two descriptions establishes phase reduction as an accurate and computationally efficient framework for large-scale exploration of delayed CPG networks.

papers.title: Challenge-Aware Knowledge Recruitment with Meta-Agent Supervision for Medical Multi-Agent Reasoning
papers.abstract: Large language models perform strongly on standard medical QA but degrade on harder reasoning tasks, where multi-agent debate often fails to beat strong single-model prompting. We argue that a key limitation is that existing systems select experts and retrieve knowledge from the question alone, rather than from gaps that emerge during reasoning. We propose challenge-aware adaptive recruitment: an external CHALLENGER inspects the evolving reasoning trace and identifies specific factual or expertise gaps. These signals trigger targeted knowledge retrieval or mid-discussion specialist recruitment. On the MEDAGENTSBENCH hard subset (862 questions across nine biomedical datasets), upfront retrieval provides little benefit, while challenge-aware in-between retrieval performs better; on a multi-specialist backbone it improves accuracy on 8 of 9 datasets and adds 6 percentage points over Challenger Only. Ablations indicate benefits from both retrieval timing and gap-specific query signals, and a live web-search experiment shows that the timing advantage persists across retrieval backends. For specialist recruitment, self-triggered adaptation is unreliable, whereas Challenger-triggered recruitment raises GPT-4.1-mini MedQA accuracy from 46% to 54%, with positive direction on all tested generalization datasets. Naively combining retrieval and specialist recruitment degrades performance, highlighting the need to coordinate adaptive intervention channels. These results show that when and why external resources are recruited is a key design choice in multi-agent medical reasoning.

In clinical practice, complex diagnoses often require expertise from multiple specialties. Hospitals therefore convene multidisciplinary teams (MDTs), bringing together specialist clinicians to discuss a case and agree on a diagnosis or treatment plan. By combining knowledge from several domains, MDTs can address problems that would be difficult for any individual clinician to solve alone.

Hospitals therefore convene multidisciplinary teams (MDTs), bringing together specialist clinicians to discuss a case and agree on a diagnosis or treatment plan. By combining knowledge from several domains, MDTs can address problems that would be difficult for any individual clinician to solve alone.

However, an MDT is neither a fixed committee nor a group working from a predetermined body of evidence. The relevant specialties often become apparent only as the discussion unfolds. A radiological interpretation may reframe the clinical question, or an unexpected laboratory result may raise a possibility that had not previously been considered, prompting the team to seek an additional specialist opinion. Medical evidence is consulted in much the same way: not necessarily at the outset, but when a specific question becomes important to the team’s decision.

A similar idea has recently been explored in AI through multi-agent systems, in which multiple language-model agents with different roles or areas of expertise collaborate to solve a problem [14, 9]. papers.title: Hall-Density Collapse as Direct Evidence for Percolative Conduction Onset in Monolayer MoS$_2$ Transistors
papers.abstract: The origin of the apparent metal-insulator transition in two-dimensional electron systems remains debated. Using temperature-dependent transport and Hall measurements on industry-relevant MoS$_2$ monolayer FETs with amorphous HfO$_2$ dielectrics, we establish classical percolation as the underlying mechanism. We report two complementary signatures of disorder-driven conduction onset: a temperature-independent Hall-density collapse as a function of absolute gate voltage and a vanishing activation energy at a characteristic carrier density $n_{\mathrm{c}}$, identified as the percolation threshold. These findings identify dielectric-interface disorder, rather than channel quality alone, as the key parameter governing device turn-on. The extracted activation barriers reach values substantially exceeding room-temperature thermal energies, indicating that disorder-driven conduction onset remains relevant well beyond cryogenic transport.

papers.title: Self-Supervised Pretraining for Label-Efficient Facial Expression Recognition using Smart Glasses
papers.abstract: Facial Expression Recognition (FER) on optomyographic (OMG) smart glasses such as OCOsense enables privacy-preserving, camera-free affect sensing for health and well-being. Most FER systems are fully supervised, i.e., they rely either on hand-crafted expert features with classical machine learning, or on end-to-end deep models trained from labelled data. Both depend on large quantities of labelled expressions, which are costly to collect and limit deployment in real-world, personalized settings. We investigate Self-Supervised Learning (SSL) as a route to label-efficient FER on these glasses. We pretrain a Vision Transformer with a masked-autoencoder objective on unlabelled OCOsense recordings and finetune it for five-class FER under person-independent cross-validation. Across label budgets from 5% to 100%, pretraining consistently improves performance; with only 5% of the labels, the pretrained model outperforms the from-scratch model trained with all labels. Our results show that SSL pretraining is a practical way to reduce labelling cost for smart eyewear FER, and we discuss the implications for future personalization and continual adaptation.

papers.intro:
Mental-health and well-being disorders are among the leading causes of disability worldwide, affecting roughly 16–20% of the population in many regions, yet most individuals rarely receive timely or personalized support (Arias et al., 2022). Wearable devices now make continuous, in-the-wild behavioral and physiological monitoring feasible at scale, opening the door to earlier and more personalized well-being sensing (Broulidakis et al., 2023). A persistent obstacle, however, is robust generalization across users, devices, and real-world conditions. Behavioral and affective signals vary substantially from person to person, and models that perform well on a training cohort often degrade on new, unseen users (Han et al., 2024). Methods that adapt to individuals without demanding large per-user labelled datasets are therefore key to enabling practical well-being sensing with smart devices.

Smart eyewear is becoming a practical platform for continuous, context-aware health and well-being sensing. Because the frame sits stably on the face and head, it can host sensors that observe facial-muscle activity and head motion without a camera pointed at the wearer, sidestepping the positioning and privacy problems that limit camera-based facial analysis on wearables. They typically extract hand-crafted features for classical machine learning classifiers or train deep networks end-to-end, in both cases depending on labelled expression data. Because facial and expression morphology varies across users, models trained on one cohort transfer imperfectly to new, unseen users—the person-independent domain-shift problem in wearable sensing (Han et al., 2024). This limitation is shared by the OMG-based OCOsense systems on which we perform our experiments (Archer et al., 2023; Kiprijanovska et al., 2023; Marinova et al., 2025).

papers.title: Approximation and Hardness for the Data Validation Problem
papers.abstract:
Finnah, G\"onsch and Otto [Eur. J. Oper. Res. 2025] recently introduced the Data Validation Problem (DVP): Given a transitive directed acyclic graph $G$ on $n$ vertices (resp. tasks) and $m$ edges (resp. precedences) and a probing budget, a policy can successively pay a probing fee and probe an edge in $G$ as long as the total probing fees do not exceed the budget. If a probe succeeds, the targeted edge $e$ is removed from $G$ and we receive a reward; if the probe fails, the edge stays in $G$ and cannot be probed again. We seek a policy with maximum expected cumulative reward. Crucially, $G$ must stay transitive throughout the probing process, so a policy can only challenge the precedence between consecutive tasks, that is, only probe edges in the transitive reduction of the current precedence graph.
  We show that DVP is strongly NP-hard and W[1]-hard with the probing budget $T$ as a parameter, even in the deterministic case (when every probe has probability $0$ or $1$ to succeed) and with unit probing costs and rewards. For the same setting, we give an approximation-preserving reduction from the Densest $k$-Subgraph (D$k$S) Problem, with the consequence that there is no polynomial-time $2^{(\log n)^{1-\delta}}$-approximation algorithm and no FPT $\sqrt{T}$-approximation algorithm for DVP, assuming the Almost-Exponential Time Hypothesis and the Strongish Planted Clique Hypothesis, respectively.
  We also present the first known policies with provable worst-case guarantees for DVP, namely an $m$-approximation algorithm for instances with uniform probabilities and probing costs, a $2T/p_{\min}^T$-approximation algorithm for general instances, where $p_{\min}$ is the minimum probing success probability, and an exact FPT algorithm on tournament graphs, in the deterministic setting.
papers.intro:
Scheduling under precedence constraints is a classic topic in theoretical computer science and operations research. In a precedence-constrained scheduling instance, a set of tasks is given together with a partial order ≺\prec, which is the set of precedence constraints. The partial order can also be encoded as a so-called precedence graph. Given two tasks t,t′t,t^{\prime}, whenever t≺t′t\prec t^{\prime}, task tt must be completed before task t′t^{\prime} can start. Tasks that are incomparable in the partial order ≺\prec may be processed in any order. The focus of the literature for scheduling with precedence constraints has considered the partial order as an input and has been primarily focused on scheduling tasks according to some objective function depending on when tasks are assigned on a time line. Many variations of precedence constraints have been studied, where the structure of the partial order ≺\prec can strongly affect both the computational complexity of the problem and the optimal objective value [19]. A more basic question has received much less attention: how is the precedence structure obtained in the first place? In practice, the precedence constraints are rarely given explicitly with full confidence and must first be determined. This is a question that has been considered in the operations research community as the Data Validation Problem (DVP) introduced by Finnah, Gönsch and Otto [7]. However, to the best of our knowledge, the computational complexity or approximation bounds for this problem have not been studied from a theoretical perspective. In this paper, we initiate the theoretical study of the problem of determining the precedence structure of a scheduling problem. We give complexity results and approximation guarantees for this problem and several natural variants.

In such processes, the relation between every pair of tasks is rarely documented explicitly and an expert must be consulted to determine it. papers.title: AtomicFaaS: Offloading Side-Effect Compensation to the Serverless Platform
papers.abstract:
Function-as-a-Service (FaaS) simplifies distributed application development by offloading operational concerns to the platform, but developers remain responsible for recovering from failures. Retries require idempotent functions, which means that developers have to write complex, error-prone code that undoes or skips the already completed operations of a failed function.
  To address this, we propose AtomicFaaS, a platform extension that provides semantic atomicity for the external side effects of a function invocation, whether the function fails or its instance crashes, without developer-written compensation code. AtomicFaaS intercepts outbound calls and records their effects in a fault-tolerant log, from which the platform compensates leaked effects outside the failed instance. Compared with a manually implemented saga, AtomicFaaS eliminates compensation code and leaves no compensatable effects after any tested failure, while adding ~1 ms per intercepted call. Under load, it lowers the sustainable throughput of CPU-bound functions, while its latency overhead becomes negligible once calls to external services dominate the invocation time.
