papers.intro:
Function-as-a-Service (FaaS) aims to simplify distributed application development by letting developers focus on business logic rather than operational concerns. The platform handles infrastructure provisioning, resource management, scaling, and fault tolerance (Jonas et al., 2019). Developers write applications as small, often stateless functions that the platform invokes in response to events (Hellerstein et al., 2018; Shahrad et al., 2020).

Function-as-a-Service (FaaS) aims to simplify distributed application development by letting developers focus on business logic rather than operational concerns. The platform handles infrastructure provisioning, resource management, scaling, and fault tolerance (Jonas et al., 2019). Developers write applications as small, often stateless functions that the platform invokes in response to events (Hellerstein et al., 2018; Shahrad et al., 2020).

Failure handling, however, has only partly moved to the platform. It may re-execute a failed invocation, which is safe only for idempotent functions that developers must implement (Jangda et al., 2019), and hence the consequences of a failed execution remain the developer’s responsibility. Ensuring idempotency can be challenging (Sreekanti et al., 2020; Ding et al., 2023), especially as functions often rely on external services to perform stateful operations (Eismann et al., 2021). A function may perform several operations with side effects before it fails, so developers must either undo already performed operations or roll forward through them when the function is retried. While the rollback itself runs within the function instance and cannot protect against failures of that instance, rolling forward requires additional persistence and coordination outside the function for every operation (Zhang et al., 2020; Jia and Witchel, 2021). Either way, developers have to reason about failure scenarios and write error-prone code that distracts from the business logic, which contradicts the simplicity that FaaS promises.

Following the idea that the system rather than the application should run compensations (Breitbart et al., 1993; Georgakopoulos et al., 1995), we introduce AtomicFaaS, which brings it to serverless platforms. Under AtomicFaaS, an invocation either commits all of its external side effects, or the platform compensates those that were already applied, independent of the failure cause. To provide this guarantee, AtomicFaaS logs the outbound calls of a function and, if the invocation fails, issues compensating calls from outside the failed instance, using a catalog of inverses maintained by the platform or the service providers. Once every effect of an invocation has been compensated, it can be retried without producing duplicate effects, and developers write only the simple forward path of their functions.

papers.title: CrossPressor: Scalable Cross-View Fusion for Feed-Forward 3D Gaussian Splatting
papers.abstract: Feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting (3D-GS) becomes increasingly difficult to scale to long multi-view sequences. Anchor-based compression methods such as ZPressor alleviate representation growth by decoding Gaussians only from a compact set of anchor feature maps, but keeping these anchors fixed forces each one to aggregate an increasing number of support views. We identify this representation--fusion mismatch and introduce \textbf{CrossPressor}, a training-free method for scalable anchor-based fusion. CrossPressor preserves all decoder-facing anchor queries while constraining the view-growing support sequence through coverage-cycled evidence routing, distributing retained spatial evidence across support views and fusion layers while keeping all support views represented. Routing before K/V projection, together with joint context packing, further reduces support-side fusion cost without retraining. CrossPressor maintains reconstruction quality close to dense fusion while achieving up to $26.12\times$ faster cross-view fusion and $1.43\times$ end-to-end acceleration on long input sequences. Our project page is at: https://yuhsihu.github.io/CrossPressor.

Feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting (3D-GS) is an effective paradigm for generalizable novel view synthesis. Given a set of calibrated images, recent methods directly predict an explicit Gaussian representation in a single forward pass [3, 5, 28], avoiding scene-specific optimization while retaining the efficient rendering properties of 3D-GS [12]. However, as feed-forward reconstruction expands from sparse observations to longer sequences, both the reconstructed representation and the cross-view computation used to construct it become increasingly difficult to scale. A model that is efficient for a few input images may therefore become impractical when processing tens or hundreds of views.

Given a set of calibrated images, recent methods directly predict an explicit Gaussian representation in a single forward pass [3, 5, 28], avoiding scene-specific optimization while retaining the efficient rendering properties of 3D-GS [12]. However, as feed-forward reconstruction expands from sparse observations to longer sequences, both the reconstructed representation and the cross-view computation used to construct it become increasingly difficult to scale. A model that is efficient for a few input images may therefore become impractical when processing tens or hundreds of views.

Recent methods [26, 25] have begun to address the issue of scaling in representation size. For instance, ZPressor [25] partitions the input images into a fixed number of groups using camera poses. It selects one anchor view from each group and fuses the remaining support views into the corresponding anchor feature maps. Only these updated anchor features are passed to the pixel-aligned Gaussian decoder. Since the number of anchor views remains constant, adding additional support views to provide further scene information does not directly increase the input to the Gaussian decoder or the number of Gaussians.

This exposes a growing support-to-anchor fusion bottleneck even though the decoder-facing representation remains fixed.

papers.title: BudgetSplat: Budget-Controllable Generalizable Gaussian Splatting
papers.abstract: Feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting enables efficient generalizable novel view synthesis, but existing pixel-aligned methods often generate highly redundant Gaussian primitives, causing the final representation size and rendering cost to grow rapidly with image resolution and the number of input views. We propose BudgetSplat, a budget-controllable feed-forward framework that adapts the final Gaussian representation to a user-specified preservation ratio. Rather than treating compaction as simple importance ranking, we formulate it as a joint problem of importance estimation, spatial coverage, and cross-view redundancy. A single trained model supports varying numbers of context views and multiple test-time budgets without per-budget retraining or per-scene compression. To realize this formulation, Intra-Cross Mask Supervision provides structure-, coverage-, and redundancy-aware guidance for learning Gaussian importance, while budget-conditioned feature modulation adapts Gaussian opacity and attributes to the requested preservation ratio. Coverage-Aware Budget Selection further combines patch-wise pre-selection, view-wise opacity ranking, and 3D redundancy suppression to construct compact yet spatially distributed Gaussian representations. Experiments on indoor reconstruction and cross-dataset generalization demonstrate consistent quality--size trade-offs across different input view counts and preservation ratios, substantially reducing final representation storage and rendering cost while preserving rendering quality.

3D Gaussian Splatting (3D-GS) [9] represents scenes using explicit anisotropic Gaussians and enables high-quality real-time novel view synthesis. However, it requires costly per-scene optimization. Recent generalizable methods predict Gaussian representations from input images in a feed-forward manner, substantially improving reconstruction efficiency and generalization to unseen scenes [2, 5, 20, 23, 11].

3D Gaussian Splatting (3D-GS) [9] represents scenes using explicit anisotropic Gaussians and enables high-quality real-time novel view synthesis. However, it requires costly per-scene optimization. Recent generalizable methods predict Gaussian representations from input images in a feed-forward manner, substantially improving reconstruction efficiency and generalization to unseen scenes [2, 5, 20, 23, 11].

Most feed-forward 3D-GS methods decode one or more Gaussians from each pixel. Although this pixel-aligned formulation provides strong geometric anchoring, its representation size grows rapidly with image resolution and input-view number. Overlapping observations additionally produce many redundant Gaussians, increasing the storage and rendering costs of the final scene asset. Existing methods reduce pixel-aligned Gaussian redundancy through different designs. Geometry-aware fusion [20, 21] and view compression [18] consolidate overlapping pixel-aligned predictions across views; voxel-aligned prediction [19] predicts Gaussians in a shared 3D volume, whereas global scene encoders [1, 8] compress multi-view observations into a compact set of scene tokens before decoding the Gaussian representation. The latter demonstrate that a fixed-capacity Gaussian set can be sufficient on some benchmarks, but its output size remains tied to the scene token capacity.

These developments raise a practical question: Can a single feed-forward model adapt its final Gaussian representation to different user-specified budgets? Existing approaches generally fall into two categories. Fixed-capacity methods [1, 8] tie the representation size to a particular token or decoder configuration, so substantially larger or more complex scenes may require retraining a higher-capacity model. Post-hoc compression methods [7] reduce an already reconstructed Gaussian set, but introduce additional per-scene processing or optimization. In practice, deployment conditions may require the same model to operate under different representation budgets. Simply applying a budget-unaware Top-KK rule to a conventionally trained pixel-aligned model is suboptimal: it may over-allocate Gaussians to salient or high-opacity regions, leaving weakly textured areas under-covered. We therefore view budget-controlled Gaussian compaction as a joint problem of importance estimation, spatial coverage, and cross-view redundancy, rather than simple candidate ranking. These limitations motivate a feed-forward model whose final Gaussian representation can be adjusted at test time while retaining the geometric advantages of pixel-aligned reconstruction.

papers.title: Anomaly Detection on Resource-Constrained Devices with Reservoir Computing
papers.abstract: Anomaly detection at the edge requires the deployment of models that achieve competitive performance, while minimizing computational cost and memory footprint. In this article, we investigate the suitability of the Mahalanobis Distance of Reservoir States (MDRS), an unsupervised time-series anomaly detection method, for resource-constrained devices and propose two optimizations to reduce its computational requirements. Specifically, we replace random reservoir connectivity (MDRS-Rand) with a circular shift (MDRS-Circ) and show that the anomaly score for an entire time series can be computed from the final reservoir state alone. Furthermore, we show that exploiting the reservoir's temporal memory enables more efficient input preprocessing, further reducing computational cost. We evaluate the MDRS variants on the MLPerf Tiny anomaly detection benchmark against the reference autoencoder and other anomaly detection methods, and deploy their inference kernels on a NUCLEO-F401RE microcontroller to assess latency, estimate energy consumption, and measure memory footprint. Among the evaluated methods, only MDRS and the autoencoder meet the benchmark's performance target, with MDRS requiring fewer operations and smaller models. With optimized preprocessing, MDRS achieves an ROC AUC of 0.869, a model size of 24 KB, an estimated energy consumption of 24 uJ per inference, and a latency of 0.32 ms, corresponding to a 75.9x speedup over the autoencoder with standard preprocessing.
papers.intro:
IoT and resource-constrained devices are increasingly used to perform tasks at the edge. Many of such tasks fall into the category of anomaly detection applied to time-series [1]. For example, networking intrusion detection systems require methods that analyze incoming packets and infer whether they compose an ongoing cybersecurity attack. Another example is the analysis of environmental conditions (e.g., video or audio signals) to monitor processes and identify suspicious deviations from the normal conditions. To achieve the near real-time performance necessary for carrying out these tasks successfully, computations need to be performed locally. Offloading them to the cloud is often not viable, as the communication overhead is non-negligible. However, given the limited computational capabilities of resource-constrained devices, it is crucial to develop computationally-efficient methods.

Tiny machine learning (tinyML) [2] has emerged as an area specifically targeting these settings, enabling the deployment of ML models on resource-constrained devices with limited memory, storage, and computational capabilities. To stimulate the development of methods for tinyML, the MLPerf Tiny benchmark [3] provides a standardized framework for evaluating such models, including an anomaly detection task based on acoustic machine-condition monitoring. By defining target detection performance and measuring computational efficiency, the benchmark supports the evaluation of trade-offs between accuracy and deployment cost.

By defining target detection performance and measuring computational efficiency, the benchmark supports the evaluation of trade-offs between accuracy and deployment cost.

Reservoir computing is a family of randomized recurrent neural networks promising for tinyML [4]. In reservoir computing, most network weights are initialized randomly and remain fixed, and only the output weights are trained [5]. This architecture drastically reduces training cost compared to fully-trainable neural networks, making reservoir computing particularly suitable for resource-constrained deployment. Building on this foundation, Tamura et al. recently proposed the Mahalanobis Distance of Reservoir States (MDRS) [6], an unsupervised anomaly detection method that detects point-wise anomalies by measuring the deviation of reservoir states from an estimated distribution of normal conditions. Unlike previous reconstruction- or prediction-based reservoir computing methods, MDRS produces temporally stable anomaly scores and avoids the need for supervised training of the output weights, making it a promising candidate for unsupervised anomaly detection on resource-constrained devices.

In this article, we investigate the suitability of MDRS for anomaly detection on resource-constrained IoT devices and propose two optimizations to reduce its computational requirements. First, we replace the random reservoir connectivity with a circular shift operation [7, 8], eliminating the need for a dense recurrent matrix multiplication. Second, we introduce an end-only score that computes the Mahalanobis distance only for the final reservoir state rather than at every time step. We evaluate the MDRS variants on the MLPerf Tiny anomaly detection benchmark against the reference autoencoder and other anomaly detection methods (Section III) in terms of detection performance, computational cost, and memory footprint (Section V). Among the evaluated methods, only MDRS and the reference autoencoder meet the MLPerf Tiny performance target, with MDRS requiring fewer operations and a smaller model. Moreover, since the reservoir integrates its input over time, MDRS can process single frames without the temporal stacking required by the autoencoder to meet the performance target, allowing further reductions in computational cost. When deployed on a NUCLEO-F401RE microcontroller (Section VI), MDRS achieves 6.9×\times lower latency and estimated energy consumption than the autoencoder with identical inputs. With optimized preprocessing, these improvements reach 75.9×75.9\times while meeting the MLPerf Tiny performance target with a model size of 24 KB.

papers.title: PersonaCodeBench: Evaluating Coding Agents in Persona-driven Human-Interactive Sessions
papers.abstract: Coding agents must deliver correct software while respecting users' expertise, preferences, and working conditions. Existing benchmarks increasingly incorporate interaction, yet personalized requirement fulfillment remains underexplored. We introduce PersonaCodeBench, which turns user characteristics into verifiable obligations in persona-driven multi-turn coding sessions. Our persona pool spans roles, technical abilities, interaction preferences, and practical constraints, yielding task-grounded evolved requirements for implementation, permissions, testing, explanation, and delivery. At runtime, a controller governs user simulator responses and requirement disclosure, using online requirement evaluation to provide feedback and advance the interaction. Requirements emerge progressively, with their content, disclosure conditions, and acceptance criteria fixed before evaluation. A completion verifier and a personalization verifier separately assess native correctness and persona fulfillment. Joint pass requires both adherence to the declared budget and compliance with validity conditions. We evaluate all major frontier agents, establish a comprehensive leaderboard, and conduct detailed experimental analyses to validate effectiveness. PersonaCodeBench supports reproducible evaluation of coding agents' ability to meet explicit, personalized user expectations alongside coding objectives.

Real coding sessions involve users clarifying goals, inspecting changes, and requesting revisions (Baumann et al., 2026). A correct patch can remain unsuitable for its user: an analyst may lack permission to change a schema, a student may need an explanation, and a shop owner may be unable to install software. Success therefore depends on completing the task in a way that respects the user’s expertise, preferences, and working conditions.

Copilot Arena collects developer preferences in actual workflows (Chi et al., 2025). Building on these advances, we ask: can a coding agent complete the software task while satisfying the particular user’s requirements? Controlled evaluation must connect user characteristics to observable obligations and distinguish functional correctness from personalized acceptance.

papers.title: From Early Concepts to Lunar Hypertelescopes Roadmap for Next-Generation Optical Astronomy on the Moon
papers.abstract: Since the dawn of the Space Age, the Moon has been considered one of the most promising locations for astronomical observations. The absence of atmosphere, exceptional mechanical stability, access to the permanently shielded radio-quiet far side, and the possibility of constructing extremely large apertures have motivated numerous concepts for lunar observatories over the past six decades. Despite extensive studies conducted during the Apollo era, most proposed lunar astronomy projects remained unrealized due to technological limitations, shifting scientific priorities, and the high cost of sustained lunar operations. Today, renewed international interest in lunar exploration, combined with advances in robotics, autonomous systems, additive manufacturing, precision optics, and formation flying, is reopening the prospect of large-scale astronomical infrastructures on the Moon. In particular, lunar hypertelescope concepts offer the possibility of achieving unprecedented angular resolutions through diluted optical arrays spanning hundreds of meters to several kilometres. This paper reviews the historical evolution of lunar astronomy concepts, analyses the reasons behind previous failures, examines current technological developments, and proposes a roadmap toward future lunar hypertelescope facilities capable of transforming observational astronomy during the twenty-first century.

papers.intro:
The Moon has occupied a unique place in human imagination since antiquity. Long before becoming a destination for scientific exploration, it inspired mythology, religion, philosophy, literature, and early astronomy. The invention of the telescope transformed humanity’s perception of the Moon. Galileo’s telescopic observations of the Moon in 1609 revealed mountains, valleys, and other irregular surface features, challenging the Aristotelian view of celestial perfection. These discoveries initiated a profound transformation in natural philosophy that culminated with Newton’s law of universal gravitation, demonstrating that the same physical laws govern both terrestrial and celestial phenomena [24, 39, 38]. Over subsequent centuries, lunar observations became central to the development of modern astronomy.

During the Industrial Revolution and the rapid development of modern engineering, humanity began to dream of travelling to the Moon, a vision reflected in literature (e.g., From the Earth to the Moon by Jules Verne, 1865) and early cinema (e.g., A Trip to the Moon by Georges Méliès, 1902). This dream became reality on July 20, 1969, with the successful landing of the Apollo 11 mission on the lunar surface. Since then, the Space Age has transformed the Moon from a distant object of observation into a potential platform for scientific exploration. Following the Apollo program, scientists began to consider the establishment of astronomical observatories on the lunar surface [18].

papers.title: From Earth's Harshest Landscapes to Lunar Horizons: Engineering NEA Telescopes for Extreme Environments
papers.abstract: Near-Earth Asteroids (NEAs) represent both a scientific opportunity and a potential threat to human civilization. While current survey programs have successfully detected most large NEAs, a significant observational gap remains for objects smaller than approximately 140 m, which can still produce regional-scale devastation. Ground-based surveys are intrinsically limited by atmospheric conditions, weather, and solar avoidance constraints, which leave a significant fraction of near-Sun objects difficult to detect. In particular, Earth-based observatories remain largely blind to objects approaching from the Sun-ward direction, reducing available warning times. Future lunar observatories offer a promising solution to this limitation. A telescope operating on the Moon could enable observations of regions inaccessible from Earth, provide enhanced sensitivity, and significantly improve early detection capabilities. However, the lunar environment imposes severe engineering constraints, including thermal cycling, dust contamination, radiation exposure, and autonomous operation requirements. We propose the AMAS(Atacama-Mongolia-Antarctica-Sahara) project, an international initiative using Earth's most extreme environments as analogue sites for future lunar astronomical facilities. By deploying and testing specialized NEA survey telescopes in these environments, key technologies for future lunar observatories can be validated under realistic operational conditions. This paper presents the scientific rationale, engineering challenges, site selection strategy, and long-term roadmap toward a global Earth-Moon network for planetary defense.

papers.intro:
Asteroid impacts have profoundly influenced the history of Earth, acting both as destructive agents and as fundamental drivers of planetary and biological evolution. Throughout the age of the Solar System, collisions with asteroids and other small bodies have repeatedly modified Earth’s geology, atmosphere, climate, and biosphere. While impacts are often associated with catastrophic destruction, they have also played a crucial role in shaping the conditions that enabled the emergence and evolution of life [12].

While impacts are often associated with catastrophic destruction, they have also played a crucial role in shaping the conditions that enabled the emergence and evolution of life [12].

One of the most significant epochs in Earth’s early history was the Late Heavy Bombardment (LHB), approximately 4.1 billion years ago. This period is believed to have been triggered by orbital resonances between the giant planets, particularly Jupiter and Saturn, which destabilized large populations of asteroids and sent them toward the inner Solar System [7]. During this era, countless impacts reshaped the surfaces of the terrestrial planets. Asteroids may also have delivered a substantial fraction of Earth’s water and volatile compounds, contributing to the conditions necessary for the emergence of life [13].

During this era, countless impacts reshaped the surfaces of the terrestrial planets. Asteroids may also have delivered a substantial fraction of Earth’s water and volatile compounds, contributing to the conditions necessary for the emergence of life [13].

Large impacts may have influenced biological evolution in ways that extend beyond simple destruction. Geological evidence associated with the S2 impact event, produced by an asteroid estimated to be between 30 and 60 km in diameter approximately 3.2 billion years ago, suggests that asteroid collisions could simultaneously generate severe environmental disturbances and chemically reactive environments favourable to prebiotic chemistry [5]. While such events may have locally sterilized portions of the Earth’s surface through intense heating and ocean vaporization, they also released nutrients and energy sources capable of stimulating biological activity.

At the opposite extreme, asteroid impacts have repeatedly caused major biological crises. The most famous example is the Chicxulub impact approximately 66 million years ago. The impactor, estimated to have been 10–12 km in diameter, excavated a crater approximately 180 km wide on the present-day Yucatán Peninsula in Mexico [15]. The resulting global environmental catastrophe contributed to the extinction of nearly 75% of Earth’s species, including all non-avian dinosaurs.

papers.title: Hamilton cycles in bicirculants with non-coprime connection sets
papers.abstract:
A bicirculant is a regular graph that admits an automorphism having two vertex-orbits of the same size. A bicirculant can be described as follows. Given an integer $m \ge 1$ and sets $R, S, T \subseteq \mathbb{Z}_m$ such that $R=-R$, $T=-T$, $0 \not\in R \cup T$ and $0 \in S$, the graph $B(m;R,S,T)$ has vertex set $V=\{u_0,\dots,u_{m-1},v_0,\dots,v_{m-1}\}$ and edge set $E=\{u_iu_{i+j}| \ i \in \mathbb{Z}_m, j \in R\} \cup \{v_iv_{i+j}| \ i \in \mathbb{Z}_m, j \in T\} \cup \{u_iv_{i+j}| \ i \in \mathbb{Z}_m, j \in S\}.$ Some of the well known bicirculants include the generalized Petersen graphs and Cayley graphs of dihedral groups.
  In 1983, Brian Alspach proved that the only non-hamiltonian generalized Petersen graphs are $G(m,2)$ where $m \equiv 5 \pmod 6$. In a recent paper we conjectured that this is the only exception among regular connected bicirculants of degree at least two, and we have verified the conjecture for bicirculants with $|S|\le 3$. Results of Alspach, Chen and Dean imply that the conjecture also holds for all bicirculants with $m$ even and $\gcd(m,S)=1$. In this paper, we show that the conjecture holds for all bicirculants with $|S| \geq 4$ and $\gcd(m,S)>1$ such that $R\cup T$ contains an element that is not coprime to $\gcd(m,S)$ and, if $m$ is odd, is also not divisibile by $\gcd(m, S)$ or $R \cap T$ contains an element that is coprime to $\gcd(m,S)$.

papers.title: On generalized $k$-token graphs with distinguishable tokens and a maximum capacity of $s$ tokens per vertex
papers.abstract: Supertoken graphs \(F^s_{k\times1}(G)\), also known as generalized token graphs, model configurations of \(k\) distinguishable tokens on a graph \(G\), with at most \(s\) tokens at each vertex. We study structural and metric properties of these graphs in terms of the base graph. For regular \(G\), we characterize when \(F^s_{k\times1}(G)\) is regular. We show that bipartiteness is inherited from \(G\) and characterize it for complete base graphs. For \(s\ge2\), we characterize connectedness and show that \(t\)-vertex-connectivity of \(G\) implies \(t\)-vertex-connectivity of the supertoken graph. We obtain exact diameter formulas in several regimes, including complete graphs and stars, and derive lower bounds and a conjectured formula for odd cycles. We also determine the clique number, give bounds and equality conditions for the chromatic number, and characterize planarity for complete base graphs.

papers.title: The Price of List Replicability: Tight Bounds for Bias Estimation
papers.abstract:
We study the sample complexity of list replicable algorithms for estimating the biases of $d$ coins. An algorithm is $(k,\varepsilon,\delta)$-list replicable if for every bias vector $\mathbf{p}\in[0,1]^d$, there is a set of outputs $L_{\mathbf{p}}\subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$ of at most $k$ elements such that every $\mathbf{y}\in L_{\mathbf{p}}$ satisfies $\lVert\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{p}\rVert_\infty\leq\varepsilon$, and the algorithm output is in $L_{\mathbf{p}}$ with probability at least $1-\delta$. Prior work gave a $(d+1,\varepsilon,\delta)$-list replicable algorithm with sample complexity $\widetilde{O}\left(\frac{d^3}{\varepsilon^2}\right)$, but no nontrivial sample complexity lower bound was known.
  We establish the first non-trivial sample complexity lower bound for this problem and give an improved algorithm that matches it up to polylogarithmic factors. Together, these results determine the optimal sample complexity for list size $d+1$ to be $\widetilde{\Theta}\left(\frac{d^2}{\varepsilon^2}\right)$, showing that the quadratic dependence on dimension is inherent up to polylogarithmic factors. More generally, for every $k\in[d+1,2^d]$, we establish matching upper and lower bounds of $\widetilde{\Theta}\left(\frac{d^2}{\varepsilon^2\log k}\right)$ on the total sample complexity.

papers.intro:
Typically, learning algorithms observe samples from an unknown distribution and produce an output. In general, such algorithms are not replicable: two different runs of the algorithm observe two different samples (though drawn from the same distribution), resulting in potentially different outputs. Motivated by this, various notions of replicable learning have been introduced in the recent literature. In particular, the work of [23] formalized a notion of replicability called ρ{\rho}-replicability, and the works of [10] and [5] introduced the notion of list replicability. Since then, the notion of replicable learning has received considerable attention and has been studied in various contexts such as PAC learning, Reinforcement learning, multi-armed bandits, etc. [21, 3, 4, 13, 9, 12, 22, 11, 1]. A basic problem studied in this area is dd-CoinBiasEstimationProblem: given sample access to dd coins with unknown biases, estimate every bias to within additive error ε\varepsilon. The dd-coin bias estimation problem is a basic instance of high-dimensional mean estimation over Bernoulli product distributions and captures central challenges in designing replicable algorithms and understanding their limitations.

papers.title: Morpheus.AI: agents autonomously generate, execute and refine virtual tissue models
papers.abstract: Virtual tissue models link observations to mechanistic hypotheses, but building them demands expertise in biology, mathematics and programming. Here, large language model (LLM) agents paired with the simulator Morpheus (Morpheus.AI) autonomously built such models from fifteen benchmark studies, five without a published model. With a frontier LLM, agents that ran their simulations met 83-86% of study-specific criteria in under two hours and for under US\$4 per model. Such agents could make in silico modeling routine.

papers.title: The Logic of Emergence
papers.abstract: ``Emergence'' refers to the fact that different mathematical languages and theories seem to be required to describe scientific theories that operate at different spatial and temporal scales. Highly circumscribed, special cases of emergence have been investigated using many different formal tools, including coarse-graining (over space and / or time), renormalization, dimension reduction, broken symmetry, and various formulations of causality. Here we extend the mathematics of model theory to unify and extend these earlier investigations. As a preliminary application of our framework, we investigate canonical examples of emergence, including the emergence of genetics from chemistry, of psychology from neurobiology, and of different forms of collective behavior from the laws governing their constituent parts. By exploiting the power of model theory we also uncover many aspects of emergence that were previously obscured. In particular, we uncover some of the rich hierarchical structure that relates different scientific fields. For example, we show that scientific fields can be related via a collection of multiple partial orders, all defined over the same set. On the other hand, under an alternative relation among scientific fields, one which allows cycles, we show that it is possible that the set of all of scientific fields must collapse into a single scientific field. Going forward, these investigations point to the formal tools that might need to be developed in order to arrive at a deeper understanding of this emergent hierarchy of scientific reality.

papers.title: Rough-to-frozen transition in non-integrable dimer models
papers.abstract: The transition from rough to frozen phases in models of random surfaces is expected to be governed by the Pokrovsky-Talapov law, which predicts a $\varepsilon^{3/2}$-type singularity of the macroscopic height profile (limit shape), as the distance $\varepsilon$ from the frozen phase (facet) is sent to zero. This has been proved so far only in exactly solvable cases, notably the classical, determinantal, 2D dimer model. In this paper we prove the validity of the Pokrovsky-Talapov law for a non-integrable 2D dimer model on the hexagonal lattice, whose Gibbs weight depends upon a weak plaquette interaction among dimers. Our proof is based on a multiscale analysis (constructive fermionic Renormalization Group), which allows us to identify two different regimes with distinct scaling properties and to explain the universality of the Pokrovsky-Talapov exponent $3/2$, in contrast with the interaction-dependent critical exponents characterizing the rough phase. The first regime, corresponding to smaller distances, is characterized by an effective quadratic dispersion relation, while the second comes with an effective linear dispersion relation, typical of Luttinger liquid behavior. As a byproduct of our construction, we control the scaling limit of the interacting dimer model uniformly in the distance from the frozen phase.

papers.intro:
The study of random surfaces revealed the emergence of deep universality phenomena in many different models, ranging from dimer coverings of planar graphs to interlaced particle systems and stochastic partial differential equations, with unexpected connections with random matrix theory. Universal fluctuation properties, characterized by a Gaussian Free Field (GFF) behavior or by a Tracy-Widom-type distribution, have been observed in seemingly disparate systems [33, 11, 32]. Among these, the dimer model on planar bipartite graphs plays a prominent role due to its exact solvability: correlation functions can be computed explicitly via the Kasteleyn formalism, starting from which its scaling limit can be rigorously analyzed [23, 19]. As such, the dimer model provides an ideal laboratory for investigating the universal properties of random surfaces.

Dimer models on planar, periodic, bipartite graphs exhibit a rich phase diagram with three distinct phases, each characterized by specific properties of the height function distribution and of the large distance behavior of the dimer correlations [23, 24]. In the frozen phase, the random surface becomes flat on a microscopic scale: the height function is deterministic and dimer configurations are rigidly ordered. In the gaseous or smooth phase, the variance of height fluctuations is bounded uniformly in the system size but, differently from the frozen phase, the system has positive configurational entropy. Truncated dimer-dimer correlations do not vanish, but they decay to zero exponentially fast at large distances, so that the height fluctuations at faraway points are essentially independent. The rough or liquid phase exhibits the richest structure: the height function converges at large scales to a profile with non-trivial curvature, whose form depends upon the shape of the domain and the boundary conditions, and can be computed as the solution to a variational problem involving the surface tension (or free energy) of the model; moreover, at large distances fluctuations around the average profile converge to a GFF, after appropriate rescaling. At the microscopic level, dimer-dimer correlations decay polynomially to zero at large distances, signaling a critical behavior analogous to the one displayed by statistical mechanics systems at a second order phase transition. In this phase, the scaling limit of height fluctuations displays conformal invariance properties [22].

In a series of previous papers [16, 15, 17, 18] we considered a class of non-integrable dimer models, for which we proved that, well-inside the rough phase, the scaling limit of height fluctuations around the average height profile is described by a GFF, like in the case of integrable dimer models; on the other hand, the critical exponents characterizing the large distance decay properties of dimer correlations change, in general: in particular, in [15, 17, 18] we prove that the critical exponent associated with the oscillatory part of the two-point dimer correlations is a non-trivial analytic function of the interaction strength, equal to the ‘stiffness’ coefficient of the GFF. The results of [16, 15, 17, 18] hold in the weak coupling regime, i.e., they require that the interaction strength λ\lambda, which measures the distance from a reference integrable model, is small enough, a priori non-uniformly in the distance ε\varepsilon from the rough-frozen (or rough-smooth) boundary.

If so, does the GFF behavior of height fluctuations, as well as the Kadanoff universality relation between the stiffness of the GFF and the dimer-dimer critical exponent, hold in the whole rough phase, up to the transition line? Does the exponent 3/2, characterizing the speed at which the height profile within the rough phase approaches an affine profile, remain unchanged, or is it modified by the interaction? papers.title: Topological localization in unentangled random braids
papers.abstract: In 2015, P. Serna, G. Bunin, and A. Nahum numerically investigated fluctuations in a bunch of unentangled random threads. They showed that fluctuations of an individual thread in a braid are qualitatively different from those of a thread embedded in a medium of fixed parallel lines. In particular, Serna et al. observed a logarithmic increase in the average transverse span, $\left<|x_N|\right>$, of a thread with polymer length, $N$. This behavior highlights the collective nature of topological interactions, in which each polymer fluctuates and constrains the motion of the others. Studying this problem both numerically and analytically, we propose the following interpretation: the logarithmic regime is transient, and sufficiently long polymers exhibit topological localization, where $\left<|x_N|\right>$ approaches a finite limit at $N\to\infty$. Unlike localization induced by quenched external disorder, this phenomenon arises solely from collective topological constraints. We study braids within a locally free approximation and support the localization by analytical investigation of Brownian bridges on the asymptotic Cayley graph of a locally free group. We further conjecture that topologically induced localization emerges as a phase transition: for a small number of threads, $n \sim 2\div 5$, the span, $\left<|x_N|\right>$, grows algebraically, with the usual scaling $\left<|x_N|\right>\sim N^{1/4}$ at $N\gg 1$; by contrast, for sufficiently large $n$, each thread in a long braid ($N\gg 1$) asymptotically localizes, approaching $\left<|x_N|\right>\sim \mathrm{const}$.

papers.intro:
Topology gives rise to interactions that are fundamentally different from conventional energetic ones. While energetic interactions are local, i.e. depend directly on interacting objects, topological constraints are global – they restrict the space of accessible configurations [19, 33]. Such constraints are responsible for many remarkable properties of extended objects, like for example polymeric systems, ranging from the rheology of melts to chromosome organization and ring-polymer statistics [10, 15, 28, 30]. Despite essential progress in understanding and description of topological interactions, yet the understanding collective statistical mechanics of topologically constrained many-body systems still remains a challenging task. Even in the absence of energetic interactions, topology alone can generate strong correlations extending over the entire system, and the mechanisms by which these correlations emerge are remain often out of a clear understanding.

Directed polymer fibers provide one of the cleanest realizations of a purely topological many-body problem. Consider an ensemble of nn directed polymer threads, each consisting of NN steps, connecting two parallel planes (from top to bottom). Such a configuration can be viewed as a ”braid” [1]. Since polymers cannot pass through one another, each configuration belongs to a particular isotopy class of braids. Two configurations are topologically equivalent if one can be continuously deformed into the other while keeping the endpoints fixed and forbidding strands from passing through one another. The statistical ensemble of braids is therefore naturally decomposed into sectors labeled by elements of the braid group [1, 27].

The statistical ensemble of braids is therefore naturally decomposed into sectors labeled by elements of the braid group [1, 27].

The simplest, yet very conceptually rich, sector is the trivial braid, i.e., the braid isotopic to a collection of parallel straight threads. Geometrically, however, a trivial braid need not resemble straight lines. A large number of local strand exchanges may occur, provided they cancel globally so that the braid word reduces to the identity. Such random trivial braids represent highly disordered configurations constrained only by global topological triviality. They form a natural model of directed polymer melts in which all polymers remain collectively unentangled.

In 2016, P. Serna et al. [31] performed extensive numerical simulations of directed polymer melts restricted to the trivial braid sector. Their work showed that topological constraints alone dramatically suppress transverse fluctuations compared with those of unconstrained directed polymers. More importantly, they found that the fluctuations of an individual thread in a random trivial braid differ qualitatively from those of a single topologically trivial thread embedded in an array of fixed parallel lines. The latter corresponds to an individual topological constraint, whereas the former is an intrinsically collective problem in which every polymer fluctuates while simultaneously acting as a topological constraint on all the others. Their simulations therefore provided compelling evidence that collective topological interactions cannot be reduced to an effective external disorder generated by a regular array of threads treated as immobile obstacles. The origin and interpretation of this collective localization have remained open questions. In our view, [31] is a seminal yet underappreciated work that raised fundamental questions deserving careful investigation.

This leads to the spontaneous localization of unentangled threads. Since all threads are identical, this behavior results in emergent localization in the whole trivial braid: each thread fluctuates within a narrow strip around its straight configuration.

papers.title: Post-Inference Model Chaining: A Problem Statement and a Model-based Bootstrap for Training End-to-End Digital Twins
papers.abstract: End-to-end digital twins can be constructed by fitting separate stage models and connecting them after inference. We investigate the Frequentist prediction properties of a commonly used Monte Carlo simulation scheme that forwards complete predictive draws through such a chain when measured stage outputs contain independent normal errors, but the latent stage means are deterministic. Analytical two-stage examples show persistent asymptotic interval and coverage inflation and, with quadratic propagation, mean bias dependent on the parameters to be estimated. Simulations of four- and eight-stage linear-quadratic univariate chains with 7, 15 or 30 training runs demonstrate pronounced input-dependent distortions. A diagnostic using error-free latent training predictors shows that the effect is mainly not attributable to errors in variables, but to the MCSim approach even showing underestimation of coverage. We propose a model-based bootstrap: an initial chain forwards fitted means, bootstrap chains are refitted on fixed-center bootstrap data while forwarding their mean prediction, and a target-stage future error enters a studentized prediction root. Across the investigated scenarios, relative mean bias is substantially reduced, and coverage is closer to the nominal 90%. At sample size 30, the eight-stage bootstrap has mean width ratios of 1.16-1.42 relative to the known-parameter normal reference, compared with 4.11-4.97 for observed-to-observed MCSim. These results support improved endpoint prediction in the tested setting. Further investigations of the bootstrap scheme in the supplement for a bivariate 6-stage process show similar satisfactory results.

papers.title: A Dichotomy for Terminal Cyclability
papers.abstract: Given an undirected graph $G$ and a set $R \subseteq V(G)$ of terminals, Terminal Cyclability asks whether $G$ contains a simple cycle visiting every vertex of $R$. We establish a complexity dichotomy for this problem on red-minor-closed classes of annotated graphs. In particular, we show that Terminal Cyclability is polynomial-time solvable on every such class excluding any annotated planar graph. The problem is NP-complete whenever the class contains all annotated planar graphs. More precisely, we give an $|G|^{2^{\mathbf{poly}(b)}}$-time algorithm, where $b$ is the bidimensionality of $(G,R)$. Our main technical contribution is the introduction of a weak irrelevant vertex rule. Rather than removing irrelevant vertices until the treewidth becomes constant, we only remove irrelevant vertices until the treewidth is logarithmic in the graph size. Such a weakening is necessary as a parameter-only treewidth threshold for an irrelevant vertex rule in this setting is known to be impossible to realise. Combined with a single-exponential algorithm for Terminal Cyclability parameterized by treewidth, this yields the polynomial-time algorithm for our dichotomy.

papers.intro:
The Hamiltonian Cycle problem asks if a given graph contains a cycle spanning all of its vertices. The problem belongs to Karp’s original list of NP-complete problems [30] and is known to remain NP-complete even when restricted to planar graphs [21]. It is one of the oldest and most studied computationally hard problems. The fact that Hamiltonian Cycle is NP-complete on planar graphs gives rise to a neat delineation of the problem’s tractability within minor-closed graph classes: Hamiltonian Cycle is NP-complete in every minor-closed graph class containing all planar graphs. On the other hand, the celebrated grid theorem of Robertson and Seymour [43] states that any minor-closed class that excludes some planar graph has bounded treewidth, implying the existence of polynomial-time algorithms for Hamiltonian Cycle within such classes (see for example [14]).

The task is to arrange a sequence of English words of length nn in a cycle, changing exactly one letter at each step, including from the last word back to the first. papers.title: Exact certification for conic optimization over quadratic modules: partitions of unity and recession directions
papers.abstract: We consider linear conic problems whose cone is a product of truncated quadratic modules, the sum-of-squares (SOS) side of the moment-SOS hierarchy. A floating-point solution is turned into an exact rational certificate in three steps: rounding, repair of each block residual by a constant, and absorption of the constants along a recession direction of the problem. The repair relies on strict partitions of unity in the quadratic modules. We characterize their existence, relate the canonical one to the analytic center of the dual pseudo-moment cone, Christoffel-Darboux polynomials and Pell equations, and we derive closed-form rational partitions for balls and boxes. The loss incurred by the certification is the optimal value of a recession problem, equal to a support function of the masses of the dual feasible pseudomoments. The method is illustrated on polynomial optimization, volume computation and positivity of polynomials along D-finite trajectories.

papers.title: Quasinilpotency of commutators under a weakened Kleinecke--Shirokov condition
papers.abstract: Kramar and Kramar Fijav\v{z} proved that a commutator $Y=AB-BA$ of two complex square matrices is nilpotent whenever $Y$ commutes with an iterated commutator $\delta_Y^{k}(A)$, where $\delta_Y(T)=YT-TY$, and asked whether this result can be generalized to bounded operators on infinite-dimensional spaces. We show that for $k\geq 2$ such a commutator need not be quasinilpotent. On the other hand, for every $k$ it is quasinilpotent whenever it is compact, or more generally whenever it is a Riesz operator or $AY-YA$ is compact. Moreover, its Riesz projection at any non-zero isolated point of its spectrum always has infinite rank.

papers.title: Non-induced inherent graphs
papers.abstract:
Concepts of avoidable paths and inherent two-rooted graphs were recently introduced for the case of induced subgraphs. In this paper, we translate this framework to the setting of not necessarily induced (NNI) subgraphs, where the structural constraints, as well as conclusions, are significantly relaxed. We develop a new sufficient condition for inherence, and use it to provide complete characterizations of inherent two-rooted paths and forks. We show that for these families, the obvious necessary condition for inherence from the induced case is sufficient in the NNI setting. To complement these results, we introduce two general methods for proving non-inherence and apply them to demonstrate the non-inherence of several classes of two-rooted trees.
  Keywords: subgraph, two-rooted graph, two-rooted tree, avoidable two-rooted graph, inherent two-rooted graph

papers.intro:
In graph theory, graph properties are often characterized by forbidden or mandatory substructures. These substructures are analyzed in two main ways: as induced subgraphs, which preserve all adjacencies from the parent graph, or as the more flexible not necessarily induced (NNI) subgraphs, which require only a subset of vertices and edges.

The concept of “avoidability,” central to our work, has its roots in the study of chordal graphs. The foundational result is Dirac’s theorem [8], which states that every chordal graph contains a simplicial vertex—a vertex whose neighborhood forms a clique. Recognizing that not all graphs have simplicial vertices, Ohtsuki, Cheung, and Fujisawa introduced in 1976 the concept of an avoidable vertex: one for which every induced path of length two centered at this vertex is part of an induced cycle [13]. They proved that such a vertex exists in every graph. The term ‘avoidable vertex’ was introduced by Beisegel et al. [1]; an alternative term used in the literature is ‘OCF-vertex’ (see, e.g., [3, 4, 12]).

Recall that NNI stands for “not necessarily induced”. The present work pivots from the induced to the NNI setting. This transition is a natural and crucial step, as the structural constraints are significantly relaxed, in the sense that a non-induced copy of a graph HH can exist in many more contexts than an induced one; on the other hand, in general, there are more extensions in the NNI setting than in the induced one. We adopt the two-rooted graph framework but redefine the core concepts for NNI subgraphs. Our goal is to determine how this added flexibility impacts the property of inherence and to identify classes of two-rooted graphs that are robust enough to be inherent in this more general setting.

A powerful sufficient condition for a copy of (H,s,t)(H,s,t) to be avoidable in a graph GG is that the subgraph induced by the vertices not in the copy is connected. Any extension of such a copy would have its new vertices within this subgraph and would therefore be closable; in particular, the copy is avoidable. It turns out that for certain two-rooted graphs, the mere absence of simplicial copies guarantees the existence of such a copy of HH. Such two-rooted graphs are called complementary connected or simplicial (CCS) graphs. By definition, CCS graphs are inherent. The converse implication is open.

papers.title: Can Magnetic Reconnection Accelerate Energetic Particles in the Heliosheath?
papers.abstract: The mechanism for accelerating energetic particles in the outer heliosphere is still under debate. The termination shock, turbulence, and magnetic reconnection have all been proposed as viable mechanisms. We investigate compression-driven particle acceleration during magnetic reconnection in the heliospheric current sheet using the MHD--SDE framework that incorporates energetic-particle feedback into the MHD evolution. For the heliosheath conditions considered here, we find that reconnection-driven acceleration is inefficient downstream of the termination shock, whereas reconnection near the heliopause can generate stronger compression and produce a power-law differential intensity spectrum $J(\varepsilon)\propto\varepsilon^{-5.4}$. However, even the hardest spectrum achieved during magnetic reconnection remains much steeper than the typical $J(\varepsilon)\propto\varepsilon^{-1.5}$ spectrum observed in the heliosheath. This indicates that magnetic reconnection alone is insufficient to explain the acceleration of energetic particles in the heliosheath.

papers.intro:
Energetic particle populations in the outer heliosphere, including pickup ions (PUIs) and anomalous cosmic rays (ACRs), have been observed from several keV to tens of MeV through both in-situ measurements and remote sensing [25, 36, 58, 13, 30, 55, 54]. The origin of these energetic particles is a long-standing problem. Voyager measurements beyond the termination shock revealed persistent nonthermal energetic ion populations with power-law spectra extending from tens of keV to tens of MeV, with differential intensity approximately following J⁡(ε)∝ε−1.5J(\varepsilon)\propto\varepsilon^{-1.5} [13, 30]. The Interstellar Boundary Explorer (IBEX) identified a globally distributed energetic neutral atom (ENA) flux over energies of roughly 0.5–6 keV, providing remote evidence for heliosheath ions in this energy range [24, 55, 14, 54]. The Interstellar Mapping and Acceleration Probe (IMAP) will extend ENA measurements with enhanced spectral and angular resolution, enabling unprecedented characterization of energetic particle distributions in the outer heliosphere [56, 81, 66].

The heliospheric termination shock has long been proposed as the primary site of energetic particle acceleration in the outer heliosphere [65, 41, 42, 27, 28]. However, when Voyager 1 crossed the termination shock, the ACR intensity did not peak but continued to rise in the heliosheath, suggesting other acceleration mechanisms or a modified shock theory is needed [71, 72, 11]. Later studies have considered that shock acceleration [57, 31, 43, 68, 10], turbulence-driven acceleration [21, 22, 40], and magnetic reconnection [45, 18, 19, 74] as possible mechanisms.

The sectored heliosheath region (see Figure 1) consists of alternating magnetic-polarity sectors separated by folded heliospheric current sheets (HCSs), formed as the ballerina-skirt-like HCS crosses the termination shock and is compressed and distorted by plasma compression and flow deflection in the heliosheath [8, 12, 67, 2]. As the sectored magnetic field piles up toward the heliopause, the spacing between neighboring sector boundaries is expected to decrease and become spatially nonuniform [12, 18]. The HCSs are possible sites for magnetic reconnection and energetic-particle acceleration. Lazarian and Opher [45] proposed first-order Fermi acceleration in fast turbulent reconnection, where particles gain energy by bouncing between converging reconnecting magnetic fluxes in the sectored heliosheath. Drake et al. [18], Drake et al. [19] instead emphasized first-order Fermi acceleration in merging magnetic islands in the heliopause sector region. However, it remains unclear whether magnetic reconnection under heliosheath conditions can produce the observed nonthermal ion spectra. In particular, the particle-in-cell (PIC) simulations of Drake et al. [18] failed to produce clear power-law energy spectra, making it difficult to compare theoretical predictions with observations. Over the past decade, a number of studies have shown that low-β\beta magnetic reconnection can effectively produce power-law energy spectra [49, 50, 51, 77, 78, 34, 35, 63, 16]. It is also shown that flow compression is the main particle acceleration mechanism during magnetic reconnection, especially in the weak guide field regime [47, 20, 59]. Applying the compression acceleration model to the near-Sun heliospheric current sheet HCS, recent studies have shown that magnetic reconnection typically produces a power-law spectrum J⁡(ε)∝ε−3J(\varepsilon)\propto\varepsilon^{-3} or softer, consistent with observations by Parker Solar Probe [61, 60]. However, HCS acceleration in the heliosheath is in a very different plasma environment. In this paper, we revisit whether magnetic reconnection can accelerate particles to high energy in the heliosheath.

Global MHD models and Voyager-based studies indicate that plasma conditions vary significantly across the heliosheath, from high-β\beta, PUI-dominated plasma downstream of the termination shock to more magnetically compressed, lower-β\beta plasma toward the heliopause [18, 15, 1, 5]. Zenitani and Miyoshi [76] has shown that plasma β\beta controls the plasma compressibility and reconnection outflow dynamics, and it is therefore expected to strongly influence compression-driven particle acceleration. A goal of this study is to determine how reconnection-driven PUI acceleration changes across the plasma-β\beta conditions expected from the termination-shock region to the heliopause.

Zenitani and Miyoshi [76] has shown that plasma β\beta controls the plasma compressibility and reconnection outflow dynamics, and it is therefore expected to strongly influence compression-driven particle acceleration. A goal of this study is to determine how reconnection-driven PUI acceleration changes across the plasma-β\beta conditions expected from the termination-shock region to the heliopause.

Previous fully kinetic PIC simulations provide insight into particle injection and reconnection microphysics and have been widely used to study particle acceleration in low-β\beta magnetic reconnection [62, 48, 20, 32, 33, 50, 51]. Recent hybrid-PIC simulations have begun to explore reconnection in regimes with higher β\beta [29]. However, in high-β\beta plasmas like heliosheath, the magnetic free energy available per particle is relatively small, so capturing the development of a nonthermal tail can require longer integration times [18]. Applying PIC-based simulations directly to the heliosheath is difficult also because the characteristic sector spacing is on the order of several AU, and the typical PUI gyroradius is several orders of magnitude less. Energetic particle transport equations provide a macroscopic description of energetic-particle transport and acceleration on MHD fluid scales, without requiring the gyroradius to be resolved [64, 7, 75]. This approach has been used to study compression-driven particle acceleration in fluid-scale magnetic reconnection regions [49, 46, 70, 69, 61, 60]. Here, we use the MHD–SDE framework developed in Seo et al. [70], in which Parker’s transport equation is solved using the stochastic differential equation (SDE) method [49, 46] and the resulting nonthermal particle pressure is coupled back to the MHD equations. This feedback is essential to consider as PUIs contribute a substantial pressure component in the heliosheath, similar to our earlier studies [70, 69]. Several other macroscopic approaches also include energetic-particle feedback. The kglobal and MHD-gPIC model evolves energetic particles using guiding-center equations and couples their anisotropic stress back to the MHD plasma, allowing pressure anisotropy and the firehose constraint to regulate reconnection [17, 3, 37]. However, its original formulation does not include any spatial diffusion or pitch-angle scattering. The MHD-PIC method includes the Lorentz-force backreaction of energetic particles but requires their gyromotion scale to be resolved [4]. We apply the MHD–SDE framework to model reconnection-driven particle acceleration across heliosheath conditions, from the downstream region of the termination shock to near the heliopause. Our results show the hardest spectrum achieved during magnetic reconnection remains much steeper than the typical J⁡(ε)∝ε−1.5J(\varepsilon)\propto\varepsilon^{-1.5} spectrum observed in the heliosheath, indicating that magnetic reconnection alone is insufficient to explain the acceleration of energetic particles in the heliosheath.

papers.title: PARGAR: Pilot-Aware Graph Attention for Sparse-Pilot Neural OFDM Receivers
papers.abstract: Reliable channel estimation and symbol detection in 5G New Radio (NR), as well as emerging 6G radio systems, rely on demodulation reference signals (DMRS). The density and placement of these pilots on the orthogonal frequency-division multiplexing (OFDM) time--frequency resource grid affect both receiver reliability and spectral efficiency. Sparse DMRS layouts increase the time--frequency distance between pilot observations and data resource elements (REs), which can make pilot information harder to exploit with purely local processing. This paper proposes \textbf{PARGAR (Pilot-Aware Graph Attention Receiver)}, a graph-attention neural receiver that represents the OFDM resource grid as a graph for bit detection. The graph combines local time--frequency edges with pilot-anchor links from data REs to selected pilot REs, and we further study a channel-scaled pilot-anchor rule based on approximate coherence time and coherence bandwidth. Using Sionna-generated OFDM simulations, we evaluate \textsc{PARGAR} against DeepRx, a convolutional neural network (CNN)-based receiver, across dense, two-symbol sparse, and single-symbol sparse DMRS layouts under channel-mismatch scenarios. Under the considered SISO uncoded setup, channel-scaled \textsc{PARGAR} explicitly injects pilot-aware inductive bias and yields lower BER in selected sparse-pilot scenarios while remaining competitive under dense pilots.

papers.intro:
Fifth-generation (5G) New Radio (NR) and emerging sixth-generation (6G) radio systems rely on demodulation reference signals (DMRS) for channel estimation and coherent detection. The 5G-Advanced evolution and Release-20 6G study items target mobility, non-terrestrial networks, sensing, and AI-native air interfaces [1]. DMRS density directly controls a practical tradeoff. More pilot resource elements (REs) provide more frequent channel observations and can improve receiver reliability, but they also reduce the number of REs available for data transmission. Reducing pilot density improves the data-RE fraction but increases the time-frequency distance between pilot observations and data REs. In this setting, the receiver must infer channel information over longer pilot-to-data separations, and interpolation errors can affect subsequent equalization and bit detection under delay spread, Doppler, and frequency-selective fading.

Neural-network-based receivers, hereafter referred to as neural receivers, offer an alternative by learning channel estimation and data detection directly from received OFDM resource grids. DeepRx showed that CNNs can perform direct bit detection from resource-grid inputs [2], and subsequent work extended neural receivers toward multi-user multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) systems, adaptation, continual learning, lightweight implementations, and neuromorphic architectures [3, 4, 5]. These receivers process the grid through convolutional operations, which are effective for local time–frequency neighborhoods. However, sparse pilots create nonlocal pilot-to-data dependencies: a data RE may need information from pilot REs several OFDM symbols or subcarriers away. Capturing such dependencies with only local convolutions can require many layers or large receptive fields.

Capturing such dependencies with only local convolutions can require many layers or large receptive fields.

Graph neural networks (GNNs) provide a complementary inductive bias by propagating information over explicitly defined relationships [6], and graph attention networks (GATs) learn adaptive weights for neighboring nodes [7]. In wireless systems, many GNN methods model users, antennas, links, or resource-allocation relationships for MIMO detection, beamforming, tracking, and scheduling [8, 9, 10]. Our earlier work used OFDM resource-grid graphs for NR channel estimation [11], without performing end-to-end bit detection or introducing pilot-anchor connections between data and pilot REs. This paper instead uses the OFDM resource grid itself as the graph and explicitly adds pilot-anchor edges to support bit detection.

Robustness under channel mismatch is a second concern. In this paper, channel mismatch refers to test conditions in which the channel profile, terminal speed, or delay spread differs from the training configuration. Neural receivers can be sensitive to the channel distribution used during training [12], and VERITAS [13] showed that such mismatches can degrade receiver performance, while also suggesting that training on harder conditions may generalize better to easier ones. These observations lead to three research questions: 1) How to explicitly propagate sparse pilot information to data REs for neural OFDM detection? 2) How to select pilot anchors using channel correlation rather than only grid geometry? 3) How does the resulting graph receiver compare with neural and classical baselines under pilot sparsity and channel mismatch? They are addressed as follows. We propose PARGAR (Pilot-Aware Graph Attention Receiver, a graph-attention receiver for OFDM bit detection in 5G NR- and 6G-oriented radio links, and make the following contributions: • We introduce a pilot-aware graph-attention neural receiver whose graph combines local time–frequency edges with pilot-anchor edges between data and pilot REs. • We study a channel-scaled anchor-selection rule that normalizes time and frequency separations by approximate coherence time and coherence bandwidth. • We combine practical model-based node features with iterative channel-feature refinement and evaluate PARGAR against DeepRx, least-squares minimum mean-square error (LS-MMSE), and genie-aided MMSE (Genie-MMSE) under dense, two-symbol sparse, and single-symbol sparse pilot layouts with channel-distribution mismatch.

papers.title: Interactive World Simulation with Cosmos for Physical AI
papers.abstract: We present a shared framework that adapts Cosmos world foundation models for real-time interactive world simulation in Physical AI. By streaming visual observations in response to actions and scene controls, the framework enables users and embodied agents to interact with evolving virtual environments. It supports both predicting the visual consequences of actions and generating observations from physical state maintained by an external simulator. We demonstrate this approach across camera navigation and robot manipulation, controllable video transfer, and multi-view autonomous vehicle (AV) simulation. These examples provide a shared foundation for developing interactive virtual environments for Physical AI training and evaluation. Our code and model checkpoints are available at https://github.com/nvidia/cosmos and https://huggingface.co/collections/nvidia/cosmos3-examples. The project website is available at https://research.nvidia.com/labs/cosmos-lab/cosmos-simulation.

papers.title: Fault-tolerant shallow recurrent decoders for sparse sensing with missing sensor measurements
papers.abstract: Real-world sensing systems are inherently imperfect: sensors may fail, intermittently disconnect, operate with asynchronous sampling rates, and be subject to noise, leading to measurement streams that are irregular, incomplete, and heterogeneous. Nevertheless, sensing strategies for real-time state reconstruction typically assume synchronous and continuously active sensors, a constraint that substantially limits their applicability in operational environments. In this work, we introduce fault-tolerant sparse sensing strategies in the context of shallow recurrent decoders (SHRED) to enable high-dimensional state estimation from sparse, asynchronous, and missing sensor measurements. Specifically, we consider naive imputation strategies, fault-tolerant recurrent temporal encoders, and we introduce four different transformer-based masking mechanisms to make SHRED explicitly aware of sensor availability through the binary data-availability mask. Moreover, we further introduce a multi-step decoding training objective for SHRED, resulting in smoother latent trajectories and more robust predictions. Throughout a synthetic benchmark and three real-world problems in hydrodynamic and ocean modeling, we show that (i) transformer-based masking mechanisms outperform standard imputation techniques and fault-tolerant recurrent architectures, (ii) the multi-step decoding training objective enhances reconstruction fidelity and robustness in the presence of heterogeneous missing-data patterns, while (iii) the computational efficiency of SHRED is preserved, with no additional inference-time overhead.

papers.intro:
Many real-world dynamical systems evolve in high-dimensional state spaces that cannot be directly observed in their entirety [1, 26]. This challenge arises across a wide range of scientific and engineering applications, including fluid and solid mechanics, weather and climate modeling, plasma physics, and structural health monitoring. In these systems, sensors provide the primary interface between theory and reality, yet their deployment is inevitably limited by cost, reliability, physical inaccessibility, and operational constraints. However, being able to access local measurements is crucial to, e.g., inferring full state dynamics, designing feedback control strategies, or predicting quantities of interest.

Recovering the state of a dynamical system from partial observations enables downstream tasks such as monitoring, forecasting, anomaly detection, and control, while avoiding expensive and impractical full-field measurements. Traditional approaches to state reconstruction are grounded in linear algebra frameworks. The singular value decomposition (SVD) – also known as proper orthogonal decomposition (POD) [35, 31, 6, 4] – provides an optimal low-rank approximation of high-dimensional state data through a linear projection onto a low-dimensional basis of spatial functions capturing most of the data variability. After computing the dominant POD modes from the training data, the coefficients of the low-rank representation can be estimated from a limited number of point measurements by solving a linear inverse problem, provided that the sensing matrix is well-conditioned [22, 49]. However, the requirement for a well-conditioned sensing matrix imposes constraints on both the number and placement of sensors, leading to an NP-hard optimization problem for identifying the optimal configuration [12, 29, 30] and potentially limiting its applicability in real-world settings [11, 36]. Moreover, the reconstruction accuracy of this method is bounded by the expressiveness of the POD modes used, so that fine-scales or nonlinear features of the field cannot be recovered entirely when only a few modes are retained.

The advent of scientific machine learning has introduced new data-driven methods for addressing limitations of traditional linear methods [23, 5, 40]. Neural networks and, in particular, shallow decoder networks (SDNs), leverage the universal approximation theorem of feedforward architectures [14] to learn an end-to-end nonlinear mapping from sensor measurements directly to the corresponding high-dimensional state [8, 42, 19, 34], without requiring an explicit basis representation as in POD-based methods. Similarly, the Senseiver [43] employs an attention-based architecture inspired by the Perceiver IO [28] to reconstruct spatio-temporal fields at arbitrary query locations from sparse observations. Once trained on a set of snapshots, these strategies can capture nonlinear spatial correlations in the data that are inaccessible to linear methods and have been shown to outperform linear POD-based architectures in field reconstruction, particularly in ill-posed settings, i.e., with few or poorly placed sensors. Nevertheless, POD-based methods, SDNs, and the Senseiver all share an intrinsic limitation: they operate on static snapshots, treating each time instant independently and discarding the temporal dynamics of the measurement signal. The temporal history of observations, naturally available whenever sensors operate continuously over time, is essential for capturing intrinsic dynamical features, such as temporal correlations between consecutive measurements.

The shallow recurrent decoder (SHRED) framework proposed by Williams et al. [51] addresses this limitation by combining a recurrent temporal encoder with a shallow spatial decoder. The encoder, which is typically modeled via recurrent neural networks such as, e.g., long short-term memory (LSTM) [25, 33] or gated recurrent unit (GRU) [10] networks, processes a sliding window of lagged sensor measurements, compressing their temporal history into a latent representation, which is subsequently mapped to the full field by a SDN. Thanks to the temporal history of sensor readings, SHRED achieves dramatically lower reconstruction errors than classical techniques, even with a very limited number of randomly placed sensors. Different SHRED extensions have recently been proposed in the literature. For instance, Riva et al. [41] take into account an ensemble of SHRED models to cope with noisy measurements. Moreover, the SHRED framework has been extended to parametric systems [47, 46], demonstrating that the temporal history of a handful of sensors suffices to reconstruct and control high-dimensional fields across varying physical and geometrical parameters. Gao et al. [24], instead, introduce a regularization based on sparse identification of nonlinear dynamics (SINDy) [7] to promote interpretable latent dynamics, further improving forecasting performance and explainability in challenging scenarios. papers.title: A First Closed-Form Robin Parameter for Optimized Schwarz Waveform Relaxation as a Function of Iteration Count, Overlap, and Time Window Length
papers.abstract:
Schwarz waveform relaxation (SWR) is a parallel-in-time iterative method for the solution of evolution problems and belongs to the class of Parallel-in-Time algorithms that have received increasing attention over the past three decades. For parabolic problems, SWR converges linearly over long time intervals and exhibits superlinear convergence on short time intervals. Since the introduction of optimized variants (OSWR) nearly three decades ago, determining the optimized Robin parameter when OSWR is applied on bounded time windows has remained an open problem.
  We introduce here a new analytical approach that, for the first time, yields a closed-form expression for the optimal Robin parameter in the transmission conditions for the one-dimensional heat equation with two overlapping subdomains. The resulting formula explicitly characterizes the dependence of the optimal parameter on the iteration number, the overlap size, and the length of the time window. Beyond resolving this long-standing optimization problem, our analysis provides a framework that can be extended to more general settings, including higher-dimensional problems, multiple subdomains, and higher-order transmission conditions.

papers.intro:
The convergence behaviour of classical and optimized Schwarz Waveform Relaxation (SWR) methods for parabolic partial differential equations (PDEs) differs markedly from that of Schwarz methods for elliptic problems [12], owing to the non-normal nature of the time derivative operator. It is known that classical SWR methods (i.e., with Dirichlet transmission conditions) converge superlinearly on bounded time intervals, but such convergence deteriorates as the time interval length TT goes to infinity; in the limit, convergence is only linear [10, 13, 11]. As the iteration progresses, the convergence curve exhibits different phases: there is an initial rapid phase, then a slowdown, and finally an acceleration to superlinear convergence [9]. Moreover, when Robin transmission conditions are used, the best Robin parameter pp that minimizes error reduction depends on the number of iterations nn one intends to take, rather than a fixed constant [4].
