The classical approach to finding best parameters via Fourier analysis, see [3], is unable to capture this dependence on nn. Indeed, such an analysis does not even yield superlinear convergence estimates (but see [9] for a Kernel Fourier analysis that uses the heat kernel to restore superlinearity in the estimates). As a result, superlinear estimates typically employ kernel techniques [10, 11] or Laplace transforms [7, 14, 8]. The latter is useful when the iteration function in Laplace space admits a closed form inverse Laplace transform, or can be expressed as a convergent series of such inverse transforms. This is feasible for Dirichlet and Neumann transmission conditions, but not for Robin transmission conditions. As a result, the problem of finding nn-dependent best Robin parameters remains so far an open problem, even for the simple case of the one-dimensional heat equation in two subdomains. Note that in the discrete-time setting, it is possible to find the best Robin parameter by numerically minimizing the norm of the appropriate iteration matrix, whose size is proportional to the number of time steps, see [1, 2].

The goal of this paper is twofold. The first goal is to introduce a theoretical tool for estimating the error of domain decomposition methods with simple Laplace transforms, even when the inverse transforms do not have closed form formulas. The tool relies on a simple relationship between the Laplace and Fourier transforms, together with the Plancherel theorem. Although the tool is easy to understand, its application is not so widespread in the domain decomposition literature; we therefore illustrate its utility by giving a new convergence analysis of the classical SWR method for two subdomains, for which we are able to recover the known superlinear estimates using only a few lines of calculations. The second goal of the paper is to use the same techniques to fully analyze the convergence of optimized SWR (OSWR), first as a function of the Robin parameter pp, and then by choosing the parameter pp to minimize this contraction estimate for a given number of iterations nn. Note that this is the first time we are able to truly optimize pp in the superlinear regime, even though the algorithm exists and has been used for three decades. In each case, we use numerical examples to illustrate the sharpness of our estimates.

papers.title: Regret Bounds for Market Making with Persistent Orders
papers.abstract: We study adversarial market making with orders that remain active until execution. The maker operates on two markets: a primary market where orders are made and a secondary market where the resulting positions are hedged. In each round, the maker posts a quote on the primary market before observing both primary and secondary market prices. An order executes when the primary price reaches its quote, and the resulting position is immediately offset at the secondary price. When both price sequences are chosen by an adversary over $T$ rounds, we give a simple deterministic policy with regret of order $\log T$ against the best fixed quote (static comparator) and $\sqrt T$ against the best quote for each submission date (dynamic comparator), plus two terms measuring exposure to future primary and secondary prices. These rates remain optimal even when both exposure terms vanish and lower bounds show that the exposure terms are necessary. Our policy naturally extends to simultaneous bids and asks, where we show that static and dynamic regret are both characterized (up to constant factors) by the exposures terms (where the primary price exposure $V_T^{\mathrm{two}}$ now accounts for both bids and asks) and a term of order $\sqrt{V_T^{\mathrm{two}}\log T}$. Our policy is simple, efficient and fully parameterless. We extend this setting by demonstrating how natural assumptions on the price processes lead to improved guarantees without changing the policy.

papers.intro:
A market maker quotes prices at which they are willing to buy and sell an asset. After a trade, they can offset their position in another (secondary) market. The difference between the quoted price and the price of this offsetting trade determines the maker’s profit. We revisit the simple sequential model of Cesa-Bianchi et al. (2025), where the maker submits a bid and ask pair to an incoming trader in each round. Unlike that setting, where an unaccepted quote does not remain available to later trades, we study what happens when: (1) orders remain active until they trade, (2) orders cannot be canceled. In our model the maker continues submitting orders even though the previous ones may still be outstanding. An ask therefore determines both a sale price and an execution date: a higher ask may earn more if it trades, but it may trade later. Hence, even though every executed position is immediately offset, outstanding orders remain exposed to future prices, and many orders can become exposed to the same later change in the hedging cost. Our model has two exogenous price sequences (one for the primary and one for the secondary market), both revealed after each decision. An outstanding ask executes the first time the primary price becomes at least as large as its quote, and the maker buys back the asset at that round’s secondary price. The execution delay of outstanding asks is monotonic in their quote, as a lower quote cannot execute later than a higher one. Finally, our setting also includes bids, which are defined symmetrically to asks.

We study two notions of regret: static regret, where we compare the maker with the best fixed quote submitted on every round, and dynamic regret, where the comparator chooses the best quote separately on every round and knowing the entire price path. In both cases, the regret after TT rounds is controlled by two measures of price exposure plus a horizon-dependent term. The first measure is defined on the primary prices and counts the width of the intervals of quotes that wait and eventually execute. The second measure is defined on the secondary prices and records the possible change between the last observed hedging price and a future execution price. These measures can be small even when some orders wait a long time. The horizon-dependent term, instead, is Θ⁡(log⁡T)\Theta(\log T) for static regret and Θ⁡(T)\Theta\big(\sqrt{T}\big) for dynamic regret. These bounds are obtained by the same policy using two different learning rates that depend neither on the horizon nor on the price exposures. We also prove lower bounds showing that this difference between static and dynamic regret is necessary, even when the primary price never increases and the secondary price is constant. Separate constructions also establish the need for both exposure terms. Our policy is simple, efficient, and naturally extends to bid-ask pairs.

papers.title: Performance Portability of Out-of-Kernel Optimizations on GPUs: A Molecular Docking Case Study
papers.abstract: Achieving performance portability is challenging for irregular scientific applications built as repeated multi-kernel GPU pipelines, because throughput depends on out-of-kernel decisions as much as on kernel efficiency. Using molecular docking as a representative case study, we propose an out-of-kernel tuning methodology that treats batching policy, worker concurrency, and per-worker memory allocation as explicit optimization parameters, replacing backend-dependent occupancy-driven choices with a more portable execution strategy based on explicit resource bounds. We implement this methodology in the muDock mini-app under a manager/worker execution model where multiple host workers share a GPU through independent streams. We then evaluate the methodology on NVIDIA, AMD, and Intel GPUs across CUDA, HIP, and SYCL implementations. Across all evaluated platform/backend pairs, the memory-bounded formulation exceeds the peak throughput of the occupancy-guided baseline. The fully tuned methodology improves the end-to-end throughput on all tested configurations, achieving an average speedup of 1.53x over the baseline.

papers.intro:
High-performance computing (HPC) plays a central role in reducing the time-to-solution of large-scale scientific applications. As production systems increasingly rely on GPU acceleration, however, achieving this objective across different vendors and software ecosystems becomes more difficult in practice. Deploying a scientific application across platforms requires not only functional portability, but also tuning choices that remain effective despite differences in compilers, runtimes, and hardware resource behavior [1, 2, 3]. This problem is particularly relevant for applications that are not dominated by a single monolithic kernel, but instead execute long sequences of repeated kernel launches. In these applications, throughput depends on how inputs are grouped and submitted across the full pipeline, not only on the efficiency of one kernel in isolation. As a result, achieving portable performance requires looking at the full application pipeline, not only at kernel-level code generation.

As an example, biological applications consume a significant fraction of HPC resources, and virtual screening is a representative throughput-oriented workload in which a speed-up directly increases the screening capacity. Structure-based virtual screening uses docking to rank large libraries of compounds, called ligands, against one or more protein targets, allowing researchers to focus downstream experimental validation on the most promising candidates [4, 5, 6]. Because docking simulations are much cheaper than experimental screening, modern campaigns increasingly target very large chemical libraries, sometimes reaching hundreds of millions of compounds [7, 8, 9]. This trend makes portable GPU efficiency a first-order concern for docking pipelines. Docking is also a challenging workload for portable performance. Ligands differ in atom count, flexibility, and interaction patterns, so the cost and memory footprint of processing each ligand can differ substantially [10]. This irregularity makes batching, resource usage, and concurrent device use especially important for end-to-end throughput. Prior work on out-of-kernel optimizations has already shown that these decisions can be as important as kernel-level tuning [11].

Because docking simulations are much cheaper than experimental screening, modern campaigns increasingly target very large chemical libraries, sometimes reaching hundreds of millions of compounds [7, 8, 9]. This trend makes portable GPU efficiency a first-order concern for docking pipelines. Docking is also a challenging workload for portable performance. Ligands differ in atom count, flexibility, and interaction patterns, so the cost and memory footprint of processing each ligand can differ substantially [10]. This irregularity makes batching, resource usage, and concurrent device use especially important for end-to-end throughput. Prior work on out-of-kernel optimizations has already shown that these decisions can be as important as kernel-level tuning [11].

In this paper, we study this problem using muDock [12, 13], a compact molecular docking mini-app designed to preserve the key computational patterns of larger docking codes while enabling systematic experimentation across platforms and backends. Our goal is to study whether a more portable out-of-kernel formulation can improve throughput in a repeated multi-kernel GPU pipeline. Instead of relying on occupancy-driven batch sizing, which depends on backend-specific information and assumptions, we study an alternative formulation based on explicit resource bounds. In particular, we focus on batching policy, worker concurrency, and per-worker memory allocation as coupled tuning dimensions, and evaluate how these choices transfer across CUDA, HIP, and SYCL implementations.

papers.title: A brief overview of the baryon cycle in galaxies
papers.abstract: Galaxy formation and evolution is governed by the continuous exchange of gas between the cosmic web, the circumgalactic medium (CGM), and the interstellar medium (ISM) of galaxies. This brief review summarises our current understanding of this baryon cycle, from the accretion of gas onto galaxies to its conversion into stars, and the feedback processes that regulate the growth of galaxies. Several open questions will be highlighted, that will encourage progresses in cosmological simulations, multiwavelength observations, and theory to resolve.

papers.intro:
In the Λ\Lambda Cold Dark Matter (Λ\LambdaCDM) paradigm (see reviews by [161, 167]), the gravitational collapse of baryons within the initial distribution of dark matter haloes led to the formation of a complex structure of voids, filaments, and nodes known as the cosmic web, ubiquitous in the observed Universe (see, e.g., [193, 234] for a brief overview, [204, 105, 36] for empirical evidence, and [194, 33, 21] for theoretical predictions). Galaxies are assembled primarily within filaments, whereas voids are the most underdense regions of the Universe, and nodes host galaxy clusters. Further growth of galaxies is regulated by the interplay between gas accretion from the cosmic web to the circumgalactic medium (CGM) and down to the interstellar medium (ISM) of galaxies (reviewed by [177, 170, 209, 162, 60]) and feedback from stellar activity [235, 201, 205] and active galactic nuclei (AGN; [59, 88, 87]). A comprehensive theoretical and observational framework for galaxy formation and evolution therefore requires connecting physical phenomena spanning approximately ten orders of magnitude in spatial scale and several orders of magnitude in time-scale. Galaxy assembly within the cosmic web occurs on Gpc-to-Mpc scales over Gyr time-scales, and gas accretion proceeds on Mpc-to-kpc scales, again over Gyr time-scales. Once inside the galaxy, gas cools and settles dynamically on kpc-to-pc scales over Myr time-scales, before star formation and AGN activity take place on pc-to-km scales over time-scales as short as a Myr. The multi-scale nature of galaxy formation and evolution is not the only challenge. The baryon cycle [162], which describes how gas accretes onto galaxies, cools to form stars, and is partially returned to the CGM through stellar- and AGN-driven outflows, depends on galaxy mass [183], galactic environment [15], and cosmic time [68, 222]. This renders galaxy formation and evolution not only an inherently multi-scale problem, but a complex dynamical puzzle that requires input from cosmological simulations, multiwavelength observations, and analytic theory in equal measure. This brief review covers several aspects of the baryon cycle. Section 2 discusses gas accretion from the CGM to the ISM; the process of star formation is presented in Sect. 3, and the impact of stellar feedback on the baryon cycle is described in Sect. 4; the feeding of supermassive black holes (SMBHs) at the centres of galaxies and the contribution of AGN outflows to the baryon cycle are discussed in Sects 5 and 6, respectively. Concluding remarks, including a brief summary of the open questions, are given in Sect. 7.

papers.title: Timed Games under Environmental Interference with Real-Time Objectives
papers.abstract: Classical Timed Games formulations may be unsuitable, or require substantial modeling effort, to capture complex interaction patterns between a controller and its surrounding environment, in which non-determinism must be resolved after the controller has chosen which action to perform. In this paper, we develop the theory of Timed CLTLoc Games (TCGs), a Timed Game variant designed to facilitate the modeling of such patterns. Unlike classical Timed Games formulations, TCGs partition locations rather than transitions, and use Constraint Linear Temporal Logic over clocks (CLTLoc) to specify the controller's objectives. We develop algorithms for solving TCGs and synthesizing winning controller strategies for games whose objectives include formal properties such as reachability and safety. For reachability objectives, our synthesis algorithm yields winning controller strategies that minimize the number of moves required to reach a goal state. Solving reachability TCGs is EXPTIME-complete, matching the complexity of solving reachability Timed Games. All of our algorithms operate backwards and are implemented in our C++ region-based library TARZAN, leveraging OpenMP for efficient parallelization. Experimental results demonstrate the feasibility of TARZAN.
papers.intro:
The interactions between a reactive system (Harel and Pnueli, 1985) and its environment are naturally modeled as game-theoretic problems, in which the system represents a controller acting against an adversarial opponent. Ensuring safety and functional correctness properties is essential, as the environment may introduce interference under which the controller must still guarantee correct behavior. A canonical domain is robotics, in which autonomous robots act as controllers in dynamic environments shared with other robots and human operators.

When timing constraints are involved, tg defined over ta address the controller synthesis problem in real-time settings (Maler et al., 1995). Typical tg semantics (refer to (Nicolas Markey, 2025b) for an introduction), as implemented in state-of-the-art tools such as Uppaal Tiga (Behrmann et al., 2007b), focus on the concurrency between two players: the controller and its environment. Informally, after both players choose an action and a delay, the action corresponding to the shortest delay is executed, breaking ties in favor of the environment. While effective for modeling concurrent interactions, this semantics may be unsuitable, or require substantial modeling effort, to capture interactions in which the non-determinism over transitions and, in some cases, also delays, must be resolved after the controller chooses the action to perform (and possibly also an associated delay).

To facilitate the modeling of such interactions, we propose a novel tg variant, called tcg, in which the controller always chooses an action to perform, and its objectives (hereafter referred to as the winning condition) are specified by using cltloc (cltloc) formulae (Bersani et al., 2016; Bersani et al., 2017). The non-determinism over transitions is then resolved by the environment; non-determinism over delays depends on whether a location belongs to the controller or the environment. Notably, tcg partition locations rather than transitions, better capturing environmental interference that may occur after the controller has chosen an action. For instance, when the environment consists of human operators, a robot may require human intervention to complete some tasks (Askarpour et al., 2019; Lestingi et al., 2024); here, tcg facilitate the modeling of the following hri (Goodrich and Schultz, 2007) phenotypes from Hollnagel’s foundational taxonomy (Hollnagel, 1998): delay/premature action—an action is executed at an unintended time—and insertion/intrusion—an action not included in the original plan is executed. These interaction patterns and phenotypes, in which the environment resolves non-determinism after the controller has chosen an action, cannot be faithfully encoded under the standard tg semantics, where the controller retains the ability to interfere with the environment’s timing and uncontrollable transitions carry no liveness obligation (de Alfaro et al., 2003; Behrmann et al., 2007a); thus, tcg and standard tg target different application domains.

These interaction patterns and phenotypes, in which the environment resolves non-determinism after the controller has chosen an action, cannot be faithfully encoded under the standard tg semantics, where the controller retains the ability to interfere with the environment’s timing and uncontrollable transitions carry no liveness obligation (de Alfaro et al., 2003; Behrmann et al., 2007a); thus, tcg and standard tg target different application domains.

For instance, consider a manufacturing robot (the controller) cooperating with a human operator (the environment). The robot determines which task the operator must perform, but it controls neither the outcome of the task nor its duration: given the same command, the operator may react in different ways and at a controller-unpredictable time. Since controllability in standard tg is associated with transitions, a single transition cannot simultaneously represent a controller-selected command while leaving both the delay and the resolution of the resulting non-determinism to the environment. To encode such an interaction, the model must decouple the command and its execution into two consecutive steps: a controllable transition issuing the command and leading to an auxiliary location, followed by uncontrollable transitions exiting from that location, each representing one possible reaction of the operator. However, since the environment controls the resolution of uncontrollable transitions, it may choose to never fire any of them when a location has only outgoing uncontrollable transitions, allowing the game to remain indefinitely in the auxiliary location. Avoiding this behavior requires equipping the auxiliary location with an invariant, thereby imposing an artificial upper bound on the operator’s reaction time. Besides introducing an auxiliary location for each command, this modification alters the modeled system itself. In tcg, instead, a single environment location is sufficient: the robot selects the action, then the operator determines the delay and subsequently resolves the non-determinism by selecting one of the enabled transitions. Thus, tcg decouple controllability from timing and outcome resolution in a natural way, allowing the original interaction to be modeled without auxiliary locations or artificial timing assumptions.

tcg are further distinguished by cltloc’s linear-time nature, which facilitates the specification of constraints over the timeline of the interaction between a controller and its environment. As a result, the same model can be reused among different winning conditions, avoiding structural modifications whenever the specification changes.

papers.title: Sobolev--Poincar\'e inequalities for piecewise $W^{2,p}$ functions over general polytopic meshes
papers.abstract: We establish Sobolev--Poincar\'e inequalities for piecewise $W^{2,p}$ functions in two and three dimensions over families of general polytopic (including shape-regular simplicial and Cartesian) meshes, allowing for degenerate facets. The proposed inequalities feature control by either the broken Hessian or, more naturally for general fourth-order problems, the broken Laplacian. Important tools in their derivation are a Helmholtz decomposition in Banach--Sobolev spaces and Sobolev--Poincar\'e inequalities for piecewise $W^{1,p}$ functions; we avoid the use of any inverse inequality. We provide estimates with fairly general Lebesgue exponents. Applications to the stability analysis of nonconforming discretizations for second- and fourth-order, linear and nonlinear problems are exhibited.

papers.title: Delay-Doppler Synchronization for Distributed Uplink Interference Nulling in LEO Networks
papers.abstract: Cooperation among low-Earth-orbit (LEO) satellites provides spatial diversity for mitigating uplink interference that is difficult to suppress with a single onboard array. Coherent interference cancellation across satellites, however, requires compensation of the relative delay and Doppler of a common interferer. We analyze two-branch interference nulling with finite training and derive a closed-form approximation to the mean residual interference-to-noise ratio (INR). The approximation separates wrong acquisition, local synchronization errors, and weight-learning losses, linking performance to input INR, branch power imbalance, training length, and effective search size. Under a Gaussian surrogate with small errors and efficient, approximately unbiased refinement, correct acquisition yields a high-INR plateau of $2/N_v$, where $N_v$ is the valid training length. Synchronization and weight learning contribute equally to this limit, whereas persistent alignment bias adds a penalty that grows with input power. Monte Carlo experiments compare dense FFT/zoom and coarse FFT/gradient acquisition using matched final FIR refinement, branch-noise normalization, and independent test blocks. Both approach the predicted plateau at high input INR. Coarse search reduces measured search time by $6.7\times$ at an approximately 0.7-dB acquisition-threshold penalty. Controlled power-ratio sweeps show how branch imbalance delays reliable acquisition at fixed stronger-branch INR. A separate Starlink snapshot evaluation demonstrates comparable nulling performance under changing satellite geometry.

papers.title: Intra-Cell Spatial Reuse in LEO Downlinks: Beam-Leakage-Aware Satellite Scheduling
papers.abstract: Dense low-earth-orbit (LEO) constellations offer an opportunity to increase local broadband capacity by serving multiple terminals in the same cell through concurrent satellite beams. However, interference between overlapping beams limits spatial reuse, and satellite selection based solely on link strength or angular separation may result in suboptimal performance. This paper proposes beam-leakage-aware satellite scheduling for Ku-band LEO downlink transmissions. With matched transmit and receive beamforming, we formulate a fixed-cardinality sum-rate maximization problem that jointly accounts for satellite-dependent received powers and pairwise receive-array leakage. A beam-leakage-aware branch-and-bound (BL-BnB) algorithm combines an admissible upper bound with greedy-plus-swap initialization to obtain globally optimal schedules for the reference-point model. We evaluate the method using a 24-h ephemeris-derived Starlink visibility trace with antenna and transmit-power models calibrated to public SpaceX filings. The results show that total capacity increases with beam count, but less than proportionally. With eight concurrent beams, BL-BnB improves mean per-beam capacity by 27.2% over nearest-satellite selection, primarily benefiting weaker links. BL-BnB achieves millisecond-scale runtimes in our evaluation, supporting the computational feasibility of optimal scheduling.

papers.intro:
Local traffic demand in low-Earth-orbit (LEO) broadband networks can exceed the capacity of a single satellite beam, motivating concurrent service from multiple simultaneously visible satellites [1]. In a recreational vehicle (RV) park or at rural terminal densities, active terminals can be too close together to be served by non-overlapping spot beams. Concurrent beams from multiple satellites can increase local capacity by reusing the same time–frequency resource. The resulting intra-cell spatial reuse, illustrated in Fig. 1, depends on how effectively the terminals can separate desired and interfering downlinks.

Concurrent beams from multiple satellites can increase local capacity by reusing the same time–frequency resource. The resulting intra-cell spatial reuse, illustrated in Fig. 1, depends on how effectively the terminals can separate desired and interfering downlinks.

Regulatory developments further motivate the study of overlapping beams. To protect geostationary-satellite-orbit (GSO) systems under the International Telecommunication Union (ITU)’s interference limits [2], the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) initially restricted Starlink Gen2 to one co-frequency, co-polarization beam per location in the 12.2–12.7 and 19.7–20.2 GHz bands [3]. Then, its January 2026 waiver permitted up to eight overlapping Ku-band beams with 4∘4^{\circ} GSO-arc avoidance [4]. The framework adopted in April 2026 introduced an alternative that does not explicitly limit the number of overlapping beams but instead relies on GSO-link performance protection and 3∘3^{\circ} arc avoidance in the United States [5]. These developments make the capacity benefits and interference costs of concurrent beams increasingly relevant.

The most critical challenge is that satellite visibility does not directly translate into usable spatial reuse. For a compact cell, satellite transmit footprints substantially overlap, so interference rejection relies primarily on the ground terminals’ receive arrays. Selecting the nearest satellites favors short propagation paths but can also end up with highly correlated arrival directions. Conversely, enforcing a large angular separation can be unnecessarily restrictive, sacrificing desired-link strength without minimizing the actual array response to interference. Since each active satellite contributes interference to all other scheduled links, the achievable sum rate depends jointly on individual received powers and aggregate beam leakage.

Prior work has explored spatial processing and resource allocation to control satellite interference. Massive multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) transmission combines statistical channel information and space-angle-based user grouping for full-frequency reuse, but considers a single satellite serving all scheduled users [6]. Cooperative downlinks jointly optimize hybrid beamforming and user scheduling, assuming inter-satellite data exchange [7]. Game-theoretic transmit covariance optimization mitigates uplink jamming, assuming cooperative satellite reception [8]. Interference prediction and hybrid receive beamforming improve long-term rates through receiver adaptation rather than satellite subset selection [9]. Coordinated beam hopping balances loads using spatially isolated transmission patterns [10], restricting simultaneous illumination of the same cell. These approaches leave open the achievable intra-cell reuse from satellite selection alone with fixed matched beamformers.

More closely related, ephemeris-based min–max satellite selection (E-MMS) greedily minimizes the largest receive-array correlation with already selected satellites [1]. This criterion measures spatial separability. However, the desired received power (the beamformed signal power from the intended satellite) varies across candidate links with propagation distance, antenna gain, and transmit power. Each link’s rate also depends on the sum of interference from all other selected satellites, which the largest pairwise correlation alone does not capture. Thus, correlation-based selection does not guarantee the maximum sum rate. Computing the globally optimal sum rate under the same model provides a reference for assessing heuristic selection.

We select a prescribed number of satellites at each scheduling interval using a common cell reference point. papers.title: Go-Go-Go: the game of Go without turns
papers.abstract:
The study of variants of classic games has a long history, with chess alone inspiring countless variants that have been proposed, analyzed, and studied. The game of Go, despite rivaling chess in age, cultural relevance, popularity, and strategic depth, has seen drastically fewer variants.
  We introduce Go-Go-Go, a variant of the classic game of Go where there are no turns, and players play stones simultaneously and asynchronously on the board. The variant (which is to be played through a computer) includes a basic mechanism to avoid excessive spamming of moves, by imposing a minimal delay between moves that depends on their relative spatial distance. Apart from the lack of time discretization, most of the ruleset of the original game is either directly maintained or adapted in a natural way that preserves the original spirit. The first playtesting indicates that this results in the preservation of much of the emerging strategies and "flavor" of Go, while replacing the long strategic reasoning with fast paced, instinctive action fueled by quick reflexes. Play testers also report the need to balance immediate but suboptimal reactions with more reasoned but slower plays.
  We offer a publicly available, playable, OpenSource, and online reference implementation of Go-Go-Go at http://gogogo.di.unimi.it

The exploration, analysis, and study of the variants of classic games has a long history. Variants of Chess in particular are the subject of a large literature covering their impact, implications, design aspects, et cetera [1, 2, 3, 4, 5].

The game of Go (also known as Weiqi, Banka, Baduk, Igo) has a prominent place among classic games, rivaled only by Chess. It predates Chess by millennia [6, 7]; it is among the most popular games in East Asia, home to a large share of humanity [8]; despite the extreme simplicity of its rules, it exhibits extraordinary strategic depth, as reflected by the recentness of the ability by computer programs to beat professional players [9], which occurred two full decades after Chess [10]. Despite this prominence, variants of the game of Go are much rarer, almost nonexistent, and overlooked by literature, compared to other classic games such as Chess.

In this work, we introduce, design, and experiment with a variant of Go consisting in the removal of the time discretization (turns) in favor of a time continuum where players are allowed to play asynchronously, without waiting for each other. Playing a move causes a temporary unplayable area around the played location, which shirks over time and delays subsequent moves in its proximity.

papers.title: Linear-length cycles in the supercritical percolated hypercube
papers.abstract: Let $Q_p^d$ be the random subgraph of the $d$-dimensional binary hypercube obtained by retaining each edge independently with probability $p$. A long-standing folklore conjecture states that the emergence of the giant component in $Q_p^d$, at $p\approx 1/d$, is accompanied by the emergence of cycles of linear length. We confirm this conjecture and determine the order of the longest cycle near the phase transition. Specifically, for every sufficiently small constant $\varepsilon>0$, we show that if $p=(1+\varepsilon)/d$, then with high probability the longest cycle of $Q_p^d$ has length $\Theta(\varepsilon^2 2^d)$. The dependence on $\varepsilon$ is optimal up to constant factors.

papers.title: Flow-Optimal Separators for Minor-Free and Induced-Minor-Free Graphs in Linear Time via Follow the Regularized Leader
papers.abstract:
We give a new algorithm for finding balanced separators in minor-free and induced-minor-free graphs. A key technical idea is a new connection to online learning: we formulate a continuous, non-convex optimization problem and solve it using the Follow the Regularized Leader (FTRL) framework. Our implementation of each FTRL step yields a purely combinatorial algorithm that assigns and adjusts vertex weights over multiple rounds. For graphs with $n$ vertices and $m$ edges, we obtain the following results.
  (1) For $H$-induced-minor-free graphs, we find a balanced separator of size $O(\log(|V(H)|)\sqrt{|V(H)|+|E(H)|}\sqrt{m})$ in expected linear time for fixed $H$. As a corollary, we find balanced separators of size $O(\sqrt{m})$ in string graphs in expected linear time, without requiring string representations.
  (2) For $K_h$-minor-free graphs, we find a balanced separator of size $O(h\log h\sqrt{n})$ in expected linear time for fixed $h$. Our algorithm unifies two long lines of work on separators in minor-free graphs, dating back to Alon, Seymour, and Thomas (1990): one optimizing separator size and the other optimizing running time. It also gives a natural interpretation of the vertex weighting scheme in a recent linear-time algorithm by Bonnet, Korhonen, Le, Li, and Masarik (2026).
  The separator bounds for both graph classes are flow-optimal: techniques based on flow-cut duality, including ours, cannot yield balanced separators of asymptotically smaller size.

Though their separator’s size is worse than that of Alon, Seymour and Thomas [AST90], subsequent results [Spa25, Le26] followed this technique, along with recent advances with padded decomposition for KhK_{h}-minor-free graphs by Conroy and Filtser [CF25], to bring the separator size to a nearly-optimal bound of O⁡(h​log⁡h​n)O(h\log h\sqrt{n}). papers.title: System-Theoretic Analysis of Extended Cellular Potts Models for Tumor Invasion
papers.abstract: The Cellular Potts Model has emerged as a standard framework for modeling multicellular systems and metastatic progression. Yet, computational extensions incorporating cell movement within spatial gradients of Extracellular Matrix (ECM), an important element of the tissue microenvironment, lack theoretical foundations. This work provides a system-theoretic formulation and analysis of Extended Cellular Potts Models (ECPMs) that explicitly couple tumor dynamics with ECM degradation. We reformulate the ECPM as an interconnected dynamical system: a stochastic process describing a network of locally interacting tumor cells coupled to a jump-linear system describing ECM evolution. By exploiting the sparse energy structure of the model, we characterize asymptotic ECM behavior, transition probabilities with uniform bounds, and global system convergence. In one-dimensional settings, we derive closed-form expressions for invasion time probabilities, revealing how mean invasion time depends on local ECM gradients, number of cells and their tendency to maintain a target volume. Numerical simulations validate theoretical predictions, establishing a principled foundation for analyzing haptotaxis-driven invasion in Potts-based models.

papers.intro:
Understanding the complex mechanisms governing tumor invasion and progression is a crucial goal in cancer research. Mathematical modeling plays a pivotal role in replicating the underlying principles of tumor dynamics, offering a structured framework to test hypotheses and interpret experimental findings. One class of models, the Cellular Potts Model (CPM), has emerged as a versatile tool to describe multicellular systems, capturing spatially resolved cell behaviors and interactions across multiple scales. A tumor can be viewed as a complex system with local interactions, in which agents (cells) interact locally with their neighbors and with a shared environment, giving rise to emergent collective behaviors such as invasion. Traditionally, CPMs depict tissues as ensembles of cells governed by energy-based rules that account for cell adhesion and volume constraints. This approach allows the emergent behavior of cellular assemblies to be studied as a consequence of local, cell-cell interactions. However, real tumor environments are far more complex, shaped not only by intercellular adhesion but also by interactions between cells and their surrounding extracellular matrix (ECM). These interactions give rise to a key process in tumor invasion where cells move along gradients of ECM concentration or adhesion strength. Classical CPMs account only for the intercellular interaction network, and neglect the feedback between the cells and the evolving environment. Building on the foundational analysis provided in [1], which discusses the theoretical properties of standard CPMs, our work focuses on a specific subclass of Extended Cellular Potts Models (ECPMs) that explicitly incorporates cell-ECM interactions to model haptotaxis [2]. Within this framework, we extend classical CPM theory by leveraging system-theoretic tools to address more realistic tumor invasion models, thus offering new insights into the mechanisms by which cell-ECM coupling influences invasion dynamics.

In the following, we present the literature review divided into three categories: (i) early theoretical studies on CPMs, (ii) applied CPMs in cancer biology and their extensions ECPMs, and (iii) related works in the systems-and-control community.

In the following, we present the literature review divided into three categories: (i) early theoretical studies on CPMs, (ii) applied CPMs in cancer biology and their extensions ECPMs, and (iii) related works in the systems-and-control community.

Early work [3] introduces CPMs to simulate cell sorting via differential adhesion and energy minimization principles. Subsequent mathematical studies analyze critical behavior, phase transitions, and Gibbs measures to establish equilibrium properties in Potts models [4, 5, 6]. Rigorous analytical frameworks further characterize CPM dynamics—including ergodicity, convergence, and parameter sensitivity [1]—and connected discrete stochastic rules to continuum PDE limits [7, 8]. Despite these advances, most theoretical analyses have focused on the statistical mechanics or continuum limits of CPMs without explicitly incorporating ECM dynamics or cell–environment feedback, which are central to haptotaxis-driven invasion.

In biological applications CPMs have successfully modeled morphogenesis [9], cancer invasion driven by intercellular adhesion [10], and drug treatment failure dynamics [11]. Recent extensions, i.e. ECPMs for tumor invasion, explicitly incorporate ECM interactions, modeling tumor invasion [12], angiogenesis driven by matrix gradients [13], dynamic ECM remodeling in wound healing [14], and broader tissue organization [15, 16]. While these works provide powerful computational tools, they largely remain simulation-oriented, with limited theoretical formalization and results on the underlying dynamics. papers.title: Faster Approximate Text-to-Pattern Hamming Distances via Near-Optimal Sumset Estimation
papers.abstract:
\emph{Text-to-Pattern Hamming Distances} is one of the most studied problems in string algorithms: given a text $T$ of length~$n$ and a pattern~$P$, the task is to compute the Hamming distance between~$P$ and every length-$|P|$ substring of~$T$. As exact algorithms have been stuck at time~$\tilde O(n^{3/2})$ for decades, a long line of work has turned to the $(1+\epsilon)$-approximate version of the problem. Milestones include Karloff's $\tilde O(\epsilon^{-2} n)$-time algorithm [IPL '93], followed by randomized improvements to $\tilde O(\epsilon^{-1} n)$ by Kopelowitz and Porat [FOCS '15] and recently to $\tilde O(\epsilon^{-0.915} n)$ by Chan, Jin, Vassilevska W., and Xu [FOCS '23].
  In this work, we significantly improve this bound to $\tilde O(\epsilon^{-2/3} n)$, using a considerably simpler algorithm. Our algorithm follows the framework of Chan, Jin, Vassilevska W., and Xu, which reduces the problem to a variant of 3SUM that we call \emph{Sumset Estimation}. We solve Sumset Estimation optimally (up to logarithmic factors) by replacing their matrix multiplication techniques with ideas from sparse recovery. Specifically, we adapt the classic Count Sketch by replacing its random signs with random complex roots of unity---a simple idea that may find further applications for other additive problems.
  Finally, we give evidence that our running time might in fact be optimal: we show that the $\epsilon^{-2/3}$ dependence is \emph{best possible} for a certain natural class of algorithms, including ours and all previous algorithms.

papers.title: The Complexity of Unpredictability
papers.abstract:
We initiate the study of middle-bit predictors: functions that take as input a string with one missing bit and try to predict that bit. These are closely related to next-bit predictors, a classical object in pseudorandomness.
  We study the deterministic complexity of computing an unpredictable distribution (UNPRED). Given a list of middle-bit predictors in circuit form and a parameter $\epsilon>0$, output a multiset of strings such that each predictor succeeds with probability less than $1/2+\epsilon$ on a uniformly sampled string from the multiset. We write $\mathsf{UNPRED}^{\mathsf{TC}^1}$ for the restriction to $\mathsf{TC}^1$ predictors.
  We show that UNPRED offers a unified route towards resolving several major open problems in catalytic computation, the biggest of which is whether deterministic polynomial time (P and FP) can simulate catalytic logspace (CL and SearchCL). It is believed that $\mathsf{SearchCL}\subseteq\mathsf{FP}$. We prove $$\mathsf{UNPRED}\in\mathsf{FP}\implies\mathsf{SearchCL}\subseteq\mathsf{FP}\implies\mathsf{UNPRED}^{\mathsf{TC}^1}\in\mathsf{FP}.$$ Thus, the questions of whether UNPRED is in FP and whether SearchCL is contained in FP are almost equivalent, up to the restriction to $\mathsf{TC}^1$ circuits.
  We also show that any deterministic polynomial-time algorithm for $\mathsf{UNPRED}^{\mathsf{TC}^1}$ must exploit properties of $\mathsf{TC}^1$ circuits, either in the algorithm itself or in its analysis. To our knowledge, this would also be the first algorithm to use the structure of $\mathsf{TC}^1$ circuits in this way to solve a natural problem, thus advancing our understanding of Boolean circuits.
  Together, our results provide strong evidence that middle-bit predictors could be the key to unlocking several major open problems in catalytic computation, pseudorandomness, and Boolean circuit complexity.

papers.title: Grounding in the Dark: Text-Only Training for Zero-Shot Video Temporal Localization
papers.abstract: Video-LLMs are typically trained on paired video-text data for temporal tasks, yet collecting precise temporal annotations and training on large-scale video datasets are both costly. We investigate whether a text-only LLM, with no vision-language pretraining, can be trained on textual video descriptions alone to perform temporal grounding and receive video only at inference time. This setting removes paired video data from training altogether and is a step toward training multimodal models without paired annotations. We generate a 134K-example corpus of textual sequences with up to 100 time steps, adapt Qwen3-8B with LoRA on CLIP or LLM2CLIP text embeddings, and evaluate on Charades-STA and QV-Highlights without training on videos from either benchmark. LLM2CLIP, whose text encoder supports longer inputs, represents detailed descriptions better than CLIP (61.54 versus 53.86 mtIoU on Temporal-TextVid) and transfers them better to video. Still, replacing text with frame embeddings at inference yields only 4.99 mtIoU on Charades-STA and 11.12 on QV-Highlights, revealing a large modality gap. To bridge it, we propose Nearest Entity Replacement (NER), a training-free mapping that represents each video frame by the normalized mean of its nearest text-entity embeddings, so that the model receives the kind of input it was trained on. NER reaches 14.45 mtIoU on Charades-STA and 20.72 on QV-Highlights, outperforming the strongest of four families of modality-gap baselines by 5.00 and 1.71 points. NER thus enables partial transfer from text to video, while more reliable grounding will likely require encoders with better-aligned text and visual representations.

Video large language models (Video-LLMs) can describe videos, answer questions about them, and localize events in time [21, 35, 9, 40]. Recent trained temporal-grounding variants encode time with dedicated tokens [39], numbered frames [41], sequential transfer from images and short clips [2], or reinforcement-learning objectives [1]. Although their architectures differ, these systems learn from paired video and language (Fig. 1). Marking event boundaries requires close inspection by annotators, while storing and repeatedly decoding long videos adds training cost.

This setup tests whether a temporal model trained on text embeddings can use visual embeddings without retraining.

Our experiments use 134K synthetically generated training examples and evaluate zero-shot performance on Charades-STA [5] and QV-Highlights [19], without using any videos from either benchmark to train the temporal-localization model. We first examine whether the base LLMs can localize events from textual sequences and find that they are capable of doing so (Table 2). The next challenge is transferring this ability to video, where textual descriptions are replaced by visual embeddings. We find that the choice of encoder plays an important role in this transfer. While CLIP struggles with detailed descriptions, LLM2CLIP represents them more effectively, achieving 61.54 mtIoU compared to 53.86 on Temporal-TextVid, and also transfers better to video (Table 2). Based on these results, we adopt LLM2CLIP with detailed descriptions as our main configuration. However, the gap between text and visual representations remains substantial. When evaluated directly on video, the text-trained model achieves only 4.99 mtIoU on Charades-STA and 11.12 mtIoU on QV-Highlights. This motivates us to explore methods for bridging the modality gap. Across the matched encoder and caption configurations, NER improves mtIoU over raw visual features and caption-memory projection on both video benchmarks.

papers.title: SO3LR Tauri: Generally Applicable Force Fields for Reactive (Bio)Molecular Simulations Covering the Periodic Table
papers.abstract: Machine-learned force fields (MLFFs) aim to create a unified model that describes all major classes of (bio)molecules at quantum-mechanical accuracy. We present SO3LR Tauri, a family of MLFFs developed toward this goal, coupling a fast SO3krates network to explicit, physics-based interaction modules: pair-specific short-range repulsion, environment-dependent dispersion, and electrostatics, each improved beyond its original formulation. The models are trained on 148 million structures spanning 85 elements, drawn from several quantum-chemical datasets. Against coupled-cluster references, the models accurately reproduce nucleobase-pair and charged protein-ligand interactions, carbohydrate conformer ordering, and molecular dipoles. They also resolve the transition pathways of organic and enzymatic reactions. Dynamical simulations recover experimental densities of water and organic solvents, the hydration structure of mono- and divalent ions, the pKa values of amino-acid side chains, and the structure and dynamics of proteins, membranes, nucleic acids, glycoproteins, and metal-containing biomolecules, all without system-specific fitting. Released in three sizes, the models reach 0.7-3.2 $\mu$s/atom and scale to 27-84 million atoms on a single GPU. Much work remains to be done: achieving predictive accuracy for static and dynamic liquid properties, reaction barriers, coverage of chemical and conformational space, and the sampling and inference speed needed to describe biomolecular processes.

papers.intro:
Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations have become a central tool for studying biomolecular structure and function [54], and their reliability rests on the accuracy of the underlying force field. For decades this role has been filled by classical, empirical force fields, whose careful parametrization has made them both efficient and remarkably successful across a vast range of biological problems [119, 59, 66]. Given their simple functional forms, accuracy is achieved by fitting separate parameter sets for each class of biomolecules, with dedicated models for water, ions and metal centers [65, 67, 86]. These force fields are well established for proteins and lipids, while nucleic acids and carbohydrates remain more challenging [31, 115]. Simulating several classes of biomolecules together therefore requires combining independently developed parameters [136], which were not designed for use together.

Machine-learned force fields (MLFFs) hold a different prospect [123, 125, 76, 6]. With far greater descriptive power, a single model could in principle represent all of these classes consistently and with close to quantum-mechanical accuracy. Biomolecular applications further require that such a model scale to large assemblies and include the long-range electrostatic and dispersion interactions that shape their structure and dynamics [57, 130]. Its first version, trained on 4M PBE0+MBD structures over eight elements and scaling to 200k atoms on a single GPU, demonstrated the promise of this approach for biomolecular simulation [70].

papers.title: Combinatorial Boolean Matrix Multiplication in $n^3 / 2^{\Omega(\sqrt{\log n})}$ Time
papers.abstract:
For over fifty years, combinatorial algorithms for Boolean matrix multiplication (BMM) and triangle detection saved only polylogarithmic factors over cubic time. At STOC 2024, Abboud, Fischer, Kelley, Lovett, and Meka broke this barrier with a deterministic $O(n^3 / 2^{\Omega((\log n)^{1/7})})$-time algorithm, and asked whether $n^3 / 2^{\Omega(\sqrt{\log n})}$ time is achievable. We answer this question in the affirmative, giving deterministic combinatorial algorithms for both BMM and triangle detection running in $O(n^3 / 2^{\Omega(\sqrt{\log n})})$ time.
  Following Abboud et al., we decompose $(A,B)$ into pairs of submatrices $(A_k,B_k)$, called \emph{pieces}, each of which is either sparse or pseudorandom in a sense that forces $A_k\star B_k$ to be nearly all-ones on its vertex sets. Whereas their decomposition produces $2^{O(d^7)}$ pieces at regularity parameter $d$, we obtain $2^{O(d^2)}$ pieces, directly improving the runtime exponent from $(\log n)^{1/7}$ to $\sqrt{\log n}$. Prior work found pseudorandom pieces by repeatedly restricting to denser submatrices, paying worst-case vertex losses at each step that compounded across nested recursion levels, together with an expensive derandomization step. We eliminate the extra powers of $d$ by matching the vertex loss at each step to the size of its density jump so losses telescope across scales, derandomizing witness search via $L_d$-norm estimation so the sampler length stays $2^{O(d)}$, and bounding overlap across the recursion with a fractional density-weighted volume budget rather than raw submatrix volume.

papers.title: Forget What Comes Next: LLM Unlearning via Statistical Independence
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can memorize and reproduce fragments of their training data, raising privacy and legal concerns that motivate machine unlearning. Yet poisoned training examples can remain statistically detectable after unlearning, which raises the question of whether current unlearning objectives remove what the model has memorized at all. In this work, we introduce PINT, a novel algorithm for machine unlearning that uses the Hilbert-Schmidt Independence Criterion (HSIC) to reduce the statistical dependence between tokens to be forgotten and the internal representations used to predict them. We formally relate our HSIC-based objective to Exact Memorization through a computable upper bound, connecting the training objective directly to the model's ability to reproduce the forgotten tokens. In extensive experiments, we compare forgetting-utility trade-offs across eight settings with models up to 7B parameters and demonstrate scalability to 70B parameter models. Our evaluations cover unlearning Gaussian poisons, personal information, hazardous knowledge in biology and cybersecurity, and copyrighted books and news articles. PINT achieves the strongest forgetting-utility trade-off on average and is the only method to make Gaussian poisons undetectable while maintaining near-original model utility. Code is available at: https://github.com/shkabrii/PINT

papers.intro:
The tendency of large language models (LLMs) to memorize and reproduce fragments of their training data, including personally identifiable information and copyrighted text (Carlini et al., 2021; Carlini et al., 2022), poses significant privacy and legal concerns. With the right to be forgotten now formalized in major data protection frameworks across the EU, the US, and China (European Parliament and Council of the European Union, 2016; California State Legislature, 2018; Standing Committee of the National People’s Congress, 2021), there is a growing need for methods that can remove the influence of specific training examples without the prohibitive cost of retraining from scratch. A growing body of work on approximate machine unlearning has made empirical progress in this direction (Jang et al., 2023; Maini et al., 2024; Li et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2024). Nevertheless, significant gaps remain: Pawelczyk et al. (2025) show that current methods may fail to unlearn poisoned examples injected during training, leaving them statistically detectable even after an unlearning attempt.

papers.title: Decision Models as Scalable Economic Surrogates that Capture Human Variation
papers.abstract: Decision Models (DMs), a new class of AI models, give fast responses and return a probability distribution over a fixed set of options. These properties make them candidate human surrogates in economic simulations and surveys, a role increasingly filled by Large Language Models (LLMs), which are costly at scale and under-represent the variation in human behaviour. We present a first evaluation of DMs as human surrogates in economics, comparing 10 DMs with 8 LLMs in three economic settings: a household spending survey on consumption, several classic economic games and a labour-market field experiment. Frontier DMs, those that score highest on general decision-making benchmarks, reproduce the variation in human responses more closely than LLMs in all three settings. They capture the modal human response as well as LLMs in the spending survey, but less well in the economic games. Frontier DMs are also roughly ten times faster than the fastest LLM and can be over a hundred times cheaper. Together, these results suggest that DMs capture the heterogeneity of human behaviour better than LLMs and make large-scale economic simulations more feasible.

papers.intro:
AI agents are increasingly used as human surrogates in surveys or agent-based simulations, with recent applications spanning political preferences (Argyle et al., 2023), consumer choices (Maier et al., 2025) and strategic economic games (Horton et al., 2023; Mei et al., 2024). AI agents address the core challenge in socio-economic modelling of balancing agent adaptability with behavioural realism. Traditional agent-based simulations rely on fixed, hand-written behavioural rules (Farmer and Foley, 2009). Because people adapt when policy changes, these rules may not generalise to new policies, a problem known as the Lucas critique (Lucas Jr, 1976). To address this critique, economic models have used perfectly optimising rational expectations agents, an assumption that does not align with real human behaviour (Conlisk, 1996; Kahneman and Tversky, 2013; Thaler, 2016). While surrogates such as LLM-agents are imperfect approximations of humans (Gao et al., 2025), they can capture many human behavioural biases while adapting dynamically to policy changes (Horton et al., 2023). They therefore provide a much-needed alternative to the unrealistic behavioural assumptions of the status quo, enabling simulations that can generate more reliable answers to policy questions.

While surrogates such as LLM-agents are imperfect approximations of humans (Gao et al., 2025), they can capture many human behavioural biases while adapting dynamically to policy changes (Horton et al., 2023). They therefore provide a much-needed alternative to the unrealistic behavioural assumptions of the status quo, enabling simulations that can generate more reliable answers to policy questions.

However, using LLMs as human surrogates faces two major limitations. First, while LLMs often successfully replicate the modal human response, they fail to capture the full distribution of behaviour, leading to significantly less heterogeneity than is found in human populations (Bisbee et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2026). This compromises economic modelling for policy, as human heterogeneity is a driver of both macroeconomic outcomes (Kirman, 1992) and collective social dynamics (Granovetter, 1978; Wu et al., 2026). Although persona prompting and demographic conditioning can recover some of this lost variation (Vezhnevets et al., 2023), they require extensive sampling, which leads to the second challenge: operational latency and computational cost. Generating autoregressive text for multiple, sequential decisions across large-scale populations is slow and computationally expensive, forcing researchers to trade off the size of their simulated economies against agent diversity.

Decision Models (DMs), a rapidly growing class of AI models (Duan et al., 2026; Ling et al., 2026; Almeida, 2026), are in a good position to address these challenges. They are fine-tuned to take as input natural language questions and scenarios and make decisions between provided options. Crucially, rather than generating free-form text, DMs are designed to directly assign probabilities to the available choices. They are also faster and cheaper than LLMs, potentially allowing simulations with orders of magnitude more agents. This makes them a promising candidate for representing human behaviour as they are adaptable, provide structured choice probabilities, are fast and can be sampled cheaply to generate variation in simulated decisions.

In this paper, we test whether DMs are a viable additional tool for representing humans in economic modelling. We choose our experiments so that we explore a range of economic settings (consumption, games and labour) and question types (binary choices vs multiple choices and qualitative vs quantitative). The human data we compare to varies from surveys to economic experiments and realistic field experiments. We consider survey answers on changes in consumption in response to a future earnings shock (Federal Reserve Bank of New York, 2026), a variety of classic economic games (Mei et al., 2024) and a field experiment on labour preferences (Mas and Pallais, 2017). By replicating these experiments and surveys with DMs and LLMs, we assess how well DMs are able to act as human surrogates for economic research compared to LLMs.

We choose our experiments so that we explore a range of economic settings (consumption, games and labour) and question types (binary choices vs multiple choices and qualitative vs quantitative). By replicating these experiments and surveys with DMs and LLMs, we assess how well DMs are able to act as human surrogates for economic research compared to LLMs.

Our results show that “frontier” DMs, those that lead on standard decision-making benchmarks, capture the variation in human behaviour better than LLMs, and do so faster and more cheaply. In all three settings, frontier DMs are closer to the human distribution than LLMs on our distributional measures. In the consumption survey, they also capture the modal human response as well as LLMs, although on the economic games, LLMs represent the modal human response better. In the labour experiment, frontier DMs reproduce the gradual shift in human choices as a wage gap changes, whereas LLMs switch abruptly from one job to the other. Taken together, we find that frontier DMs can be an effective and scalable tool for modelling human behaviour, especially where capturing the variation in responses matters.

Our work fits into a broader agenda of integrating AI models into economic research. Reinforcement Learning has been used in macroeconomics (Gabriele et al., 2025) and firm competition environments (Calvano et al., 2020). A growing body of work has also studied LLMs, both to understand their behaviour and to assess whether they are viable human surrogates, with encouraging results across a range of single-shot and multi-turn games (Horton et al., 2023; Mei et al., 2024; Manning and Horton, 2026). LLMs have also been used within agent-based models (ABMs), in diverse settings such as macroeconomics (Li et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2025; Feng et al., 2025), status signalling (Cross et al., 2026) and trading markets (Henning et al., 2025; del Rio-Chanona et al., 2025; Saxena et al., 2026), with platforms such as Concordia allowing such simulations to be built quickly and flexibly (Vezhnevets et al., 2023).

However, the use of LLMs as human surrogates remains contested: LLMs tend to capture only a narrow, modal part of the human distribution (Bisbee et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2026), and the outcomes of LLM-based ABMs can be sensitive to prompting (Ye et al., 2026a). Several works have therefore aimed to make LLMs better represent human distributions. For example, conditioning LLMs on personas or backstories can widen the part of the human distribution they capture (Argyle et al., 2023; Park et al., 2024), although this approach can be brittle to the exact wording of the prompt (Lutz et al., 2025).

papers.title: Ni ordering in the van der Waals gap of Ni-intercalated 2H-NbS$_2$: from disorder through $2\times2$ and $\sqrt{3}\times\sqrt{3}$ order to stripe order
papers.abstract: We report a synchrotron x-ray diffraction study of Ni-intercalated 2H-NbS$_2$ over the range $0.18 \le x \le 0.57$, with Ni contents measured by energy-dispersive x-ray spectroscopy. Powder diffraction on the whole series shows that the NbS$_2$ host is preserved, while the Ni ions in the van der Waals gap evolve from a disordered arrangement to $2\times2$ order at $x=1/4$ and $\sqrt{3}\times\sqrt{3}$ order at $x=1/3$, through a range where both motifs coexist, to an orthorhombic stripe-type order at $x=0.57$. The in-plane lattice parameter increases with Ni content, whereas the interlayer spacing remains nearly constant except for a pronounced minimum at $x=1/4$, which density-functional calculations reproduce for the ordered structure. Single-crystal diffraction on the two commensurate phases shows that the $x=1/4$ structure, with Ni on a single site and a trimerized Nb lattice, is free of stacking faults, whereas the chiral $x=1/3$ structure contains Ni on the nominally empty site, inversion twins and stacking faults of the Ni layers. The comparison between powders and crystals shows that grinding mainly degrades the stacking of the Ni layers. These results establish the structural phase diagram of Ni$_x$NbS$_2$ and the intercalant disorder to be taken into account in the interpretation of its magnetic properties.

papers.intro:
Transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs) of general formula T​X2TX_{2}, where TT is a transition metal and XX a chalcogen, form one of the most versatile families of layered van der Waals materials. Within each layer, TT and XX are strongly covalently bonded, while adjacent T​X2TX_{2} layers are held together only by weak van der Waals forces [13]. This anisotropy makes TMDs easy to exfoliate down to the monolayer, but it also opens a second, less exploited route to tailoring their properties: the intercalation of foreign atoms into the van der Waals gap. Because the layers are only weakly coupled, intercalation can proceed over a wide and continuously tunable range of concentrations without destroying the T​X2TX_{2} sublattice, in contrast to substitution within the layers themselves [10, 39].

Composition series have been reported for CoxNbS2 [21] and, more recently, for FexNbSe2 [43], but in the former the Co content was estimated from the nominal synthesis ratio rather than measured. We first use high-resolution synchrotron powder diffraction on the whole series (Sec. III) to identify the compositions at which 2×22\times 2 and 3×3\sqrt{3}\times\sqrt{3} Ni superstructures appear, coexist, or give way to disorder and to a stripe phase, to follow the lattice parameters, compared with density-functional calculations of the ordered structures, and to estimate the correlation lengths of the Ni order. papers.title: Follow or Surpass? Collaboration, Sound, and the Recognition of Influence in Lineages of Jazz Trumpet Players
papers.abstract: Cultural fields cohere not only horizontally, through collaboration, but also vertically, through lineages of artistic influence. Considerable attention has been devoted to collaboration networks in various fields of creative production; however, we know less about the structure of artistic influence that is nevertheless key to individual artistic development and the evolution of genres. We examine the structure of such an influence network in a genealogy of 52 prominent jazz trumpet players, combining musicians' discographies, demographic characteristics, geographical locations, and audio analysis of more than 16,000 recordings with exponential random graph models. Direct collaboration, overlap in collaborators, and sonic context similarity, that is, the similarity of the recordings on which players appear, are each associated with an ascribed influence tie, net of the others. Not surprisingly, ascribed ties connect musicians whose recordings share a similar sonic context, but musicians also tend to collaborate with their influences and share collaborators with them. However, players whose recordings share a sonic context and who move in the same circle of collaborators can be thought of as peers or rivals, rather than as influences of each other, because lineage implies a succession predicated on difference as much as on continuity. Taken together, our findings suggest that a field's account of its own evolution is neither a record of who played together nor a map of shared sonic contexts, but a selective ordering that requires both. While our data do not permit a causal account, our aim is to provide a rich and varied methodological strategy and descriptive as well as inferential tools to understand the yet understudied vertical integration of cultural fields through influence ties.

papers.intro:
Creativity today is increasingly understood as a collective phenomenon, with collaborative communities emerging in a wide range of fields (Becker, 2008; Bourdieu, 1983; Crane, 1992; Crossley, 2019; Lutter, 2014). We witness the increasing dominance of teams in science (Wuchty et al., 2007), applied and fine arts (White and White, 1993), music (Lena, 2012), and filmmaking (Cattani and Ferriani, 2008). In all of these fields, creators build on each other’s ideas as they strive to craft successful products, weave creative careers, and leave a mark. Consequently, a long line of research has examined how collaboration networks affect the creativity and success of individuals or teams (Vedres and Stark, 2026; Burt, 2004; De Vaan et al., 2015; Lutter, 2015), and how artists influence each other (Lena and Pachucki, 2013; Burgdorf et al., 2024; Basov et al., 2017). Several researchers have studied collaboration in the context of jazz music as well, focusing on network positions that elevate jazz musicians’ success (Vedres and Cserpes, 2021; Vedres, 2017), and how the structure of collaboration relates to genres and styles (Kirschbaum, 2015; Phillips, 2011; Phillips, 2013).

Several researchers have studied collaboration in the context of jazz music as well, focusing on network positions that elevate jazz musicians’ success (Vedres and Cserpes, 2021; Vedres, 2017), and how the structure of collaboration relates to genres and styles (Kirschbaum, 2015; Phillips, 2011; Phillips, 2013).

Cultural fields do not cohere only horizontally through collaboration networks. They also organize their histories vertically through lineages: selective accounts of who carried whose work forward. Practitioners, critics, and educators produce such accounts when they locate artists within a succession and distinguish historically consequential relations from the many sources on which creators draw (Bourdieu, 1983; Becker, 2008; Anheier et al., 1995). A lineage, in this sense, is a classification (DiMaggio, 1987; Bowker and Star, 2000): a retrospective and selective representation of descent that a field produces about itself. This article asks what such a classification records. Musicians are connected to one another in many ways: they play together, they draw on the same circles of collaborators, and they record in similar sonic contexts. Which of these proximities does an expert account of descent treat as lineage, and by what logic does it select among them?

To address this question, we take an expert-curated genealogy of jazz trumpet players, with ties we call expert-ascribed influence relations, as a starting point for our investigation. We consider two forms of proximity that can each inform ascribed influence: social proximity, captured by direct collaboration and by overlap in collaborators, and proximity in sonic context, captured by audio embeddings of the recordings on which musicians appear. We speak of sonic context rather than of a player’s sound because the embeddings are computed from complete recordings rather than from isolated trumpet parts: they describe the ensemble, arrangement, and recording within which a player’s work was heard, of which the player’s own playing is one component. We enrich the genealogy with musicians’ discographies, demographic characteristics, geographical locations, and sonic information on over 16,000 recordings, and analyze this combination of data sources using exponential random graph models (Lusher et al., 2013), which allow us to assess the conditional association of each form of proximity with expert recognition while accounting for the structure of the influence network itself.

Most existing accounts of cultural influence measure it by tracing how artists refer to one another’s work — musicians who sample their peers’ records (Lena and Pachucki, 2013), filmmakers who reference each other’s movies (Burgdorf et al., 2024). Such designs infer the outcome from the same class of data as their predictors. Our article instead starts with a judgment by a jazz expert explicitly concerned with influence and takes the relational structure the expert identified as its dependent variable. The genealogy we model was drawn by the jazz trumpeter and educator John McNeil and re-published in Paul F. Berliner’s Thinking in Jazz (Berliner, 2009), where Berliner records that the figure is “based on sketch provided by John McNeil, Sept. 1993” (p. 763) and refers readers to McNeil’s own discussion of the depicted relationships for their substance (McNeil, 1993, 26–27). Our ambition is to explore the correlates of influence ties systematically and measure the extent to which sonic context similarity and collaborative network alignment inform expert-recognized influence. We do not pretend to causally explain influence, but to shed light on the logic experts use to order a field’s tradition into predecessors and successors.

We combine archival data covering most jazz recordings made in the 20th and 21st centuries (Vedres, 2017; Kirschbaum, 2015; Phillips, 2013) with machine-learning techniques for quantifying the content of recorded music (Diwakar and Gupta, 2024). After digitizing and manually enriching McNeil’s genealogy with musicians’ demographic characteristics, we retrieve their discographies from the Jazz Discography Online (Lord, 2020), yielding more than 5,000 unique recorded sessions and about 18,000 collaborators of the focal musicians. From these sessions, we construct two distinct social measures. The first is direct collaboration: whether two genealogy players themselves appeared in a recording session together, a condition of co-presence and direct exposure. The second is overlap in collaborators: the share of one player’s collaborators that is shared with another, a measure of common position in the wider community rather than of contact. We then obtain audio for more than 16,000 tracks and compute artist-level sonic context profiles from the full recordings using the pre-trained VGGish embedding, widely used in genre classification and recommendation (Hershey et al., 2017a), from which we derive pairwise sonic context similarity. Finally, we bring all three measures together in exponential random graph models (Lusher et al., 2013).

papers.title: The Cone Fixing the Reals of $\mathrm{HOD}^{M_{2n}(x)}
papers.abstract: For a cone of reals $x$, the reals of $\mathrm{HOD}^{L[x]}$ are precisely the reals in $Q_3$, or equivalently, the set of reals in $M_1$, the minimal proper class mouse with a Woodin cardinal. We show that if $z$ is any real coding $M_1|\delta^{+M_1}$, then $z$ is the base of such a cone (so $M_1^{\#}$ is such a base). We also establish a kind of optimality for this result, by identifying a real $x$ such that $M_1\subseteq L[x]$ but $\mathbb{R}\cap\mathrm{HOD}^{L[x]}\not\subseteq M_1$, although there is a base for the cone in a generic extension of $L[x]$. We prove analogous results for $M_{2n}(x)$ for all $n$, with the optimality result holding for all $n$.

papers.title: Uniqueness of the hexagonal lattice's universal optimality
papers.abstract: We build on a recent proof of the universal optimality of the planar hexagonal lattice. We extend this result to demonstrate that, up to Euclidean motion, the hexagonal lattice is the only periodic configuration with this property.
