papers.title: A Framework for Context Enrichment and Selective Robustness in LLM Social Agents
papers.abstract: Researchers use large language models as agents in social simulations, where agents are prompted with observations and background information intended to shape their actions. Yet LLM agents have been shown to substantially change their behavior under meaning-preserving prompt variations, creating a validation problem for social simulation. One plausible hypothesis is that this brittleness reflects a lack of grounding and can be reduced by enriching the context provided to the agents. Whether richer context improves robustness remains unclear, in part because context richness and robustness are rarely defined in ways that support controlled comparisons. We address the first need with controlled context enrichment, a set of prompt substitution rules that systematically enriches distinct types of context: neutral padding, generic social background, descriptive decision grounding, and normative decision grounding. We address the second by introducing selective robustness as a validation criterion: insensitivity to meaning-preserving prompt variation combined with a directional response to decision-relevant changes in the social world. We demonstrate the framework in a Prisoner's Dilemma-like game, showing how it can be used to identify which forms of context enrichment produce more desirable and robust agent behavior. We find that these forms of enrichment produce distinct behavioral patterns that vary between the two models tested.

papers.title: DefectSkills: Guiding AI agents through first-principles calculations for point defects in semiconductors and insulators
papers.abstract: First-principles defect calculations can now be performed autonomously by AI agents, enabled by established computational methods and open-source Python toolkits. However, reliable and repeatable defect calculations require clear scientific and technical guidance that helps agents resolve ambiguities and avoid errors in calculation setup, execution, postprocessing, and analysis. Here, we present DefectSkills, a set of structured prompts that provides human-in-the-loop guidance to AI agents performing first-principles calculations of point defects in semiconductors and insulators using the Vienna Ab initio Simulation Package (VASP). The prompts encode human expertise and guide agents through unit-cell relaxation, electronic-structure and dielectric calculations, phase-stability and chemical-potential analysis, charged-defect supercell generation and calculations, finite-size corrections, formation-energy calculations and thermodynamic analysis, and data backup. By packaging this expertise as reusable agent skills, DefectSkills supports consistent workflow execution across agentic AI systems and reproducible defect calculations.

papers.title: Emission-associated energy deposition and Cherenkov-dose proportionality in megavoltage photon beams
papers.abstract: Background: Quantitative Cherenkov-to-dose conversion depends on beam spectrum, field size, depth, and material properties. Purpose: To distinguish dose contributions with and without accompanying Cherenkov production and assess their implications for calibration. Methods: Geant4 simulations paired dose and local Cherenkov distributions in water for flattened 6, 10, and 15 MV and flattening-filter-free (FFF) 6 and 10 MV beams with $3 \times 3$ and $10 \times 10$ cm$^2$ fields. Energy deposition was tagged by whether its transport step produced at least one Cherenkov photon. Component fractions were calculated over the phantom. Distributions were independently normalized within a shared reference region and compared using voxelwise ratios, lateral profiles, and spatial partitioning. Results: Emission-tagged fractions were 37%-61%, increasing with beam energy and lower for FFF beams. Fractions differed by less than 1.3 percentage points between field sizes. Emission-tagged ratios clustered near unity, with 98.4%-99.9% between 0.95 and 1.05 across the evaluated regions, whereas total and non-emission-tagged ratios varied with depth and lateral position. Emission-tagged profiles generally showed smaller residual differences. Conclusions: Emission-tagged deposition closely tracked local Cherenkov production. Departures of the total Cherenkov-to-dose ratio followed spatial variations in the emission-tagged dose fraction, indicating where calibration needs correction. The classification reflects actual photon production and depends on transport settings; dedicated electron-energy scoring is needed to isolate sub-threshold contributions.

papers.title: VA-TDM: A Unified View for Improving Few-Step Diffusion Models by Velocity Adversarial Distillation
papers.abstract: Few-step distillation offers efficient generation with diffusion and flow models, but preserving quality with only a few sampling steps remains challenging. Distribution-matching methods via score distillation provide a strong foundation, yet they rely on accurately tracking the student's changing distribution. At intermediate generation steps in few-step sampling, student-score estimation can be difficult, and commonly used estimators may describe a different distribution from the one used to update the student. Flow matching allows a more flexible approach to supervision through velocity fields constructed from the student's sampling process. Building on this perspective, we introduce Velocity Adversarial Distillation (VAD), which uses a learned critic to compare student and teacher fields and turn their disagreement into feedback for learning. VAD unifies score distillation, Fisher-based matching, and moment matching, also explaining existing heuristic MMD updates and delivering new training objectives. We further develop VA-TDM, which follows trajectory distribution matching: providing supervision for partial denoising along the student trajectory. Beyond this, VA-TDM combines transition-aware online velocity learning and dual-form VAD supervision across intermediate student transitions. Extensive results show that VA-TDM is powerful for learning few-step generators, achieving state-of-the-art four-step performance in both text-to-image and text-to-video generation across various backbones and scaling effectively to 33B MiniMax-H3. In particular, our VA-TDM-H3 notably outperforms the few-step Fast-H3 and is closer to the original many-step H3 according to human preference.

authors.name: Yihong Luo
authors.institution: Chinese Academy of Medical Sciences & Peking Union Medical College

papers.title: From Handcrafted to Generative: RLVR-Optimized Icon Generation for Alexa+
papers.abstract: Alexa+ devices with screens display animated icons during conversations to visually reinforce what is being said. The original set of these icons was hand-drawn by designers one at a time, a process that produces polished results but is time-consuming and cannot scale to the range of topics encountered in open-ended conversation. We describe an automated pipeline, deployed in production, that generates these vectorised animated icons from a text description alone and surfaces relevant animations to customers based on their ongoing conversation. The pipeline decomposes icon creation into a sequence of stages (image generation, semantic decomposition, vectorisation, styling, and animation). Its quality is determined at the very first of these, image generation, on which every downstream stage depends. We therefore focus on improving this first and most critical stage. Because the icons are rendered on small display canvases under strict design guidelines, generations are often unsuitable for production. Supervised fine-tuning is not viable, as no dataset of line-art icons exists under these constraints. Instead, we design objective verifiers that automatically flag generations violating the design guidelines, and use them to fine-tune a flow matching image generation model via reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards (RLVR). The fine-tuned model raises the pass rate from 15.7% to 58.7% (3.7x) under a VLM judge that is independent of the reward model. Both the trained model and the verifier are deployed in the production pipeline, where the verifier also serves as the automated quality gate before final design review.

papers.title: PCF All The Way Down
papers.abstract:
We prove that a finite surjective post-critically finite self-map of a variety in characteristic zero remains post-critically finite on every preperiodic integral effective divisor after passing to its periodic image with its return map. Iterating this result proves PCF all the way down.
  A detailed report on AI usage is contained in the manuscript.

papers.title: GraphSeal: Graph-Augmented Speech Deepfake Detection via Temporal-Spectral Artifact Propagation
papers.abstract: Current speech deepfake detectors treat each utterance as a flat sequence of frames, limiting their ability to capture long-range spectral inconsistencies that span non-adjacent regions of an audio signal. We propose \textbf{GraphSeal}, which constructs a temporal-spectral graph over short speech segments and propagates artifact cues through graph attention layers before a global readout produces the bonafide-vs-spoof decision. Each node in the graph corresponds to a fixed-length segment; edges encode temporal adjacency and spectral similarity, letting the network attend to distant frames that share suspicious spectral patterns. A multi-head graph attention mechanism weights neighboring nodes according to both learned features and edge attributes, and a hierarchical readout aggregates node representations into a single utterance-level embedding for binary classification. GraphSeal is front-end agnostic: it operates on top of any self-supervised or handcrafted feature extractor. On ASVspoof 2019~LA, ASVspoof 2021~LA, ASVspoof~5, and the In-the-Wild dataset, GraphSeal achieves equal error rates of 0.52\%, 2.41\%, 8.17\%, and 5.24\%, respectively, matching or outperforming prior methods that rely on fixed-topology graph networks or purely sequential architectures.

authors.name: Lee Seung-woo
authors.institution: Wyss Institute for Biologically Inspired Engineering

papers.title: What Does 4-Bit Microscaling Cost a Wearable Activity Recognizer?
papers.abstract:
Wearable sports sensors can recognize actions on the device itself, where lower-precision numbers reduce model storage and memory traffic. Two 4-bit block-scaled formats, MXFP4 from the Open Compute Project, introduced in 2023, and NVFP4 from NVIDIA, introduced in 2025, are drawing interest. Published evaluations cover general deep-learning benchmarks and large language models; to our knowledge, nobody has yet measured what they cost a small wearable-sensor model.
  We train a 159,492-parameter 1D CNN to recognize four basketball actions from wrist-accelerometer data in Hang-Time HAR and test it on players it has never seen, using five-fold cross-validation grouped by player. Every comparison between number formats is made fold by fold.
  In full precision the model reaches 69.26\% macro-F1. Measured TFLite FP16 and INT8 models lose at most 0.16 percentage points. In simulation, 4-bit weights cost 1.45 points with MXFP4 and 0.72 points with NVFP4. When activations are quantized to 4 bits as well, MXFP4 loses 5.14 points and NVFP4 only 0.75, and NVFP4 comes out ahead in all five held-out-player folds.
  The ranking survives two alternative simulator settings, with NVFP4 leading by 3.49 to 4.40 points. A $2 \times 3$ ablation with 4-bit weights and activations (two block sizes and three scale rules) points to scale selection as the main source of MXFP4's loss. The reference MXFP4 conversion we simulate rounds the scale down, which can pick scales that are too small, so many blocks clip their largest values. Rounding the scale up recovers 3.18 points with 32-value blocks and 3.63 points with 16-value blocks, and switching to an 8-bit floating-point scale, as NVFP4 does, adds another 0.84 and 1.20 points. Block size matters less. Under this round-down rule, 16-value blocks score 0.44 points below 32-value blocks in all five folds; under the other two rules there is no consistent effect.

papers.title: Found by Search, Broken by a Shortcut: Transfer and Tampering of Searched Intrinsic Rewards
papers.abstract: Can a search over innate drives find intrinsic rewards that help a reinforcement-learning agent learn, transfer to a task it never saw, and resist an exploit that was absent during the search? Each candidate reward combines four generic events (a new view, a pickup, a drop and a toggle), each with a weight, a relief and a refill rate. We ran three pre-registered stages; the search protocol was locked in a public, timestamped commit before any search result existed. CMA-ES and an equal-budget random search used 1,560 PPO training runs, and the final evaluation and tamper test used 340. On the held-out task, KeyCorridorS3R2, the CMA-ES-selected reward (E) beat task-only PPO, episodic novelty and the random-search-selected reward (R) in all 3 registered comparisons, all of them meaningful by the registered size rule. Among these generic rewards E transferred best; the earlier paper's satiation reward, which on this task is given hand-wired key and locked-door events, did better (20 of 20 seeds solved against 4 of 20; descriptive). On UnlockPickup, where that reward uses generic events, E's mean area exceeded it by 0.276 (descriptive). On the training tasks there was no registered difference between E and R: both E-over-R tests missed. A free reset action, absent during the search, collapsed E's learning on DoorKey-8x8 (mean area 0.829 without it, 0.136 with it; registered) to below task-only PPO (descriptive). The searched drives helped on every task tested, but a reward given task-specific events did better on the held-out task, and selection gave E no protection against an exploit absent from the search.

papers.title: Translate, then decide: asymptotic optimality of latent-space control in bistable systems
papers.abstract: This paper asks whether an optimal decision can be separated from the physical dynamics on which it acts. It studies this question through minimum-energy barrier crossing in scalar bistable systems. It characterizes the finite-horizon optimal feedback and shows that, as the horizon grows, it converges to a law that doubles and reverses the drift while it opposes crossing, and switches off once the barrier is passed. In physical coordinates, this law inherits the plant's nonlinearity, entangling decision and dynamics. We show that a plant-specific translation of state, input, and time maps every double well in the considered class to the same unit-rate linear world model, allowing a downstream decision stage to use a single plant-independent control primitive. This separation generally loses optimality at finite horizons because the translation does not preserve the physical control energy. Nevertheless, we prove that the excess physical energy of the layered controller vanishes as the horizon grows and that its limiting feedback reproduces the asymptotic optimum exactly. Thus, translation and optimization generally do not commute at a finite horizon, but commute in the asymptotic limit.

papers.title: Decompose the Distillation: Interpretable Single-Pass Guidance for Diffusion Models
papers.abstract: Classifier-Free Guidance is a widely used inference-time guidance rule for conditional image generation with diffusion models, which exposes a guidance scale that adjusts conditioning strength after training. This flexibility requires conditional and unconditional model evaluations at every sampling step, so an N-step trajectory takes 2N forward passes. Single-pass alternatives reduce such cost, yet most collapse CFG's two components into one opaque guided prediction, losing the separable base flow and guidance direction that support per-step control and diagnostics, even when the scale remains adjustable. This work introduces CtrlFlow, a single-pass guidance method that preserves CFG's separable base-flow and guidance-direction interface. To preserve both components at one-pass cost, CtrlFlow attaches two lightweight LoRA adapters to a frozen backbone, each adding 2.5% parameters, and predicts the base flow and guidance direction from one pass of the shared frozen backbone. Because the guidance scale multiplies the guidance direction only after the forward pass, one evaluation yields the guided velocity at any scale, so a single trained checkpoint remains adjustable at inference without retraining. Preserving two outputs introduces a training mismatch: inference amplifies guidance-direction errors by the chosen scale, while naive component-wise losses weight both outputs equally. To align training with this composed inference-time error, CtrlFlow uses a unified multi-scale distillation loss. Residual guidance errors can still persist at extreme scales, where even small guidance-direction errors are amplified by the guidance scale. To reduce this inference-time error, CtrlFlow applies scale-adaptive modulation to damp velocity-field errors and time-grid warping to concentrate solver evaluations where the trajectory changes most rapidly.

papers.title: Closed-Loop Adaptive Sampling on a Generative Ocean Model
papers.abstract: Adaptive sampling can substantially improve the value of sparse ocean observations by directing mobile robots toward measurements that are most informative for an evolving environment. Recent learned generative ocean models can produce high-resolution forecasts and ensembles at substantially lower computational cost than traditional numerical models, creating an opportunity to use rich predictive forecasts directly in closed-loop robotic sampling. However, these models do not natively provide the explicit uncertainty representations assumed by classical informative-planning methods, and their forecasts often evolve in learned latent spaces rather than directly in physical ocean variables. We develop a multi-robot closed-loop adaptive sampling framework that uses a single learned generative model for forecasting, uncertainty estimation, planning, and measurement assimilation. The model forecasts an ensemble in latent space, decodes it to physical ocean states, and uses ensemble statistics to construct A- or D-optimal sampling objectives. We select sampling locations subject to robot reachability under predicted currents. The collected measurements are assimilated back into the latent state using observation-conditioned diffusion sampling. Across 120 test scenarios A- and D-optimal sampling generally outperforms static, random, and systematic-coverage baselines while adding little planning overhead. Our experiments uncover several scenarios in which model uncertainty diverges from forecast error, motivating future work in uncertainty quantification.

papers.title: Agentic Wireless Optimization: Workflow Automation, Algorithm Design, and Multi-Timescale Network Operations
papers.abstract: Optimization is fundamental to wireless communications, from characterizing channel capacity and designing transmission schemes to allocating network resources. However, conventional workflows require substantial expertise and manual effort, particularly for high-dimensional or nonconvex problems, black-box objectives, and interdependent decisions across time scales. Recent advances in agentic artificial intelligence (AI), particularly agents based on large language models (LLMs), offer new opportunities to address these challenges by integrating reasoning, tool use, and numerical feedback. This article presents an overview of agentic AI for wireless optimization, focusing on workflow automation, algorithm design, and multi-timescale network operations. First, LLM-based agents streamline optimization workflows by automating problem formulation, code generation, numerical solution, and result verification in a closed loop. Second, they facilitate algorithm design by combining and configuring existing numerical methods and refining learning-based optimizers, using numerical feedback to improve solution quality and computational efficiency for nonconvex and black-box problems. Third, they support multi-timescale network operations by decomposing coupled problems into interdependent subtasks and coordinating their solutions to satisfy network-level objectives and service requirements. A multicast beamforming case study demonstrates performance gains from agent-developed solvers, particularly in execution time, and a network energy-saving example illustrates how agents coordinate dynamic base station activation, user association, and beamforming across time scales. Finally, we discuss open challenges and research opportunities in agentic wireless optimization.

authors.name: Ya-Feng Liu
authors.institution: Harbin University of Science and Technology

papers.title: LumiTac: Compact, High-Rate Six-Axis Optical Tactile Sensing for Human-Robot Interaction
papers.abstract: Integrating six-axis tactile feedback into robotic interfaces requires compact sensors with accurate load measurement and rapid online reconstruction. This paper presents LumiTac, a low-profile, camera-free optoelectronic tactile sensor combining spatially distributed illumination with spectral encoding. Five photoemitters and five RGBW photoreceivers are mounted on opposing circuit boards coupled through translucent silicone. Load-induced interlayer motion modulates the internal light field under compression, shear, bending, and torsion. The sensing head measures 12 mm in diameter and 4.75 mm in thickness, weighs less than 2 g, and has a component cost of approximately USD 7. A compact multilayer perceptron reconstructs three force and three moment components from 20 optical channels. Independent testing yielded coefficients of determination (R-squared) of 0.9657-0.9941, with mean absolute errors of 0.054-0.190 N for forces and 0.304-1.419 mN m for moments. Online prediction achieved an average update rate of 303.57 Hz and a median software processing latency of 0.722 ms. Experiments involving combined loading, light weights, and rapid tapping evaluated load tracking, sensitivity to small forces, and transient response, respectively. Robotic demonstrations further validated its applicability to tactile-guided manipulation and physical human-robot interaction. This study paves the way for compact, high-rate optical tactile sensing in robotic manipulation and human-robot interaction.

papers.title: Reglos: A Self-Evolving Personal Memory Agent with Recursive Self-Improvement
papers.abstract: Personal agents draw on past conversations to tailor their responses to each user. Their memory systems store and update what each user says, and coding agents now also rewrite the harness that turns this memory into the model's context. Such patches risk overfitting, because one tested only on the failures it targets can fix those cases and help nowhere else. We present Reglos, a training-free personal memory agent that tests whether harness changes help beyond the failures they were written to fix. Its self-evolving memory adds to each user's append-only record with every conversation, as new preferences supersede old ones and facts can be forgotten. Its harness improves through recursive self-improvement, in which a coding agent proposes patches from failure traces and a critic from a second model family screens each one for benchmark gaming. After the harness is frozen, a fixed evaluator decides which further patches to accept. With the same backbone behind every system, Reglos outperforms state-of-the-art memory systems such as Mem0, MemOS and EverOS, reaching 61.3% and 84.0% on PersonaMem-v2 and LongMemEval-S with Qwen3.8-27B, and 57.5% and 87.2% with GPT-5.6 Luna.

papers.title: CARE-FL: Federated Fine-Tuning of Multimodal LLMs in Resource-Constrained Edge Networks
papers.abstract: Domain-specific adaptation of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) in privacy-sensitive edge environments requires federated fine-tuning, yet client selection remains challenging due to heterogeneous multimodal data and modality availability, dynamic system conditions, and evolving client utility during training. We propose Constraint-Aware Reinforcement Learning for Efficient Federated Fine-Tuning (CARE-FL), a constrained online client-selection framework for federated MLLM Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) fine-tuning. CARE-FL formulates client participation as a sequential decision process and employs Q-value decomposition to address the large combinatorial joint action space through scalable client-level long-term utility estimation. These utilities are learned online using a modified Double Deep Q-Learning (DDQL) scheme, while constraint-aware $\epsilon$-greedy execution selects feasible client subsets under per-round latency and bandwidth constraints. Complementing client selection, an adaptive aggregation mechanism further controls potentially unstable global updates and places greater weight on the previous model when needed. Experiments on the CrisisMMD disaster-response task in emulated heterogeneous wireless edge environments show that CARE-FL achieves higher and more stable test accuracy than the compared client-selection baselines across different system settings, while satisfying the imposed latency and bandwidth constraints.

authors.name: Nuocheng Yang
authors.institution: Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications

papers.title: Data-Driven Likelihood-Ratio Construction for Radar Detection via Bernstein Induction Operators
papers.abstract: Accurate likelihood-ratio (LR) construction is challenging when clutter statistics are unknown. Prespecified clutter models may not adequately describe the observed data, and evaluating target-present densities may require computationally expensive marginalization. This paper proposes a data-driven LR construction framework based on a Bernstein polynomial model (BPM) and a Bernstein induction operator (BIO). The BPM weights are estimated from clutter-only samples, whereas the target-induced responses of the Bernstein basis densities are approximated offline in the same basis to construct column-stochastic matrices. These matrices map clutter-density weights to target-present density weights at specified signal-to-clutter ratios (SCRs), and mixtures of the matrices account for target fluctuations. For a fixed target model and basis representation, the matrix library is independent of the clutter-density weights and can be reused across clutter distributions. The resulting LR construction avoids repeated online evaluation of the physical-induction integrals. Simulations under analytical clutter models show close agreement with the reference LRs and detection probabilities, with lower online computation times in the non-Gaussian cases considered. Experiments using synthetic target echoes embedded in measured sea clutter further show improved detection probabilities relative to the evaluated baselines in the weak-target regime.

papers.title: HarnessFlow: MCTS-Guided Harness Optimization for LLM Agents
papers.abstract: The performance of large language model (LLM) agents depends on both the underlying model and the harness that governs interaction with tools and the environment. Yet harness design remains largely manual, and automating it requires navigating an open-ended search space through costly end-to-end evaluations. We introduce HarnessFlow, a framework for optimizing complete executable harnesses under a limited candidate-evaluation budget, with the model and task environment held fixed. HarnessFlow organizes candidates and their evaluation histories in a refinement tree, using a Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS)-based policy to balance exploitation and exploration. A coding agent refines selected harnesses using archived code, execution feedback, and a library of reusable harness mechanisms. With 15 refinement attempts per benchmark, HarnessFlow achieves the highest mean test scores among the compared methods on six benchmarks spanning agentic tasks, coding, and web interaction. The optimized harnesses achieve an average score of 69.48%, outperforming the initial harnesses and Meta-Harness by 10.89 and 3.95 percentage points, respectively, while incurring lower average per-task execution costs than hand-engineered baselines. These results suggest that structured harness search offers a promising route toward automating the design of capable and efficient LLM agents.

authors.institution: Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai

authors.institution: Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen

papers.title: AmbiHTMLBench: A Benchmark for HTML-based Visually Rich Document parsing
papers.abstract: Traditional document parsing systems use Markdown as their output representation, which is effective for linear text but does not fully preserve fine-grained spatial structure, table geometry, visual hierarchy, or rendering semantics. We show that HTML is advantageous for heterogeneous and layout-sensitive documents whose representations must remain editable, inspectable, and reusable, and introduce AmbiHTMLBench to systematically study this setting. In this benchmark, given a real-world document, a model must recover executable HTML that preserves its content, organization, and visual appearance. The benchmark contains 1,115 diverse pages with structured annotations and evaluates predictions in two different ways: The objective protocol aligns ground-truth and predicted rendered blocks and measures table fidelity, page-level text error, and a two-dimensional layout consistency; a complementary reference-anchored protocol measures perceived fidelity by aligning LLM judges with human preferences. Across ten primary multimodal systems, the best objective score is 0.8092, while the subjective winner is different, demonstrating that automatic decomposition and human-perceived fidelity capture complementary properties. We further fine-tune a small-parameter expert model and find that task-specific adaptation yields good performance on document-to-HTML reconstruction task. These results position AmbiHTMLBench as a diagnostic testbed for building smarter and more logical document parsing systems.

authors.name: Linhan Pang
authors.institution: State Key Laboratory of Applied Organic Chemistry

papers.title: Trick-or-Treat: Adversarial Evaluation of Multimodal Medical Reasoning with Synthetic Images
papers.abstract: We used medical image synthesis to create a challenging multimodal evaluation framework that exposes hallucination behaviors in frontier models. Evaluating multimodal reasoning has historically been difficult because existing medical datasets rarely pair different image modalities, such as radiographs and external clinical photographs. To address this gap, we introduce Trick-or-Treat, an adversarial multimodal medical benchmark that pairs real chest radiographs with synthetic clinical photographs to challenge models' cross-modal reasoning. For each of a wide range of conditions, we created two pairs of images, where the pairs share a single chest radiograph but contain different external photographs. In matched pairs, the chest radiograph and photograph both contain findings suggesting the same disease (e.g., varicella pneumonia suggested by lung opacities and crusted skin lesions seen in chickenpox). In mismatched pairs, the photograph depicts an alternative clinical finding that would not lead to the same unifying diagnosis (e.g. replacing crusted skin lesions with ordinary acne). Synthetic photograph generation allows clinical findings to be varied while the person's features and photographic setting stay consistent, reducing confounding. In an investigation of three frontier models, we found that models hallucinated clinically significant photograph findings in 45-57.5% of mismatched pairs, up from 25-37.5% for the same photographs shown alone. When faced with mismatched pairs, models tended to ignore mismatches and instead hallucinated findings that better matched the radiograph (e.g. misreading acne as crusted skin lesions to justify diagnosing chickenpox). Trick-or-Treat both demonstrates concerning error pattern in frontier models' medical reasoning and provides a proof of concept for the use of synthetic images in adversarial multimodal evaluation.

papers.title: Turns Matter: Advancing Streaming Video RL via Turn-Level Credit
papers.abstract: Streaming video understanding requires models to repeatedly decide whether to respond or continue observing. Recently, Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) has been applied to this setting, with existing approaches emphasizing reward design while retaining a single trajectory-level advantage across turns. Such shared credit can reinforce redundant replies after earlier successes and discourage useful follow-ups after earlier failures. We propose TurnWise, a turn-level GRPO framework that aligns learning with individual streaming decisions. TurnWise addresses the mismatch between trajectory-level feedback and turn-level interaction, promoting informative responses and reducing redundancy. Specifically, turn-level credit assignment uses silence-completed prefix scoring to construct group-relative advantages from each decision's remaining return, separating its learning signal from earlier rewards. Turn-mean policy optimization averages token losses within each turn and then across turns, giving response and waiting decisions equal weight regardless of output length. These complementary designs improve streaming policy learning without a learned critic or additional rollouts. Extensive experiments show our method outperforms prior RL approaches for streaming video understanding.

authors.name: Haowen Hou
authors.institution: Guangdong Laboratory of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Economy (Shenzhen)

authors.name: Xuehui Wang
authors.institution: University of Chinese Academy of Sciences

authors.name: Jiaqi Wang
authors.institution: Harbin University of Science and Technology

papers.title: Generalized Sorting via Four-Cycles
papers.abstract:
We study the generalized sorting problem where only a subset of the pairs can be compared. Equivalently, we are given an $n$-vertex $m$-edge graph $G=(V, E)$ where the vertex set $V$ is to be sorted, and the edge set $E$ indicates possible comparisons. The goal is to sort $V$ with as few (adaptive) queries to $E$ as possible.
  When $G$ is the complete graph, the problem is equivalent to standard sorting for which $\Theta(n \log n)$ queries are sufficient and necessary. All classical sorting algorithms crucially rely on the ability to compare any pair and do not imply an $o(n^2)$-query algorithm in the general case. This was improved 15 years ago by Huang, Kannan, and Khanna [FOCS'11] who achieved a bound of $\widetilde{O}(n\sqrt{n})$. Kuszmaul and Narayanan [FOCS'21] later gave a bound of $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{m n})$, which is more efficient for sparse graphs, but matches the $\widetilde{O}(n\sqrt{n})$ barrier for dense graphs.
  In this paper, we present an algorithm for generalized sorting that makes at most $\widetilde{O}(n^{4/3})$ queries, therefore breaking the longstanding $\widetilde{O}(n\sqrt{n})$ barrier for all graphs. The key to our result is to query edges that belong to many (specific types of) four-cycles. We show that querying such edges allows the algorithm to verify the direction of many other edges (specifically, their opposing edges in the four-cycles) and thus achieve a much better amortized query cost.

papers.title: SAUCE: Summary Analysis Using Conversation Entailment
papers.abstract: With the growing need for evaluating Large Language Models (LLMs) and their applications to speech, challenges persist in summarizing and evaluating conversations that lack a clear end goal. We introduce SAUCE -- a reference-free, fact-based evaluation pipeline for cross-lingual conversational speech summarization. It measures the accuracy and the fact coverage of a summary through the entailment between conversation and text. We compare SAUCE against several popular summarization metrics and demonstrate the effectiveness of capturing information loss due to transcription and translation error and identifying broken summaries. Crucially, unlike black-box LLM evaluators or dense embedding metrics, SAUCE is inherently explainable: it maps summary scores to discrete, verifiable facts, allowing users to pinpoint exact hallucinations or omissions. We illustrate how this interpretability helps developers systematically profile LLM behaviors and gives end-users an actionable tool to verify summary accuracy in noisy, real-world conditions. Preliminary investigations show SAUCE strongly align with human judgment.

papers.title: Motion-guided Contrastive Regularization For Latent World Models
papers.abstract: JEPA-style world models learn action-conditioned latent dynamics without reconstructing observations, but distributional regularization alone does not ensure that their representations preserve information needed for control. We identify static collapse, a failure mode in which the encoder preserves episode-specific static content while suppressing manipulation-relevant state changes. Because static content is temporally predictable yet diverse across episodes, this failure can persist despite regularizers such as SIGReg. A controlled study on OGBench-Cube shows that introducing randomized backgrounds substantially degrades planning performance while leaving the underlying manipulation task unchanged. To address this problem, we propose motion-guided contrastive regularization. Our approach compares predicted latent transitions with transitions to candidate observations from the same episode, reducing the usefulness of static background identity for distinguishing action outcomes. Optical-flow similarities provide soft contrastive targets, allowing candidates with similar motion to receive similar supervision. Combined with latent prediction and SIGReg, our objective encourages representations to preserve within-episode state distinctions and similarities between related transitions. Our method improves planning success over LeWorldModel (LeWM) from 52% to 78% on OGBench-Cube with randomized backgrounds and from 14% to 54% on LIBERO-Object, while maintaining comparable performance on four other visual-control benchmarks.

papers.title: FlowReconBench: Accuracy, calibration and cost of learned and classical flow reconstruction from sparse sensors
papers.abstract: Reconstructing full flow fields from sparse sensors requires prior assumptions about unmeasured regions and physical variables. Yet it remains unclear when learned models outperform classical estimators and which aspects of their predictions can be trusted. FlowReconBench evaluates ten learned and five classical methods on three regimes: a laminar cylinder wake across Reynolds numbers, two-dimensional Kolmogorov turbulence and a large-scale three-dimensional (3D) isotropic turbulence. Methods share leakage-controlled splits and sensor draws and are scored on per-channel error, ensemble spread, calibration, spectra and cost. The leading method changes for each regime. Classical methods perform strongly in low-order and dense-sensing regimes. On the cylinder wake, linear stochastic estimation and gappy proper orthogonal decomposition lead, including for unobserved pressure. In 3D, inverse-distance weighting matches the best learned methods on observed channels. Data-driven methods become superior at decreasing sensor density or poor sensor observability. On Kolmogorov flow, continuous ranked probability score and error yield different method rankings: generative models offer broader but underdispersed ensembles, while deterministic models prioritize pointwise error. Generative models balance this tradeoff through their sampler budget, with a larger budget improving ensemble quality at higher computational cost. In 3D, scaling tests demonstrate that queryable methods are flat in memory, while full-grid construction methods run out of memory. Observing only 2 of 4 fields leaves the problem kinematically underconstrained, yet a latent model can reproduce structural similarities to the ground truth.

papers.title: The Galois actions on braided fusion categories
papers.abstract: This note harmonizes two classical topics: minimal modular extensions of braided fusion categories and the Galois action on modular fusion categories. Their common generalizations are Galois-modular extensions, which always exist when a braided fusion category $\mathcal{B}$ is pseudounitary. Each extension induces a Galois action on the simple objects of $\mathcal{B}$. Up to integral equivalence, the Galois-modular extensions of $\mathcal{B}$ form a torsor over an explicit group of homomorphisms from $\mathrm{Gal}(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}/\mathbb{Q})$ to the invertible objects of order dividing two in the symmetric center $\mathcal{E}$ of $\mathcal{B}$. If $\mathcal{E}$ is Tannakian and $\mathcal{B}$ has a minimal modular extension, all minimal modular extensions induce one canonical Galois action. We prove that many facts about the modular data of modular fusion categories extend to pseudounitary premodular fusion categories as well via the Galois action.

papers.title: Alignment Myopia in Generative AI
papers.abstract: Current generative AI alignment relies on a myopic paradigm that prioritizes immediate conversational satisfaction. By relying on short-horizon feedback, this approach ignores the profound, longitudinal externalities of persistent human-AI interaction, which can lead to adverse outcomes such as cognitive atrophy, social erosion, and diminished human agency. To address this, we propose a paradigm shift toward long-horizon alignment that accounts for how AI reshapes human experience over time. To this end, we map the tensions between near-term utility and long-term costs of AI use across four facets of human well-being to reveal outcomes that current reward models fail to capture. Ultimately, we advocate for moving beyond simple preference optimization toward alignment strategies that actively foster long-term human well-being by navigating these complex temporal scales.

authors.name: Michael Madaio
authors.institution: University of Massachusetts Chan Medical School

authors.name: Himabindu Lakkaraju
authors.institution: Harvard–MIT Division of Health Sciences and Technology

papers.title: Probabilistic Steering of Generative Priors for Lab-in-the-Loop Antibody Optimization
papers.abstract: Therapeutic antibody development is often framed as comprising two discrete stages: initial discovery of novel binders followed by iterative optimization to refine these hits into therapeutic-grade molecules. Models and methods often reflect these stages, with generative structure models applied to discovery and probabilistic black-box optimization methods applied to refinement. Here we propose to unify these stages by smoothly transitioning a generative discovery model into iterative optimization, allowing the handoff between the structure-based prior and supervision from wet lab data to be guided by the posterior uncertainty of a probabilistic surrogate. We show that this yields improvements in optimization efficiency in the low-N regime, as well as improved diversity amongst the optimized molecules.

papers.title: Sketchpad: certified exact arithmetic with a small vision-language model
papers.abstract: Language models are accurate on most long-arithmetic problems, but their accuracy is estimated on samples and carries no guarantee for an unseen input; tool use is exact but moves the computation outside the network. We show that exactness at all input lengths becomes a finite, checkable property of a network when each of its steps reads only a bounded view of an external working memory. In Sketchpad, Qwen3.5-0.8B with a low-rank adapter executes arithmetic procedures on a rendered sheet. Each forward pass reads a three-cell view and emits one step: a digit, a carry or borrow, and the next operation. A fixed runtime moves the view and writes no digit of a result. We prove in Lean that the model is then exact on all inputs of any length if and only if it is exact on the finite set of views the runtime presents, that no finite test suffices when steps also read earlier steps, and that the guarantee tolerates bounded numerical perturbation and extends to compositions of procedures. All 2,446 views pass on the deployment device, a laptop GPU running the model in a web browser. The certified model performs signed addition and subtraction, long multiplication and division, square roots and greatest common divisors at arbitrary length. It solved 200 of 200 pre-registered problems in the browser, and 220 of 220 sums of up to 1,000 digits and products of up to 20 digits, of which GPT-6.1 Sol, the strongest of ten other models, solved 217. A symbolic runtime built on these procedures solves, expands and factors polynomials with every number computed by the model, and a multiplicative gate on the adapter recovers the base model exactly when the sheet is not in use.

papers.title: Universal Hardness From Masking Channels
papers.abstract: We prove a broad learning-theoretic generalization of the celebrated hardcore lemma concerning the average-case complexity of computing a Boolean function (Impagliazzo, 1995). Our starting point is the observation that the classic notion of a hardcore measure, which reweights a function's input distribution, is equivalent to an input-dependent masking channel that injects randomness into the function's output distribution until it appears fully pseudorandom. The analogue of density of the measure is the fidelity of the channel. From this viewpoint, we develop a general framework for certifying hardness that allows for non-Boolean functions $f$ and a wide range of notions of hardness besides the classic 0-1 loss, by choosing the right notion of fidelity via convex duality. We show the difficulty of learning $f$ using a class $\mathcal{C}$ to minimize a convex loss is tightly characterized by the maximum fidelity possible for a masking channel, which measures the least amount of noise the channel must add to hide the structure of $f$ and make it $\mathcal{C}$-indistinguishable from random noise. Using our framework, we derive a number of multiclass generalizations of the hardcore lemma, and reveal some unexpected subtleties in going to larger alphabets. We construct a universal masking channel that applies to many natural notions of hardness simultaneously. Such channels are dual to omnipredictors, which optimize multiple losses at once (Gopalan, Kalai, Reingold, Sharan, and Wieder, 2022). We observe a symmetry between masking channels and generalizations of the hardcore lemma using pseudoentropy. We present a tight characterization of pseudoentropy using the MaxEnt algorithm from machine learning. A long line of research has shown that learning and hardness are two sides of the same coin; our framework gives a crisp and general formulation of this principle via convex duality.

papers.title: Quasicrystals are Functionally Graded Materials
papers.abstract: Quasicrystals exhibit long-range order without translational periodicity, posing challenges to compute their electronic properties. Here we show that a quasicrystal can be represented exactly as a periodic approximant with a spatially graded phason, establishing a connection to functionally graded materials. Building on this connection, we develop a controlled quantum theory of quasicrystals. We derive a state-dependent control parameter governed by the quantum metric of local Bloch states, determining when finite approximations are reliable. We further construct a Hamiltonian that correctly predicts Bragg gap positions, quasimomentum equivalence, and quasiperiodic eigenstates to all orders in phason strain within a finite Fourier window. We verify the theory numerically and propose a diffraction-based experimental test of the gap shift induced by phason strain. Our framework opens a route to predicting the electronic structure and functional properties of quasicrystals using methods developed for functionally graded materials.

authors.name: Mingda Li
authors.institution: Xi'an Institute of Optics and Precision Mechanics

papers.title: From Activation to Intervention: Interpreting Sparse Visual Features through Reconstruction
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) decompose visual representations into individual features, offering a promising basis for explaining model behavior. Interpreting these features typically relies on images or pixel regions that most strongly activate them. However, this evidence becomes ambiguous when multiple features with different semantics frequently activate in the same locations, such as texture and color in the same patterns. We propose Reconstructive SAE Intervention (RecSAEI), a framework that shifts feature explanation from passive observation to active visual reconstruction. By intervening on representations along SAE decoder directions and reconstructing the visual output, we provide direct evidence of a feature's semantic meaning. We demonstrate that our method successfully disambiguates feature meanings across multiple datasets and vision encoders. Furthermore, our framework grounds [CLS] SAE interventions in a sparse set of patch SAE decoder directions. Beyond stable target response, this attribution also exposes the compositional relationship between elementary visual patterns and high-level semantics. Our results advocate for intervention reconstruction as an essential complementary signal for explaining neural networks.

authors.name: Jacob Beattie
authors.institution: The University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center

authors.name: Xi Xiao
authors.institution: China Tobacco Hunan Industrial Co., Ltd. (China)

authors.name: Sara Beery
authors.institution: MIT Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory

papers.title: On the Detectability of Compact Multi-Planet Systems via Gravitational Microlensing
papers.abstract: Compact multi-planet systems orbiting ultracool dwarfs, such as TRAPPIST-1, may be a major population of terrestrial worlds with poorly constrained demographics. Individual close-in planets are expected to escape microlensing detection, but whether a compact system can produce a detectable collective signal remains to be quantified. We calculate the microlensing signal from each TRAPPIST-1 planet, and of all seven combined, if the system were a lens toward the bulge. For a 0.09 $M_\odot$ lens at 4 kpc, $R_E \approx 1.21$ AU, placing the planets at $s = 0.010$--$0.051~\theta_E$, 12--63 times interior to the lensing zone. We measure each signal as the residual after fitting a single-lens model, which accounts for the barycentric dipole. Because the quadrupole term cancels between the two images to first order, the residual scales as the octupole ($q s^3$), reaching $|\delta A / A| \sim 10^{-6}$. The seven planets combined yield $\Delta\chi^2 \sim 10^{-3}$ even at 1~mmag precision, five orders of magnitude below the standard detection threshold. Detection requires increasing all planet masses by a factor of $\sim$300, whereas the resonant chain loses its guarantee of Hill stability at a factor of $\sim$7. Only a lens within $\sim$15 pc of the source or the Sun places the outer planets in the lensing zone. The Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope is therefore not expected to detect a TRAPPIST-1-like system through microlensing, whereas its transit channel in the same fields can detect such planets in large numbers, marking a sharp boundary in the Galactic census between microlensing and transit sensitivity.

papers.title: Just the Facts: How Dialogues with AI Reduce Conspiracy Beliefs
papers.abstract: Personalized dialogues with AI substantially reduce conspiracy beliefs. To identify why, we conducted two experiments with U.S. adults recruited online (total N = 2,193) that removed possible causes one at a time. The debunking effect was robust to disclosing the AI's persuasive goal, framing the exchange as a debate, instructing the AI to inform rather than persuade, halving its response length, altering how beliefs were measured, and replacing the dialogue with a single tailored message. Only instructing the AI to persuade without factual evidence and arguments substantially reduced the debunking effect. Content analyses of the AI's output and participants' own accounts linked larger reductions in conspiracy beliefs to factual argumentation rather than rapport, storytelling, or appeals to empathy. AI dialogues appear to reduce conspiracy beliefs primarily by supplying relevant, well-reasoned counterevidence. Our results suggest that humans might be similarly effective if they could supply comparable evidence.

papers.title: Sublinear Metric Distortion for Matching
papers.abstract:
We study metric distortion in one-sided matching. Given $n$ agents and $n$ items in an unknown metric space, our goal is to match agents to items so that the total distance between matched pairs is small. However, instead of direct access to the distances in the metric, we are only given each agent's ranking of the items by distance. What is the smallest worst-case approximation factor (called the distortion) that a mechanism can guarantee in expectation? Despite significant interest over the last decade, the best-known guarantee has been the $O(n)$ distortion of Random Serial Dictatorship since the beginning.
  We give a matching mechanism with distortion $O(n^{\log_4 3})$, the first sublinear upper bound. The key idea is to use a partial matching derived from a truncated version of either Random Serial Dictatorship or the Probabilistic Serial rule. We then complete this matching using a new, general-purpose cluster completion algorithm that ensures unmatched agents receive nearby items. Along the way, we pin down the optimal distortion of Random Serial Dictatorship and Probabilistic Serial up to logarithmic and constant factors, respectively, and give improved lower bounds for truthful mechanisms.

authors.name: Moses Charikar
authors.institution: Rutgers, The State University of New Jersey

papers.title: Continuous-Discrete Dual-Domain Co-Design for Optimized Digital Control of Power Converters
papers.abstract: Optimizing digital control for power converters typically involves designing continuous-time controllers and discretizing them via Euler, Tustin, or Generalized Bilinear Transform (GBT) methods. However, the intrinsic coupling between continuous-domain control parameters and discrete-domain implementation parameters remains underexplored, often leading to suboptimal performance. To bridge this gap, this paper first establishes a Non-Uniqueness Theorem, elucidating the coupling mechanism between dual-domain parameters. Based on this, two co-design methodologies are proposed to derive optimized parameter sets: the Explicit Frequency-Domain Analytical Method (EFDAM) and the Implicit Computer-Aided Search Method (ICASM). The EFDAM derives closed-form solutions by maximizing the crossover frequency and resonant magnitude via logarithmic frequency stability criteria, while minimizing discretization errors using Taylor-series bounds. The ICASM formulates the search for optimized parameters as a constrained multi-objective optimization problem, balancing bandwidth, resonant magnitude, and fundamental magnitude. To solve ICASM efficiently, two algorithms are introduced: the Multi-Start COBYLA (MS-COBYLA), which employs Latin Hypercube Sampling for physics-informed initialization to escape local optima, and the PSO-COBYLA hybrid algorithm, which couples global particle swarm exploration with local refinement. Experimental results on a 5-kW single-phase inverter with a Proportional-Integral-Resonant (PIR) regulator validate that the proposed methods outperform the conventional benchmark, achieving a 43.3\% reduction in the peak-to-peak current ripple measured at the zero-active-power operating point and an 11.7\%--35.9\% decrease in THDi across various harmonic profiles.

authors.name: Shen Chen
authors.institution: National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University

authors.name: Jinjun Liu

authors.institution: Harbin University of Science and Technology

papers.title: Transmission Expansion with Large, Discrete Data Center Realization Uncertainty
papers.abstract: Large data center projects introduce a distinct transmission planning uncertainty because of their large scale, discrete project realization nature, and strong locational impacts on the transmission network. On the one hand, conventional deterministic treatments can either overbuild the network by assuming that all candidate projects materialize; on the other, they can leave the system underprepared by prematurely screening out projects. This paper develops a project-realization-based framework for systematically modeling, planning, and evaluating transmission expansion under uncertain data center realization. Candidate data center projects are represented through alternative realization scenarios and associated probabilities, enabling different planning strategies to be modeled and quantitatively assessed under a common framework. Within this framework, numerical case studies demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework and the benefits of stochastic planning approach. The results show that stochastic planning can use realization probabilities to hedge multiple plausible futures, providing a more balanced tradeoff between transmission investment and reliability exposure than deterministic approaches under correctly specified and misspecified realization probabilities.

papers.title: Look Before You Move: Multimodal Sensing-Aided Trajectory and Beamforming Design for 6DMA
papers.abstract: Six-dimensional movable antenna (6DMA) technology allows a base station (BS) to adjust the three-dimensional (3D) positions and 3D rotations, i.e., the 6D poses, of its surfaces. Many existing 6DMA designs select the poses based on prior channel knowledge. However, the channels at a new pose can be estimated only after the surfaces have moved to this pose, and the limited movement speeds of the surfaces restrict the poses reachable at the next time step. To address these challenges, we propose a learning-based multimodal sensing-aided trajectory and beamforming design for multiuser 6DMA systems with mobile users and surrounding objects. The BS observes the users and surrounding objects with RGB images, LiDAR point clouds, and GPS positions, independently of the poses of the surfaces. Since a surface may need several time steps to reach a favorable pose, the BS designs a 6DMA trajectory over several future time steps and executes only its first step, following receding-horizon control. We propose a neural network, in which user-centric cross-modal attention and temporal self-attention modules relate each user to the scene and its sensing history, and surface-to-user attention relates each surface to the users. A projection layer keeps the poses feasible under the geometric and kinematic constraints, and a graph attention module allocates the transmit power along the pilot-based beamforming directions. Performance evaluations using the CARLA driving simulator and Sionna ray tracing (RT) demonstrate significant minimum-rate gains of the proposed design over fixed-position antennas. Ablation studies validate the contributions of multimodal sensing and the proposed attention modules to these gains. The results further highlight the importance of designing the trajectory several time steps ahead, which is more beneficial under tighter speed limits of the surfaces.

papers.title: On Wilker-Type Properties
papers.abstract: Wilker-type properties record how a compact set can be split along a binary open cover, and they are precisely the continuity conditions for the union operation on open lattices, governing the topology of power and function spaces. We give a unified treatment of the four properties $\W$, $\Ww$, $\Wi$ and $\Win$. We prove that $\Wi$ and $\Win$ are hereditary for arbitrary subspaces, whereas $\W$ and $\Ww$ are hereditary only for closed subspaces; all four are preserved by continuous retracts, and $\Ww$, $\Wi$, $\Win$ are finitely additive over topological sums. For KC-spaces $\Ww$ and $\Wi$ coincide, and spaces whose compact subspaces are Hausdorff belong to $\Win$. Using Kov\'ar's compact KC-space $M_0$ and its variant $\QQ^{+}$, we obtain countably infinite compact KC-spaces in $\Wi\setminus\W$, showing $\Wi$ is strictly weaker than $\W$. Conversely, we construct compact $T_1$ spaces whose product fails $\Ww$, proving the classes $\Ww$ and $\Wi$ are not reflective. We further show Vietoris constructions need not preserve $\Wi$, and prove that $\Ok(M_0)\cong \Ck(M_0,\Sier)$ is not sober and fails property~$S$. Open problems are collected at the end.

papers.title: Constant-Time Dynamic Edge Coloring via Dynamic Splitting and LLL
papers.abstract:
We give a dynamic algorithm that maintains a near-optimal edge coloring in constant expected time per update. For every fixed $\epsilon>0$, the algorithm maintains a $(1+\epsilon)\Delta$ edge coloring under edge insertions and deletions in $\mathrm{poly}(1/\epsilon)$ worst-case expected update time against an oblivious adversary, provided $\Delta\ge\Delta_\epsilon=\widetilde\Theta(1/\epsilon^2)$. The previous constant-time algorithm of Bhattacharya, Costa, Panski, and Solomon (BCPS) required $\Delta\ge(\log n/\epsilon^4)^{\Theta(\log(1/\epsilon)/\epsilon)}$, where $n$ is the number of vertices. We remove this dependence on $n$, answering their open question.
  Our approach differs substantially from that of BCPS, which relied on coloring in locally tree-like subgraphs. Instead, we draw on distributed algorithms that organize partial coloring through successive applications of the Lov\'asz Local Lemma (LLL). We develop a dynamic LLL solver with worst-case expected update bounds and a dynamic splitting algorithm that partitions edges into low-degree subgraphs. A key technical contribution is a bottom-up method for iterative splitting, which avoids the logarithmic overhead of maintaining successive levels. It achieves constant expected update time by adaptively choosing which levels to inspect and repair, rather than inspecting every level after each update. We believe these dynamic splitting and LLL tools can be of interest beyond edge coloring.

papers.title: To lift or not to lift: Operator inference for nonlinear PDEs with boundary control
papers.abstract: Operator inference (OpInf) provides a nonintrusive framework for learning projection-based reduced-order models directly from data, but its standard formulations do not explicitly account for the fact that boundary actuation changes the admissible solution space of a PDE. This paper develops and evaluates a boundary-consistent, lifting-based OpInf formulation for nonlinear PDEs with time-varying inhomogeneous boundary conditions. The proposed approach decomposes the state into a known lifting component that satisfies the prescribed boundary conditions and a homogeneous component represented in a POD basis. Substituting this decomposition into the governing dynamics reveals a boundary-consistent reduced model structure in which the learned dynamics includes bilinear state-input and quadratic input-input interactions for quadratically nonlinear PDEs. The resulting operators are inferred from data, preserving the nonintrusive character of OpInf while guaranteeing boundary condition satisfaction by construction. Numerical experiments on boundary-actuated heat, Burgers, and lid-driven cavity problems show that the lifted formulation improves boundary compliance and can enhance prediction accuracy, solver stability, and computational efficiency, although these gains vary across problems and reduced model dimensions. Overall, this study establishes lifting as a principled extension of OpInf for boundary-actuated PDEs, clarifies when and how this formulation improves performance, and indicates that standard OpInf can remain an effective alternative in certain regimes.

papers.title: Measuring Risk, Not Harm: Detecting Psychological Harm Risk Factors in LLM Conversations
papers.abstract: Psychological harms from interactions with large language models cannot be monitored directly because they may emerge over repeated interactions and depend strongly on subjective individual user context. We propose measuring risk, not harm: detecting observable AI behaviors that constitute risk factors for psychological harm at the AI response level and aggregating these signals to support longitudinal monitoring. We operationalize eight such behaviors and construct a synthetic multi-label corpus of 47,062 AI responses and 373,873 response-factor labels, with targeted human annotations for validation and evaluation. We then compare trained embedding-based classifiers, direct LLM judging, and a classifier--judge cascade. All detectors are model-agnostic and operate only on LLM outputs, requiring no access to internal model states. We apply these detectors to several out-of-distribution human-AI conversation data sets from prior research. On held-out human-labeled data, the best cascade achieves macro precision of 0.86, recall of 0.76, and F1 of 0.79. On WildChat, it reduces LLM-judge calls by 97.1\% relative to direct judging. On DelusionEval, risk-factor detections cluster within conversations. Together, our results show that response-level behavioral risk-factor detection can provide a scalable measurement layer for longitudinal psychological-safety monitoring without conflating observable AI behavior with latent user harm.

papers.title: Twisted Diophantine approximation: asymptotic and uniform results
papers.abstract: Fix an $m\times n$ matrix $A$; twisted Diophantine approximation studies how well we can approximate the affine form $A {\bf q}-{\bf b}$ by an integer $m$-vector, depending on the choice of $m$-vector ${\bf b}$. We report on two companion papers in twisted Diophantine approximation, covering two setups: asymptotic and uniform. The asymptotic paper gives an exact Khintchine-type Lebesgue zero--one law, a null--conull criterion for badly approximable shifts, and Hausdorff-measure tests yielding exact power-law dimensions under a critical divergence condition. The uniform paper computes Hausdorff dimensions of sets of uniformly approximable vectors. It also gives Hausdorff zero--full laws, uniform-exponent spectra, and a sharp escape-of-mass bound. In both cases the results are established for arbitrary approximation functions from suitable regularity classes, and the arguments use a homogeneous lattice count involving all successive minima to record clustering in every independent direction.

papers.title: TB-Transolver: Parallelized and Coherent Long-Horizon Rollouts via Temporal Bundling for Time-Dependent PDEs
papers.abstract: Transolver has recently gained widespread adoption for solving diverse physical problems on unstructured geometric meshes by leveraging its Physics-Attention mechanism, which seamlessly extends standard softmax attention to handle physical domains at scale. For time-dependent problems, existing literature relies on time-conditioned or autoregressive rollouts to preserve temporal causality while retaining Physics-Attention as the spatial backbone. However, a fundamental limitation of this formulation is its sequential execution model, wherein computational costs scale linearly with the temporal horizon, rendering standard Transolver inefficient for transient problems despite its exceptional spatial efficacy. This bottleneck has historically hindered its broader application in time-dependent physical modeling. To address this limitation, we introduce TB-Transolver (also referred to as Temporally Bundled Transolver), an efficient framework built on temporal bundling that scales Transolver for time-dependent PDEs. Furthermore, we propose \emph{spatiotemporal coherence} (${\rm C(K)}$) as a general metric to systematically quantify snapshot correlation within a temporal bundle, enabling the \emph{a priori} selection of optimal bundle widths using training data alone, thereby avoiding expensive grid searches. We demonstrate the computational efficacy of TB-Transolver across four physically distinct domains, namely, plasticity, fluid dynamics, reaction-diffusion, and global weather forecasting; achieving training speedups of up to $29\times$ over conventional autoregressive and time-conditioned baselines. Finally, these computational gains are further amplified through distributed multi-node and multi-GPU parallelism, yielding aggregated speedups of up to $45.6\times$ at optimal bundle widths for systems exhibiting high spatiotemporal coherence compared to single-GPU implementations.

papers.title: SCRUB: Contact-Based Surface-Frame Estimation for Force-Motion Control with an Armless Quadruped
papers.abstract: Wiping, sanding, and inspection robots press a sliding tool on a surface with controlled force. Controlling that force needs the surface normal, which is unknown on real-world, unmapped surfaces. Surface-normal estimators can help estimate the surface normal, but they either need a friction model or assume that the instantaneous tool velocity lies along the surface; however, walking violates this assumption. We propose SCRUB, a contact-based surface-frame estimator, which lets an armless quadruped slide a body-mounted tool along near-vertical surfaces in the absence of known, axis-aligned, or vision-predicted normals. SCRUB's predictive controller presses and slides the tool using a Kalman-filter estimate of the normal from two cues: 1) A force cue measures the estimate's tilt across the motion. If friction directly opposes the motion, the cue is zero exactly when that tilt is zero, for any friction coefficient. However, if the cue's sliding direction is wrong, friction appears as a false tilt. 2) A velocity cue measures tilt along the motion. Walking and pressing move the tool in and out. SCRUB therefore subtracts the commanded press rate from the tool velocity, averages the result over each gait cycle, and treats this mean as lying along the surface. On Unitree Go1 hardware at nominal speed and load, SCRUB completed every wall traverse and column orbit. No orbit completed with either cue removed, without gait averaging, or with a fixed normal.

papers.title: Discrete Poincar\'e and Bogovskii operators for higher order finite element de Rham complexes
papers.abstract: We present discrete Poincar\'e and Bogovskii operators for the common finite element discretizations of the de Rham complex of arbitrary polynomial order. We first discuss how such operators arise from a decomposition of the finite element spaces into a lowest order component and a remainder. This results in a fast algorithm for computing grad, curl, and div potentials. We then introduce a nonlocal Poincar\'e operator on contractible domains, which generalizes existing constructions based on cone operators to arbitrary order by integrating over cones against extended test forms. This requires developing commuting extension operators, which turn out to be related to rational forms. We also show how the nonlocal construction is modified to obtain a discrete Bogovskii operator preserving homogeneous boundary conditions. We further discuss how the ideas of the construction fit into the theory of finite element systems.

papers.title: Wandering continua, renormalization, and Lebesgue measure on Julia sets
papers.abstract: We study the Lebesgue measure of wandering continua and related invariant sets in Julia sets, using the hyperbolic area method recently developed by Ye. For entire functions of finite type, we show that a wandering continuum of positive area must escape to infinity uniformly. For infinitely renormalizable unicritical polynomials, we show that almost every point in the renormalization core (the intersection of the orbits of little Julia sets) is recurrent and contained in the postcritical set. The main tool is a conservativity theorem: if $f$ is injective on a forward invariant measurable subset $E$ of the Julia set, then $f|_E$ is conservative and almost every point of $E$ is recurrent and contained in the postsingular set.

papers.title: Constrained defined-contribution pension management: A reparameterized neural network approach
papers.abstract: This paper studies constrained defined contribution (DC) pension management under a two-factor financial market model. The pension participant is allowed to invest in cash, two nominal bonds, an inflation-linked bond, and a stock index. Moreover, they can also purchase term life insurance to manage pre-retirement death risk. Unlike traditional literature, we consider a pension member restricted to a general non-empty, closed, and convex trading constraint set that includes no short-selling, no borrowing, and portfolio-mix constraints as special cases. Such restrictions reflect common limits on pension-account trading. To solve the problem, we construct a family of unconstrained artificial markets, in which the original trading constraints are satisfied by adjusting the drift terms of the risky assets. Using a duality transformation, we derive the Lagrangian dual problem and propose a reparameterized neural network method to compute lower and upper bounds on the primal value function. We calibrate our model with U.S. data using a Kalman filter method, and find that our method produces a smaller duality gap than the benchmark methods. We also compare the constrained results with the unconstrained explicit solution and find that trading constraints substantially change wealth accumulation, portfolio strategies, and insurance demand. This highlights that unconstrained solutions may provide misleading guidance for pension management in practice.

papers.title: ExaTune: Exhaustive Hyperparameter Landscape Exploration at Scale
papers.abstract: Hyperparameter optimization (HPO) returns a single optimal configuration, systematically discarding the explored performance landscape that encodes how results depend on configuration choices. Fitness landscape analysis comprises a robust collection of methods from evolutionary computation offering ruggedness indices, autocorrelation functions, and fitness-distance correlation that have never been applied to machine learning hyperparameter spaces at scale, given that fine-grained ground-truth enumeration data has not existed. We present ExaTune, an open-source HPC system to produce a new artifact class: the hyperparameter landscape map. ExaTune exhaustively evaluates every point on a discretized hyperparameter grid via $K$-fold cross-validation, aggregates results into reproducible parquet benchmarks, and applies a suite of five formalized landscape metrics: spatial autocorrelation (Moran's $I$), ruggedness, local optima density, fitness-distance correlation (FDC), and variance-based parameter importance. We release a benchmark collection of 8 complete landscape maps (totalling 285,080 exhaustively evaluated configurations) spanning five model families (SVMs, random forests, XGBoost, ridge regression, and $k$-nearest neighbors) across six classification and two regression benchmarks, hosted on HuggingFace. Empirical analysis demonstrates that Bayesian optimization, Optuna, Hyperband, and Random Search at standard trial budgets systematically miss instability regions, secondary optima, and parameter interaction effects that are visible in complete landscapes; information that is structurally unavailable to any optimizer by design.

papers.title: Stacking-Based Weighting for Large Language Bayes in M-Open Settings
papers.abstract: Large Language Bayes (LLB) transforms a natural language problem description into a collection of candidate probabilistic programs and performs inference within each model, combining their predictions using Bayesian model averaging. While this provides a flexible framework for probabilistic inference without manual model specification, the resulting candidate model set is often misspecified in practice, and likelihood-based aggregation can concentrate on a single model, under-representing uncertainty across the sampled models. We propose a stacking-based aggregation method for LLB that selects model weights by optimizing predictive performance rather than marginal likelihood, while preserving the original language-model-driven model generation and within-model inference pipeline. Because leave-one-out predictive quantities are intractable in latent-variable models, we derive a variational lower bound that yields a tractable ELBO-based stacking objective. Across real-world probabilistic inference tasks, our method achieves comparable predictive performance to Bayesian model averaging while yielding more dispersed model weights, reducing concentration on a single candidate model under misspecification.

papers.title: Reachability Diameter: Beyond the Square-Root Barrier, with Polynomial Hardness
papers.abstract:
The reachability diameter of a directed graph is the maximum finite shortest-path distance across all pairs of vertices. It has received recent attention under this name, although the underlying quantity has long played a central role in shortcut set and parallel reachability. Notably, Bals et al. establish hardness for every polynomial-factor approximation in nearly-linear time for weighted digraphs. Yet they give $n^{1/2+o(1)}$-approximation in the unweighted regime with nearly-linear running time, and their conditional lower bounds rule out certain constants only, leaving open whether polynomial loss is necessary.
  We give a randomized algorithm that estimates the reachability diameter of an unweighted digraph within a factor $n^{1/3+o(1)}$, with high probability, in $\widetilde{O}(m+n)$ time. We complement our algorithm with a lower bound conditional on the 3-uniform Hyperclique hypothesis, ruling out an $n^{2/15-\varepsilon}$-approximation in $\widetilde{O}(m+n)$ time for every fixed $\varepsilon\in(0,2/15)$, establishing the necessity of polynomial loss for nearly-linear time algorithms.

papers.title: Constructing Cospectral Hypergraphs Using Adjacency Preserving Permutations
papers.abstract: In this paper, we use permutations of the vertices of hypergraphs that preserve their adjacency matrices defined in banerjee 2021. These permutations form a group which lies between the automorphism group and the full symmetric group $S_n$ where $n$ is the number of vertices. Using elements from that group which are not automorphisms, we construct cospectral non-isomorphic hypergraphs. We use hypergraph structure coming from finite projective planes to show existence of infinitely many families of such hypergraphs. Also this method is very specific to uniform hypergraphs with uniformity greater than or equal to 3, i.e not applicable to graphs.

papers.title: Controls on the deformation and reorientation of mafic enclaves during magma mingling: A computational study
papers.abstract: Mafic microgranular enclaves in granitic plutons record magma mingling, and their shapes are often interpreted as a record of the flow that deformed them. We investigate how a dense, low-viscosity droplet deforms in a lighter, much more viscous host under shear and gravity, using 96 two-dimensional Level-Set simulations.
