papers.title: Geometric ergodicity of the block Gibbs sampler for Bayesian linear mixed models with scale mixtures of normal random effects
papers.abstract: We study a Bayesian linear mixed model whose random effects follow a scale mixture of normal distributions with an arbitrary mixing distribution, a class that contains the Student-t, slash, contaminated normal, normal-generalized inverse Gaussian and Laplace laws. Conditionally conjugate priors lead to a three-block Gibbs sampler that alternates between the variance components, the latent precision weights, and the regression coefficients together with the random effects. Using a drift function built from fractional powers, we give sufficient conditions for geometric ergodicity of this chain, which involve a moment of the mixing distribution of some order larger than 1/2 and its behaviour near the origin. An equivariance of the sampler under rescaling of the design then shows that the conditions hold for all the families above, including Student-t random effects with any degrees of freedom, for every random-effects design matrix, full rank or not, with the rank entering only the conditions on the priors of the variance components. Together with posterior moment bounds, geometric ergodicity justifies Monte Carlo standard errors and effective-sample-size stopping rules for the regression coefficients and the log-variance components. Simulations examine these procedures at practical run lengths: joint confidence regions need a correction for the number of batches, and under sequential stopping their observed coverage remains slightly below the nominal level. We illustrate the methods with longitudinal beta-HCG measurements from early pregnancies, in which the latent weights reveal larger between-subject variability among abnormal pregnancies.

papers.title: Projected and Reflected Sliced Wasserstein Kernels for Persistence Diagrams
papers.abstract: Persistence diagrams do not naturally live in a Hilbert space. Carri\`ere, Cuturi, and Oudot embedded them in kernel methods through the Sliced Wasserstein kernel, built from the Sliced Wasserstein distance $\mathrm{SW}_1$, which is conditionally negative definite (CND). We study the projected ($\mathrm{SW}_p$) and reflected ($\mathrm{RW}_p$) Sliced Wasserstein distances for every order $p\ge1$, and compare them with the $p$-Wasserstein distance $d_p$ and with a reflected variant $d_p^r$, in which projection onto the diagonal is replaced by reflection across it. We show that $2^{1/p}d_p\le d_p^r\le 2d_p$ with sharp constants, so that $d_1^r=2d_1$ and $d_p^r$ inherits the stability of $d_p$, although it is a metric only for $p=1$. The distances $\mathrm{SW}_1$ and $\mathrm{RW}_1$ are CND metrics, and $\mathrm{RW}_1$ gives rise to a new positive definite kernel, stable with respect to $d_1$. For $p>1$, neither $\mathrm{SW}_p$ nor $\mathrm{RW}_p$ satisfies the triangle inequality, and rigorous interval-arithmetic certificates prove that $\mathrm{SW}_2$ and $\mathrm{RW}_2$ are not CND; numerical experiments suggest that the CND property fails for every $p$ above some $p^*\in(1,1.2]$. On diagrams with at most $N$ points, $\mathrm{SW}_p$ and $\mathrm{RW}_p$ are metrically equivalent to $d_p$ and $d_p^r$, with sharp upper constants. On an orbit recognition benchmark, the kernels built from $\mathrm{SW}_1$ and $\mathrm{RW}_1$ reach about 85% accuracy, outperform the persistence scale space kernel, perform on par with the persistence weighted Gaussian kernel, and are about one percentage point below the kernel built from $\mathrm{SW}_2$, which is not positive definite.

papers.title: Diophantine definability from addition and divisibility over rings of $S$-integers
papers.abstract: Let $K$ be a number field, let $S$ be a finite set of places of $K$ containing the archimedean places, and let $\mathcal{O}_{K,S}$ denote the ring of $S$-integers of $K$. We prove that multiplication is positive-existentially definable in $(\mathcal{O}_{K,S},0,1,+,\mid)$ if and only if the unit group $\mathcal{O}_{K,S}^\times$ is infinite. This extends a 1977 theorem of Lipshitz for rings of integers to rings of $S$-integers. One of the key ingredients is a uniform bound for unit equations due to Evertse, Schlickewei and Schmidt, which we use to recover multiplication on the unit group.

papers.title: CoordX Protocol: Peer to Peer Cryptographically Verified Shared Records
papers.abstract:
People, companies and software agents often must work on shared records even when they do not trust each other. Today they usually give those records to a central server. The server keeps the canonical copy, authenticates users, and decides who has permissions to act on the record. The CoordX Protocol removes the need for that central server.
  In the CoordX protocol the author of a record holds full permission over it. Permission for any other party to create, read or update the record is assigned by explicit grants and keys. An invitation only starts contact between two parties. It gives no permission. Each record is a causal tree of signed entries, and each entry is immutable. Each entry names the permission that allowed it. Any party can get the proof of that permission and check it without help from anyone. Two honest parties that check the same bytes, with the same keys and local settings, always get the same answer. The content is encrypted, so the relays that may carry it in transit see only sealed bytes. To exclude a party from future content, the other parties move to new keys. The protocol does not choose a winning version, does not put entries in time order, and does not need global agreement. Applications decide what the entries mean above the level of the protocol.

papers.title: Finite Spectral Depth Controls Gaussian Entrance Rank and Avoidance of the First Gradient-Flow Saddle
papers.abstract: Matrix factorization provides a simple model for studying the training dynamics of neural networks. Recent studies of gradient flow under small initialization have analyzed how trajectories escape from a neighborhood of the origin and approach their first nonzero stationary point. In this paper, we study continuous-time dynamics that applies a finite number of Newton-Schulz iterations to the normalized matrix gradient (Muon). We show that the number of Newton-Schulz steps can change the rank selected during the early stages of training and allow the resulting trajectory to bypass the first nonzero stationary point approached by gradient flow. Under an additional residual-inertia condition, we prove that bypass occurs for all sufficiently large finite Newton-Schulz depths and provide an explicit sufficient threshold. We also construct an example in which the bypass threshold is four.

papers.title: C-WFDM: A ControlNet-Guided Wavelet-Fusion Diffusion Model for Multimodal Brain MRI Completion
papers.abstract: Multimodal brain MRI provides complementary anatomical, tissue, and pathological information to support downstream artificial intelligence (AI) applications. However, modality availability is uneven across public and pooled neuroimaging datasets: T1-weighted (T1w) MRI is widely represented, T2-weighted (T2w) and fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) MRI are less consistently available, and gadolinium-enhanced T1-weighted (T1Gd) MRI is relatively scarce. Pooled datasets therefore contain participants with different combinations of acquired MRI contrasts, reflecting variation in the study designs, acquisition protocols, and clinical or research objectives of the contributing studies. Many missing-modality benchmarks simulate incomplete MRI by withholding contrasts from complete four-modality cases, which may not represent the observed availability patterns in pooled datasets. To address this gap, we introduce C-WFDM, a ControlNet extension of our Wavelet-Fusion Diffusion Model (WFDM), for subject-specific missing-modality completion. C-WFDM is built on an earlier BrainScape snapshot comprising 157 public MRI datasets and 45,880 preprocessed scans. The pretrained WFDM backbone retains target-modality and metadata conditioning, while target-specific ControlNet adapters use MRI contrasts from the same participant to guide synthesis. C-WFDM synthesizes T2w from T1w, FLAIR from T1w and T2w, and T1Gd from T1w, T2w, and FLAIR. Acquired conditioning contrasts are used when available, and generated intermediate contrasts are used only when required. We compare C-WFDM with ALDM, cWDM, and Pix2Pix using paired structural similarity index (SSIM), peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR), and mean absolute error (MAE). In the BrainScape completion experiment, C-WFDM achieves the best T2w and FLAIR results among the evaluated models, with SSIM values of 0.9232 and 0.8904, respectively.

papers.title: Geometric Multigrid Preconditioners for conforming Finite Element Methods on Arbitrarily Agglomerated Meshes
papers.abstract: Geometric multigrid methods for conforming finite element discretisations classically require a nested mesh hierarchy, forcing coarse meshes to be conforming, which is unsuitable for general domains. In order to eliminate this geometric constraint, we introduce and analyse a family of multilevel auxiliary space preconditioners. At the first level, a conforming Lagrangian discretisation on a fine simplicial mesh is preconditioned by a non-conforming polytopal discretisation posed on an arbitrarily agglomerated coarse mesh. At the subsequent levels, the coarse problem is solved by a geometric multigrid method for that polytopal discretisation on further agglomerated meshes, so that the whole hierarchy is generated from the fine mesh by agglomeration alone. We consider two polytopal discretisations, a symmetric interior penalty discontinuous Galerkin method and a hybrid high-order method. The prolongation operator at the first level is an element-wise interpolation onto the fine mesh followed by nodal averaging, preceded in the hybrid high-order case by a local potential reconstruction. For point-Jacobi and vertex-star patch additive Schwarz smoothers, we prove that the condition number of the preconditioned system is bounded by $O((H/h)^3)$, where $H/h$ is the coarsening ratio, and by $O((H/h)^2)$ for the DG variant with penalty proportional to $H/h$. Numerical experiments in two and three dimensions, on structured and unstructured meshes with agglomerates generated by automatic clustering algorithms, confirm the robustness of the preconditioners.

papers.title: Honest Small Decision Models for Finance: Scale, Specialization Collapse, and Mixed-Corpus Remediation
papers.abstract: Financial workflows need fast, calibrated, auditable decisions, not just generated text. We train System-1 decision models, small language models fine-tuned to answer typed questions (choice/score/noul) with a probability in a single forward pass, across two model families (K2-Horizon and Qwen3.5/3.8) and nine rungs from 0.8B to 32B parameters, using one frozen LoRA recipe on a public decision benchmark and two new finance corpora: a programmatic-gold policy corpus (rule-reading with exact labels) and a reality-labeled outcome corpus (19,640 realized forward-return questions in walk-forward splits, plus a sealed 2026 test of 1,360 questions). Narrow fine-tuning costs general decision competence 9-45 percentage points, a data-mixture effect that shrinks with model scale and is associated with narrow-gradient volume. On reality-labeled questions, every trained rung from 0.8B to 32B lands at the horizon-conditioned prior baseline (accuracy 0.37-0.38, no detectable conditional edge under our controls); the models respond with flat, well-calibrated probabilities that track per-horizon base rates: naturally honest uncertainty, with a mid-scale calibration sweet spot (ECE 0.026 at 2B, degrading to 0.043-0.044 at 9-32B under prior drift). A mixed-corpus remediation carries all competencies in one adapter at modest cost: it matches or slightly exceeds the generalist specialist on the public benchmark while holding the policy ceiling and near-specialist outcome calibration, yielding a deployable artifact with per-domain temperature regimes and a band-dispatch escalation analysis: sharp, dispatchable bands where rules determine answers; flat, review-routing bands where reality does not.
papers.intro:
A trading desk, a compliance team, and a credit officer all need the same primitive: given a state and a typed question, a probability, not a paragraph. Recent “System-1” decision models (TypeSafe AI, 2026) make this primitive architectural: the model consumes a state and typed questions (choice over options, score on an ordinal scale, noul returning P⁡(yes)P(\mathrm{yes})) and emits calibrated probabilities in one forward pass, at latencies and sizes suitable for production gates. Production deployments exist at exactly this shape (Cloudflare’s clef is a 27B decision model post-trained from Qwen3.8-27B (Cloudflare, 2026); the this-that model serves typed decisions in 30 ms at a millionth of a cent (Cheng et al., 2026)), and a growing open ecosystem (imajev (mohit67890, 2026), strands-decider (strands-labs, 2026), decider (Mapika, 2026), kev (Palmer, 2026)) publishes recipes and leaderboards.

Recent “System-1” decision models (TypeSafe AI, 2026) make this primitive architectural: the model consumes a state and typed questions (choice over options, score on an ordinal scale, noul returning P⁡(yes)P(\mathrm{yes})) and emits calibrated probabilities in one forward pass, at latencies and sizes suitable for production gates. Production deployments exist at exactly this shape (Cloudflare’s clef is a 27B decision model post-trained from Qwen3.8-27B (Cloudflare, 2026); the this-that model serves typed decisions in 30 ms at a millionth of a cent (Cheng et al., 2026)), and a growing open ecosystem (imajev (mohit67890, 2026), strands-decider (strands-labs, 2026), decider (Mapika, 2026), kev (Palmer, 2026)) publishes recipes and leaderboards.

But three questions matter before an institution fine-tunes its own small decision layer, and the open literature answers none of them for the finance domain. (1) What happens to probability quality when the labels come from reality? Decision-model training sets use clean or programmatically-solved labels; financial outcomes are noisy, regime-drifting, and close to unpredictable from standard technical features. (2) What does domain fine-tuning destroy? papers.title: DRAP: Dynamics-Risk Adaptive Plasticity for Continual Learning in Physical AI
papers.abstract: Continual learning in physical AI differs from conventional continual learning because small per-step policy errors can accumulate over a trajectory. Each deviation may move the agent outside the training distribution, increase subsequent prediction errors, and ultimately cause closed-loop task failure. This work introduces Dynamics-Risk Adaptive Plasticity (DRAP), a replay-free method that estimates the historical importance of adaptable model tensors from sample-level action gradients weighted by local trajectory-amplification risk. A ridge-regularized local linear model is fitted to expert state-action transitions, and the largest singular value of its state-transition matrix provides a policy-independent, Lyapunov-inspired estimate of one-step perturbation amplification. After each task, risk-weighted squared gradients are accumulated in a tensor-level importance memory. During subsequent tasks, DRAP uses normalized cumulative importance to scale the effective AdamW learning rate of each tensor, immediately reducing the plasticity of components that supported previous behavior at dynamically sensitive trajectory points. We instantiate DRAP on a fixed KappaTune-selected subnetwork of OpenVLA and evaluate replay-free sequential adaptation across the LIBERO Spatial, Object, and Goal suites. Compared with standard AdamW fine-tuning and EWC, the results show substantially improved retention of previously learned behaviors while preserving strong new-suite acquisition.
papers.intro:
Continual learning in physical AI differs from conventional continual learning because small changes in a policy can alter future observations and amplify into closed-loop task failure. In embodied control, an action error changes the next physical state, modifies the next observation, and may place the policy outside the training distribution. Subsequent errors can therefore compound over the remainder of the trajectory [1, 2].

Vision-language-action (VLA) models combine visual perception, language grounding, and low-level control within a single pretrained policy. OpenVLA provides an open 7B VLA with tokenized actions and a pretrained vision-language backbone [3]. OpenVLA-OFT later demonstrated that continuous actions, action chunking, and optimized decoding can substantially improve success and inference efficiency [4]. These advances strengthen task acquisition, but do not remove the continual-learning problem: sequential fine-tuning can overwrite behavior required by earlier manipulation skills.

Existing continual-learning strategies offer complementary trade-offs. Replay remains a strong baseline but requires storing or regenerating previous observations. Expansion and routing methods isolate tasks but add modules or routing mechanisms. Parameter-regularization methods preserve a previous solution but can restrict acquisition. Direct update-suppression methods reduce future plasticity according to past update history, but can become too restrictive for large heterogeneous models.

Unlike reference-based consolidation methods, the proposed Dynamics-Risk Adaptive Plasticity (DRAP) does not penalize parameter displacement from a previously stored checkpoint. Instead, similar to CLASSP [5], it uses accumulated historical importance to directly regulate future plasticity. Protection is therefore active from the first update of each subsequent learning stage and does not require storing reference copies of the adaptable parameters.

Section III describes the sequential LIBERO evaluation protocol. Section IV motivates the dynamics-risk signal from the compounding-error perspective of imitation learning, and Section V formalizes the replay-free continual learning problem. Section VI presents the DRAP method, including the KappaTune-based subnetwork selection, the local dynamics-risk estimator, the risk-weighted tensor importance, and the tensor-specific learning-rate control. Section VII reports the experimental results, including ablations of KappaTune selection and of dynamics-risk weighting. Finally, Section VIII concludes and outlines directions for future work.

papers.title: Same Origin, Different Verdicts: Text Production Conditions Confound Machine-Generated Text Detection in Russian
papers.abstract: Automated detection of machine-generated text is applied where the verdict carries a cost for the author, yet origin is a property of the production process, not an observable property of the text. The conditions under which a text is produced push it in the same direction in which a generative model is presumed to push it. This study measures the contribution of these conditions while origin is held fixed. The Russian-language corpus of 1882 documents comprises a machine part, generated by four generation channels (each backed by its own model family) across 45 tasks in three task modes, and an archival human part annotated for source regimentation level before the texts were read. The primary contrast is computed within the machine corpus: both halves of a pair are generated by the same model for the same task and differ only in task wording. Machine-likeness is measured by four operationalisations: an interpretable index with weights fixed before data collection, a trained classifier, a zero-shot metric on an open model, a judge model. The main result is disagreement between procedures: changing the task mode shifted the scores of all four, but three gave a negative shift, the judge a positive one, and none of the four intervals covers zero. The comparison plan and the specifications of procedures 2-4 were fixed after the result of procedure 1, before procedures 2-4 ran; the disagreement survived correction of a corpus defect and of the nested validation. A baseline on the source identifier alone reaches a median AUROC of 1.0000 on the thirteen group splits where it is defined, and removing emphasis markers flipped a confident machine verdict to human without changing the full text by a single character. The scores are properties of a specific measurement system and corpus: they reflect data collection, repetition, formatting, and preprocessing decisions as well as linguistic style.

Automated assessment of text origin is applied where the decision carries a cost: checking student work, moderating platforms, screening contractors, editorial policies. A verdict of "machine-written"carries consequences for the author, and so the question of what exactly a detector measures stops being a technical one.

In the accusatory scenario, therefore, what decides is not average accuracy but the detector’s behaviour at a low false positive rate — and on this characteristic systems diverge dramatically.

papers.title: SRRM: A Retrieval-Reconstruction Benchmark for Evaluating Long-Context Memory in Small Language Models
papers.abstract: Small Language Models (SLMs) are increasingly deployed on consumer-grade hardware, yet their ability to preserve information across progressively longer contexts remains insufficiently understood. Existing benchmarks primarily evaluate retrieval-oriented tasks, providing limited insight into whether successful retrieval reflects comprehensive long-context memory preservation. To address this limitation, this paper introduces Simple Retrieval-Reconstruction Memory (SRRM), a lightweight and fully reproducible benchmark that jointly evaluates Targeted Retrieval and Global Information Reconstruction. This study also proposes the Memory Preservation Ratio (MPR), a benchmark-level metric that quantifies the relationship between retrieval and reconstruction performance. SRRM was evaluated using a synthetic dataset on three Qwen2.5 models (0.5B, 1.5B, and 3B parameters) across context loads ranging from 10 to 100 factual statements. Experimental results show that reconstruction performance deteriorated substantially faster than retrieval accuracy as contextual information increased, indicating that retrieval alone is insufficient to characterize long-context memory preservation. Among the evaluated models, Qwen2.5-1.5B achieved the highest retrieval accuracy (86.7%), reconstruction performance (45.7%), and MPR (0.53), outperforming the larger Qwen2.5-3B model (72.2%, 18.5%, and 0.26, respectively). These findings demonstrate that increasing parameter count does not necessarily improve long-context memory preservation. Overall, SRRM provides a reproducible and extensible benchmark for systematically evaluating long-context memory while revealing complementary memory behaviors that remain hidden under retrieval-only evaluation frameworks.

papers.title: Deterministic Network Interface Naming on Multi-NIC Linux Systems: A Boot-Time Convergence Approach
papers.abstract: Network interface naming on multi-NIC Linux systems suffers from a well-documented race condition in systemd-udevd that has remained unsolved since 2017. When multiple network interfaces are present, parallel udev worker threads attempt to rename interfaces simultaneously, causing EEXIST failures when a target name is temporarily occupied by another interface awaiting its own rename. The upstream systemd project has classified this as "not-a-bug" and declines to implement a fix. The problem, previously cosmetic under NetworkManager, has become critical as the industry migrates to systemd-networkd, which matches interfaces by name rather than MAC address, turning a failed rename into a complete loss of network connectivity. This paper presents a boot-time convergence approach that combines systemd .link file declarations with a retry-based init service that detects and recovers from rename failures before dependent services start. Deployed across diverse multi-NIC hardware configurations, the solution achieves 100% deterministic interface naming. The approach is OS-agnostic and applicable to any systemd-based Linux distribution.

papers.title: Streaming OS Installation from Compressed Partitioned Images on Memory-Constrained Bare-Metal Hosts
papers.abstract: Bare-metal server provisioning systems typically decompress OS images into RAM before writing them to disk. When servers have insufficient RAM to hold the decompressed image (increasingly common as OS images grow due to AI/ML toolkits, GPU drivers, and firmware stacks), provisioning fails entirely. This paper presents a streaming installation technique that combines partial decompression for metadata extraction with pipeline-based disk writing, enabling OS installation on hosts where available RAM is less than the decompressed image size. The method decompresses only the first 30MB of a compressed image to extract the GPT partition table, calculates the target filesystem offset, then streams the full image through a kernel pipe buffer (64KB) directly to disk at the calculated offset, never storing the decompressed data in memory or on disk. Deployed across a production fleet of memory-constrained bare-metal servers, the technique achieves 100% provisioning success where the standard approach fails entirely.

papers.title: Unlocking Turing Tensor Cores: A Measured Throughput Account of From-Scratch Pre-training on a Single 22G RTX 2080 Ti
papers.abstract: The RTX 2080 Ti (TU102) ships full second-generation Tensor Cores in hardware, yet the vendor throttles FP16 matrix multiplication at the driver level, leaving usable tensor throughput well below the hardware peak. turing-unlock lifts this restriction with a kernel module that, before the nvidia driver binds the device, writes the FP16 speed selectors (SS0=0x88888888, SS1=0x8) and releases the ACR mutex; published measurements report cuBLAS FP16 matmul throughput rising from 55.7 to 91.4 TFLOPS (about 1.6x). On the same 22G 2080 Ti and under the same from-scratch pre-training protocol as the companion memory ledger (five tiers of Chinese encoder-decoder models, 2,451 steps per tier, 16,384 tokens per step, seed 42), we obtain a before/after throughput account: the small tier (75.7M parameters, 512-wide, 8+8 layers, activation checkpointing on) improves in steady-state throughput from 6,480 to 7,246 tok/s (+11.8%) with wall time cut from 1.77h to 1.61h (9.0% saved); the tiny tier goes from 15,150 to 15,866 tok/s (+4.7%) with wall time savings of 3.8%; the three smaller tiers (pico-micro) gain at most +0.3%; per-tier peak memory stays bit-identical, and final quality metrics are bit-identical or consistent within 10^-3. We conclude that the unlock gain is a function of matrix size, rising monotonically with tier -- imperceptible for pico-micro, visible from tiny upward, and cashed out as a double-digit percentage at small -- and that it is a pure throughput gain that leaves training dynamics untouched.
papers.intro:
[1] presents a complete memory ledger for from-scratch pre-training of Chinese encoder–decoder models on a single 22G RTX 2080 Ti: every line item of static parameters, optimizer state and activations is laid out, and activation checkpointing together with gradient accumulation squeezes a 75.7M-parameter model onto one card. The memory ledger answers “can we afford to train”; once the answer is yes, the immediate next question is “how long”. Under a fixed budget of 16,384 tokens per step and 2,451 steps per tier, throughput (token/s) maps one-to-one onto wall time: throughput is cost.

The TU102 ships full second-generation Tensor Cores, but since the Turing era NVIDIA has throttled FP16 matrix multiplication at the driver level on consumer cards, keeping usable tensor throughput far below the hardware peak. papers.title: Logarithmically Slim Polygons
papers.abstract:
We study the relationship between the large-scale geometry of a geodesic metric space and the slimness of its geodesic polygons. We show that if there is a uniform constant $\delta$ such that every geodesic polygon in an unbounded geodesic metric space is $\delta$-slim, then the space has asymptotic Assouad--Nagata dimension one.
  We further consider graphs of bounded valency and allow the slimness constant of an $n$-gon to grow logarithmically with $n$. More precisely, under an explicit logarithmic bound on the slimness of geodesic $n$-gons, we prove that the graph has asymptotic Assouad--Nagata dimension one. Thus, sufficiently strong logarithmic control on the slimness of geodesic polygons forces one-dimensional large-scale geometry.
  We also obtain two criteria for graphs, outside the hyperbolic setting, to have asymptotic Assouad--Nagata dimension one. In particular, these criteria show that one-dimensional large-scale geometry can be detected from quantitative restrictions on the slimness of geodesic polygons, without requiring the space to be hyperbolic.

papers.title: The Search for the Top Quark
papers.abstract: The discovery of the top quark in 1995 completed the roster of the matter particles, quarks and leptons, expected in the Standard Model and in many of its suggested extensions. However, the top quark does not conform to the pattern set by its sister quarks and has come to be a critical component of the ongoing searches for physics beyond the prevailing paradigm. (Prepared for the Proceedings of the 4th International Symposium on the History of Particle Physics, CERN, Nov. 2025.)

papers.title: Hybrid Spark: Adaptive Speculative Decoding That Lets the Content Choose the Drafter
papers.abstract: Speculative decoding (SD) speeds up large language model (LLM) serving, but its gain depends on the workload's \emph{shape}, such as batch size and context length, and on its \emph{content}. A model-based drafter proposes a short block on any content, while a model-free drafter such as n-gram lookup proposes long copies at almost no cost when the output repeats its input, as in code editing. Adaptive verification spends a batch-wide verification budget on the draft tokens most likely to be accepted, but it supports only one model-based drafter. Model-free drafters provide no per-token confidence, so they cannot take part in budget allocation, and deployments must either fix one drafter or split their GPUs between drafters. We present \sys, a framework that runs a model-based and a model-free drafter on every step and gives each request the better of their chains, within adaptive verification and entirely on the GPU, which keeps asynchronous scheduling intact. The key idea is a price per verified draft token: the goodput that slot would earn elsewhere in the batch. Once the model-free drafter's tokens carry calibrated acceptance estimates, fit once on general text, this price puts both drafters' chains on one scale. Instantiated with \dspark and an n-gram drafter in vLLM, \sys achieves 1.10--1.62\x the output throughput of \dspark on code editing at batch size~4 and 1.04--1.27\x at batch size~128, while staying at 0.97--1.01\x of it on chat at temperature~0. A single deployment can therefore serve both workloads.
papers.intro:
Decoding dominates the cost of serving large language models (LLMs). At each step, the model reads its weights and KV cache to produce one token per request, leaving much of the available compute idle in memory-bound regimes (Pope et al., 2023). Speculative decoding (SD) (Leviathan et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2023) exploits this idle compute: a cheap drafter proposes several tokens, and the target model verifies them in a single forward pass while preserving the output distribution. The benefit depends on how many tokens are accepted relative to the cost of drafting and verification.

This tradeoff changes with both batch size and content. At small batch sizes, verifying additional tokens is relatively cheap, and longer drafts can substantially improve throughput. As the batch grows, verification becomes more expensive, and verifying too many tokens can make SD slower than vanilla decoding (Liu et al., 2026c; Liu et al., 2024). Adaptive verification, as in TurboSpec (Liu et al., 2024), DSpark (Cheng et al., 2026), and D-cut (Liu et al., 2026b), addresses this problem by adjusting the verification budget at each step and allocating it to draft tokens most likely to be accepted. The budget also responds to content: low-entropy domains such as coding and math tend to accept longer drafts than roleplay or creative writing (Abramovich et al., 2026).

Yet adaptive verification assumes that the drafter has already been chosen. It decides how much of a draft to verify, but not which drafter should produce it. This distinction matters because different drafters exploit different kinds of predictability. Model-based drafters learn to predict the target’s continuation and work across general text. Model-free drafters instead exploit repetition, copying tokens from the prompt or previously generated text. The best drafter therefore depends not only on how predictable the next tokens are, but also on where that predictability comes from.

Model-free drafters instead exploit repetition, copying tokens from the prompt or previously generated text. The best drafter therefore depends not only on how predictable the next tokens are, but also on where that predictability comes from.

Code editing makes this difference particularly clear. Given an existing program and a request to modify it, the model often reproduces large portions of the original code, changing only a few regions. A model-based drafter can predict these tokens, but its draft length is limited. An n-gram drafter can instead copy much longer continuations directly from the prompt, at little cost. On the NextCoder code-editing workload with Qwen3-4B at batch size (BS) 4, DSpark, which drafts seven tokens per step, achieves 4.17–5.00×\times speedup over vanilla decoding across edit distances from 0% to 70%. An n-gram drafter that proposes up to 15 tokens achieves 7.42×\times speedup when the output is nearly identical to the input, but falls to 1.80×\times on heavy rewrites (Figure 1). Neither drafter is uniformly better: copying wins when the output repeats the input, while model-based drafting is more robust when the output changes substantially.

This creates a practical problem for serving systems. A deployment serving both editing and general requests must either choose one drafter for all traffic or maintain separate deployments for different workloads. The former leaves performance on the table: using DSpark everywhere misses the gains from copying on light edits. The latter fragments GPU capacity across pools whose traffic varies over time, requiring each to be provisioned for its own peak. Ideally, a single deployment would use the better drafter for each request, and adapt that choice as generation progresses.

Combining drafters, however, is not as simple as running both and taking the longer draft. The two drafters produce different kinds of predictions, compete for the same verification budget, and must be compared at every decoding step without introducing overhead. This raises three challenges: • (C1) Estimating acceptance for model-free drafts. Model-based drafters provide token confidences, but an n-gram match only identifies a possible continuation, not how likely the target is to accept it. Without acceptance estimates, model-free drafts cannot participate in adaptive verification or be compared with model-based drafts. • (C2) Choosing between competing draft chains. Each request now has two candidate chains that may agree, diverge, or differ entirely. Verifying both requires tree attention or increases verification cost, while choosing one requires a common scale and a price that reflects the rest of the batch. Existing hybrids (Oliaro et al., 2025) select the model-free chain when its score exceeds a fixed threshold, ignoring both the changing cost of verification and what other requests could gain from the same slots. • (C3) Making the decision practical at serving scale. Drafter selection must run at every decoding step, entirely on the GPU and at negligible cost, without host-device synchronization. Otherwise, it undermines asynchronous scheduling and CUDA graph execution. Existing CPU-based hybrid approaches (Oliaro et al., 2025) incur this synchronization. The system must also preserve the target model’s output distribution.

papers.title: Quadratic reset bounds for finite maximal prefix codes
papers.abstract: Let $C$ be a finite maximal prefix code of maximum codeword length $k\ge2$. We prove that, whenever the literal decoder of $C$ is synchronizing, it has a reset word of length at most $(k-1)(4k-5)$. The bound is independent of the alphabet and the number of decoder states. Its main ingredient is a short-detection theorem: a linear observation of the decoder, with terminal weight constant on states of depth $k-1$, is either identically zero or nonzero on a word of length at most $2k-3$. The proof uses a first-return decomposition in noncommuting variables and cancellation of a highest-degree coefficient. For codes whose codeword lengths are $k-1$ and $k$, we prove the sharper bound $2(k-1)^2-1$ and characterize equality. The binary code with the single short word $a^{k-1}$ attains this bound for every $k\ge2$; an age representation and a potential on circular arcs give the matching lower bound. Both upper bounds yield polynomial-time constructions in the explicit code size. The mathematical results and the algorithms are formalized in Lean, with polynomial work bounds in a specified binary cost model.
papers.intro:
A prefix code can be decoded as soon as a complete codeword has been read. If the starting position is unknown, however, different parsings may persist. A reset word removes this uncertainty: after reading it, every possible state of the decoder is the same. For the code {a,b​a,b​b}\{a,ba,bb\}, the letter aa is a reset word. The decoder is either at the root or has just read bb, and in both cases aa completes a codeword. For the code {a​a,a​b,b​a,b​b}\{aa,ab,ba,bb\}, no word resets the decoder, since the two possible depth parities remain different.

papers.title: Toward an Optimal Configuration for Tree Species Classification from Bark Images: A Leakage-Safe Ablation Study
papers.abstract: Background: The automatic identification of tree species from bark photographs is of practical interest for forestry inventory and the wood-processing industry, yet the design choices that govern the accuracy of deep-learning approaches have not been studied systematically, and some prior results may be inflated by leakage of images of the same trunk across training and test partitions. Methods: A systematic ablation study is conducted on the public BarkNet 1.0 dataset (20 species) under the established tree-level, leakage-safe partitioning scheme. Using ConvNeXt-V2 backbones, the following factors are varied in turn and evaluated by five-fold cross-validation: patch size, the strategy by which per-patch predictions are aggregated into an image-level decision, the training regime (single- versus two-stage), backbone capacity, the whole-image baseline, and the number of patches available at inference. Results: Per-patch accuracy rises monotonically with patch size (from 75.6% at 160 px to 89.6% at 512 px), and image-level accuracy rises in step, plateauing near 94.9% around 512 px. Learned aggregation exceeds majority voting by at most 0.7 pp, an advantage that shrinks as patches grow and attention becomes near-uniform. Backbone capacity (pico to tiny) alters accuracy by less than a point, and two-stage training offers no advantage over one-stage. Whole-image classification (91.9%) trails patch-based aggregation, since it admits no bag to average over; accuracy increases with the number of patches at inference, saturating around 64. Conclusions: The study yields a simple recommended configuration: patches as large as possible while leaving enough to average over (around 512 px here), with a nano backbone. It also quantifies the second-order role of learned aggregation and model capacity, providing a reproducible reference point for practitioners and future research
papers.intro:
The identification of tree species is a routine but labour-intensive task in forest inventory, ecological monitoring, and the grading and pricing of timber in the wood-processing industry, and automating it with computer vision has attracted sustained interest over the past decade [1, 2]. Most automated systems identify plants from leaves, flowers, or fruit [1], which are seasonal and frequently out of reach on a standing trunk. Bark, by contrast, is visible throughout the year and remains accessible on both standing and felled trunks, and its texture varies comparatively little with season; these properties have made it an attractive cue for automated identification [3, 4, 5, 6].

Bark, by contrast, is visible throughout the year and remains accessible on both standing and felled trunks, and its texture varies comparatively little with season; these properties have made it an attractive cue for automated identification [3, 4, 5, 6].

Early approaches to bark recognition relied on hand-crafted texture descriptors, such as local binary pattern variants and statistical radial binary patterns [3, 5]. The feasibility of learning such features directly was established by Carpentier et al. [6], who released the BarkNet 1.0 dataset and reported strong accuracy by classifying image crops with a convolutional network and aggregating the per-crop predictions through hard majority voting. Subsequent work has pursued higher accuracy with more capable backbones; Cui et al. [4], for example, reported near-saturated single-image accuracy on an extended dataset using a ConvNeXt architecture [7]. Beyond BarkNet 1.0, larger bark benchmarks have since been released, including Bark-101 [8] and the recent CentralBark dataset [9].

Viewed more abstractly, bark recognition is an instance of fine-grained visual categorization [2]: the classes are visually similar sub-categories separated by subtle, texture-like cues rather than by object shape. It also shares its computational structure with a broader family of tasks in which a single image is too large or too heterogeneous to classify directly and is instead tiled into patches whose predictions are aggregated into an image-level decision. This tile-and-aggregate paradigm is central to computational pathology, where gigapixel whole-slide images are split into thousands of patches and combined by multiple instance learning [10, 11, 12], and it recurs in remote sensing and document analysis. The design questions examined here, namely how large each tile should be, how many are needed, and how their predictions should be combined, are therefore not specific to bark, and the conclusions may inform other tile-based fine-grained recognition tasks.

Despite this progress, two issues limit the practical value of the existing literature. First, the design choices that determine accuracy (the resolution at which bark is sampled, the manner in which patch-level evidence is combined, the training procedure, the capacity of the backbone, and the number of patches required at inference) have largely been adopted by convention. Individual choices have been studied in isolation, for instance patch extraction and majority-voting rules for bark by Misra et al. [13], but they have not been compared jointly and on a common footing, so no consolidated guidance exists as to the configuration a practitioner should adopt. Second, when a dataset contains several photographs of the same trunk, partitioning the data at the level of individual images rather than at the level of trees allows near-identical views of a trunk to appear in both training and test sets; the resulting leakage can inflate the reported accuracy and obscure the true difficulty of the task. This is a failure mode documented across many machine-learning-based sciences [14] and guarded against, for example, by patient-level splitting in computational pathology [11]. On BarkNet 1.0, Carpentier et al. [6] adopted a tree-level split, which we retain; some more recent studies instead report image-level results that, as this study shows, can be optimistic.

Accordingly, the present study does not seek to introduce a new architecture or to maximise a single headline figure. Instead, a systematic and leakage-safe ablation study is conducted, in which each principal design choice is varied in isolation and its effect on accuracy is quantified under a common, tree-level evaluation protocol. The aim is to establish which configuration is most effective for bark-based species classification, and by how much each factor matters, so that the result may serve as a dependable starting point for both industrial deployment and future research.

papers.title: Incremental Minimum Spanning Trees on a Napkin
papers.abstract: In the incremental minimum spanning forest problem, weighted edges arrive one at a time. After each insertion we must report the edge that leaves the minimum spanning forest, and queries ask for the bottleneck distance of two vertices: the smallest possible maximum edge cost on a path between them. Link-cut trees solve both in $O(\log n)$ amortized time. In 2021 we wrote the folklore BottleneckTree, a short competitive-programming structure that stores one parent pointer and one cost per vertex, and conjectured that it also runs in $O(\log n)$ amortized time. We show that this conjecture is false: on a family of inputs, its amortized cost per operation is $\Omega(\sqrt{n})$. We then present a structure with the same state, two arrays and a single loop, and prove that it runs in $O(\log n)$ amortized time per insertion and per query. Unlike the AM-tree of Ding, Gu and Sun, which attains the same bound, it stores no subtree sizes and maintains no balance invariant. For a connected graph with distinct costs, the structure can be viewed as an implicit link-cut tree on the Kruskal reconstruction tree: each rotation corresponds to exactly one preferred-child change, and each skip acts on a stale path-parent pointer. In experiments it is 1.3-2.1 times faster than the folklore BottleneckTree on insertions, up to 480 times faster on its adversarial input, and 6.3-16 times faster than an explicit link-cut tree.

papers.title: Toward a Compositional Knowledge Architecture for a Shared Organizational Cortex
papers.abstract: Organizations accumulate evidence in conversations, documents, decisions and relationships, but they act on interpretations: judgements assembled from several observations, resting on assumptions, and revised as circumstances change. Existing retrieval, knowledge graphs and agent memory keep the records and lose the interpretation. We propose a four-layer architecture, Signals, Domains, Claims and Dimensions, in which interpretations persist with their justifications and standing, a truth-maintenance network revises that standing as evidence changes, and validated, versioned Dimensions position interpretations on named axes. We call the result a shared organizational cortex. In a registered retrieval experiment, the Dimension term gains 0.028 nDCG@10 (p = 0.002). In system-level comparisons, the full retrieval configuration improves nDCG@10 by 0.081 over Signals-only and 0.053 over graph-augmented Signals-only retrieval (both reported p < 0.001). The architecture gives organizations a persistent, revisable basis for shared judgement.

papers.title: An Asymptotic for E. P. Stein Numbers
papers.abstract:
Epstein's put-or-take-a-square game is an impartial combinatorial game in which a player may, in each turn, add or subtract the largest square not exceeding the current integer. We study E. P. Stein numbers, the positions from which both legal moves lead directly to positive squares, and prove the following asymptotic formula for the counting function $S_2(X)$ of these positions: \[
  S_2(X)=\frac{1}{\pi^2}X^{1/4}\log X+O(X^{1/4}). \]

papers.title: Homogeneous Polynomial Carleson Operators Along the Paraboloid
papers.abstract: In this paper, we prove boundedness on $L^p(\mathbb{R}^{n+1})$, $1<p<\infty$, of polynomial Carleson operators along the paraboloid with phase belonging to a class $Y$ of homogeneous polynomials. For $n,d\ge 2$, let $\mathcal{P}^{n,d}$ denote the class of all real-valued homogeneous polynomials in $n$ variables of degree $d$. We may take the class $Y$ to be an arbitrary linear subspace $Y \subseteq \mathcal{P}^{n,d}$ such that $\dim Y \le M_{n , d}$, where $M_{n , d}$ is a constant depending only on $n$ and $d$. The main novelty of our result is that we may allow a large collection of homogeneous polynomials of the same degree, in contrast to earlier results that relied on distinct degree assumptions. The heart of our proof is a $TT^*$ method, and the derivation of new estimates for oscillatory integral kernels involving interactions between homogeneous polynomial phases and the paraboloid.

papers.title: AssameseLM-E2B: An Open-Weight Assamese Language Model for Efficient Consumer-Grade Deployment
papers.abstract:
While Large Language Models (LLMs) excel in high-resource languages, their performance often degrades in low-resource languages due to tokenization inefficiencies, generative instability, and linguistic interference. This paper presents AssameseLM-E2B and its instruction-tuned variant, AssameseLM-E2B-it, a 2-billion-parameter model adapted specifically for low resource Assamese language. Built upon the Gemma-4 architecture, the model incorporates an expanded byte-level BPE vocabulary to reduce tokenization overhead by nearly 500% compared with multilingual 2B--3B baselines. We employ a parameter-efficient Continual Pre-Training (CPT) pipeline with Hybrid LoRA, followed by Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) on a balanced, multi-domain dataset to enhance instruction-following and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) capabilities.
  Evaluation demonstrates a Bits-per-Byte (BPB) score of 0.7488 on FLORES-200, alongside an overall RAG score of 96.7% and 100% refusal accuracy on adversarial unanswerable prompts. Comparative analysis reveals significant limitations in general-purpose baselines, including receptive-productive decoupling, generative degradation on Romanized Assamese, and unintended Bengali script assimilation. These results demonstrate the potential of parameter-efficient adaptation for developing capable, locally deployable language models for low-resource languages under constrained computational resources.

papers.title: One Strategic Woman: Sharp Ranks and a Persistent Core
papers.abstract: In a balanced random stable-marriage market, one fixed woman manipulates men-proposing deferred acceptance to obtain her best attainable partner. We prove that the women's expected average true partner rank is asymptotic to $(\ln n)^2$, improving the previous $O((\ln n)^4)$ bound, while the men's is asymptotic to $n/(2\ln n)$. The men's and women's average ranks, normalized by $n/\ln n$ and $\ln n$, converge jointly in distribution to $(U,U^{-1})$, where $U$ is uniform on $(0,1)$. Under optimal truthful truncation, the span of women's average ranks within the reported stable core, divided by $\ln n$, converges in distribution to $U^{-1}-1$.

papers.title: Exhaustive Search Is Hard to Beat in Constant Depth for Hyperclique and Orthogonal Vectors
papers.abstract:
A hyperclique in an $r$-uniform hypergraph is a set of vertices in which every $r$-subset is an edge. A simple exhaustive search algorithm detects a hyperclique on $\ell$ vertices in an $r$-uniform hypergraph on $m$ vertices by checking all $\binom{m}{\ell}$ sets of $\ell$ vertices. This algorithm can be expressed as a depth-two circuit with at most $m^\ell$ gates and wires. For hypercliques of *constant* size, Amano (2010) showed that this circuit is almost optimal: for large $r$, constant-depth circuits need $m^{\ell(1-O(\log r/r))}$ wires. We prove that this circuit remains hard to beat even for hypercliques of *polynomial* size. More precisely, circuits of depth $h$ need $m^{\Omega(\ell)}$ gates for $\ell\leq m^{1/h-\varepsilon}$, and $m^{\ell(1-O(\log r/r))}$ gates for $\ell=m^{o(1)}$ that tends to infinity.
  Our hyperclique bound and the method behind it also lead to lower bounds for two central problems of fine-grained complexity. First, we extend the bound $n^{k/4}$ of Rossman (2008) for $k$-Clique from cliques of *constant* size to cliques of *polynomial* size: circuits of depth $h$ detecting a clique on $k$ vertices in an $n$-vertex graph need $n^{\Omega(k)}$ gates for $k\leq n^{1/(h-1)-\varepsilon}$. Second, a reduction of Choudhury, Limaye, Sreenivasaiah, and Srinivasan (2026) turns our hyperclique bound into a lower bound of $n^{k-\varepsilon}$ gates for $k$-Orthogonal Vectors ($k$-OV) at every fixed depth for vectors of dimension $\log^{O(1)} n$; this proves the $k$-OV Conjecture for constant-depth circuits in polylogarithmic dimension.
  Finally, for $2$-OV in logarithmic dimension, we give a simple proof that depth-three circuits need $\Omega(n^2)$ wires, which answers a question of Kane and Williams (2019).
papers.intro:
Fine-grained complexity aims to explain why the textbook algorithms for many problems have resisted improvement for decades: it connects these problems by reductions to a few core problems and conjectures that the known algorithms for the core problems are essentially optimal [Vas18]. For example, the 3SUM problem asks whether three of nn given integers sum to zero, and the conjecture that it requires time n2−o⁡(1)n^{2-o(1)} gives lower bounds for many problems [GO95, Păt10, AV14, AVW14, KPP16]. A natural way to prove them goes through Boolean circuits: every multitape Turing machine running in time TT can be simulated by circuits of size O⁡(T​log⁡T)O(T\log T) [PF79], so a lower bound on circuit size implies a lower bound on running time. This paper studies two classical problems for which, despite decades of effort, no known algorithm is much faster than exhaustive search, which tries every candidate solution. The first is kk-Cliquen\textup{{Clique}}_{n}, in which one is given an nn-vertex graph and needs to decide whether it contains a clique on kk vertices. It is one of Karp’s 21 𝖭𝖯\mathsf{NP}-complete problems [Kar72] and the canonical 𝖶⁡[1]\mathsf{W}[1]-complete problem of parameterized complexity [CFK+15]. The second is kk-Orthogonal Vectors (kk-𝖮𝖵n,d\mathsf{OV}_{n,d}), in which one is given kk lists A1,…,AkA_{1},\ldots,A_{k}, each of nn binary vectors of dimension dd, that is, from {0,1}d\{0,1\}^{d}, and needs to decide whether one can choose a vector from each list so that the coordinatewise product of the chosen vectors is zero. Exhaustive search decides kk-Clique by checking all (nk)\binom{n}{k} sets of kk vertices, and kk-OV by checking all nkn^{k} choices of vectors.

papers.title: Zuse: A Decision Model for European Languages
papers.abstract: Decision models read a document and return a probability for each of a fixed set of options instead of generating text. Several appeared in 2026, but none has published results outside English. We describe Zuse, three decision models (4B, 9B and 27B) that train a low-rank adapter and a pointer head on frozen open-weight bases, targeting 27 European languages, and use them to study how this design behaves across languages and tasks. On a broad European suite of 11 sources excluded from training, covering 9 task groups and 27 languages, a development set that also guided model selection, the 27B model reaches 87.5% accuracy with a pooled expected calibration error of 0.016, and 0.035 when weighted per source. Post-hoc analyses of these single-seed results give three findings. First, miscalibration is structured by task rather than language: on parallel reading and topic items in 26 languages the confidence gap varies about as much as sampling noise, while across sources it spans -0.07 to +0.09, with knowledge tasks overconfident and acceptability judgements underconfident at all three sizes, so one fitted temperature cannot correct both. Second, the share of decisions that can be automated at a 5% error budget follows chance-corrected skill (Spearman 0.97 over 33 source and model pairs) more closely than raw accuracy (0.91). Third, reach beyond the training languages is set by the base model: across 210 languages, changing the training run moved scores by at most about 2 points within a size, while languages outside the base's documented list trail by 23 to 28 points at every size. On English public suites Zuse is behind Jev and Kev, including Kev models on the same bases. We also report two pitfalls in building multi-source training data: label-word collision between topic schemes, and an injection augmentation that taught a shortcut. Zuse can be tried at https://bineric.com/zuse.
papers.intro:
Many operational uses of language models require a choice among known options rather than generated text. Ticket routing, policy checks, moderation and form extraction all have this shape. A decision model suits such tasks: it reads a document and a set of questions, then returns a probability for each option. Because it cannot produce text, its output stays inside the options supplied, and its probabilities can be used to decide which cases to automate and which to send to a person.

We ask whether the decision-model design carries across European languages, and what governs calibration and automation there. We study this with Zuse, a family of three decision models targeting 27 European languages. We make six contributions:

1. A per-language evaluation of decision models. We report results for 27 European languages, 11 sources and 9 task groups, and reach across 210 languages. To our knowledge this is the first such evaluation for any decision model. 2. Calibration under source shift. Miscalibration depends on the task, in the same direction at all three sizes, with no detectable language effect on parallel items. Pooled calibration error understates per-source error by a factor of two. 3. Automation limits. The automatable share tracks chance-corrected skill and how well confidence ranks right answers above wrong ones. Thresholds chosen in-sample do not transfer between splits. 4. Base-model effects. On identical data, base choice outweighed parameter count, and reach outside the training languages came from the base. 5. Two pitfalls for multi-source decision data, each with a diagnostic others can run: label-word collision, and accuracy that rises under attack. 6. papers.title: Small 5-chromatic unit-distance graphs in disks of radius 3/2, 5/4 and 23/20
papers.abstract: We give three explicit unit-distance graphs in the plane with chromatic number 5 whose vertices lie in small disks: a graph with 773 vertices inside an open disk of radius 3/2, one with 5713 vertices inside an open disk of radius 5/4, and one with 8168 vertices inside an open disk of radius 23/20. The smallest examples previously reported for these radii have 11725, 11725 and 31171 vertices. All coordinates are exact elements of Q(sqrt3, sqrt5, sqrt11). In each case 5-chromaticity is certified by an explicit 5-colouring and a DRAT proof that no 4-colouring exists. The 773-vertex graph is vertex-critical.
papers.intro:
A unit-distance graph is a graph whose vertices are points of the plane, two of them adjacent when they are at distance 11. The chromatic number of the plane is the largest chromatic number of such a graph. De Grey [1] found a unit-distance graph with chromatic number 55, and a second proof was given by Exoo and Ismailescu [2]. The search for small examples went on in the Polymath16 project; the smallest known 55-chromatic unit-distance graph has 509509 vertices and is due to Parts [4], after a 553553-vertex graph of Heule [3]. Parts also gave a proof of χ⁡(ℝ2)≥5\chi(\mathbb{R}^{2})\geq 5 that can be checked by hand [5], and de Grey and Parts [12] gave lower bounds on the number of vertices of kk-chromatic unit-distance graphs. Related colouring questions for the plane are studied in [7, 11, 8, 13, 10], for two forbidden distances in [6], for odd distances in [9], and in higher dimension in [14].

papers.title: Building a Method: Challenges and Lessons from Developing an Impact Evaluation Framework for Public Investment in Open Source Software
papers.abstract: Modern societies and institutions depend on an invisible layer of open digital infrastructure: foundational, openly accessible digital technologies that support a broad range of social and economic activities. Open source software is a core component of this infrastructure, underpinning everyday technologies and critical systems in various critical sectors. As open source software becomes increasingly recognised, funded, and governed as open digital infrastructure, policymakers face growing demands for accountability, transparency, and credible evidence of impact. However, methods for evaluating public investment in open source software remain underdeveloped, with no widely accepted methodological standard. This paper describes the Sovereign Tech Agency's transition from qualitative reporting and funding-recipient self-assessment towards a mixed-methods approach that incorporates quantitative, goal-oriented evaluation to inform funding decisions. Drawing on the development of this framework, it examines its initial design, the practical and structural challenges encountered, and the responses adopted. The work identifies three central challenges: evaluation indicators must reflect heterogeneous project goals and contexts; quantitative assessment relies on fragmented and fragile data infrastructure; and observed changes before, during, and after investment do not establish causal attribution without additional research designs. The paper argues that evaluating investment in open source software is not only a methodological task but also a governance practice, dependent on sustainable open research infrastructure, community knowledge, and ongoing methodological refinement.
papers.intro:
Open source software (OSS) is software whose source code is made available under a licence that permits anyone to inspect, use, modify, and redistribute it. It is often developed and maintained collaboratively and in a decentralized manner, and is typically available at no cost. OSS underpins much of the digital infrastructure on which contemporary society and the economy depend. Over 96% of codebases contain OSS ([1]), and roughly 70-90% of any software stack consists of OSS ([2]).

It is often developed and maintained collaboratively and in a decentralized manner, and is typically available at no cost. OSS underpins much of the digital infrastructure on which contemporary society and the economy depend. Over 96% of codebases contain OSS ([1]), and roughly 70-90% of any software stack consists of OSS ([2]).

While used by many, projects are often maintained by small groups of people or, in some cases, individuals. Despite its criticality and widespread use, OSS maintenance work remains inadequately compensated. Those in the open source community have increasingly been expressing concerns [3] around widespread commercial freeriding on the labour of volunteers [4], security vulnerabilities and maintainer burnout [5], both of these fueled by the increasing appearance of AI reporting [6].

This prevalence of OSS across modern codebases, and its presence in various systems of critical infrastructure such as finance and energy [7] has given it the recognition as open digital infrastructure (ODI). ODI refers to foundational and openly accessible digital technologies that make crucial contributions to society, serving as input resources for a broad range of downstream productive activities [8]. As the infrastructural role of OSS has gained recognition, its sustainability has become an increasingly important public policy concern. In response, various governments have adopted measures to address this issue, primarily through direct investment in OSS maintenance. Recent European examples include the Next Generation Internet (NGI), funded by the European Comission, the Sovereign Tech Agency in Germany and the European Sovereign Tech Fund pilot implemented through the EDIC Digital Commons.

Recent European examples include the Next Generation Internet (NGI), funded by the European Comission, the Sovereign Tech Agency in Germany and the European Sovereign Tech Fund pilot implemented through the EDIC Digital Commons.

With the growth of budgetary expenditure in OSS, the question of measurement becomes increasingly important: how can public institutions determine that public investment strengthens those open source components? Evaluating the results of investment can provide insights into what kind of instruments work, which ones don’t, and how changes in the well-being of the projects can be attributed to the different interventions. Establishing causality in those changes, however, requires complex research designs. As such, impact evaluation for OSS funding is an ongoing research area, with no widely accepted methodological standard.

papers.title: Representation embeddings and the third Brauer--Thrall conjecture
papers.abstract: Let $A$ be a representation-infinite finite-dimensional algebra over an algebraically closed field $k$. We prove that for every infinite cardinal $\kappa$ there is an indecomposable $A$-module $M$ with $\dim_k M=\kappa$. Over algebraically closed fields, this settles Simson's conjecture, also called the third Brauer--Thrall conjecture, that every representation-infinite finite-dimensional algebra has indecomposable modules of arbitrarily large cardinality. To construct these modules, we extend Bongartz's representation embedding from finite-dimensional Kronecker modules without a simple injective summand to such modules of arbitrary dimension. The extended functor commutes with direct sums and filtered colimits and preserves the dimension of infinite-dimensional modules. Applying it to the indecomposable Kronecker modules of every infinite dimension constructed by G\"obel and Simson yields the required $A$-modules.

The algebra AA is called representation-finite if there are only finitely many isomorphism classes of finite-dimensional indecomposable AA-modules, and representation-infinite otherwise. The Brauer–Thrall conjectures concern the indecomposable modules of a representation-infinite algebra; see Ringel [20] for their origin. The first Brauer–Thrall conjecture asserts that a representation-infinite algebra has finite-dimensional indecomposable modules of arbitrarily large dimension. Roiter [24] proved it for finite-dimensional algebras over any field, and Auslander [2] proved the analogue for Artin rings, with length in place of dimension. The second Brauer–Thrall conjecture asserts that, over an infinite field, a representation-infinite algebra has infinitely many positive integers dd for which there are infinitely many pairwise non-isomorphic indecomposable modules of dimension dd. papers.title: Horndeski Gravity as an Effective Dark Energy Fluid in Cosmological N-body Simulations
papers.abstract:
Unraveling the nature of the cosmic expansion, driven by Dark Energy (DE), remains one of the key challenges in modern cosmology. Modified Gravity (MG) models provide an alternative to the standard cosmological constant paradigm. These models predict distinct signatures in the growth of structure, yet analytical predictions are challenging due to the highly non--linear equations involved.
  To overcome this problem, we study MG as an effective DE fluid. To this end, we have incorporated linear DE perturbations into the N--body code $\texttt{CO}N\texttt{CEPT}$, which relies on the Einstein--Boltzmann solver $\texttt{CLASS}$. We replaced the $\texttt{CLASS}$ version used by $\texttt{CO}N\texttt{CEPT}$ with $\texttt{mochi\_CLASS}$, a patched version that includes Horndeski family models. By writing linear DE perturbations ($\delta\rho_{\rm DE}$, $\delta P_{\rm DE}$, $\theta_{\rm DE}$, and $\sigma_{\rm DE}$) in terms of metric perturbations in the synchronous gauge, the N--body code is able to evolve the effective fluid using the Boltzmann equation. Our current simulations encompass a range of cosmological scenarios ---$w_0w_a$CDM, Hu--Sawicki $f(R)$ and cubic Galileon--- each extended to include massive neutrinos.
  For each of the models, we have found deviations from General Relativity close to what is predicted in the linear regime: a sub-$0.2\%$ relative difference for $\Lambda$CDM, up to $40\%$ for $f(R)$ and a sub-$25\%$ for cubic Galileon. Since our code is the first to implement Horndeski gravity into an N--body code, its validation is a non--trivial computational task. Our novel code opens the door to explore a vast number of modified gravity models in the context of current and future cosmological surveys.

papers.title: CoRTeC: A Differentially Private Release for Synthetic Tabular Data, Decodable by Any Generator
papers.abstract: The records that could train the most useful models, such as a hospital's patient files, are often the ones an institution cannot share. We propose CoRTeC, a method that releases synthetic versions of such records under differential privacy. Differential privacy places a proven limit on what the synthetic data can reveal about any person, and in particular on membership inference. CoRTeC spends the privacy budget once, on a small file of noisy counts designed for training a classifier. For each group of records, the file gives the group's size, its balance of outcomes, a histogram of every column for each outcome and the outcome rate in each of several non-overlapping cells. A reviewer can check every number before the file leaves the institution. Anyone can then turn the counts into synthetic rows, as often as they like and at no further privacy cost. A maximum-entropy decoder can do this without any language model, and so can each of the five frozen language models we tested. None of them ever sees a real record. A selection step then matches the rows to the released counts. Decoded without a language model, the automatically configured release at $\varepsilon = 2$ trains classifiers to within 0.02 AUC of a real sample of the same size on the Adult dataset, across three data splits. On NHANES and bank marketing, without the selection step, it stays within 0.05 AUC. On Adult, with a fixed cohort rule, the release carries the outcome rates a deployment names more closely than a real sample does, at some cost in accuracy on pairs of columns. Four controls show that most of the utility comes from the release and the selection step, and that a language model adds what it knows from the column names. No private row ever reaches a model, and no row CoRTeC generates copies a real one. The strongest membership attack stays far below the bound the budget allows.

papers.title: Rigidity of Ricci solitons for $\varphi$-related metallic semi-Riemannian structures on para-Kenmotsu manifolds
papers.abstract: In this paper, we investigate Ricci solitons in the para-Kenmotsu setting with respect to a $\varphi$-related metallic semi-Riemannian metric arising from the underlying almost paracontact metric structure, under the assumption that the potential vector field is pointwise collinear with the Reeb vector field. We first establish the relation $\tS=S+2n\beta\bigl(g-\eta\otimes\eta\bigr)$ between the Ricci tensors of the original metric $g$ and the $\varphi$-related metallic metric $\tg$. We then show that the Ricci soliton equation implies that the original metric $g$ is of $\eta$-Einstein type. By combining this condition with the contracted Bianchi identity, we obtain a rigidity result implying $f=0$, $\lambda=\frac{2n}{C}$, $S=-2ng$, and consequently $\tS=-\frac{2n}{C}\tg$. Thus, every Ricci soliton in this setting whose potential vector field is pointwise collinear with the Reeb vector field is necessarily trivial, and both $g$ and $\tg$ are Einstein. Finally, we provide two five-dimensional para-Kenmotsu examples: one realizing the resulting trivial Einstein Ricci soliton and another showing that failure of the required Einstein condition prevents the existence of such a soliton.

Almost paracontact metric geometry provides a natural framework for studying geometric structures on odd-dimensional semi-Riemannian manifolds. Among its distinguished subclasses, para-Kenmotsu manifolds are characterized by specific differential conditions involving the structure tensors and the Levi-Civita connection. Their curvature properties impose strong restrictions on the Reeb vector field and the Ricci tensor. The basic theory and curvature identities used in this paper follow Zamkovoy [11, 12].

papers.title: Approximate minimax regret for conditionally similar tests
papers.abstract: We construct approximately minimax regret optimal tests in a scalar Gaussian instrumental variables experiment. This example shows how conditionally similar tests allow a novel approximation approach, allowing us to optimize weights over alternatives to minimize worst-case power regret. Stochastic mirror descent and averaging yield finite-iteration guarantees with exact conditional similarity. We establish bounds for exact and simulated powers and illustrate the procedure numerically. This initial algorithm shows how existing nearly-optimal test computation methods can be extended to include composite alternative hypothesis sets without the computational cost associated with maintaining size control.

papers.intro:
Conditional similarity controls rejection probabilities in the presence of nuisance parameters but generally leaves many tests to choose from (Moreira, 2003). We select among these tests by minimizing their largest power loss relative to the conditionally similar power envelope. This criterion is useful when instruments may be weak and no single test maximizes power at every alternative.

We select among these tests by minimizing their largest power loss relative to the conditionally similar power envelope. This criterion is useful when instruments may be weak and no single test maximizes power at every alternative.

Our contribution is to use conditional size control to optimize power regret across alternatives. Elliott et al. (2015), henceforth EMW, fix a weighting distribution over alternatives; weighted average power then equals power against a single mixture distribution. Their numerical search concerns a least-favorable distribution under the null, and thus the algorithm seeks to find an optimal combination of tests that satisfy these size constraints simultaneously. While Section 4.3 of EMW does account for composite alternative hypothesis sets, our conditioning construction allows for a save on compute time, as we maintain size guarantees by construction. Aradillas Fernández et al. (2025) then develop stochastic mirror descent (SMD) for the corresponding finite-null, single-alternative problem, thus attaining approximation guarantees not present in the algorithm of EMW. That formulation also accommodates a fixed alternative mixture representing a weighted-average-power (WAP) criterion (for a discussion, see Section 3.8 of Lehmann and Romano (2005)), restricting the problem to that of a composite null and a singleton alternative.

We instead impose conditional similarity within every best response. This removes the need to optimize null weights to enforce size and allows the iterative search to focus on alternatives at which power falls furthest below its conditionally similar envelope. How Aradillas Fernández et al. Weighted average power remains the best-response objective, but its weights are updated to solve a minimax regret problem rather than specified in advance as the final power criterion. Our result concerns the conditionally similar class in the Gaussian experiment, instead of the unrestricted class of level-α\alpha tests, but this flexible method may lend itself to tractable results beyond Gaussian settings, which is accomplished in Aradillas Fernández et al. papers.title: One Scale, Four Texts: Gaps, Overlaps and Silent Repairs in Published Grading Schemes
papers.abstract: Category systems often reach their users as text, and readers apply them with tacit repairs. We ask what such a text determines once the repairs are removed, using diabetic retinopathy grading, where one international scale circulates in several documents. We transcribe four texts (the English screening definitions of 2025, the international scale as tabulated in 2017 and as published in 2003, and an Italian guideline of 2015) into one rule language over 24 finding variables, and make every point a text leaves open a named precisification. Exhaustive enumeration of 1,425,807,360 finding profiles, re-derived by an SMT solver and spot-checked by an OWL reasoner, shows that every text that assigns actions leaves some eyes without a category under every reading; that the 2017 tabulation has a proliferative class that is empty when read literally and a macular gap that the 2003 text lacks, so that no function maps the 2003 grades onto the 2017 grades; and that on image findings alone the English and Italian texts order some pairs of eyes in opposite ways. On 927 annotated photographs from three public datasets, with retinal thickening assumed absent, the English text and the 2017 tabulation disagree on referral for 26.8% of the eyes of one dataset (DDR) on which both decide, and in a pre-registered experiment classifiers trained on each text's labels side with their own text. Thickening cannot be seen on a colour photograph; left free, every disagreement involving England becomes undecidable, so it rests on what the camera cannot show. In a second pre-registered study, language models that answered without deliberating repaired most gap and overlap items even when told to read literally, while Claude Sonnet 5.5 and Claude Opus 5.5 reported the defects far more often; within two models, deliberation reduced silent repair without removing it.
papers.intro:
Much institutional categorisation is written down before it is applied. A grading scheme or a triage table is a text, and whoever applies it reads it with conventions the text does not state: take the worst category when two apply, choose the nearest sensible one when none does, ignore a literal reading that would be absurd. These repairs are silent, and they stop working when a text is executed rather than read: coded into software, used to define labels for machine learning, matched against another text in a crosswalk that pools data, or handed to a language model. This paper asks what a published category system determines on its own. We take the texts at their word, turn every open point into an explicit choice among admissible readings, and ask which defects survive every choice.
