The question is not whether guidelines leave room for clinical judgement. A text may leave a decision to the grader on purpose, and we keep every such opening as a named reading rather than resolve it. A gap is something else: an eye that no category covers under any admissible reading, so that the text applied as written returns nothing. An overlap returns two categories with different actions, and an order inversion means that two texts rank the same pair of eyes in opposite ways. A grader absorbs the first two without noticing, but software, a label generator or a language model has to return something definite, and what it returns is then decided by the implementation, not by the text. Knowing where a text is silent or contradictory, and whether two texts that share a name define the same categories, is a precondition for pooling labels across them.

Section 4 reports the gaps, overlaps, empty classes and order inversions that survive every reading, including a change between the 2003 and 2017 versions of the international scale that no relabelling can undo. Section 5 measures how often annotated photographs fall into these defects, shows how much of that depends on an assumption about retinal thickening, and tests in a pre-registered experiment whether classifiers trained on labels from different texts differ. Section 8 reports a pre-registered test of whether language models repair defective categories silently. Section 6 aligns the transcription with Basic Formal Ontology and standard terminologies, and Section 7 describes how every claim is checked: 15 build gates, 163 assertions over the result files, three reasoning engines, and a sabotage suite of ten cases that tests whether each gate can fail. Appendix A summarises each procedure as pseudocode (seven algorithms).

papers.title: From Certified Pairs to a Certified Hub: Reasoner-Checked Crosswalks for the Information Exchange Standard
papers.abstract: A national digital twin was conceived as an ecosystem of twins connected through mappings to a common foundation, but the roadmap that promises to confirm those mappings are valid never says what valid means. We give the test a precise form, coherence and conservativity of the merged ontology, borrowed from logic-based alignment repair, and apply it to the Information Exchange Standard (IES), first pair by pair and then to whole hubs. Crosswalks from IES into thirteen ontologies across seven sector groups, anchored on the building ontologies BOT, Brick, and SAREF4BLDG, pass through separate stages of matching, human review, certification of each SKOS correspondence against the two class hierarchies, and reasoning with HermiT. Pair by pair, the stages catch different failures: certification alone removed all 526 conservativity violations of the raw crosswalks, review alone left 73, and together they made eleven of twelve overlapping pairs coherent and conservative. Pairwise certification does not compose. Merging the three certified building crosswalks into one hub made five Brick classes unsatisfiable, through a homonym between the IES and Brick notions of a floor that only BOT's disjointness axioms expose; rejecting that one row gave a coherent and conservative hub that entails 290 cross-ontology links nobody wrote down. The core hub is inconsistent before any crosswalk is added, because two published standards, the Open Energy Ontology and BFO 2020, contradict each other; with either one left out it is coherent and conservative. A hub, not a pair, is the unit an ecosystem of twins has to certify.

papers.intro:
The UK’s national digital twin was never meant to be one model. Its founding principles define it as “an ecosystem of digital twins connected via securely shared data” [6], and the roadmap that followed rests that ecosystem on mappings: existing models and data in other vocabularies are to be connected to a common foundation, and “permanent automated mappings will allow the digital twin catalogue to be continuously refreshed” [16]. The same roadmap promises to reload the source twins “to confirm that the new mappings are valid” [16], but it does not say what makes a mapping valid. This paper proposes a test that does, applies it to every mapping and to every hub of mappings we could build around one common ontology, and reports where the ecosystem holds and where it breaks.

Such an ecosystem is only as useful as the data that flows into it, and that data arrives in whatever vocabulary its source happens to use. Building records speak the language of the construction and facilities-management community, energy records speak the language of grid models, and sensor feeds speak the language of observation ontologies. The Information Exchange Standard (IES) was designed as a common 4D ontology for exchanging information across government, with a lineage in high-quality 4D data modelling and formal upper-ontology work [10, 35]. It gives a shared backbone, but it does not, on its own, tell a data engineer how an IES class relates to the corresponding class in a building or energy ontology. That relationship has to be established by an alignment, and today those alignments are written by hand, reviewed informally, and shipped without a formal test that the result is even logically coherent.

The cost of this shows up whenever a twin has to grow. Extending the vocabulary to cover a new asset class, or connecting a new domain data source, means writing and checking new mappings by hand, and there is no agreed test that says when such a step is safe. The research community has strong machinery for each half of the problem separately. Ontology matching is a mature field with an established evaluation tradition [13], SKOS provides a vocabulary for typing correspondences [24], SSSOM provides a way to serialize and share them [22], and OWL 2 reasoners such as HermiT can decide the consistency of the merged result [14]. Using the reasoner to judge an alignment is also established: logic-based matchers repair incoherent mappings [19], reasoning support helps experts revise them [23], and the conservativity principle flags mappings that change the meaning of an input’s own terms [33]. Pointed at IES, this machinery has so far produced only unreviewed output: a recent bulk run of LogMap over defence and national-security ontologies aligned IES with several building ontologies, among many other pairs, but those alignments were not reviewed and were not tested for conservativity [9]. We are not aware of a public crosswalk that takes IES to the domain ontologies a twin consumes, reviews and types each correspondence, tests it against both class hierarchies, and reports what the reasoner makes of the merge.

Building data is plentiful and open, through public building-performance certificates [25], the building-ontology landscape is deep and well studied, and extending an IES building vocabulary to regional or national retrofit scale is exactly the kind of step that should be small and checkable rather than a project of its own. papers.title: On the geometric degree of the prolongation varieties of the differential system $x_1'=x_2^2$, $x_2'=x_1^2$
papers.abstract:
A prolongation variety of a polynomial differential system $S$ is an algebraic variety defined by the equations of $S$ and their derivatives up to a given order. We compute the geometric degree of the prolongation varieties associated with the system $x_1'=x_2^2$, $x_2'=x_1^2$ in terms of the prolongation order, thereby proving a conjecture stated by Gleb Pogudin in Section 2, Question 6 of "Some Open Problems in Differential Algebra".
  Our approach is motivated from the beginning by doing computational experiments in OSCAR in order to find the number of solutions of a zero-dimensional system using algebraic Thomas decomposition. The result will follow from a coprimality condition on a family of polynomials with integer coefficients, which is verified by showing that their roots satisfy a strong interlacing property. Finally, we propose an extension of the conjecture for the systems $x_1'=x_2^n$, $x_2'=x_1^n$ with $n>2$.

papers.title: On the geometry of real polynomials of the 7-th degree with simple complex critical points
papers.abstract: We consider real monic polynomials with simple complex critical points. Critical values of such polynomial $p$ can be considered as vertices of the uniquely defined polygon, symmetric with respect to the $x$-axis. The inverse image of this polygon is a tree-like system of ovals that touch each other externally in critical points. This system of ovals will be called the geometrical code of $p$. Let $a_1+i\cdot b_1,\ldots,a_n+i\cdot b_n$, $a_1<a_2<\ldots<a_n$ and $b_i>0$, $i=1,\ldots,n$, be the set of critical points of our polynomial $p$ in the upper halfplane, and $c_1+i\cdot d_1,\ldots,c_n+i\cdot d_n$ be their images. The order of numbers $c_k$ and the list of signs of numbers $d_k$ will be called the algebraic code of $p$. In our experimental work we study geometrical and algebraic codes of the 7-th degree polynomials and the relations between them.

papers.title: Enabling AWS Cloud FPGA Development Using High-Level Vitis HLS
papers.abstract: We present a toolchain for development of ML models on AWS EC2 F2 cloud FPGA infrastructure from high-level language, implementing a complete Vitis HLS to HDK bridge to AFI workflow that has been absent from the academic literature despite eight years of AWS FPGA availability. We introduce a four-level methodology (FP32 PyTorch, bit-accurate quantized Python, HLS C-simulation, physical FPGA) to aid in localizing errors, including FPGA-specific circuit errors. Together these tools allow coding agents to effectively implement FPGA designs from user directions, testing and debugging as needed. We document the deployment workflow, timing closure strategies, and practical HLS engineering decisions that proved crucial. We validate using TinyBERT fine-tuned for address Named Entity Recognition, implementing the embedding layer and the first of four encoder layers on the FPGA hardware. Our implementation streams weights from host DRAM, yielding poor performance compared to CPU/GPU implementations; we discuss forward paths.
papers.intro:
Engineering demanding workloads such as ML inference requires coordinated optimization between the hardware architecture and software operations. The transformer-based software stack that represents current state of the art in ML implements a neural network via matrix multiplication operations. These operations are accelerated by high-performance hardware GPUs with on-board memory. Transformer inference is increasingly constrained by memory bandwidth rather than compute [1, 2, 3, 4].

The transformer-based software stack that represents current state of the art in ML implements a neural network via matrix multiplication operations. These operations are accelerated by high-performance hardware GPUs with on-board memory. Transformer inference is increasingly constrained by memory bandwidth rather than compute [1, 2, 3, 4].

In comparison with the essentially von Neumann-based CPU/GPU architecture, Field Programmable Gate Array (FPGA) devices represent an alternative hardware platform. FPGAs offer memory distributed throughout the device and feature programmable circuitry, allowing memory and compute to be placed together in a more distributed way. These features support deterministic latency and fixed power draw independent of request rate, and could permit more efficient designs, particularly for implementing smaller models and those where GPU tail-latency variance and idle power are concerns [5, 6].

FPGAs offer memory distributed throughout the device and feature programmable circuitry, allowing memory and compute to be placed together in a more distributed way. Research in generative AI using FPGA devices has been constrained, however, by the difficulty of programming ML systems on them. Despite eight years of availability (F1 since 2017, F2 since December 2024 [7]), AWS cloud FPGA instances have not been used for ML inference in any published academic work, although their pay-on-demand cost model lowers the funding barrier for research projects. The University of Toronto noted in 2024 that F1 instances “have not been used for such large ML applications” [8]. The gap is not hardware capability; the AMD VU47P on F2 has 9,024 DSP slices, 16 GiB HBM, and 64 GiB DDR4. We identify the absence of a documented, reproducible workflow from HLS C++ kernels to deployed Amazon FPGA Images (AFIs) as the barrier.

This paper intends to close this gap. We present a complete toolchain and methodology for developing ML models on AWS EC2 F2 using the complete Vitis HLS (high level language) →\to HDK bridge →\to AFI workflow for ML workloads. Supporting contributions include a four-level validation methodology (§2.8), build time characterization for the AWS F2 HDK workflow [9] (§3.3), and a timing closure analysis for SSI FPGA devices under ML workloads (§3.2).
